This family consists of sequences found in a number of hypothetical plant proteins of unknown function. The region of interest contains nine highly conserved cysteine residues and is approximately 160 amino acids in length, and is probably a zinc-binding domain.

These sequences are derived from a number of hypothetical plant proteins. The region in question is approximately 270 amino acids long. Some members of this family are annotated as yeast pheromone receptor proteins AR781 but no literature was found to support this.

Some of the members of this family are hypothetical bacterial and archaeal proteins, but others are annotated as being cation transporters expressed by the archaebacterium Methanosarcina mazei ([swissprot:Q8PXG5], [swissprot:Q8PXG7] and [swissprot:Q8PXG8]).

The sequences making up this family are all derived from hypothetical proteins expressed by C. elegans. The region in question is approximately 160 amino acids long. The GO annotation for this protein indicates the protein to be involved in nematode larval development and to have a positive regulation on growth rate.

This domain is found in proteins expressed by bacterial or archaeal species. Some of these are annotated as being transmembrane proteins, and in fact many of these sequences contain a high proportion of hydrophobic residues. One protein containing this domain is immunity protein SdpI (swiss:O32241) from Bacillus subtilis, which provides protection for the cell against the toxic effects of its own SdpC killing factor, and also functions as a receptor/signal transduction protein [[cite:PUB00055038]].

This entry represents a putative component of efflux pumps that comprise MFP and FUSC proteins. Several members are in an operon with and have similar mutants phenotypes as an RND efflux pump and a fusaric acid resistance-like protein [[cite:PUB00093610]]. This system is involved in transporting diverse substrates including 4-hydroxybenzoate and octanoate [[cite:PUB00106931]].
This domain appears to be restricted to the Bacillales.
This family consists of hypothetical bacterial proteins of unknown function.

This family catalyses the synthesis of thymidine monophosphate (dTMP) from deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP). The physiological co-substrate has not yet been identified. Previous designation of this famliy as being thymidylate synthase from one paper, [cite:PUB00075419], has been shown to be erroneous [[cite:PUB00057368]]. The proteins are uncharacterised.

EKR is a short, 33 residue, domain found in bacterial and some lower eukaryotic species which lies between a POR (pyruvate ferredoxin/flavodoxin oxidoreductase) [pfam:PF01558] and the 4Fe-4S binding domain Fer4 [pfam:PF00037]. It contains a characteristic EKR sequence motif. The exact function of this domain is not known.

This domain of about 280 residues is found in eukaryotes. There are two conserved sequence motifs: GFC and GLL. This family is also known as UPF0704. This domain is found FAP206 [swissprot:Q23H79], a protein associated with cilia and flagella. In the ciliate Tetrahymena, the cilium has radial spokes, each of which is a macromolecular complex essential for motility. A triplet of three radial spokes, RS1, RS2, and RS3, is repeated every 96 nm along the doublet microtubule. Each spoke has a distinct base that docks to the doublet and is linked to different inner dynein arms. Knockout of the FAP206 gene results in slow cell motility and the 96-nm repeats lack RS2 and dynein c. FAP206 is probably part of the front prong and docks RS2 and dynein c to the microtubule [[cite:PUB00082324]].
This is a family of uncharacterised Clostridiales proteins.
The PGG domain is named for the highly conserved sequence motif found at the startt of the domain. The function is not known.

Members of this family carry two distinct, highly conserved sequence motifs, CPPPLYYTHL and HPHLAWLY. The family is found in eukaryotes, and the function is not known. This family lies at the C-terminus of members.
YdiH is a family of proteins found in bacteria. Proteins in this family are typically between 62 and 80 amino acids in length. The function is not known.
This family around 100 residues locates in the C-terminal of some uncharacterized proteins in various Bacteroides, Prevotella and Prevotella species. The function of this family remains unknown.

This domain is found in Rhamnogalacturonan lyase from Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron ([swissprot:Q8AAW3]) and other bacterial proteins. It shows an alpha/beta structure [[cite:PUB00100662]] and locates C-terminal to [pfam:PF07944]. The specific function of this domain is still unknown.
This family around 150 residues locates in the C-terminal of some uncharacterized proteins in various Bacteroides and Prevotella species. The function of this family remains unknown.

This family around 200 residues locates in the N-terminal of some uncharacterised proteins in various Bacteroides and Alistipes species. The function of this family remains unknown. The N-terminus of this model has been clipped by ~30 residues as it was capturing parts of collagen sequences, [pfam:PF01391].
This family around 150 residues locates in the N-terminal of some uncharacterized proteins in various Bacteroides and Prevotella species. The function of this family remains unknown.
This family around 100 residues locates in the N-terminal of some uncharacterized proteins and glucuronyl hydrolases in various Bacteroides species. The function of this family remains unknown.

This domain of around 100 residues locates at the C-terminal of some glycerophosphoryl diester phosphodiesterases and uncharacterized proteins in various Bacteroides and Prevotella species. The function of this domain is not yet clear, however, it is described as a putative glycerophosphoryl diester phosphodiesterase (PDBe:3i10).
This family around 75 residues locates in the N-terminal of F5/8 type C domain proteins and some uncharacterized proteins in various Bacteroides species. The function of this family remains unknown.
This family around 200 residues locates in the C-terminal of some uncharacterized proteins in various Bacteroides and Parabacteroides species. The function of this family remains unknown.
This is a family of unknown function, however family members such as B277 have been suggested to play a role in viral function [[cite:PUB00046115]].

The members of this family are hypothetical proteins expressed by Trypanosoma cruzi, a eukaryotic parasite that causes Chagas' disease in humans. This region is found as multiple copies per protein.
The members of this family are hypothetical plant proteins of unknown function. The region featured in this family is approximately 100 amino acids long.

Hypothetical archaeal and bacterial proteins make up this family. A few proteins are annotated as being potential metal-binding proteins, and in fact the members of this family have four highly conserved cysteine residues, but no further literature evidence was found in this regard.

In many of the family members, this region is associated with the CHK region described by SMART as being found in ZnF_C4 and HLH domain-containing kinases. In fact, one member of this family ([swissprot:Q9GUC1]) is annotated as being a member of the nuclear hormone receptor family, and contains regions typical of such proteins (Interpro:IPR000536, Interpro:IPR008946, and Interpro:IPR001628).

This is a fungal domain of unknown function. This domain can be found in DSC E3 ubiquitin ligase complex subunit 4 (Dsc4) from S. pombe, a component of the DSC E3 ubiquitin ligase complex required for the sre1 transcriptional activator proteolytic cleavage to release the soluble transcription factor from the membrane in low oxygen or sterol conditions. The complex plays also an important role in the multivesicular body (MVB) pathway and functions in a post-endoplasmic reticulum pathway for protein degradation [[cite:PUB00075404]]. This domain is also found in GLD1 from S. cerevisiae, also a component of the DSC E3 ubiquitin ligase complex involved in the targeting of the DSC complex to the Golgi apparatus and endosome membranes via the AP3 pathway to ubiquitinate Golgi/endosome membrane proteins [[cite:PUB00098082]].

The potentially novel fold is an alpha + beta fold comprising two beta sheets packed against a single helix. The enzyme is present in the cytosol.

They have no known function [[cite:PUB00029007]].

Members of this family have an important role in methanogenesis. They assume an alpha-beta globular structure consisting of six beta-strands and three alpha-helices forming the secondary structural topological arrangement of alpha1-beta1-alpha2-beta2-beta3-beta4-beta5-beta6-alpha3 [[cite:PUB00035386]].

The domain contains 12 conserved cysteines which suggests that the domain is an extracellular domain and that these cysteines form six intradomain disulphide bridges. The GO annotation for this protein indicates that it has a function in nematode larval development and has a positive regulation of growth rate.

Two structures have been solved for members of this large (>500 members) family of bacterial proteins present mostly in environmental bacteria and metagenomes (distant homologues are also present in several Plasmodium species). TOPSAN analysis for pdb:3pjy shows that there is much similarity with the other solved structure, pdb:3m7a, solved for UniProt:Q2GA55 (Saro_0823), a homologue of Thermotoga maritima TM1668, UniProt:Q9X1Z6., The homologue in Caulobacter crescentus (CC1388), UniProt:Q9A8G6, is associated with CspD, a cold shock protein (CC1387), UniProt:Q9A8G7. However, the genomic context of UniProt:Q2GA55 is most conserved with a putative xylose isomerase, suggesting a possible role in extracellular sugar processing. Saro_0821, UniProt:Q2GA57, is annotated as an AMP-dependent synthetase and ligase. PDB:3m7a structure corresponds to the C-terminal (27-165) fragment of the YP_496102 (Saro_0823) protein and it is structurally unique, as the best hits from Dali have a Z-score of 3.8 (1nt0, 2j1t, 3kq4) and it is thus a likely candidate for a new fold. Interestingly, many of the top Dali hits are involved in sugar metabolism. There are no obvious active site-like cavities on the protein surface of 3m7a (http://www.topsan.org/Proteins/JCSG/).

This entry represents a putative zinc finger domain. Proteins containing this domain typically consist of a beta-sheet region followed by an alpha-helix and an unstructured C-terminus. The beta-sheet region contains a CXCX...XCXC sequence with Cys residues located in two proximal loops and pointing towards each other. The precise function of this set of bacterial proteins is, as yet, unknown [[cite:PUB00008047]].

Members of this family are found in maltosyltransferases, and adopt a secondary structure consisting of eight antiparallel beta-strands, which form an open-sided 'jelly roll' Greek key beta-barrel. Their exact function is, as yet, unknown [[cite:PUB00025274]].
This domain is found in a set of bacterial proteins, including Cytochrome c-type protein. It is functionally uncharacterised.

Members of this family are found in 3-mercaptopyruvate sulfurtransferase, and have no known function. They adopt a structure consisting of a four-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet and an alpha-helix, arranged in a beta(2)-alpha-beta(2) fashion, and bearing a remarkable structural similarity to the FK506-binding protein class of peptidylprolyl cis/trans-isomerase [[cite:PUB00029481]].

Members of this family, which are found in a set of hypothetical bacterial proteins, contain a core of six alpha-helices, where one central helix is surrounded by the other five. This entry represents a highly conserved 100 residue coiled-coil region which is found in short coiled-coil protein (SCOC) in human and UNC-69 in Caenorhabditis elegans. In human, SCOC is required for autophagosome formation during amino acid starvation. It forms a starvation-sensitive trimeric complex with UVRAG (UV radiation resistance associated gene) and FEZ1 and may regulate ULK1 and Beclin 1 complex activities [[cite:PUB00086016]]. In C. elegans, this small, evolutionarily conserved coiled-coil domain-containing protein, UNC-69, acts as a binding partner of UNC-76. Together they participate in a common genetic pathway necessary for axon extension and cooperate to regulate the size and position of synaptic vesicles in axons. Moreover, both proteins colocalize as puncta in neuronal processes and mutations in UNC-69 preferentially disrupt membrane traffic within axons [[cite:PUB00109243]].

This conserved domain is found in Thyroid adenoma-associated proteins (THADA) and the yeast homologue, TRM732. In humans, mutations of the Trm7 homologue FTSJ1, which interacts with THADA, impair Nm32 modifications, associated with non-syndromic X-linked intellectual disability [[cite:PUB00098320],[cite:PUB00098321],[cite:PUB00098322]]. It has been suggested that these proteins may play a role in additional biological processes not related to translation. Pfam_description: This bacterial family of proteins shows structural similarity to other pectin lyase families. Although structures from this family align with acetyl-transferases, there is no conservation of catalytic residues found. It is likely that the function is one of cell-adhesion. In PDB:3jx8, it is interesting to note that the sequence of contains several well defined sequence repeats, centred around GSG motifs defining the tight beta turn between the two sheets of the super-helix; there are 8 such repeats in the C-terminal half of the protein, which could be grouped into 4 repeats of two. It seems likely that this family belongs to the superfamily of trimeric auto-transporter adhesins (TAAs), which are important virulence factors in Gram-negative pathogens [[cite:PUB00029784]] [[cite:PUB00051306]]. In the case of Parabacteroides distasonis, which is a component of the normal distal human gut microbiota, TAA-like complexes probably modulate adherence to the host (information derived from TOPSAN).

This bacterial family of proteins has no known function. However, the cis-regulatory yjdF motif, just upstream from the gene encoding the proteins for this family, is a small non-coding RNA, Rfam:RF01764. The yjdF motif is found in many Firmicutes, including Bacillus subtilis. In most cases, it resides in potential 5' UTRs of homologues of the yjdF gene whose function is unknown. However, in Streptococcus thermophilus, a yjdF RNA motif is associated with an operon whose protein products synthesise nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+). Also, the S. thermophilus yjdF RNA lacks typical yjdF motif consensus features downstream of and including the P4 stem. Thus, if yjdF RNAs are riboswitch aptamers, the S. thermophilus RNAs might sense a distinct compound that structurally resembles the ligand bound by other yjdF RNAs. On the ohter hand, perhaps these RNAs have an alternative solution forming a similar binding site, as is observed with some SAM riboswitches [[cite:PUB00109804]].

This is a bacterial family of putative lipoproteins. The structure for [swissprot:Q64U78], PDB:3fzx, the first structural template for this large family including several homologues in the human gut microbiome and in metagenomic datasets, folds into a beta barrel that topologically looks like a small-scale porin (such as FepA). [swissprot:Q64U78] is a putative exported protein, and this fold is of the YmcC-like type, with a predicted signal peptide SpI cleavage site AGAMA|QNQDC, and a Phobius server prediction of non-cytoplasmic localisation for amino acids 21-236. The possibility of it being a membrane protein can be ruled out by the hydrophilic nature of the solvent exposed surface outside the barrels. Analysis of sequence conservation suggests that an area near Glu172/Trp206 is potentially interesting. These two residues are also conserved in Dali hit PDB:2in5, a hypothetical lipoprotein classified as a new YmcC-like fold in SCOP (SCOP:159271, with a 12-stranded meander beta-sheet folded into a deformed beta-barrel) despite large structural differences between the two structures, suggesting similarity in function.

This family of proteins, found from plants to humans, is PRAT4 (A and B), a Protein Associated with Toll-like receptor 4. The Toll family of receptors - TLRs - plays an essential role in innate recognition of microbial products, the first line of defence against bacterial infection [[cite:PUB00109675]]. PRAT4A influences the subcellular distribution and the strength of TLR responses and alters the relative activity of each TLR. PRAT4B regulates TLR4 trafficking to the cell surface and the extent of its expression there [[cite:PUB00109676]][[cite:PUB00109677]]. TLR4 recognizes lipopolysaccharide (LPS), one of the most immuno-stimulatory glycolipids constituting the outer membrane of the Gram-negative bacteria. This family has also been described as a SAP-like MIR-interacting protein family.

The bacterial proteins are likely to be involved in a cell wall function as they are found in conjunction with the [pfam:PF07501] domain, which is involved in various cell surface processes. These are factors that stimulate resuscitation of dormant cells [[cite:PUB00075582]]. This domain has a beta grasp fold. Structural description of this domain revealed a structural conservation between these domains and ubiquitin, hence it is termed UBL-G5 [[cite:PUB00137668]].

This family includes the DUF34/metal-binding protein/NIF3 proteins, which are widely distributed across superkingdoms. They were previously annotated as GTP cyclohydrolase 1 type 2 [[cite:PUB00070175]] and, recently, through a comprehensive literature review and integrative bioinformatic analyses it was revealed that annotations for these members were misleading as they were based on a single set of in vitro results examining the NIF3 homolog of Helicobacter pylori [[cite:PUB00070175]]. Actually, they have varied phenotypes with the unifying functional role as metal-binding proteins [[cite:PUB00100327]]. This entry contains several NIF3 (NGG1p interacting factor 3) protein homologues. NIF3 interacts with the yeast transcriptional coactivator NGG1p which is part of the ADA complex, the exact function of this interaction is unknown [[cite:PUB00002954],[cite:PUB00019927]].

This domain of unknown function has a PLP-dependent transferase-like fold. Its genomic context suggests that it may have a role in anaerobic vitamin B12 biosynthesis. This domain is often found at the C-terminus of proteins containing DUF4213, [pfam:PF13938]. The structure of UnioProtKB:B8FUJ5, PDB:3l5o, suggests that the protein has an enolase N-terminal-like fold and this Rossmann-like C-terminal domain. Structural and bioinformatic analyses reveal partial similarities to Rossmann-like methyltransferases, with residues from the enolase-like fold combining to form a unique active site that is likely to be involved in the condensation or hydrolysis of molecules implicated in the synthesis of flavins, pterins or other siderophores. The protein may be playing a role in heavy-metal chelation [[cite:PUB00075371]].

RST1 was originally identified in a genetic screen for factors involved in the biosynthesis of epicuticular waxes [[cite:PUB00098180]]. Later, RST1 and RST1 INTERACTING PROTEIN (RIPR) have been shown to act as cofactors of the cytoplasmic exosome and the Ski complex in plants [[cite:PUB00098179]]. Structure predictions suggest that this is an alpha-helical domain with and armadillo-like fold.

This domain is specific to the human splicing factor 3b subunit 2 and it's orthologues. Splicing factor 3b subunit 2 or SAP145 is a suppressor of U2 snRNA mutations. Spliceosomes are multi-component enzymes that catalyse pre-mRNA splicing and form step-wise by the ordered interaction of UsnRNPs and non-snRNP proteins with short conserved regions of the pre-mRNA at the 5' and 3' splice sites and branch site [[cite:PUB00013034]].

This family of proteins is found in bacteria and includes YfiR from E. coli. YfiR has been shown to regulate YfiN, a diguanylate cyclase and a bifunctional protein that produces c-di-GMP in response to reductive stress and then dynamically relocates to the division site to arrest cell division in response to envelope stress in Escherichia coli. YfiR may serve as a periplasmic redox sensor that regulates YfiN activity in response to reducing conditions [[cite:PUB00088310],[cite:PUB00088309]]. HmsC in Yersinia Pestis is the orthologue of YfiR from E. coli [[cite:PUB00091013]]. HmsC is a periplasmic protein that interacts directly with the periplasmic domain (PD) of HmsD and causes proteolytic degradation of HmsD, which in turn negatively regulates Y. pestis biofilm formation [[cite:PUB00091014]].

This domain of unknown function has a PLP-dependent transferase-like fold. Its genomic context suggests that it may have a role in anaerobic vitamin B12 biosynthesis. This domain is often found at the C-terminus of proteins containing DUF4213, [pfam:PF13938]. The structure of UnioProtKB:B8FUJ5, PDB:3l5o, suggests that the protein has an enolase N-terminal-like fold and this Rossmann-like C-terminal domain. Structural and bioinformatic analyses reveal partial similarities to Rossmann-like methyltransferases, with residues from the enolase-like fold combining to form a unique active site that is likely to be involved in the condensation or hydrolysis of molecules implicated in the synthesis of flavins, pterins or other siderophores. The protein may be playing a role in heavy-metal chelation [[cite:PUB00075371]].

Two structures have been solved form this DUF, PDB:4mjf and PDB:3sbu. TOPSAN records that both proteins are the only structural representatives of Pfam PF14254, DUF4348. There are no other significant hits in FFAS. DUF4348 has ~200 proteins, all from Bacteroidetes, and all with a single domain architecture with just one DUF4348 domain. There appears to be a possible gene duplication in the protein as the N-terminal domain (approx residues 25-174) and C-terminal domain (approx residues 175-286) superimpose quite well with ~1.9A r.m.s.d. and ~30% sequence identity.

The function of this protein domain family is yet to be characterised. It is putatively thought to lie in the C-terminal domain of the DNA nucleotide repair protein, Xeroderma pigmentosa complementation group A (XPA). The function of XPA is to bind to DNA and repair any mismatched base pairs. This domain family is often found in eukaryotes, and is approximately 70 amino acids in length. There is a conserved DPE sequence motif. In humans, this protein is encoded for in the chromosomal position, Chromosome 5 open reading frame 65. Mutations in the gene lead to myelodysplastic syndromes, where there is inefficient stem cell production in the bone marrow. This suggests that the protein may have a role in forming blood cells [[cite:PUB00067380]].

This entry has been described to include subclades of DUF488 domains (namely DUF488-s, for DUF488-short subclade, DUF488-l for long subclade and DUF488-u for DUF488-standalone subclade) which all which contain the ancestral core of the domain. DUF488-s commonly pairs with the DUF488-l subclade on the genome. In the case of DUF488-l and DUF488-u, the core domain is followed by a single beta-strand that stacks at the C-terminus of the core beta-sheet and a multi-helical 'cap' [[cite:PUB00153826]]. Unlike the DUF488-s and DUF488-l subclades, DUF488-u is not found adjacent to other DUF488 subclades on the genome [[cite:PUB00153826]].

This entry represents a subclade of DUF488 domains with degenerate C-terminal core strand. Sometimes it is observed adjacent to the DUF488-s subclade, suggesting it preserves a catalytic activity comparable to other active DUF488 subclades [[cite:PUB00153826]].

It contains a characteristic EKR sequence motif. The exact function of this domain is not known.

This domain of about 280 residues is found in eukaryotes. There are two conserved sequence motifs: GFC and GLL. This family is also known as UPF0704. This domain is found FAP206 [swissprot:Q23H79], a protein associated with cilia and flagella. In the ciliate Tetrahymena, the cilium has radial spokes, each of which is a macromolecular complex essential for motility. A triplet of three radial spokes, RS1, RS2, and RS3, is repeated every 96 nm along the doublet microtubule. Each spoke has a distinct base that docks to the doublet and is linked to different inner dynein arms. Knockout of the FAP206 gene results in slow cell motility and the 96-nm repeats lack RS2 and dynein c. FAP206 is probably part of the front prong and docks RS2 and dynein c to the microtubule [[cite:PUB00082324]].

The apaG domain is a ~125 amino acids domain present in bacterial apaG proteins and in eukaryotic F-box proteins. The domain is named after the bacterial apaG protein, of which it forms the core. The domain also occurs in the C-terminal part of eukaryotic proteins with an N-terminal F-box domain. The Salmonella typhimurium apaG domain protein corD is involved in Co(2+) resistance and Mg(2+) efflux. Tertiary structures from different apaG proteins show a fold of several beta-sheets. The apaG domain may be involved in protein-protein interactions which could be implicated in substrate-specificity [[cite:PUB00009972],[cite:PUB00016988],[cite:PUB00018539],[cite:PUB00016989]].

This domain was first discovered in BPSL1050, a highly immunoreactive protein found in Burkholderia pseudomallei. The domain's structure consists of three helical regions which pack onto an antiparallel beta sheet, formed by four strands. The beta sheet is solvent exposed on one side and packs tightly against the three helices on the other side, generating a network of hydrophobic and aromatic interactions that contribute to tight packing of the protein. Is is thought that the small loop L1, the main loop L2, and part of helix alpha-3 extending until Leu120 are the three main immunogenic sequences [[cite:PUB00091370]].

This domain is found in Nude C 80 (Ndc80) proteins which can be found in species such as Homo sapiens. Ndc80 protein complexes are a core component of the end-on attachment sites for kinetochore microtubules. Ndc80 is also known as Hec1, for highly expressed in cancer 1 [[cite:PUB00049694]].

This domain can be found in EH-domain-containing ATPase 2 (EHD2) present in Mus musculus. The domain is helical in nature and has extensive contacts with the G-domain [[cite:PUB00049104]].

This domain is found in the catalytic core RABEX-5 present in Homo sapiens. RABEX, also known as Rab GTPase exchange factors, regulate endocytic trafficking through activation of the Rab families RAB5, RAB21 and RAB22. The domain is helical in nature [[cite:PUB00042275]].

This domain is found in the Telomerase protein component 1 (TEP1) and it contains an homology region to the telomerase associated protein from Tetrahymena p80 [[cite:PUB00099027]]. TEP1 is a component of the telomerase ribonucleoprotein complex and is thought to be responsible for catalysing the addition of new telomeres to chromosomes. TEP1 is also a component of the vault particle, a cytoplasmic ribonucleoprotein complex, in which it is required for vault RNA stability and its association with the vault particle [[cite:PUB00035328]]. This domain is localised between the TROVE ([pfam:PF05731]) and DUF4062 ([pfam:PF13271]) domains.

This family represents a domain of unknown function located between the Transcription factor IIIC subunit delta N-term ([pfam:PF12657]) and the Putative zinc-finger of transcription factor IIIC complex ([pfam:PF12660]) within the transcription Factor IIIC 90 kDa subunit (TFIIIC-delta/TFIIIC90, also known as general transcription factor 3C polypeptide 4). TFIIIC is a multisubunit complex that directly recognises promoter elements and recruits TFIIIB and RNA polymerase III, being absolutely required for RNA polymerase III transcription. TFIIIC90 has an intrinsic histone acetyltransferase activity with a substrate specificity for histone H3 [[cite:PUB00056254]]. This domain is likely to be involved in the interaction with other components of the TFIIIC complex.

This represents a family of archaeal, bacterial and eukaryotic glycosyl hydrolases, that belong to superfamily GH116. The primary catabolic pathway for glucosylceramide is catalysis by the lysosomal enzyme glucocerebrosidase. In higher eukaryotes, glucosylceramide is the precursor of glycosphingolipids, a complex group of ubiquitous membrane lipids [[cite:PUB00044658]]. Mutations in the human protein cause motor-neurone defects in hereditary spastic paraplegia [[cite:PUB00078737]]. The catalytic nucleophile, identified in UniProtKB:Q97YG8_SULSO, is a glutamine-335, with the likely acid/base at Asp-442 and the aspartates at Asp-406 and Asp-458 residues also playing a role in the catalysis of glucosides and xylosides that are beta-bound to hydrophobic groups. The family is defined as GH116, which presently includes enzymes with beta-glucosidase, [ec:3.2.1.21], beta-xylosidase, [ec:3.2.1.37], and glucocerebrosidase [ec:3.2.1.45] activity [[cite:PUB00044658],[cite:PUB00073615]].

This family includes members such as plant proteins AtDMPs 1-10 (Arabidopsis thaliana DUF679 domain membrane proteins 1 -10) [[cite:PUB00136742]]. The AtDMP proteins are predicted to have four transmembrane spans, with cytosolic amino- and carboxy-termini. DMP1 is a membrane protein that may be involved in membrane fission during breakdown of the ER and the tonoplast during leaf senescence and in membrane fusion during vacuole biogenesis in roots [[cite:PUB00086645]]. Several DMP proteins are expressed in senescing organs (DMP1, -3, -4) or tissues that will stall later in development (DMP1, -2, -4, -7). These expression patterns strongly suggest involvement of several DMPs in various programmed cell death processes, e.g. senescence, dehiscence and abscission [[cite:PUB00136742]]. AtDMP8 and AtDMP9 however, have been shown to facilitate gamete fusion during double fertilisation in flowering plants [[cite:PUB00093467]].

This entry represents a small protein domain found in alpha proteobacteria. Its structure is composed of a four stranded sheet packed on one side by an alpha helix. The function of these proteins is unknown.

This entry contains a set of proteins that have a predicted 6-helical hairpin fold found in a wide range of glycosyl hydrolase enzymes, suggesting a potential function for these proteins. These proteins are largely found in actinobacteria and Alphaproteobacteria.

This entry represents a family of bacterial proteins of unknown function. The domain structure includes a four stranded beta sheet which has two conserved aspartates in a DXDXG motif close to a highly conserved histidine. These three residues may for the potential active site.

This entry represents a family of small bacterial and archaeal proteins that have an SH3 like barrel structure that shows most similarity to the C-terminal domain of the ribosomal chaperone RimP [pfam:PF17384].

This entry represents a small protein that has a domain with a structure resembling a double stranded RNA-binding domain such as [pfam:PF00035]. Thus suggesting this protein may also have a dsRNA binding function. This is supported by the presence of several conserved positively charged residues.
This entry represents a bacterial protein of unknown function.
This entry represents a small domain found in a range of bacterial and phage proteins. In a few proteins it is associated with [pfam:PF11994]. This region is composed of two alpha helices.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised proteins. The possess a beta sheet packed against an alpha helical subdomain. This alignment contains three fully conserved cysteines that look like they form an Fe-S cluster or zinc binding site in the predicted structures.

This entry represents a family of bacterial proteins that have an alpha/alpha(6) toroid structure. This suggests that these proteins are likely to be an as yet uncharacterised family of glycosyl hydrolases.
This entry represents a family of small putative integral membrane proteins with two transmembrane helices.
This entry represents an uncharacterised family of bacterial proteins. Members of the family are about 250 residues in length.
Members of this family are annotated in SwissProt as Putative glycerol transporters SwissProt:Q92EU1. Members of the family contain four potential transmembrane helices.

This entry represents a small domain found in a range of phage and bacterial proteins. Structurally it is composed of a three stranded beta meander packed against an alpha helix. The function of these proteins is unknown.
This entry represents a family of Actinobacterial proteins of unknown function. AlphaFold predicts a confident dimeric arrangement. This family appears to be distantly related to [pfam:PF19887].
This family of proteins are uncharacterised. This family is distantly related to [pfam:PF06853] currently known as DUF1249.

This is a family of uncharacterised proteins. They are predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of two domains. The predicted C-terminal domain share similarity with the catalytic domains of purine and uridine phosphorylases.
The function of this family of proteins is unknown. They are predicted to adopt a five-bladed beta-propeller and are probably distantly related to apyrase.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised proteins. Proteins in this family are primarily found in Proteobacteria. The structure of these proteins contains a six stranded beta sheet.
This is a family of uncharacterized proteins.Their predicted structure shows some similarity to ADP-rybosylating toxins.

This is a family of uncharacterized proteins. They share remote similarity to both domains of proteins members of UDP-glycosyltransferase superfamily. In contrast to them, these proteins are predicted to consist of a single standalone domain.

This is a family of uncharacterized proteins. They are predicted to adopt a globular structure that resembles the conserved core of the PPPDE superfamily (after Permuted Papain fold Peptidases of DsRNA viruses and Eukaryotes) consisting of thiol peptidases with a circularly permuted papain-like fold.

This family of proteins is primarily found in proteobacteria. Proteins in this family are typically between 124 and 153 amino acids in length. Proteins in this family has several conserved histidine residues that may form zinc binding sites.
This is a domain of unknown function found in bacterial proteins. It is predicted to adopt a RIFT-type beta(6)-barrel topology with a greater similarity to FAD-binding domains.

This family of proteins is found in bacteria. Proteins in this family are typically between 135 and 154 amino acids in length. These proteins share significant sequence similarity to the central part of mammalian cell entry (MCE) protein MlaD.
This is a family of uncharacterized bacterial proteins with a length of ~140-150 residues. They are predicted to adopt an alpha-helical structure consisting of two structural repeats.

This domain is found standalone in bacteria. Its function is unknown but it has a significant sequence similarity to the C-terminal SAM-binding regulatory domain of 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR).

This entry represents a set of uncharacterised proteins found in prokaryotes. They share remote similarity to LolA and LolB outer-membrane lipoproteins. Similar to LolA and LolB these proteins are predicted to have a hydrophobic cavity consisting of an unclosed beta-barrel and an alpha-helical lid.

This family of proteins is based on the known structure of a protein from Ruminococcus gnavus PDB:3noh. The structure shows similarity to solute binding proteins. The exact function of these proteins is not yet known.

This family is found in bacterial proteins either as a standalone domain or in combination with an HTH domain that resembles lambda C1 repressor DNA-binding domain. This family has a partial sequence similarity to the RAP1 C-terminal (RCT) domain.

This entry represents a beta propeller domain composed of five blades. It is often found in large extracellular proteins in one or more copies. It is uncertain whether this domain might have an enzymatic function or a ligand binding function. Structurally this domain appears to have a sixfold symmetry, but one of the blades takes up the space of normal repeats. This unusual blade is composed of three strands of the first repeat and a final C-terminal strand from the last repeat.

This domain of unknown function is found mainly in bacterial proteins, either standalone or in combination with other domains. It is probably remotely related to the anticodon binding domain observed in histidyl, glycyl, threonyl and prolyl tRNA synthetases.
This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are probably distantly related to heme-binding proteins PhuS, ChuS, HmuS.

This domain of unknown function is found in bacterial proteins. It is probably distantly related to dodecin. It is predicted to adopt a simple fold consisting of a core of 3 strands, forming a curved sheet, and two short helices.
This domain is found C-terminal in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is probably remotely related to PemK-like, MazF-like toxins and is predicted to adopt SH3-like fold.

This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are predicted to adopt alpha/beta structure with a central nine-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet with helices packed on both sides. The predicted structure has some partial structural similarity to bacterial S-adenosylmethionine decarboxylases.

This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are predicted to fold into five-bladed beta-propeller that has similarity to apyrase but it is circularly permuted. The C-terminal two beta-strands of this domain occupy the position of the two N-terminal beta-strands in apyrase.
This family consists of several uncharacterised proteins from Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease spirochete).
This domain is found C-terminal in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is remotely related to the integrase core domain with a partly conserved active site architecture.
This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They share significant sequence similarity with immunity protein Imm5 and are predicted to adopt similar alpha-helical structure.
This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are remotely related to nucleotidyltransferases and share similar active site architecture.

This domain is found in bacterial and archaeal uncharacterised proteins. It is typically between 150 and 160 amino acids in length. It is remotely related to ribonuclease H-like nucleases but it is unlikely to possess any enzymatic activity.

This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are predicted to adopt an alpha/beta structure consisting of a central mixed beta-sheet packed on both sides with alpha-helices that is reminiscent to the common structural core of N-acetyltransferases (NAT).

This is a domain found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins either as standalone or in combination with other domains. It is remotely related to soluble lipid-binding protein MlaC and it is predicted to adopt a similar structure with a typical NTF2-like topology.

This domain is found N-terminal in a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. This domain has a significant sequence similarity to the N-terminal domains of a number of proteins members of UDP-Glycosyltransferase/glycogen phosphorylase superfamily. It is predicted to adopt the same alpha/beta structure.

This domain is found C-terminal in a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. This domain has a significant sequence similarity to the C-terminal domains of a number of proteins members of UDP-Glycosyltransferase/glycogen phosphorylase superfamily. It is predicted to adopt the same alpha/beta structure.

This is a family of bacterial proteins with unknown function. They share sequence similarity with the N-terminal part of NADAR domain and are predicted to adopt structure that is globally similar to the structure of E.coli protein YbiA, a member of the NADAR domain family.

This is a family of uncharacterised proteins found in bacteria and eukaryotes. These proteins are probably distantly related to HIT-containing uridylyltransferases and are likely to adopt the same structure.

This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They share sequence similarity to Ig-like domains found in a number of proteins such as xylosyltransferase, alkylpurine DNA glycosylase, cycloisomaltooligosaccharide glucanotransferase and are predicted to adopt the same structure.
This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are probably distantly related to uracil-DNA glycosylases and other related DNA glycosylases given their predicted structure.

This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They share significant sequence similarity with each of the specificity subunit target recognition domains of type I restriction-modification enzymes and are predicted to adopt the same structure.

This is a family of uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Gram-positive bacteria. They are predicted to be associated with the membrane and to adopt structure that has topological similarity to the common structural core of Succinate-acetate permease (SatP) superfamily proteins.

This entry represents a WH-like domain (PDB:4ro3) found at the N-terminal of an uncharacterised protein from Vibrio cholerae ([swissprot:M1RHE3]), whose function is unknown. This domain is also found in phage proteins.

This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins either standalone or in combination with other domains. It is distantly related to the type II restriction endonucleases with predicted similar active site architecture. These proteins are most likely endonucleases based on the strict conservation of the putative active site residues.
This is a domain found in a group of uncharacterised bacterial sequences whose function is unknown. This domain adopts a galactose-binding-like structure (PDBe:4lr4).

This domain is found either as standalone or in combination with other domains in a group of uncharacterised proteins. It is distantly related to EDC3 mRNA-decapping protein 3 and it could be involved in RNA-binding. It is predicted to adopt a barrel-like structure with a typical Sm-like fold. The pair of glycines responsible for maintaining the Sm-barrel curvature are also conserved in the members of this family.
This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. These proteins are enriched with hydrophobic residues and it is quite likely to be associated with the membrane.
Family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins.

This domain if found in a group of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is related to NlpC/P60 domains and it is likely to adopt similar structure as well as to possess an endopeptidase activity. All members of this family contain a conserved cysteine residue that is predicted to occupy equivalent spatial position as in the NlpC/P60 domains.

This is a family of uncharacterised proteins found in archaea and bacteria. These proteins are predicted to adopt similar structure to the members of SufE/NifU superfamily. They contain three invariant cysteine residues and a fourth semi-conserved residue either cysteine or histidine. These residues are likely to define a potential Zn-binding site similar to the binding site observed in SufU.
This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They contain highly conserved acidic residues and G[S/A]ID motif at the C terminus.

This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They share significant sequence similarity to HTH winged helix domains, in particular to the N-terminal domain of transcriptional regulator BrxR and RNA polymerase III subunit RPC82.
This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are enriched in hydrophobic residues and are likely associated with the membrane.

This is a family of small uncharacterised proteins found in bacteria and archaea. They are predicted to adopt an alpha/beta globular structure consisting of a cradle-like beta-sheet and alpha-helices packed on the convex side of the sheet.
This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins either as standalone or in combination with other domains. It is predicted to adopt an alpha-beta structure with ferredoxin-like topology.

This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to fold into a beta-barrel that has some similarity to the replication focus targeting sequence (RFTS) domain of Dnmt1 methyltransferase 1.
This family is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They share sequence similarity with several HTH winged helix domains, one of which Zinc uptake regulation protein FurB.
This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They contain conserved Pro-Gly-rich motif with a semi- conserved pattern PGRxFPGx3QGD.
This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are composed of two tandem domains with similarity to SH3 domains, in particular to YorP.

This is a family of small, about 60 residues in length, bacterial proteins. They are predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of three helices. The N- and C-terminal helices contain highly conserved aromatic residues in addition to the nearly invariant glycines located at the interhelical connecting loops.

This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are related to HlyIII family [pfam:PF03006] and are predicted to adopt the same structure consisting of seven transmembrane helices. Their predicted structure, suggests that, similarly to HlyIII, they may contain a Zn-binding site, albeit slightly rearranged as only two of the Zn-coordinating residues are in conserved positions.
This domain is found N-terminal in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is distantly related to class-II glutamine amidotransferase domains [pfam:PF13522].
This short helical domain is found in a small set of ribosomal S1 proteins. It's function is unknown.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised proteins which are predicted to form a small three helical bundle containing a beta hairpin between helices 1 and 2.

This is a domain found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins that is predicted to be helical. It contains a nearly invariant tryptophan toward the N terminus and a highly conserved motif [F/Y]GGMGSx(2)D toward the C-terminus.

This family of proteins is found in bacteria. Proteins in this family are approximately 70 amino acids in length. They are predicted to fold into a four-stranded beta-sheet meander and an alpha-helix. One face of this beta-sheet is enriched with conserved positively charged arginine and lysine residues.

This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins either standalone or C-terminal to HTH winged helix domains. It has a partial sequence similarity to ribosome associated factors that are members of [pfam:PF02482].

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins from Proteobacteria. It is predicted to adopt an alpha/beta globular structure. It has three highly conserved histidines that are predicted to cluster together in space and are likely involved in metal coordination.
Family of bacterial hypothetical proteins that is sometimes associated with GTPase domains.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins from bacteria and protostome animals. It is predicted to fold into a curved meander beta-sheet. It contains four highly conserved cysteine residues, two of which are predicted to cluster together in space and are likely involved in disulfide bond formation.
This is a domain of unknown function found at the N-terminal end.

This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins either standalone or in combination with other domains. It is probably distantly related to the C-terminal domain of CdiA toxin (CdiA-CT), known member of RNase A superfamily.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of five alpha-helices. It is probably distantly related to Wnt domains.
This entry represents a dimeric alpha/beta barrel domain from an uncultured marine organism (PDB:2op5). The function of this family is unknown.

This family of uncharacterised proteins is found in Proteobacteria. It shares significant sequence similarity with enzymes members of Heme oxygenase-like superfamily and are predicted to adopt similar structure consisting of a bundle of six alpha-helices.

This family of uncharacterised proteins is found mainly in Proteobacteria. It is likely to consists of two domains that engage in extensive contacts mainly via hydrophobic residues. The predicted structure of the N-terminal domain has similarity to chorismatases.

This is a family of uncharacterised proteins. They are predicted to adopt a globular alpha/beta structure consisting of a meander beta-sheet and two helices packed on one side on the sheet. These proteins contain three highly conserved histidines that in the predicted structure cluster close in space and could potentially form a metal binding site.
This is a family of uncharacterised proteins. They are predicted to fold into a globular structure consisting mainly of alpha-helices.

This is a domain found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. This domain occurs either standalone or in combination with other domains. It contains conserved cysteines and histidine that may be involved in Zn2+ coordination.
This entry represents an alpha-lytic protease prodomain-like domain present in a protein of unknown function from Desulfovibrio piger. It structure has been characterized (PDB:4HLB).

This family of proteins is found in bacteria. Proteins in this family are typically between 135 and 1024 amino acids in length. This family of proteins are structurally related to [pfam:PF03614] a family of transcriptional repressors of phase-1 flagellin genes. The family appears to contain two related subdomains.
This entry represents a bacterial family of unknown function.
This entry represents a family of bacterial domains of unknown function.
This entry represents a family of TIM barrel proteins that are most closely related to [pfam:PF03328]. This strongly suggests that these proteins are enzyme with a possibly related function.
This alpha helical domain is usually found at the C-terminus of proteins containing repeats of [pfam:PF12396].

This family of uncharacterised proteins is found mainly in Proteobacteria. These proteins are predicted to adopt an alpha-helical structure. They contain a highly conserved RXXXE-motif and an invariant histidine that may have a functional role.
This domain is found in a number of uncharacterised bacterial proteins that are likely associated with the membrane.
This family of proteins is found in bacteria. Proteins in this family are typically between 185 and 199 amino acids in length. There are two semi-conserved sequence motifs: HLA and GFVPYI.
This entry represents a C-terminal domain of a functionally unknown conserved protein from Bacillus anthracis (PDB:4fca).

This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are enriched with hydrophobic residues and are likely associated with the membrane. These proteins contain two conserved motifs GLDxxYxxxG and FLxxFD.
This entry represents a bacterial domain of unknown function.

This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are probably remotely related to His-Me finger endonucleases. The conservation of the putative active site residues in this family is not strict, in particular the position of the catalytic histidine. The residues involved in metal coordination are conserved. The presence in the vicinity of two invariant aspartate residues that point toward the putative active site suggests that these proteins may still function as enzymes but probably via a somewhat different catalytic mechanism. They may still retain their catalytic activity by employing these conserved aspartates that in the predicted AF2 models are well positioned to undertake a role in a potential nucleophilic attack.
This domain is found N-terminal in a group of uncharacterised proteins. It is remotely related to AbiEi winged helix domain and it is predicted to adopt the same structure.

This domain is found C-terminal in a group of uncharacterised proteins. It usually follows winged helix domain [pfam:PF22515]. This domain is related to PD-(D/E)XK nucleases and it is predicted to adopt the same structure with similar active site architecture.

This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They share significant sequence similarity with PvuII endonucleases and are predicted to adopt similar structure. The predicted structures, however, do not suggest similarity in the active site architecture.

This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are predicted to adopt alpha-helical structure. These proteins contain several invariant histidines and aspartates that may have a functional role.

This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are predicted to adopt an alpha/beta structure consisting of a cradle-like beta-sheet with alpha-helices pocked on the convex side of it. These proteins contain a highly conserved GYMDFTYF sequence motif that may be of functional importance.

This is a family of uncharacterised proteins found in Archaea. They have sequence similarity to Zincin-like metalloproteases and are predicted to adopt the same structure. Only one of the two zinc binding sites are conserved suggesting that these proteins may possess different function.
This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They share sequence similarity with DarT toxin and are likely to adopt the same structure.
This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular alpha/beta structure with a central antiparallel beta-sheet and helices packed on it.

This family of proteins is found in bacteria and archaea. Proteins in this family are approximately 160 amino acids in length. They are predicted to adopt globular alpha/beta structure. These proteins contain two highly conserved sequence motifs GxFDxWC and KRxKRLG that may be of functional importance.
This is a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. These proteins share partial sequence similarity to the collagenase catalytic core with invariant HExxH motif.

Proteins in this family are found in Firmicutes. They are approximately 120 amino acids in length and are predicted to adopt an alpha helical structure. Members of this family contain two highly conserved acid residues aspartate and glutamate.

This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of segregated alpha-helices and a five-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet. This domain contains two highly conserved sequence motifs TxxHGG and YEED that may be of a functional importance.
This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It contains a number of highly conserved positively charged residues that may have functional role.

This is a family of uncharacterised proteins found in bacteria. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of two nearly orthogonal beta-sheets and two helices that connect them. Toward the C terminus these proteins contain a highly conserved enriched with negatively charged residues region having nearly invariant EKDFxC sequence motif.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are predicted to adopt alpha-helical structure composed of six up-and-down helices. It is likely that these proteins are associated with the membrane.
This domain of unknown function is found in a group of proteins predominantly from proteobacteria. It has a LxHDGK/RRL motif and a highly conserved W residue.

This domain of unknown function is found in a group of proteins mainly from alphaproteobacteria. It is normally found N-terminal to [pfam:PF10074]. It is predicted to adopt a configuration formed mainly by beta-strands.
This is a presumed domain found at the N-terminal of phage sequences, which also have a FN3-like domain ([pfam:PF21470]) at the C-terminal.
This domain is found in a group of bacterial proteins. It is often found C-terminal to [pfam:PF18863]. It is predicted to adopt an all-alpha helical fold.

This domain of unknown function is found at the C-terminal of a group of bacterial proteins and, according to structure predictions, it may adopt a beta-barrel structure. It is often associated with an Ig-like domain ([pfam:PF08522]).
This entry represents a pair of OB fold domains found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from bacteria which have a [pfam:PF22707] domain at the C-terminal.

This entry represents a domain consisting of TPR repeats found at the N-terminal of of group of uncharacterised sequences predominantly from bacteria, which seem to be related to TOTE conflict systems as they are associated with [pfam:PF22708].

This is a domain of unknown function found at the N-terminal of proteins containing DUF3994 at the C-terminal, in most instances. According to structure predictions, this domain consists of alpha helices suggesting they are the membrane spanning region of of these sequences.
This is a family of uncharacterised proteins found mainly in actinomycetes. Their function is unknown. They are predicted to adopt OB fold with significant similarity to Rpa.
This entry represents a family of phage proteins of unknown function. AlphaFold shows confident dimer interaction.
This entry represents a beta barrel domain which is found associated with [pfam:PF10020].
This uncharacterised protein is found in the T5 bacteriophage. The function of this protein is unknown.

This domain is found in human Protein dispatched homolog 3 (DISP3) and related proteins mainly from vertebrates. DISP3 (PTCHD2), a sterol-sensing domain- containing protein, is highly expressed in neural tissue, promotes cell proliferation and alters expression of genes that are involved in tumourigenesis. The function of this domain is unknown.

This domain has a structure that resembles the galactose-binding domain. This domain is often associated with a [pfam:PF00884] sulfatase like domain. Suggesting that this domain may be part of an enzyme that modifies some kind of carbohydrate.
This entry represents an SH3 barrel like domain found in a large family of AAA proteins. The function of these proteins is uncertain.
This entry represents a helical domain found in plant proteins. The function of these proteins is unknown.
This is a domain of unknown function found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly found in worms. This is likely a transmembrane segment.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure that has significant sequence and structural similarity to MBD domains.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure that has some similarity to SRA domain ([pfam:PF18491]). The function of this domain is unknown.

This domain of unknown function is found in Lysine-specific demethylase 3B (KDM3B, also known as JmjC domain-containing histone demethylation protein 2B or JHDM2B) and related proteins. KDM3B is a histone demethylase that specifically demethylates lysine at position 9 of histone H3 [[cite:PUB00153916]]. This enzyme plays a central role in histone code. This domain is predicted to adopt an open beta-barrel with an SH3-like topology.

This domain is found N-terminal in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. This domain is predicted to adopt a globular structure that folds into a four helical bundle and has a significant sequence and structural similarity to MLKL executioner domain ([pfam:PF22215]).
This uncharacterised domain is found in a group of polysaccharide deacetylases and similar proteins from bacteria. It is predicted to adopt an alpha-helical configuration.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from Dictyostelia. It is predicted to adopt Ig-like fold with the fibronectin type III-like topology.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from Dictyostelia. It is predicted to adopt Ig-like fold with the fibronectin type III-like topology.
This entry represents a predicted ferredoxin-like domain found in a family of uncharacterized plant proteins. This group of proteins typically has this domain duplicated.
This entry represents a small domain found in a family of uncharacterized proteins in nematodes. This domain is predicted to fold as a beta-sheet composed of four anti-parallel beta-strands.
This entry represents a domain found in a family of uncharacterized proteins in nematodes. In some proteins, this domain appears internally duplicated.
This entry represents a domain found in a family of uncharacterised proteins in nematodes.
This entry represents a C-terminal domain found in a family of uncharacterised proteins in nematodes.

This is a domain of unknown function predominantly found at the N-terminal of sequences from ticks, spiders and similar sequences from arthropods. According to structure predictions this domain may adopt a alpha-helical bundle fold similar to Ty3 transposon capsid-like proteins.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised metazoan proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure with lipocalin fold. It also contains several highly conserved cysteine residues that are likely involved in the formation of intra-domain disulfide bridges.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised metazoan proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure with lipocalin fold. It also contains several highly conserved cysteine residues that are likely involved in the formation of intra-domain disulfide bridges.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised metazoan proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure with lipocalin fold. It also contains several highly conserved cysteine residues that are likely involved in the formation of intra-domain disulfide bridges.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised metazoan proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure with lipocalin fold. It also contains several highly conserved cysteine residues that are likely involved in the formation of intra-domain disulfide bridges.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised plant proteins. These proteins are probably distantly related to the plant-specific actin-binding protein SCAB1 and are predicted to contain a fusion domain composed of Ig and PH-like domains in a similar arrangement as in SCAB1 (([pfam:PF16709]) and ([pfam:PF17684])) [[cite:PUB00076164]]. The domain represented by this entry corresponds to an atypical PH-like domain.
This is a domain of unknown function mostly found in arthropods. This domain may adopt a three helical bundle fold. These sequences might be related to reverse transcriptase polymerases.
This entry represents a domain found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from Trypanosoma sp. According to structural predictions, this domain is likely to adopt a beta-propeller fold.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. This domain is predicted to fold into a globular structure that adopts a ferredoxin-like fold.
This family contains several uncharacterised Baculovirus proteins.

This domain is found N-terminal in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. It shares a significant sequence similarity with the N-terminal domain of bHLH-MYC and R2R3-MYB transcription factors ([pfam:PF14215]) and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.
This is a domain of unknown function mostly found in organisms within the Trypanosoma genus. This domain adopt a multiple helical bundle fold.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from Fungi. It shares significant sequence similarity with domains members of the Bet v1-like superfamily and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.

This domain is found in the uncharacterized protein At4g22758 from Arabidopsis thaliana and related proteins. It shares significant sequence similarity with CRIM domain and it is predicted to adopt a similar structure with ubiquitin-like topology.

This is a presumed domain found in a group of uncharacterised sequences from bacteria. According to structure predictions, this domain is found at the C-terminal and may adopt an all-beta structure consisting of eight anti-parallel beta-sheets.. These proteins also have a glycosyltransferase domain at the N-terminal ([pfam:PF13231]).

This is a presumed domain found in a group of uncharacterised sequences from bacteria. According to structure predictions, this domain is found towards the C-terminal, after a glycosyltransferase domain ([pfam:PF13231]), and it may adopt an alpha/beta structure. In some instances, this domain is followed by and all-beta domain at the very C-terminal of the sequences ([pfam:PF23157]). The function of this domain is unknown.
This is a presumed domain found at the C-terminal of sequences from Gammaproteobacteria. According to structure predictions it may have an alpha/beta fold.

This domain is found N-terminal in a group of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. These proteins are probably distantly related to Aeronamide N-methyltransferases AerE. They share two similar domains that are predicted in the same arrangement. This domain is found N-terminal to the methyltransferase domain and has a weak sequence similarity to various HTH domains.

This entry represents a domain found at the C-terminal of a group of proteins from nematodes, members of the BPI/LBP/Plunc family of proteins which share homology with cholesterol ester transfer protein (CETP) and phospholipid transfer protein (PLTP). The exact function of these proteins is unknown, however, according to their structure predictions and homology to CEPT/PLTP, they may play a role in lipid binding.

This entry represents a domain found towards the N-terminal of a group of proteins from nematodes such as Trichuris suis and Trichinella britovi, members of the BPI/LBP/Plunc family of proteins which share homology with cholesterol ester transfer protein (CETP) and phospholipid transfer protein (PLTP). The exact function of these proteins is unknown, however, according to their structure predictions and homology to CEPT/PLTP, they may be involved in lipid binding.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from digenean species.
This is a SH2 domain found mainly in nematodes such as Trichuris trichura, Toxocara canis and Trichinella sp. The function of this domain is unknown.

This is a domain of unknown function found in fungi and bacteria, which, according to structure predictions it adopts a lipocalin-like fold. This domain is found as a pair of two flattened, orthogonally packed, beta-barrels. This entry represents the C-terminal barrel of the pair.

This is a domain of unknown function found in fungi and bacteria, which, according to structure predictions it adopts a lipocalin-like fold. This domain is found as a pair of two flattened, orthogonally packed, beta-barrels. This entry represents the N-terminal barrel of the pair. In some members, the lipocalin-like domains (also referred to as AttH-like) are associated with a protein kinase-like domain at the N-terminal ([pfam:PF01636]).
This is a beta-beta-alpha zinc finger found in a group of uncharacterised sequences, mainly from fungi.

This domain is found C-terminal to the NTPase domain [pfam:PF05729] in a group of fungal proteins, including [swissprot:U7Q5X2] from Sporothrix schenckii. It is predicted to adopt an alpha-helical configuration.
This domain of unknown function is found in a fro up of fungal proteins. It is often N-terminal to several copies of ankyrin repeats. It is predicted to adopt an alpha-helical configuration.
This family consists of several uncharacterised proteins from Arabidopsis thaliana.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from actinopterygians that are distantly related and share overall similar domain organisation to the human NEDD4-binding protein 1 (N4BP1). This domain shares a weak sequence similarity to known UBA domains and it is predicted to fold into a typical three helical bundle.
This domain is found C-terminal in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of two alpha-helical repeats.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from Fungi. It shares a weak sequence similarity to the C-terminal domain of the Escherichia Coli ProQ RNA binding protein ([pfam:PF17516]) and it is predicted to adopt a similar structure with SH3-like topology.

This domain is found in Histone-lysine N-methyltransferase, H3 lysine-4 specific from Plasmodium falciparum ([swissprot:W4J2P1]) and similar sequences from alveolates. In some proteins this domain is found associated with [pfam:PF00628]. It shows a conserved motif LLxxYKxKI/LxDLL.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised plant proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure with a Cystatin-like topology consisting of a curved four-stranded beta-sheet and an alpha-helix packed on the concave side of it.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised plant proteins. It shares a significant sequence similarity with members of the GDP-fucose protein O-fucosyltransferase family ([pfam:PF10250]) and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It shares a significant sequence similarity of Ig-like domains found in Trs120 and it is predicted to adopt a structure with a similar topology.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It shares a weak sequence similarity with the Ig-like domains found in Trs130, particularly the second Ig-like domain, and it is predicted to adopt a structure with a similar topology.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. This domain is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of a four helical bundle and having structural similarity to the alpha-helical domain inserted in the third Ig domain of the Trs130 component of the TRAPPII complex [[cite:PUB00153720]].
This is a presumed domain found in a set of bacterial sequences, whose function is unknown.
This domain is found in Polyketide synthase HetM from Nostoc sp. This domain is predicted to adopt an all alpha-helical structure. Its specific function is unknown.

This presumed domain is found in a group of plant sequences related to Oberon-like proteins. According to structure predictions this domain may consist of mainly three beta-sheets and two alpha-helices.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from Fungi. This domain is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of a curved beta-sheet and alpha- helices packed on it. This domain is probably distantly related to the N-terminal domain of STE-like transcription factors ([pfam:PF02200]) based on the similarity of their predicted structures. The predicted structure of this domain has a partial similarity to pseudo Winged helix domains.
This is a presumed domain found at the N-terminal of the uncharacterised protein K02A2.6 from C.elegans and similar worm sequences. This domain may adopt a fold similar to retrotransposons.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from Arthropods. This is a relatively small domain that is predicted to contain mainly alpha-helices.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from flatworms. It is predicted to adopt a PH-like fold with similarity to the PH-like domain found in Shulin and Spt16.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised plant proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of a rubredoxin-like zinc finger capped with an elaborated alpha-helical subdomain. This arrangement is similar to the zinc finger domain found in hypA ([pfam:PF01155]).

Pfam_Description: Integral membrane domain of unknown function (DUF7087)
Pfam_name: Integral membrane domain of unknown function (DUF7087)
Pfam_description: This entry represents a four helical integral membrane domain found in nematode species. The function of this domain is unknown.
This domain is found at the N-terminal of a group of poorly characterised bacterial sequences. The function of this domain is unknown.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised proteins from halobacteria. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-beta configuration.
This entry represents a family of proteins from halobacteria. Members of this family, often annotated as ATPases, are predicted to show a central beta-sheet with alpha-helices in both sides.
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. It has a conserved motif VCRRH/YAE and conserved R, Y and W residues. Members are predicted to show an alpha-beta configuration.

This domain represents a small beta barrel domain that is found at the N-terminus of some bacterial peptidase M48 proteins. It has a PH-domain like structure. It likely acts as a chaperone for membrane protein complexes. May interact with [pfam:PF05987] members based on AlphaFold predictions.

This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. It shows two conserved motifs WP and several conserved D and R residues. Members are predicted to show beta-sheets at the N- and C-terminal ends.
This domain is found in a group of proteins from halobacteria. It shows several Y and Q conserved residues and is predicted to show an antiparallel beta-sheet and an alpha-helix.
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. They show several highly conserved motifs PVPV, LGL/MDP, AxWA, and PV/IHLEVC. Many members are annotated as nucleotidyltransferases.

This domain is found at the N-terminal end of a group of proteins from eubacteria. It is predicted to show a mainly alpha-configuration. This entry is found associated with [pfam:PF23375] and [pfam:PF23374]
This protein family includes a group of proteins from halobacteria. It shows several conserved motifs DCPH, RGCL and RPLL/VEEHHLSxY. Members are predicted to show an alpha-beta configuration.
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. It has several conserved motifs WHGP, QLWC and RxYxP. It is predicted to adopt a predominantly beta structure with a short alpha-helix.
This is a beta-propeller domain found in a group on uncharacterised proteins from fungi. The function of this domain is unknown.

This is an alpha-helical domain found at the N-terminal of a group of uncharacterised proteins from fungi. The function of this domain is unknown. Members of this entry also have a beta-propeller at the C-terminal ([pfam:PF23388]).

This is a domain found in a group on uncharacterised proteins from fungi. The function of this domain is unknown. According to structural predictions, this domain likely adopts an alpha-beta-beta-beta-beta-alpha fold. This domain is usually found associated with an alpha-helical domain at the N-terminal ([pfam:PF23391]) and a beta-propeller at the C-terminal ([pfam:PF23388]).
This domain has a restriction endonuclease-like fold. The function of these proteins is unknown. Some members of the family are annotated as nucleoporins.
This is a family of unknown function. It is structurally similar to Frag1-like domain, composed of a six-alpha-helix bundle transmembrane region [[cite:PUB00155610]].

This entry includes uncharacterised fungal sequences which consist of repeats that may adopt an alpha-solenoid structure related to ankirin repeats. The overall arrangement of these repeats may have a horseshoe conformation similar to that in leucine-rich repeats.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised domains that show similarities to members of the colipase superfamily/

This domain is found at the N-terminal end of the uncharacterised protein HVO_0731 from Haloferax volcanii ([swissprot:D4GTA0]) and similar proteins from halobacteria. It has several conserved motifs RLTR/KLxR and LVxHPxEW. It is predicted to adopt an alpha-beta structure. The function of this domain is unknown.

This domain is found at the C-terminal end of the uncharacterised protein HVO_0731 from Haloferax volcanii ([swissprot:D4GTA0]) and similar proteins from halobacteria. It is predicted to adopt an all-alpha structure. The function of this domain is unknown.

This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. It has several conserved motifs LAGV/IVDLFG, DxPHI and LxDVxYD/ExExW and five highly conserved R residues. Members are predicted to show a mainly alpha-helical structure with a small beta-sheet.

The proteins in this family are functionally uncharacterised. The proteins are around 450 amino acids long and includes Streptococcus pneumoniae Sp0239 which is structurally similar to ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) and pyruvate formate lyase (PFL). It is likely that this family represents a group of glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenases.
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. Members are predicted to show an alpha-beta configuration.
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. It has several conserved motifs AxYxET, ERxL/VxF and GYAMLK/RVR. Members are predicted to show a beta-sheet and an alpha-helix.
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. It has several conserved R, D W and Y residues. Members are predicted to show a mainly beta configuration.
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. It has several conserved motifs YVWVCD, RGF and RTQFxR. Members are predicted to show an alpha-beta configuration.
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. It has several conserved motifs GVQLIYEGLR, EPW and GR/K/QxQT/S. Members are predicted to show an all-alpha configuration.

This domain is found twice in HVO_2519 from Haloferax volcanii ([swissprot:D4GTV1]) and similar proteins mainly from halobacteria. It has several conserved motifs RTxxYR, Y/FxHxxxR an RRK. It is predicted to show an alpha-beta configuration.
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. It has several conserved motifs LGY, AERK/EWK/R, RCFV and YxWA. Members are predicted to show an alpha-beta configuration.
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. It has several conserved motifs WSYY, RxYxR and HxK/RR. Members are predicted to show a predominantly alpha configuration.
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. Members are predicted to adopt an all-alpha structure.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from archaea. It is predicted to adopt an all-helical configuration.
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-helical configuration.
This family represents a group of proteins mainly from halobacteria. Members are predicted to show an alpha- helical configuration.
This domain is found in a group of proteins from halobacteria. Members are predicted to show an alpha-beta configuration.
This domain is found in a group of proteins mainly from halobacteria. It is predicted to show an HTH fold.
This domain is found in a group of proteins from halobacteria. It has several W and R conserved residues. This domain is predicted to show an alpha-beta configuration.
