This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. Members are predicted to show an alpha-beta configuration with similarity to the KaiC domain ([pfam:PF06745]).
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. Members are predicted to show an alpha-beta configuration with similarity to the Rossmann fold of the TrkA-N domain ([pfam:PF02254]).
This family represents a group of proteins from halobacteria. Members adopt a beta configuration with high similarity to the CS domain ([pfam:PF04969]).

This domain is found in a group of small proteins mainly from Halobacteria. It contains highly conserved cysteine and histidine residues arranged in two CxxC and HxxC motifs that likely coordinate zinc. This domain is predicted to adopt a fold similar to the classical C2H2 and variant C2HC zinc fingers containing beta-hairpin and an alpha helix. In addition, it is predicted to contain an extra N-terminal strand that contributes to the formation of a three-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet. This domain also has a number of highly conserved negatively charged residues.

This domain is found in a group of small proteins mainly from Halobacteria. It contains highly conserved cysteine residues arranged in two CxxC motifs that likely coordinate zinc. The first motif could be more broadly defined as YECxxCG. This domain is predicted to adopt zinc ribbon fold.

This family contains several proteins of unknown function from C.elegans. The GO annotation suggests that this protein is involved in nematode development and has a positive regulation on growth rate.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from Halobacteria. It contains highly conserved cysteine residues arranged in two CxxC motifs that likely coordinate zinc. The first motif could be more broadly defined as a semi-conserved MWRCxxCGEM sequence motif. This domain is predicted to adopt a zinc ribbon fold with similarity to rubredoxin-like domains.

This entry is a domain of unknown function found in some PA-PLA1 family members, which consists of mitochondrial proteins that are probable phospholipases with a specific function to hydrolyze phosphatidic acid. Members of this family are involved in the metabolism of phospholipids, which are critical components of cell membranes. By hydrolyzing phosphatidic acid, these enzymes may play a role in the regulation of mitochondrial membrane composition and dynamics, as well as in signaling pathways related to lipid metabolism.
This entry represents a small family from archaebacteria based on protein PF1546. AlphaFold models show that a dimer of this protein forms a flattened 10 stranded beta barrel structure.
This domain is found in a number of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to form a a six-bladed beta-propeller with significant similarity to glucose/sorbosone dehydrogenases.

This domain is composed of 6 transmembrane alpha helices and is found at the N-terminus of a large family of bacterial signalling proteins. It is structurally related to the N-terminus of the DesK protein. That region is believed to be involved in sensing membrane fluidity.ED A0A1A9IX15.1/7-166; A0A1A9IX15.1/7-50;

This domain of unknown function is found N-terminal in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. This domain is predicted to adopt a beta-barrel with topology typical for PH domains. It has a weak sequence similarity to Dcp1 PH domain.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from Fungi. It is predicted to fold into a beta-sandwich with Ig-like topology.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from Fungi. It is predicted to adopt a beta-sandwich with Ig-like topology and is likely distantly related to the delta subunit of translocon-associated protein (TRAP-delta, [pfam:PF05404]).
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. It has sequence similarity to PB1 domain and it is predicted to adopt similar structure with typical ubiquitin-like topology.

This entry represents a family of 4 transmembrane helix domains found in archaebacteria. In some proteins these domains are associated with repeats of the [pfam:PF07411] domain. AlphaFold predicts a confident dimeric structure for this domain.
This entry represents a likely zinc-binding domain found at the C-terminus of a set of archaebacterial proteins. AlphaFold prediction show a structure forming 2-3 beta strands.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from Fungi. These proteins are likely involved in chromatin remodelling. The domain represented by this entry is predicted to fold into a globular structure with significant similarity to chromo domain ([pfam:PF00385]).
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised fungal proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular alpha-helical structure.
This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to fold into a four-helical up-and-down bundle and it is likely transmembrane.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in Trichuris sp., Trichinella sp. and similar sequences from nematodes. This domain is repeated in some sequences from Trichuris spp. (two to four times) and it may adopt a SH2-like fold.
This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It has significant sequence similarity to the alpha+beta domain found in DNA primases and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.
This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to fold into an alpha/beta globular structure with topology similar to NADH-quinone oxidoreductase subunit 16.
This domain is found in uncharacterised plant proteins. It is predicted to fold into an alpha/beta structure that is topologically similar to BRSK1/2 KA1 domain ([pfam:PF21122]).

This domain is found in related bacterial proteins. It is predicted to adopt an alpha/beta globular structure and shares significant sequence and structural similarity to members of PD-(D/E)XK nuclease superfamily, in particular, BpuSI N-terminal nuclease domain ([pfam:PF15516]).

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in bacterial proteins. Some of the members of this family might contain an EF-hand calcium binding site. The predicted structure of this domain consists of three beta sheets.

This domain is found in plant proteins that are probably related to NOMO family of proteins. The latter are components of the multi-pass translocon (MPT) complex which mediates insertion of multi-pass membrane proteins into the lipid bilayer of membranes [[cite:PUB00155613]]. The domain represented by this entry is predicted to adopt a globular beta-sandwich structure with a prealbumin-like topology.

This domain is found in Caenorhabditis elegans uncharacterized protein C01C4.2 and related proteins. It is predicted to adopt an alpha+beta barrel with some similarity to the dimeric alpha+beta barrel structures, in particular REDY-like protein Hapk ([pfam:PF11639]).

This domain is found in the Caenorhabditis elegans uncharacterised protein Clec-72 and related eukaryotic proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure with similarity to Galactose-binding domains.

This protein family includes a group of uncharacterised short sequences from actinobacteria, including the predicted secreted protein [swissprot:K5BB12] from Mycolicibacterium hassiacum [[cite:PUB00155614]].
This protein family includes a group of uncharacterised short sequences from actinobacteria [[cite:PUB00155614]].
This domain is found at the C-terminal end of a group of uncharacterised sequences from actinobacteria.
This domain is found at the N-terminal end of a group of uncharacterised sequences from actinobacteria.
This domain is found at the C-terminal end of a group of uncharacterised sequences from actinobacteria. It is normally found associated with [pfam:PF23715].

This family is equally distributed in both metazoa and plants. Annotation associated with [swissprot:Q9SLW7] suggest that it may be involved in response to viral attack in plants. However, no clear function has been assigned to this family.
This protein family includes a group of uncharacterised short sequences from actinobacteria.

This protein family includes a group of uncharacterised short sequences from actinobacteria. Many members are annotated as UbiD family decarboxylases. They are predicted to adopt an all beta configuration.

This protein family includes a group of uncharacterised short sequences from actinobacteria. Some members are annotated as ESX-1 secretion-associated proteins. They are predicted to adopt a mainly alpha-helical configuration.

This domain is found N-terminal in a group of uncharacterised proteins from Trypanosomes. It has a very weak similarity to the vWA-like domain of the SSL1 subunit of general transcription and DNA repair factor IIH and it is predicted to adopt a structure with similarity to known vWA-like domains.

This domain is found either standalone or in tandem in uncharacterised eukaryotic proteins. It has a weak sequence similarity to Nucleotide-diphospho-sugar transferases, in particular to Glycolipid 2-alpha-mannosyltransferases ([pfam:PF01793]) and is predicted to adopt similar structure.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found towards the N-terminal of fungal proteins. This domain adopts a beta-propeller like fold and may be found in association with an N-terminal F-box motif.

This protein domain is found in a variety of staphylococcus phage. It is composed of two alpha helices and a beta hairpin and shows weak structural similarity to archaeal prefoldins. The function of this protein is unknown.

This small phage protein forms a predicted strand swapped dimer using AlphaFold. It is composed of three beta strands and two alpha helices.There is also some weaker evidence for a tetramer. The function of these proteins is unknown.
This entry represents a protein domain found in phage proteins that usually contain an N-terminal [pfam:PF10979]. The function of these protein is unknown.

This domain family consists of a group of uncharacterized proteins, typically between 99 to 116 amino acids in length, found in bacteriophages that infect Microbacterium and Arthrobacter bacterial hosts. These proteins are encoded in the genomes of phages belonging to the Caudoviricetes class, primarily within the families Azeevirinae, Dismasvirus, Yangvirus, Manhattanvirus, Liebevirus, Zetavirus, and Armstrongvirus. An AlphaFold prediction shows these proteins are composed of two alpha helices. AlphaFold also predicts that these proteins likely form homodimers.
This family consists of several herpesvirus proteins of unknown function.

The DUF7170 domain family consists of several uncharacterized phage proteins of around 50 amino acids in length. The family is found in a variety of phages that infect bacterial hosts such as Escherichia, Salmonella, Klebsiella, Vibrio, Citrobacter, Shigella, Pseudomonas and Aeromonas. A few longer proteins of around 60-90 amino acids are also included.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in bacterial and phage proteins, particularly in Gordonia phages. The domain is approximately 140 amino acids in length. It contains regions of disorder at the N- and C-termini.

This entry represents a domain found in proteins typically around 200 amino acids in length. It is found in phage that infect Mycobacteria, Gordonia, and Nocardia. The exact function is unknown. The structure of the domain shows an extended beta sandwich fold where one sheet is hinged in the middle to form a kink.

This family contains a set of uncharacterized proteins found predominantly in viruses, particularly bacteriophages. The proteins are typically 130-150 amino acids in length. AlphaFold models of this family show some weak partial structural similarity to the Recombination-associated protein RdgC.

This protein is found in caudoviruses, which are tailed bacteriophages. The protein is typically around 150-180 amino acids in length. Its function is currently unknown. It is found in viruses from the Drexlerviridae family, including Rogunavirinae, Braunvirinae, Tempevirinae, and Kyungwonvirus genera.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein family found in various phages infecting Gram-negative bacterial hosts, including Salmonella, Shigella, Erwinia, Aeromonas, Vibrio and Klebsiella phages. The family typically contains proteins between 80-120 amino acids in length. The function of this protein family is currently unknown.
This family consists of short bacterial phage proteins, typically around 90 amino acids in length, that contain two transmembrane helices. The family is found in phages that infect Enterobacteria.

The domain is around 80 amino acids in length. It occurs in phage that infect a variety of bacteria including Escherichia, Salmonella, Shigella, Klebsiella, Vibrio, Pantoea, Pectobacterium, Yersinia and Serratia.

This entry describes a family of identified in phage metagenomic datasets. The family contains proteins from a variety of phages that infect actinobacteria, particularly Mycobacterium, Gordonia, and Streptomyces. The exact specificity and function of this metagenomic family is currently unknown. Some members are described as N-glycosylases but the source of that information is uncertain.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein domain found in phage, predominantly those infecting bacteria in the Enterobacteriaceae family such as Escherichia, Salmonella, Klebsiella and Vibrio. The protein is typically around 80 to 100 amino acids in length. In some phage the protein contains a predicted central coiled-coil region. The function of this protein family is currently unknown.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein that is found in a variety of phage, predominantly infecting bacteria from the Enterobacteriaceae family such as Escherichia and Salmonella. The protein is typically between 75-120 amino acids in length. These proteins have a highly conserved N-terminus.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein domain found in bacteriophage proteins, particularly those infecting Salmonella and Dickeya species. The domain is approximately 150 residues in length. The function of this domain is currently unknown.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein found in various mycobacteriophages. The protein contains a predicted transmembrane helix and is typically around 60 amino acids in length. Its function is unknown.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein domain found in various mycobacteriophages. The domain averages around 150 amino acids in length. It is found as a single domain in the phage proteins. The function of this domain is currently unknown. One protein in this family [swissprot:G8I4J4] contains an N-terminal associated domain [pfam:PF18909].

This entry represents a family of phage proteins including Enterobacteria phage T4. The family is found in various phages that infect Escherichia coli and Shigella. The function of this protein family is currently unknown.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein found in various mycobacteriophages. The protein is typically around 80 to 100 amino acids in length. It is found in phages belonging to cluster B, such as the Bclasvirinae and Coopervirus genera. The function of this protein is currently unknown.
This entry represents a small transmembrane protein found in Lactococcus 936-type phages. The function of this protein is unknown. It contains a single transmembrane helix.

This entry represents a family of small proteins of around 60 residues found in Omarvirus and related bacteriophages that infect Streptomyces species. The function of this protein family is currently unknown. Homologous proteins are also found in a small number of Streptomyces genomes. The AlphaFold model of A0A7G7BJ30 shows a pair of alpha helices at the C-terminus of the protein.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein of around 185-188 amino acids found in phages that infect Cutibacterium and Propionibacterium species. The function of this protein is currently unknown.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein of approximately 60-70 amino acids that is found in various phages, predominantly phages that infect members of the Enterobacteriaceae family such as Escherichia, Shigella, and Klebsiella.
This family consists of several eukaryotic proteins of unknown function.

This entry represents a putative membrane protein found in several mycobacteriophages, especially those belonging to the genus Cheoctovirus. The function is unknown. Most members contain a predicted transmembrane helix near the N-terminus. The family shows some length variation, especially at the C-terminus.

This family of uncharacterized proteins is found in viruses, primarily cyanophages that infect cyanobacteria such as Synechococcus and Prochlorococcus species. The family contains short sequences, generally between 45-50 amino acid residues in length. No functional information is available for members of this family.

This entry represents a bacterial domain of unknown function. The domain is around 270 to 300 amino acids in length. It is found in a variety of bacterial phyla including Actinobacteria, Bacteroidota, Pseudomonadota and Verrucomicrobiota. The domain is also found in some bacterial phages. The function of this domain is unknown. The structure of this domain shows similarity to VWFA domains.

This entry represents a family of viral proteins that are found in various bacteriophages infecting Gram-negative bacteria, such as Pseudomonas, Vibrio, Erwinia, Ralstonia, and Klebsiella. The family members are typically 800-1200 residues in length. Many are annotated as putative virion structural proteins, suggesting they may play a role in phage particle structure or assembly. However, the precise function of this family remains unknown.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein family found in viruses from the order Caudoviricetes. The family contains proteins between 199 and 219 amino acids in length. The function of this family is currently unknown.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterized bacteriophage proteins, typically around 70-80 amino acids in length. They are found in phages infecting Escherichia, Pseudomonas, Salmonella, Vibrio, and other bacterial hosts.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein domain found in viruses and bacteria, including Mycobacteriophages, Nocardia, Streptomyces and Rhodococcus species. The domain is typically between 50-99 amino acids in length. In some proteins, the domain is found at the C-terminus. AlphaFold prediction shows a small domain composed of three beta strands in a sheet with a single alpha helix between strands 2 and 3.
This entry represents a domain of unknown function. It is typically between 120 and 250 amino acids in length.

This entry represents a family of putative phage membrane proteins. It is characterized by a single transmembrane helix at the N-terminus that likely serves to anchor these proteins to the membrane. The exact functions of the proteins containing this domain remain unknown.

This family consists of several mycobacteriophage putative membrane proteins of around 99 amino acids in length. These proteins are characterized by an N-terminal transmembrane helix, a small central putative zinc binding domain containing 2 conserved cysteine and 2 histidine residues and disordered C-terminal region rich in basic and acidic residues.
The function of this family is unknown.
This family consists of several uncharacterised Chlamydia proteins of unknown function.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein found in various phages that infect bacteria including Escherichia, Salmonella, Shigella, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Citrobacter and Cronobacter. The protein ranges in length from around 66 to 98 amino acids. The protein forms a single compact domain composed of a four stranded beta sheet and two alpha helices. The structure shows some weak structural similarity to the BRICHOS domain. No clear function is known for these proteins.

This entry represents a family of phage proteins found to be associated with membranes, based on transmembrane region predictions. They are typically around 110 amino acids in length with a C-terminal membrane helix. Many also contain predicted coiled-coil region spanning the rest of the protein. The specific function is unknown. However, it could play a role in membrane fusion.

This entry describes a domain of unknown function (DUF). It is found in phage proteins, generally around 70 amino acids in length. The domain is found in a variety of phages infecting hosts such as Escherichia, Shigella, Yersinia, Erwinia, Providencia, and Pectobacterium. No functional information is known. An AlphaFold model shows this protein adopts a three stranded beta sheet structure.

These proteins are found in various phages infecting bacteria from the Enterobacteriaceae family, such as Escherichia, Salmonella, Shigella, Klebsiella, and Yersinia. They are typically around 100 amino acids in length.

This domain family is found in viruses that infect Streptococcus thermophilus bacteria. All members are from Caudoviricetes viruses. The domain is approximately 50 amino acids in length. The function of this domain is currently unknown. An AlphaFold model shows these proteins adopt a compact domain composed of a three stranded beta sheet with a single alpha helix.

This entry represents a family of phage proteins that adopt a small beta barrel-like domain. The family is found in phages infecting members of the Enterobacteriaceae, such as Escherichia, Salmonella, Klebsiella, Cronobacter, Citrobacter, Erwinia, and Pectobacterium. The exact function of this protein within the phage tail is unknown. The family shows a highly conserved length of around 60-75 amino acids, with a few members having N- or C-terminal extensions.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins including from bacteriophage T6.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein found in various bacteriophages that infect cyanobacteria and other bacterial hosts. The protein ranges in length from approximately 75 to 136 amino acids.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in large phage virion structural proteins. The domain is approximately 290 to 330 amino acids in length. It is found in a variety of phage proteins infecting bacterial hosts such as Pseudomonas, Vibrio, Ralstonia, and Erwinia, among others.

This entry represents a protein that is a component of the virion particle in several bacteriophages infecting hosts such as Bacillus, Staphylococcus, Listeria, Enterococcus and Lactobacillus. The exact function is unknown but it is likely to play a structural role. The protein is typically between 65-80 amino acids in length.
This entry represents a small domain found in a variety of uncharacterised phage proteins.
This entry represents a short highly motif that is found in some phage proteins, usually at the N-terminus. The function of this motif is unknown.

This entry represents a small phage protein that is composed of two alpha helices. According to AlphaFold prediction this protein forms a confident head to tail oriented dimer, forming a four helix bundle. The function of these proteins is unknown.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein of approximately 70-100 amino acids found in mycobacteriophages. The function of this protein is currently unknown. It is found in phages belonging to the Gracegardnervirinae subfamily, including Cheoctovirus and Terapinvirus genera. This protein forms a confident dimer according to an AlphaFold model of [swissprot:S5Z4M5]. The dimer forms a central four stranded beta sheet with two alpha helices packed orthogonally to the direction of the beta strands on each face of the sheet.

This entry represents a phage protein of unknown function. According to AlphaFold models the domain forms a four stranded beta sheet followed by a single alpha helix. This domain forms a confident dimer according to AlphaFold.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in phage proteins, typically 45-60 amino acids in length. It is found in Streptomyces phages of the Caudoviricetes order, primarily in the Arquatrovirinae subfamily. The domain does not contain any conserved motifs or residues that provide hints about its function. A structure prediction shows that it is composed of two non-interacting alpha helices.

This entry represents a family of cyanophage proteins, including Gp130, that are found in a variety of Synechococcus and Prochlorococcus phages. The family members are typically around 100 amino acids in length. Structure predictions do not show a globular fold for this protein. The exact function of this family is unknown.
This entry represents an uncharacterized protein domain found in phage and bacterial proteins.
This entry represents a small conserved sequence region found in a variety of largely mycobacterial phage proteins as well as bacterial proteins. It is often found N-terminal to [pfam:PF07498].

This entry represents a domain of unknown function. The domain is found in bacteria, primarily in cyanobacteria and their phage. It is typically around 80-90 amino acids in length. AlphaFold prediction suggests this protein is composed of two longer paired alpha helices followed by a shorter third helix.
This family contains several bacteriophage proteins of unknown function.
This short protein is found among some phage. It is possibly distantly related to the small terminase family [pfam:PF05119].

This entry represents a set of proteins that are related to the queuine tRNA-ribosyltransferase domain. Queuine tRNA-ribosyltransferase is an enzyme that catalyzes the exchange of guanine at position 34 of tRNAs with queuine. The exact function of this domain is unknown. It is found in bacteria, archaea, plants and some fungi. In bacteria, it is sometimes found on plasmids.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised proteins found in various cyanophages, bacteriophages and bacteria species. The domain is approximately 100-160 amino acids in length. Structure prediction shows this domain is alpha helical.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It is frequently found associated with ([pfam:PF22974]). This domain is predicted to adopt a globular structure with an elongated beta-sandwich topology.
This entry represents a metalloprotease-like domain found in ABC transporter permease from bacteria, predominantly Streptomyces spp. The function of this domain is unknown.

This domain is found in uncharacterised protein YnaC and related bacterial proteins. It is usually associated with ([pfam:PF22522]). This domain is a winged helix (WH) domain decorated at the C terminus with a small three stranded beta-sheet that packs on the WH domain to form a single globular structure.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins. It is usually found in combination with [[pfam:PF22515]] and [[pfam:PF22518]]. It is predicted to contain a winged helix (WH) domain that is flanked at the C terminus with a small helical subdomain. The latter packs on the WH domain to form a compact globular structure.
This domain of unknown function is found in various phage and bacterial proteins. The domain length ranges from approximately 200 to 260 amino acids.

This family of uncharacterized proteins is found in several Lactococcus phages. All members are short proteins, between 33-59 amino acids in length. The family shows some conserved polar residues at the N-terminus. These proteins appear to be disordered.
This small helical domain is found a small family of phage proteins.
This family contains several uncharacterised proteins from Neisseria meningitidis. These proteins may have a role in DNA-binding.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterized proteins found in phage and bacterial species, particularly in the Gammaproteobacteria class. Members of this family are typically short proteins, ranging from 32 to 85 amino acids in length. Many members are predicted to contain disordered regions and AlphaFold predictions show a non-globular structure.

This entry represents a family of unknown function found in phage proteins, typically 120-130 amino acids in length. Some members contain a C-terminal region enriched in basic residues that is predicted to be disordered. The N-terminus of the proteins contain a small globular domain. These proteins are found in the Ackermannviridae family of phages that infect Enterobacteria such as Salmonella, Escherichia, Shigella, and Dickeya.
This entry represents an uncharacterised phage family. A structure prediction suggests that the proteins consist of a three stranded beta meander followed by a C-terminal Alpha helix.
This domain is found in the phages infecting Mycobacterium and Gordonia. The domain is around 70-100 amino acids long.

This family represents a domain of unknown function, which is found in phage proteins ranging in length from 75 to 88 amino acids. The domain is found in phage that infect Salmonella, Shigella, Serratia, and Enterobacter species.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein found in various phages that infect bacteria. The function of this protein is currently unknown. It is typically around 300-340 amino acids in length. This protein contains a predicted coiled-coil region near its C-terminus.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised mycobacterium phage proteins.
This entry represents a protein of unknown function found in phage proteins. The domain contains approximately 77 residues and may contain a single transmembrane helix near the N-terminus.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function. It is found in uncharacterized phage proteins in the size range 90 to 120 amino acids. The domain does not appear to be related to any other known Pfam domain. The function of this domain remains to be determined.
This entry reprepsents a family of uncharacterised proteins found in mycobacterial phage.
This family contains several uncharacterised proteins found in Arabidopsis thaliana and other plants. This region is often found associated with Agenet domains and may contain coiled-coil.

This protein is found in uncharacterized proteins from various mycobacteriophages and bacterial species including Nocardia and Mycobacterium. The protein is typically around 100 amino acids in length.

This entry represents a family of small phage proteins found in a variety of mycobacteriophage genomes. The family members are typically around 70-75 amino acids in length. The function of these proteins is currently unknown.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins. AlphaFold multimer suggests this protein may form a dimeric ring arrangement.

This family of phage proteins adopt a structure composed of a pair of jelly roll fold domains with one nested within the other. This fold is suggestive of a phage head structural protein. Structure predictions suggest that these proteins can form pentameric or hexameric arrangements mediated by the outer of the two domains.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein found in various bacteriophages that infect bacteria in the family Enterobacteriaceae, including phages of Escherichia, Shigella and Citrobacter. The protein is approximately 55-60 amino acids in length. An AlphaFold model shows this domain adopts a small beta barrel structure. This domain is possibly related to the KOW motif.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein domain found in viral proteins, primarily from Mycobacterium and Gordonia phages. The domain is approximately 120 amino acids in length. These proteins are composed of a small N-terminal zinc binding domain connected by an alpha helix to a small beta barrel domain at the C-terminus.

This entry describes a domain of unknown function found in phage proteins. The proteins containing this domain average 90 to 100 amino acids in length and is found in a variety of phage proteins, particularly those from Streptomyces and Mycobacterium phages. The domain usually occurs near the middle or C-terminus of proteins. The domain forms a small beta barrel.
This entry represents an uncharacterised phage domain composed of a seven stranded beta sheet with a C-terminal alpha helix. Structure prediction suggests this protein may form a homodimer.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins that have a single transmembrane helix followed by a conserved C-terminal sequence. The family includes proteins from phage T4 and T6.
This family represents an uncharacterized protein domain found in phage proteins, mostly from Caudovirales. The domain is around 70-120 amino acids in length.
This family contains several Drosophila proteins of unknown function.
This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in phage proteins, approximately 100 residues in length. The domain is found in Microbacterium phages.
This entry represents a family of protein of unknown function found in phage. The protein are predicted to be largely disordered, with a C-terminal small beta barrel domain.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in bacteriophage proteins. The domain is around 115-125 residues long composed of a four stranded beta sheet with helices packed on one side. There is evidence for a confident dimer from structure prediction. In addition the dimer shows a strong electrostatic polarity possibly suggesting a nucleic acid binding function.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function, which is found in phage proteins, predominantly from Arthrobacter and Gordonia phages. The domain is approximately 110 amino acids in length. It shows similarity to the Phage_barrel superfamily. These proteins are often components of the phage neck complex.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins that adopt a compact domain composed of a four stranded beta sheet followed by two alpha helices packed on one side of the sheet.

This entry represents uncharacterised bacterial proteins that were predicted to possess defence functions [[cite:PUB00152882]]. They contain highly conserved aspartate and histidine residues that may have functional role.
This entry represents a domain found in uncharacterised proteins from proteobacteria. This domain is sometimes found N-terminal to [pfam:PF21832].
This entry represents a phage protein which contains a C1q and TNF superfamily domain. Structure prediction suggests that this domain forms a confident homotrimeric interaction.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins from Bacteroidota. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure with SH3-like topology. It is sometimes found N-terminal to [pfam:PF22273].
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins from proteobacteria. It is usually found C-terminal to [[pfam:PF22288]]. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure with a beta-barrel shape.
This family consists of several uncharacterised eukaryotic proteins.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins from Halobacteria. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure composed mainly of alpha-helices.
This entry represents uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria.
This entry represents uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria. They are composed of N-terminal transmembrane helix and alpha/beta globular domain.
This entry represents uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria.
This entry represents an C-terminal domain from a family of uncharacterised phage proteins. This domain has a beta sandwich fold.
This entry represents uncharacterised archaeal proteins.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins. Structure prediction suggests this protein adopts a rather open conformation of three alpha helices and a possible beta strand suggesting it must interact with other proteins to function.
This entry represents uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria. They are predicted to contain three transmembrane helices and likely associate with the membrane.

This entry represents uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria. They are likely composed mainly of alpha-helices. These proteins contain a semi-conserved GxWTDDxxAA sequence motif toward their C terminus.
This entry represents and uncharacterised family of phage proteins.
This domain is found in the homologues of uncharacterised soybean proteins.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins from phage. The structure of this family does not appear similar to any other known protein or family.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised mycobacterium phage proteins. These proteins adopt a compact three helical bundle domain.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage protein domains. The domain adopts a compact beta sheet made of six strands.
This entry represents the central alpha helical domain from a large family of uncharacterised phage proteins that typically contain three domains.
This entry represents the C-terminal domain from a large family of uncharacterised phage proteins that typically contain three domains.
This entry represents the N-terminal domain from a large family of uncharacterised phage proteins that typically contain three domains.
This entry represents a domain found various uncharacterised bacterial proteins that according to ECOD adopts a profilin-like fold.
This family represents a family of uncharacterised proteins from T even phage.
This family consists of several uncharacterised tobravirus proteins of unknown function.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein domain found in bacteriophage proteins, predominantly from mycobacteriophages and Gordonia phages. The domain is typically between 80-130 amino acids in length. It folds into a compact domain composed of a sheet of five beta strands with an alpha helix packed on one side.
This domain is found C-terminal in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It shares some similarity to the C-terminal domain of JetD [[pfam:PF09983]].

This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial and archaeal proteins. It is predicted to adopt a beta-sandwich with an Ig-like topology, similar to domains members of clan CL0073. Some proteins contain multiple copies of this domain.
This entry represents uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria.
This entry represents uncharacterised archaeal proteins.
This entry represents uncharacterised archaeal proteins.
This entry represents uncharacterised proteins found in Euryarchaeota.
This entry includes uncharacterised archaeal proteins including Uncharacterized protein AF_0763 from Archaeoglobus fulgidus [[swissprot:O29495]].
This entry represents a group of uncharacterised archaeal proteins.
This entry represents a group of uncharacterised archaeal proteins. They genes occur in pilB/pilC operons.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in enterobacteria phages. The proteins are around 80 residues in length. The proteins assume a compact domain that has four beta strands forming a sheet followed by three alpha helices packed on one side.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. A structure prediction suggests this protein forms a compact alpha helical domain followed by a disordered region.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins. These possibly have an N-terminal signal peptide followed by a small compact domain composed of a single alpha helix packed against a four stranded beta sheet.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein of approximately 54 amino acids found in T5-like bacteriophages that infect Escherichia coli and Salmonella. Homologs have been identified in several T5-like phages including bacteriophage T5, Salmonella phage vB_SenS_SB13, and Escherichia phage vB_EcoS-26175V. Structure prediction suggests that this protein forms a strand swapped homodimeric arrangement. The dimeric structure forms two four stranded sheets that are connected by two alpha helices. The C-terminal of each protein is donated to the sheet made by the other monomer.
This family of uncharacterised proteins is found in a variety of cyanophages. These proteins adopt of compact domain structure composed of four strands and one alpha helix.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein found in various bacteriophages that infect Salmonella, Escherichia, Shigella, Pantoea and Serratia species. This family includes a member in bacteriophage T5. The function of this protein is currently unknown. Structure prediction does not predict a globular compact fold for this protein.

This entry represents a family of domains found in phages that infect a variety of bacterial hosts including Streptococcus, Streptomyces, Pseudomonas and Paenibacillus species. The Domain is typically around 110-130 amino acids in length.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins. The family includes [swissprot:M9MUF4] which is annotated as a baseplate I protein. Proteins in this family are about 450 residues in length.
This entry represents an uncharacterised phage domain. In some members of the family this domain is found at the C-terminus of a longer protein which also contains [pfam:PF14594].
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins.
This family consists of several uncharacterised Arabidopsis thaliana proteins of unknown function.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. These proteins contain a small compact globular domain composed of a four stranded meander followed by a C-terminal alpha helix.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. These proteins contain a highly conserved RDR/KVL sequence motif that is likely functionally important.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins that have a small N-terminal domain composed of three beta strands and an alpha helix.

This family consists of various uncharacterized phage proteins and a few bacterial proteins. The family members range in length from 82 to 229 amino acids, with most in the 180 to 200 amino acid range. They are found in phages that infect Pseudomonas, Xanthomonas, Acinetobacter, Escherichia, Rhodobacter, Sphingomonas, Achromobacter, and Burkholderia bacteria. Bacterial proteins in the family are from Candidatus Macondimonas diazotrophica, Verrucomicrobium sp. GAS474 and Pelodictyon phaeoclathratiforme. The function of these proteins is currently unknown.

This entry describes a family of uncharacterized proteins, around 70 amino acids in length, found in mycobacteriophages. The family members share sequence similarity but their function is currently unknown. The domain is found as a single copy in the phage proteins. The domain adopts a compact globular fold with a four stranded beta sheet followed by an alpha helix.

This domain is found in uncharacterised prokaryotic proteins most of which likely associated with proteins located in pilBC operon. It is frequently found inserted in [[pfam:PF23960]]. This domain is predicted to adopt a single-stranded right-handed beta-helix with similarity to ice-binding proteins and other adhesive domains.
This entry represents a set of uncharacterised phage proteins that are related to the Pam3 phage gp33 protein.

This domain is found in uncharacterised archaeal proteins most of which likely associated with proteins located in pilBC operon. It is frequently found inserted in [[pfam:PF23960]]. This domain is predicted to fold into a globular structure with a beta-sandwich topology.
This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in uncharacterised proteins from bacteria, as well as in some plasmid pRiA4b ORF-3 family of proteins.
This entry represents a coiled-coil region found in uncharacterised archaeal proteins.
This domain is found in uncharacterised archaeal proteins.
This domain is found in uncharacterised archaeal proteins. It is predicted to fold into a single helix.
This domain is found in uncharacterised archaeal proteins. It is predicted to fold into a four-helical bundle and it is likely associated with the membrane.
This domain is found in uncharacterised archaeal proteins. It is predicted to fold into an alpha-helical hairpin and it is likely associated with the membrane.
This domain is found in uncharacterised archaeal proteins. It is predicted to fold into an alpha-helical hairpin and it is likely associated with the membrane.

This entry represents a small family of phage proteins. These proteins form a confident dimer according to structure prediction. The dimer adopts a novel fold composed of a long four stranded beta sheet with two alpha helical elements packed at each end of the twisted sheet. There is quite a bit of structural variability across the family with a variety of alternative elaborations.
This family includes a group of short archaeal proteins, that are distantly related to [pfam:PF03683].
This entry represents uncharacterised archaeal proteins.
This domain is found in uncharacterised archaeal proteins.
This family consists of several uncharacterised Mycobacterium tuberculosis and leprae proteins of unknown function.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein found in T4-like bacteriophages. It is found between the cd and pseT genes in the T4 phage genome. The function of this protein is unknown. Structure prediction suggests these proteins have a compact fold composed of five beta strands and an alpha helix.
This domain is found in uncharacterised archaeal proteins. It is predicted to fold into a four-helical bundle and it is likely associated with the membrane.
This domain is found in uncharacterised archaeal proteins. It is predicted to fold into an alpha-helical hairpin and it is likely associated with the membrane.
This entry represents a small beta barrel domain found at the N-terminus of some phage proteins.
This entry represents a small putative zinc binding motif found in a small number of uncharacterised phage proteins.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins that are glycine rich.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins.
This entry represents a small family of phage proteins. Structure prediction suggests that these proteins form a single long alpha helix.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins. Proteins in this family are around 250 residues in length.
This family consists of several uncharacterised Drosophila melanogaster proteins of unknown function.
This entry represents uncharacterised archaeal proteins. They share a semi-conserved YDxxNPXAW sequence motif.
This entry represents uncharacterised archaeal proteins.
This entry represents uncharacterised archaeal proteins. They are predicted to fold into an alpha-helical hairpin.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised domains found in a variety of phage and bacterial genomes. Structure prediction suggests the domain is composed of a small beta sheet of three strands and an alpha helix. There is some evidence from prediction that these domains might form a dimeric arrangement.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised proteins from phage. Structure prediction shows the proteins to be composed of an alpha helical N-terminal domain and a C-terminal domain composed of a 5 stranded beta meander.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein domain found in bacteriophage proteins, particularly those infecting Lactococcus species. The domain is approximately 115 amino acids in length. It is found in a small number of bacterial proteins as well.
This entry represents the C-terminal zinc binding domain of an uncharacterised family of phage proteins.
This entry represents the N-terminal domain of an uncharacterised family of phage proteins.
This family includes uncharacterised archaeal proteins that contain a HTH domain.
This entry represents the HTH domain found in group of uncharacterised archaeal proteins.
This is a presumed HTH domain found in a group of uncharacterised archaeal sequences.
This is a presumed domain found in uncharacterised proteins from archaea. It may adopt a ferredoxin-like fold.
This entry represents uncharacterised archaeal sequences containing a presumed HTH domain.
This is a presumed HTH domain found at the N-terminal of a group of uncharacterised archaeal sequences.

This domain is found N-terminal in a group of uncharacterised archaeal proteins. In some proteins, this domain precedes [[pfam:PF18069]] and [[pfam:PF18009]]. It is predicted to fold into a globular alpha/beta structure.

This family of uncharacterized proteins is found in various phages that infect bacterial hosts such as Bacillus, Staphylococcus, Enterococcus, Listeria, Lactobacillus, and Brochothrix species. The proteins in the family are typically 75 to 100 amino acids in length. The protein contains a small N-terminal domain represented by this entry followed by a C-terminal disordered region.
This family consists of several uncharacterised Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease spirochete) proteins of unknown function.
This domain is found in uncharacterised archaeal proteins. It is predicted to adopt Ig-like fold.
This is a presumed domain found at the C-terminal of a group of uncharacterised archaeal sequences, which contain an HTH domain at the N-terminal.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage domains. These domains adopt a beta sandwich structure.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from Kinetoplastida. It is found on its own or in combination with [[pfam:PF00650]]. It is predicted adopt a UBA-like alpha-helical bundle.

This domain of unknown function, which is found in a small group of bacterial proteins, shows a high structural similarity with the N-terminal domain of Magnetotaxis protein MtxA from Magnetospirillum gryphiswaldense ([swissprot:A4TUL6]).

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. The family includes the y13F protein from bacteriophage T4 [swissprot:P39499]. Structure prediction shows this protein has a compact globular fold composed of three beta strands and two alpha helices.
This domain is found in uncharacterised plant proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure with similarity to Fibronectin type III-like domains.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It is predicted to fold into a globular structure with ubiquitin-like topology elaborated with long loops. It is frequently found in combination with [pfam:PF23086].

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins from plants. It is predicted to adopt an alpha-helical bundle with ferritin-like topology. This domain is frequently found in combination with [pfam:PF01764].

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in SPbeta prophage-derived uncharacterized protein (YomG) from Bacillus subtilis (strain 168). This domain may adopt a FN3-like fold and can be found in association with a prophage endopeptidase tail domain ([pfam:PF06605]).
This family consists of several uncharacterised bacterial proteins of unknown function.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in SPbeta prophage-derived uncharacterized protein YomG from Bacillus subtilis (strain 168). This domain may can be found in association with a prophage endopeptidase tail domain ([pfam:PF06605]).

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found at the C-terminal of SPbeta prophage-derived uncharacterized protein YomG from Bacillus subtilis (strain 168). This domain may be found in association with a prophage endopeptidase tail domain ([pfam:PF06605]).

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found at the N-terminal of CHAT domain-containing, such as SwissProt:A0A100JVW6, protein from Streptomyces scabiei. This domain may be found in association with TCAD7 ([pfam:PF19973]) and CHAT ([pfam:PF12770]) domains.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in CHAT domain-containing protein, such as SwissProt:A0A100JVW6, from Streptomyces scabiei. This domain may be found in association with TCAD7 ([pfam:PF19973]) and CHAT ([pfam:PF12770]) domains.

This entry represents a small uncharacterised family of Pseudomonas phage proteins. Structure prediction suggests that these proteins adopt a pair of alpha helices. These proteins are predicted to dimerise to form a four helical bundle. In the predicted dimer there is a short C-terminal beta strand that forms an anti parallel cap at one end of the helical bundle.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins that have a predicted N-terminal transmembrane helix and a coiled-coil region. Structure prediction suggests that these proteins may adopt a trimeric coiled-coil structure. Many of these proteins are annotated as holins, however the origin of that annotation is unclear.
This entry represents a small uncharacterised domain from Staphylococcus phage. The domain is predicted to be largely composed of small alpha helices.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. These proteins range in length from 94 to 110 amino acids and adopt a small domain composed of four alpha helices.
ThiS entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. Structure prediction suggests that this protein forms a small domain that likely forms a stable dimeric complex. In this predicted complex there is a C-terminal alpha helix that binds to the opposite oligomer in a helix swapped arrangement.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins. Many of these proteins are annotated as gp11, but the origin of this annotation is unclear. Structure prediction shows this protein adopts an alpha helical fold.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It is predicted to adopt a beta-sandwich with similarity to galactose-binding domains.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. Structure prediction shows the proteins form a compact globular domain composed of a four stranded beta sheet, with a strand order of 4-1-2-3 with an alpha helix between strands 3 and 4.

This domain is found N-terminal in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to adopt a seven-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet with similarity to Mog1p/PsbP-like domains. Some proteins containing this domain have a lipoprotein attachment motif at the N-terminus suggesting they may be associated with the membrane. This domain is usually found in two copies that share little if any sequence similarity to each other.

This domain is found C-terminal in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to adopt a seven-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet with similarity to Mog1p/PsbP-like domains. Some proteins containing this domain have a lipoprotein attachment motif at the N-terminus suggesting they may be associated with the membrane. This domain is usually found in two copies that share little if any sequence similarity to each other.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. Structure prediction suggests that this protein dimerises.

This family represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins from pseudomonas phage. These proteins range in length from 114 and 130 amino acids. Structure prediction suggests the proteins adopt an open set of alpha helical segments as a monomer. However, homodimer prediction shows a confident interaction (iPTM 0.79). The dimer shows distinct charge distribution with a linear positively charged surface.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins. Structure prediction suggests these protein may form a homodimer. The dimer contains a large circular channel that is positively charged suggesting a possible DNA-binding function.

This domain is found in uncharacterised plant proteins. It is predicted to adopt an alpha/beta structure with a central four-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet and alpha helices packed on it. It has weak sequence and structural similarity to NIL domains. It is usually found N-terminal to protein kinase domains.
This domain is found in uncharacterised plant proteins. It is predicted to contain transmembrane helices that assemble in a four helical bundle.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found towards the N-terminal of CHAT domain-containing protein, such as SwissProt:A0A100JVW6, from Streptomyces scabiei. This domain may adopt a A/B hydrolase fold and is often found in association with TCAD7 ([pfam:PF19973]) and CHAT ([pfam:PF12770]) domains.
This domain is found N-terminal in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure composed mainly of alpha helices.
This domain is found N-terminal in uncharacterised nematode proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular alpha/beta structure.
This is a Ig-like domain found in a group of uncharacterised sequences, mainly from archaea.
This entry represents a group of uncharacterised archaeal sequences containing a galactose binding-like domain.
This is a group of uncharacterised sequences from archaea which are related to VapC (virulence-associated protein C) family of proteins. Members of this entry may adopt a PIN-like fold.
This entry represents a small group of archaeal sequences whose function is unknown.
This is a family of archaeal sequences of unknown function.
This entry includes uncharacterised archaeal sequences.
This entry represents uncharacterised archaeal sequences.
This is a domain of unknown function found in a group of archaeal sequences.
This family contains several bacteriophage proteins. Some of the proteins in this family have been labeled putative cro repressor proteins.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage protein. These proteins adopt a compact globular domain. The predicted structure of the domain shows a positively charged surface suggesting a possible nucleic acid binding function.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. Many of them are annotated as phage tail assembly chaperones, but there does not appear to be any evidence to support this annotation.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins from plants. It has sequence and structural similarity to domains members of Dimeric alpha/beta barrel superfamily.
This small uncharacterised phage protein has a 5 stranded beta barrel fold.

This entry represents a protein of unknown function, found primarily in phage proteins of about 60 to 75 amino acids in length. It contains a single predicted transmembrane helix in many members. Most sequences also contain a region of predicted intrinsic disorder at the C-terminus rich in basic and acidic residues. Further experimental study is required to determine the function of these proteins. Some proteins are annotated as holins but the source of this annotation is unknown.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins, that includes the L1 protein from Lactococcus phage c2 [swissprot:Q38296]. Structure prediction indicates this small protein adopts a compact domain composed of a three stranded sheet with a single alpha helix.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein found in several bacteriophages that infect bacteria such as Escherichia coli, Enterobacter, Klebsiella and Shigella. The protein is short, around 44-51 amino acids in length. It is predicted to contain a single transmembrane helix. The function of this protein is currently unknown. One representative of this family is the [swissprot:P18922] protein from bacteriophage T4.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. These proteins are around 50-60 residues in length.

This entry describes an uncharacterized protein found in several bacteriophages that infect Bacillus species. The protein ranges in length from 158 to 189 amino acids. It is found in the virions of phages from the Bastillevirinae subfamily of the Herelleviridae family. Structure prediction suggests the proteins are composed of a bundle of five alpha helices.

This entry represents a family of phage proteins. The proteins appear to contain two domains. The N-terminal domain contains a small beta sheet wrapped around an alpha helix. The second domain is composed of a pair of alpha helices. The proteins are found in several viruses within the proposed new Crassvirales order of bacteriophages.
This family consists of several uncharacterised plant proteins of unknown function.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found towards the N-terminal of some PRiA4b ORF-3-like proteins from bacteria, such as SwissProt:A0A1I7K0M5. This domain may adopt a TPR-like fold and is generally associated to PriA4_ORF3 ([pfam:PF07929]) domain.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found towards the centre of some PRiA4b ORF-3-like proteins from bacteria, such as SwissProt:A0A068QX925. This domain is generally associated to PriA4_ORF3 ([pfam:PF07929]) domain.

This entry represents the domain of unknown function found in bacterial and fungal sequences, including some F5/8 type C domain-containing proteins such as Swissprot:A0A4V0YDU8. This domain may adopt a galactose-binding domain-like fold. This domain is found in several copies, predominantly between two and six times, and it is found in association with PIG-L ([pfam:PF02585]) domain.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in some PRiA4b ORF-3-like proteins from bacteria, such as SwissProt:A0A1I7K0M5. This domain may adopt an all-helical fold and is generally found alongside the PriA4_ORF3 ([pfam:PF07929]) domain.
This entry represents a family or archaeal proteins whose function is unknown. They may adopt a dimeric alpha/beta barrel fold.
This is a small domain found in a group of uncharacterised archaeal sequences. This small domain may have an all-beta fold.
This is a domain of unknown function found in a group of uncharacterised sequences from archaea. This domain may have a beta-sandwich fold.
This is a domain of unknown function found in a group of uncharacterised sequences from archaea. It may adopt an amidotransferase-like fold.
This is a domain of unknown function found in uncharacterised archaeal sequences.
This is a C2H2 zinc finger found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from archaea.
This is a family of unknown function mainly found in archaea but also in some bacterial species. They may have a Rossmann-like alpha/beta/alpha fold.

This entry represents an uncharacterised protein family found in a range of bacteriophage including Phage T2. These proteins include a beta barrel domain. Many members of the family are annotated as IP4 internal head protein, although the source of evidence for this annotation was not found.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. Structure prediction suggests these proteins are composed of a three stranded beta sheet packed against a pair of alpha helices.

This entry represents an uncharacterised family of proteins. Structure prediction suggests these proteins form a four stranded beta sheet with a helix packed on one side. Structure prediction also suggests a confident dimer. The structure shows some weak similarity to large ribosomal subunit protein eL38.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage domains. This domain is found in one to two copies per proteins. It seems likely that the proteins with a single copy of the domain form homodimers.
This entry represents a small uncharacterised enterobacterial phage protein family. Structure prediction suggests these proteins might adopt a pair of alpha helices.

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein domain found in various phage and bacterial proteins. The domain is approximately 60-80 amino acids in length. The domain is composed of four alpha helices that form a small bundle. The surface of the domain is negatively charged.
This entry represents a small uncharacterised family of phage proteins. It adopts a novel triangular beta prism structure.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised mycobacteria phage proteins that adopt a zinc binding domain composed of 5 potential ligand residues. The zinc binding motif is composed of a CXXC and a CXXHH motif.
This family consists of several uncharacterised Streptomyces proteins as well as one from Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The function of these proteins is unknown.

This entry represents an uncharacterised family of phage integral membrane proteins. The proteins are found in phage of S. aureus and B. subtilis. These proteins contain three potential transmembrane helices. There is a conserved GXXPL motif that is highly conserved between helices 1 and 2.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised enterobacterial phage proteins.

This entry represents a small family of phage proteins. The family includes members from Phage T2 and T6. These proteins contain a small three stranded beta domain. Some members have an additional small C-terminal domain composed of a beta-alpha-alpha-beta hairpin domain.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised mycobacterial phage proteins. The proteins have a domain that contains a four helical bundle.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised lipoproteins. The family includes a range of both bacteria and phage proteins.

This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in bacteriophage proteins. The domain is around 90-95 amino acids in length. It is found in uncharacterized proteins from phages that infect Enterobacteria such as Salmonella and Shigella species as well as Dickeya. The specific function of this domain remains unknown. Structure prediction suggests that these proteins may form a homotetramer (iPTM=0.88). The domain contains a three twisted stranded beta sheet.
This entry represents an uncharacterised domain found in phage proteins.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins. Family members are largely found in mycobacterial phage.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. The structure of this family is predicted to be composed of a four stranded beta sheet and a single alpha helix.
This entry represents a family of small uncharacterised proteins found in mycobacterial phage.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins.

This entry represents the domain of unknown function found towards the C-terminal of some MACPF domain-containing proteins from fungi, such as SwissProt:A0A2P4PCT2. It is found associated with MACPF_1 ([pfam:PF22693]) domain.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins that are composed of two small domains connected by an alpha helix. Structure prediction suggests that these proteins may homodimerise or tetramerise. These proteins are primarily found in Gordonia phage.

This entry represents a small region that is found in a variety of uncharacterised mycobacterial phage proteins. Structure prediction suggests it adopts an alpha helix and beta hairpin structure that likely homodimerises.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised mycobacterial phage proteins. Structure prediction suggests that this protein forms a single alpha helix. It is quite hydrophobic with a negatively charged C-terminus. Some proteins are annotated as RDF proteins but there does not appear to be any evidence to support their function as recombination directionality factors.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterized proteins found in Mycobacterium phages. The family members are typically around 67 amino acids in length. Structure prediction suggests these proteins form a small compact domain composed of four beta strands followed by an Alpha helix. The domain possibly shows weak structural similarity to integrase arm-type binding domain.
This domain is found at the C-terminal end of a group of archaeal sequences that contain [pfam:PF01978] at the N-terminal. It is predicted to adopt an alpha-beta configuration.
This domain is found at the C-terminal end of a group of archaeal sequences that contain [pfam:PF01978] at the N-terminal. It is predicted to adopt an all-alpha configuration.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterized proteins found in bacteriophages. The function of this protein family is currently unknown. The family appears to be conserved across various phage species that infect Escherichia coli and related bacteria. The family includes members from Phage T2 and T6.Members of this family are typically short proteins of around 60-67 amino acids in length. The structure of these proteins is predicted to be composed of two alpha helices that pack together. Structure prediction suggests these proteins may homodimerise (iPTM=0.83).

This entry represents a family of small putative transmembrane proteins found primarily in Streptomyces phages and some bacteria. The family is characterized by a conserved transmembrane region typically located between residues 20-45 of the alignment. Many members of this family are around 70 amino acids in length. The function of this protein family is currently unknown.

This entry represents a protein family of unknown function found in various bacterial phage proteins. The family typically consists of proteins around 140-160 amino acids in length. It is found in phages that infect bacteria such as Salmonella, Escherichia, Shigella, and Dickeya. The function of this family remains unclear. Some members of this family are annotated as uncharacterized or hypothetical proteins. AlphaFold predictions suggest the proteins in this family contain two distinct domains, with a central domain composed of a three stranded beta sheet and a C-terminal small 3-helix bundle domain.

This entry represents a conserved domain found predominantly in bacteriophage proteins. The domain is characterized by a highly conserved YDRH motif, which likely plays an important role in the domain's function or structure. This family includes proteins from various phages that infect cyanobacteria, particularly Synechococcus and Prochlorococcus species. The proteins contain a central small domain composed of a three stranded beta sheet with an alpha helix inserted between the second and third strands.

Pfam_Description: Phage membrane protein Family of unknown function (DUF7442)
Pfam_name: Phage membrane protein Family of unknown function (DUF7442)
Pfam_description: This entry represents a family of putative membrane proteins found in various bacteriophages. The proteins in this family typically contain two transmembrane helices. The function of these proteins is currently unknown. They are predominantly found in phages infecting Salmonella, Escherichia, and other enterobacteria. The proteins in this family are generally short, with most members being around 80-81 amino acids in length

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein family found in bacteriophages. The function of this family is currently unknown. Members of this family are typically around 90-100 amino acids in length. The family includes proteins from various phage species infecting bacteria such as Salmonella, Klebsiella, and Proteus. Some members of this family contain disordered regions, particularly in their C-terminal portions. Conserved basic and acidic residues are present in many family members, which may be functionally important. This entry represents the globular N-terminal domain of these proteins.

This entry represents a conserved family found in various bacteriophages, particularly those infecting Escherichia, Klebsiella, and other Enterobacteriaceae. The function of this domain is currently unknown. This family is commonly found in phages belonging to the Drexlerviridae family, including genera such as Webervirus, Tempevirinae, and Tunavirinae. This entry shows some structurally similar features to [pfam:PF24227].

This entry represents an uncharacterized protein family found in mycobacteriophages. The function of this protein is currently unknown. The family is approximately 147 amino acids long. These proteins contain two small domains. The most N-terminal one contains a CXXC and HXXC motif that likely bind to zinc.

This entry represents a highly conserved domain found in various bacteriophages, particularly those infecting Salmonella and related bacteria. The domain is also present in some bacterial species, suggesting possible horizontal gene transfer. The function is unknown, but the high degree of conservation implies an important role in phage biology. A conserved motif DVT is present centrally in many family members. The aspartate and threonine form side chain hydrogen bonds that help stabilise the dimeric interaction. Structure prediction suggests these proteins form a confident homodimer (iPTM=0.83).

This entry represents an uncharacterized family found in various bacteriophage proteins. It is predominantly found in phages infecting diverse bacterial species including Burkholderia, Bacillus, Streptomyces, Listeria, and Caulobacter. The proteins are typically around 100-150 amino acids in length. Many of the proteins containing this domain are annotated as uncharacterized or hypothetical proteins. The proteins form a compact domain composed of a four stranded antiparallel beta sheet.

This entry represents a conserved viral protein domain of unknown function (DUF4241). The domain is approximately 130-160 amino acids in length and is found in various bacteriophages and large DNA viruses. The alignment shows several conserved residues, including a highly conserved DCC motif. The protein contains a beta sandwich domain structural.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in pseudomonas phage. The protein contains a compact domain composed of two alpha helices followed by four beta strands that form a beta sheet.
This family consists of several uncharacterised Drosophila melanogaster proteins of unknown function.

This entry represents a group of uncharacterised proteins from bacteria that, according to structure predictions (SwissProt:A0A7C3HQW7 or SwissProt:A0A5C6D6K5), they may contain novel repeats that fold into twisted long beta-hairpins different from typical beta-barrel hairpins and they do not exhibit homology to any beta-barrel.

This entry represents a presumed domain found in a group of uncharacterised sequences from bacteria. According to structure predictions, this domain may adopt and all-beta configuration with beta-strands of different lengths. This domain is usually associated with DUF7450 ([pfam:PF24247]).
This entry represents a presumed domain found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from bacteria. This domain may adopt an all-beta configuration.

This entry represents a group of uncharacterised sequences from bacteria. According to structure predictions, these proteins may comprise novel repeats consisting of an arrangement of four beta-strands in which the second one is longer and curved. This arrangement is repeated eight times in SwissProt:A0A5B9QB27, which form a closed repeat.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins from a set of mycobacterial phage including phage Bxb1 (gene 86). The members of the family range in length from 50 to 90 residues. Structurally, the domain shows some weak similarity to the N-terminal domain of IF5, which adopts an SH3 like barrel fold.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised actinobacterial zinc binding domains. The proteins contain a characteristic CXHH motif. Only the second of those two histidines acts as the zinc ligand according to structure prediction (ipTM = 0.94).
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised proteins found in Mycobacterial phage. The family includes gene 48 from phage Bxb1.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. This family includes gene 78 from Phage Bxb1.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised mycobacterial phage. Some members are annotated as DNA primase. The family includes gene 53 from phage Bxb1.

This entry represents an uncharacterised protein domain found in a mycobacterial phage proteins. These domains form a zinc binding cluster where 8 cysteine and histidine residues bind two zinc ions according to structure prediction (iPTM=0.87).
This is a short conserved region found in some transposons. Structural modelling suggests this domain may bind nucleic acids [[cite:PUB00070793]].
This entry represents a small uncharacterised mycobacterial phage domain composed of two alpha helices and three beta strands. The family includes Phage Bxb1 gene 81.

This entry represents a small uncharacterised family of mycobacterial phage proteins. The family includes gene 71 from phage Bxb1 [swissprot:Q9B050]. Structure prediction suggests this protein may form a pair of alpha helices that form a helical hairpin structure.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised mycobacterial phage proteins. The family includes Phage Bxb1 gene 76. These proteins are short around 40 residues in length.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised mycobacterial phage proteins. The family includes gene 82 from mycobacterial phage Bxb1.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. The family includes the gene 83 from the mycobacterial phage Bxb1 [swissprot:Q9B038]. This family shows structural similarity to [pfam:PF09926]. These proteins have an SH3 like barrel structure.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins. The family includes Phage Bxb1 protein 85 [swissprot:Q9B036].

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins. Structurally these are composed of a pair of alpha helices. Structure prediction suggests these proteins may homodimerise (iPTM=0.89). These proteins are annotated as RDF proteins but the source of this annotation is uncertain.
This entry represents a beta sandwich domain found in a variety of bacterial cell surface proteins.

This entry represents a conserved protein family found in cyanophages that infect marine Synechococcus and Prochlorococcus. The function of this protein is unknown. It is typically 70-100 amino acids in length. The protein appears to be specific to cyanophages and is not found in their cyanobacterial hosts.
Members of this family are uncharacterised proteins found in cyanobacteria that grow with a filamentous morphology [[cite:PUB00154605]].

This family is a family of eukaryotic membrane proteins. It was previously annotated as including a putative receptor for human cytomegalovirus gH [[cite:PUB00019476]] but this has has since been disputed [[cite:PUB00044752]]. Analysis of the mouse Tapt1 protein (transmembrane anterior posterior transformation 1) has shown it to be involved in patterning of the vertebrate axial skeleton.
This family includes a group of short proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-helical structure.
This family includes a group of short proteins from archaea.
This family includes a group of short proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-helical structure.
