This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-helical structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt a mainly alpha-helical structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-helical structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from nematodes.

This entry represents a domain consisting of a novel repeat fold which containing five repeats, each of them comprising three antiparallel beta-strands and a short alpha-helix, according to structure predictions (e.g SwissProt:S8CFV9). This domain is found in Casein kinase 1-like protein HD16 from rice, a protein involved in the regulation of flowering time through gibberellin (GA) signaling and independently of photoperiod [[cite:PUB00155615]].

This entry represents a domain containing a novel repeat fold, according to structure predictions. It may comprise six repeats, each of them consisting of two antiparallel beta-strands and a short alpha-helix.
This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It contains four invariant cysteines and it is predicted to adopt a Zn-ribbon fold.

This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. These proteins contain a highly conserved lipoprotein-type signal peptide sequence at the N terminus and two invariant cysteine residues within this domain suggesting their extracytoplasmic localisation.
This entry represents a group of uncharacterised sequences from bacteria. They may consist on repeats with a novel fold which is organised in three units with twisted beta-strands each.

This entry includes a group of uncharacterised sequences from bacteria and archaea, which, according to structure predictions, they may have a novel repeat fold. They may consist of 5-6 antiparallel beta-strands decorated with short alpha-helices.

This entry includes uncharacterised bacterial sequences that may adopt a novel fold consisting on three repeat units, each of them are type of beta-sandwich with three beta-strands on one side and four or five on the other.

This entry represents an uncharacterised family of phage proteins. These proteins consist of two domains. The first is composed of four alpha helices that are contributed by both the N and C-terminus of the protein. The second domain is a central beta domain. Structure prediction suggests that these proteins might form a large homo-oligomeric ring of 8-10 subunits, but the iPTM scores are marginal.

This entry represents a group of uncharacterised sequences that, according to structure predictions. they may consist on a novel repeat fold which comprise beta-hairpin-beta units organised in four and five units, forming two domains.

This entry represents a group of uncharacterised sequences from viruses. They may have a novel repeat fold consisting of two domains at the N- and C-terminal with beta-hairpin-beta-alpha configuration that are connected by nine alpha-helices linked by loops.
This entry represents a domain from uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Campylobacterota. Members of this entry contain two highly conserved cysteine residues.
This entry represents a domain from uncharacterised proteins mainly found in Actinomycetes. They are predicted to adopt an OB fold-like beta-barrel.
Archaeal domain of unknown function. This domain has been solved as part of a structural genomics project and comprises of segregated helical and anti-parallel beta sheet regions.
This domain is found in uncharacterised archaeal proteins. Members of this family have a PGF-CTERM motif [pfam:PF18204] at the C-termini.
This is a coiled-coil region found at the C-terminal of a group of uncharacterised sequences from fungi.
This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in fungal sequences. It may adopt a Ig-like fold similar to that in Auxiliary Activity family 9 (AA9), [pfam:PF03443].
This is a domain of unknown function found in uncharacterised sequences from fungi. Some of these sequences are annotated as sphingosine kinases. This domain may adopt a PH-like fold.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from Epsilonproteobacteria. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure with a beta-sandwich topology.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised eukaryotic proteins. It contains six highly conserved cysteines which are predicted to form disulfide bonds. This domain is predicted to adopt structure similar to C-type lectins.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised eukaryotic proteins. It is predicted to fold into Ig-like beta-sandwich.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised eukaryotic proteins. It contains two highly conserved cysteines. This domain is predicted to fold into Ig-like beta-sandwich.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised eukaryotic proteins. It contains two highly conserved cysteines. This domain is predicted to fold into Ig-like beta-sandwich.

This entry represents uncharacterised proteins found in Chlamydiia. They adopt a globular alpha/beta structure consisting of a curved mixed beta-sheet and alpha-helices packed on both sides (PDB:6UXC).
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised archaeal proteins. They contain three highly conserved negatively charged (aspartate and glutamate) residues.

This entry represents a group of uncharacterised proteins found in Halobacteria. They contain three invariant cysteine residues and a histidine that probably constitute a metal binding site. These proteins are probably C2HC zinc fingers that are variant of the classical C2H2 zinc finger domains.
This entry represents a group of uncharacterised archaeal proteins.

This entry represents a group of uncharacterised archaeal proteins. These proteins are short in size (~50 residues long), contain a highly hydrophobic helix and are likely associated with the membrane.
This entry represents a group of uncharacterised archaeal proteins. They contain the typical P-loop motif and are probably structurally related to the P-loop NTPases.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from nematodes. These proteins contain a semi-conserved PPChHPGQ motif (where h is a hydrophobic residue) and are predicted to fold into a incomplete beta-sandwich.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from parasitic secernentean nematodes. It is predicted to adopt an OB-fold.

This domain of unknown function is found in multiple copies in a number of bacterial proteins. It is closely related to domains represented by DUF11 ([pfam:PF01345]). Similarly to DUF11, this domain contains a conserved N-terminal lysine and a C-terminal asparagine with central aspartate/glutamate residues suggesting that it may contain an isopeptide bond. In addition, it contains a semi-conserved TNTGNV sequence motif in which a highly conserved asparagine probably plays a role in stabilising the rod structure formed by repetitive copies of this domain.
This domain is found in uncharacterised prokaryotic proteins. Is has significant sequence similarity to GIY-YIG endonuclease domains and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from Halobacteria. It has detectable sequence similarity to domains members of the N-(deoxy)ribosyltransferase-like superfamily and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.

This family contains several plant, cyanobacterial and algal proteins of unknown function. The family is exclusively found in phototrophic organisms and may therefore play a role in photosynthesis (personal obs:Moxon SJ).

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised archaeal proteins. They are predicted to have a structure composed of seven nearly orthogonally packed strands, four of which are located at the N-terminus and three at the C-terminus. The N- and C-terminal strands clamp to form a beta-sandwich. They are separated by a ~50 aa long disordered region which contains a repetitive SPY sequence motif.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised archaeal proteins. It is predicted to fold into a three-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet. It contains a highly conserved tryptophan residue located at the beginning of the third beta-strand.
This entry represents a family of small uncharacterised proteins from Halobacteria. They are predicted to fold into a single alpha-helix and contain a highly conserved LYxGYG sequence motif.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins from Halobacteria. It has a detectable sequence similarity to TRAM domains and it is predicted to adopt a similar structure. It is found as standalone domain.
This domain is found in uncharacterised eukaryotic proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure composed of alpha-helices.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised metazoan proteins. It has a detectable sequence similarity to HTH winged helix domains and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised metazoan proteins. It has a detectable sequence similarity to HTH winged helix domains and it is predicted to adopt similar structure. In some proteins, this domain is found two copies and usually associated with [pfam:PF24359].

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised metazoan proteins. It is predicted to adopt a structure typical for HTH winged helix domains. This domain is usually found associated with [pfam:PF24359] and [pfam:PF24360].
This family includes a group of short from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-helical structure in the N-terminal and show a disordered C-terminal region.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt a mainly alpha-helical structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-beta structure.

This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to be organised into two domains, an N-terminal with an all-alpha configuration and a C-terminal with an alpha-beta structure.

This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to be organised into two domains, an N-terminal with an all-beta configuration and a C-terminal with a mainly alpha-structure.
This family includes a group of short archaeal proteins. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-helical configuration.
This family includes a group of short archaeal proteins. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-beta configuration.
This domain of unknown function is found at the C-terminal end of a group of archaeal proteins. It is predicted to adopt an alpha-beta structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-beta structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-beta structure.
This domain contains is found in many copies in a variety of uncharacterised fly proteins. This domain has a Ly6/uPAR/alpha-neurotoxin-like domain structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an all-alpha structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-beta structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-beta structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-helical structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-helical structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha structure.
This family includes a group of short proteins from archaea.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt a mainly beta structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt an alpha-beta structure.
This family includes a group of proteins from archaea. Members are predicted to adopt a mainly alpha structure.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised enterobacterial phage proteins. These proteins adopt a compact domain composed of a small three stranded beta sheet, with an alpha helix inserted between the first and second strand.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria. They are predicted to adopt a structure consisting of four alpha-helices.

This entry represents a family of small uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria. They are predicted to adopt a globular alpha/beta structure consisting of three-stranded beta-sheet and two alpha-helices one of which is packed on the beta-sheet.

This entry represents a family of small uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria. They are predicted to adopt a globular alpha/beta structure consisting of five-stranded beta-sheet and an alpha-helix packed on it.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised prokaryotic proteins. They are likely associated with the membrane and consists of several transmembrane helices.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria. These proteins are likely to form a dimer structure as predicted by AlphaFold with significant ipTM score.
This entry represents a group of uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria. These proteins are likely associated with the membrane.
This entry represents a group of uncharacterised archaeal proteins. These proteins probably do not adopt a globular structure.
This entry represents a group of uncharacterised archaeal proteins. They are predicted to fold into a four helical bundle.

This entry represents a group of uncharacterised archaeal proteins. They are predicted to adopt alpha/beta structure consisting of five-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet and five alpha-helices protruding from it.
This family is predominated by ORFs from Circoviridae. The function of this family remains to be determined.
This entry represents a group of small uncharacterised archaeal proteins. They are predicted to fold into a single alpha-helix.
This entry represents a domain found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from Halobacteria. This domain contains a pair of highly conserved cysteine residues.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from Halobacteria. It is frequently found in combination with [pfam:PF24420].
This is a small family of uncharacterised archaeal proteins. They are predicted to fold into a helical hairpin.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in archaea. These proteins are likely associated with the membrane. They are predicted to fold into a single helix.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in Halobacteria. These proteins are likely associated with the membrane. They are predicted to fold into a three helical bundle.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in archaea. These proteins are predicted to be largely disordered. They contain a semi-conserved VIADxx[DE]xAW sequence motif.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in archaea. They may be part of toxin/antitoxin system.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in archaea. They contain four pairs of conserved cysteines as well as several conserved histidines. It is likely that these residues are involved in metal coordination.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in archaea. They contain two pairs of conserved cysteines that are likely involved in metal coordination. It is predicted to structurally resemble Zinc-beta ribbon domains.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in archaea. They contain two pairs of conserved cysteines that are likely involved in metal coordination. It is predicted they may structurally resemble Zinc-beta ribbon domains.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in archaea. They contain two pairs of conserved cysteines that are likely involved in metal coordination. These proteins are predicted to structurally resemble treble-clef zinc fingers.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in archaea. They contain two pairs of conserved cysteines that are likely involved in metal coordination. These proteins are predicted to structurally resemble treble-clef zinc fingers.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in archaea. They contain two pairs of conserved cysteines that are likely involved in metal coordination. These proteins are predicted to structurally resemble Zinc beta-ribbon domains.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in Haloferacales. They contain two pairs of conserved cysteines that are likely involved in metal coordination. These proteins are predicted to structurally resemble treble-clef zinc fingers.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in archaea and eukaryotes. These proteins contain two pairs of conserved cysteines and two pairs of conserved histidines that are probably involved in zinc coordination. These proteins likely resemble two classical C2H2 zinc fingers that pack on each other and form a compact globular structure.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised proteins from phage. Structure predictions suggest the protein is composed of a larger N-terminal domain with an 8 stranded beta sheet. Followed by a C-terminal helical domain.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in Halobacteria. They contain two pairs of conserved cysteines that are likely involved in metal coordination. These proteins are predicted to structurally resemble Zinc beta-ribbon domains.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found in Halobacteria. They contain two pairs of conserved cysteines that are likely involved in metal coordination. These proteins are predicted to contain two subdomains one of which is consisting of a five-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet and a helix packed on it followed by a zinc beta-ribbon domain.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria. They contain two pairs of conserved cysteines that are likely involved in metal coordination. These proteins are predicted to structurally resemble treble-clef zinc fingers.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins. The proteins are composed of an N-terminal three helical bundle followed by an alpha helical region at the C-terminus.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria. They contain four pairs of conserved cysteines that are likely involved in metal coordination.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised mycophage proteins. These proteins form a compact domain composed of 5 or 6 antiparallel beta strands that curve around a C-terminal alpha-helix.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Halobacteria. They contain two pairs of conserved cysteines that are likely involved in metal coordination.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins.
This domain is found in uncharacterised eu- and prokaryotic proteins. It contains four invariant cysteines and it is predicted to adopt a Zn-ribbon fold.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised archaeal proteins. They contain two pairs of conserved cysteine residues and are predicted to adopt a fold typical for Treble-clef zinc fingers.

This entry represents a domain found in uncharacterised proteins from prokaryotes. It contains two pairs of conserved cysteines that are likely involved in metal coordination. This domain is predicted to structurally resemble Zinc beta-ribbon domains.

This domain is found in uncharacterised eukaryotic proteins. It is sometimes found in tandem. This domain is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of alpha helices with some similarity to SAM domains.
This domain is centrally located in a group of uncharacterised plant proteins. It is often found associated to [pfam:PF12371]
Family of eukaryotic proteins with unknown function, which are induced by tumour necrosis factor.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised eukaryotic proteins. It has a detectable sequence similarity to protein kinase domains and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.
This domain is found in uncharacterised sequences from fungi. It may adopt a nucleotidyl transferase-like fold.
This is an Ig-like domain found in a group of uncharacterised sequences from nematodes. The function of this domain is unknown.
This is an Ig-like domain found in the middle region of a group of uncharacterised sequences from nematodes.
This is a presumed domain found at the N-terminal of uncharacterised sequences from Strongyloides species. This domain may consist of a beta-sandwich fold.

This domain is found in bacterial uncharacterised proteins that probably belong to the penicillin-binding protein-type class of thioesterases. This domain is predicted to fold into a meander beta-barrel consisting of eight antiparallel beta-strands. It contains a semi-conserved GxWxW sequence motif near the N terminus.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins predominantly from fungi. It has a detectable similarity to ADP ribosyltransferase domains and it is predicted to adopt a similar structure.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. It is predicted to adopt an alpha-helical structure consisting of four helices. This domain contains several conserved aromatic hydrophobic residues that may have a functional role.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. It is predicted to fold into a six-stranded beta-barrel. Inserted in this barrel is an alpha-helix that packs on the barrel side and it is enriched with positively charged residues which may have a functional importance.

Pfam_Description: Borrelia burgdorferi protein of unknown function (DUF759)
Pfam_name: Borrelia burgdorferi protein of unknown function (DUF759)
Pfam_description: This family consists of several uncharacterised proteins from the Lyme disease spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from Fungi. It has a detectable similarity to known galactose-binding domains, in particular to the C-terminal domain of Bacillus sp. alkaline serine protease, and is predicted to adopt similar structure.
This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in proteins from C. elegans and related sequences from Caenorhabditis species. It may adopt a CUB-like domain fold.
This is a domain found in uncharacterised sequences from Caenorhabditis spp. In SwissProt:O45754, it represents the second domain. It may adopt a CUB-like fold.
This domain of unknown function is found in uncharacterised fungal sequences.
This entry represents a domain of unknown function found in uncharacterised plant sequences. This domain may have a beta-propeller structure.
This is a GNAT-like domain found at the N-terminal of uncharacterised sequences from nematodes.
This domain is found in uncharacterised plant proteins.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised fungal proteins. It is predicted to adopt an all-alpha configuration.
This is a domain of unknown function found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from plants and some fungal species. This domain is usually found associated with [pfam:PF23704] and [pfam:PF04182].
This family contains several uncharacterised plant proteins.
This domain of unknown function is found once or twice in a group of fungal uncharacterised proteins. It is predicted to adopt a mainly beta configuration.

This domain is found in tandem in a number of bacterial proteins which are likely associated with the bacterial cell surface. It is predicted to fold into a beta-sandwich. Some members of this entry are likely to contain an intramolecular isopeptide bond connecting their N- and C-terminal strands. This family is closely related to [pfam:PF19407].
This domain is found in uncharacterised sequences from Plasmodium falciparum and related sequences from Apicomplexa. The function is unknown.
This entry includes uncharacterised fungal sequences. It represents a long alpha-helix found near the C-terminal.

This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is usually associated with von Willebrand factor type A domain (e.g. [pfam:PF00092]), which is inserted into the domain core. Members of this entry are likely to contain an intramolecular isopeptide bond. The domain represented by this entry is predicted to fold into a beta-sandwich but does not include the two N-terminal strands that precede the von Willebrand factor type A domain.
This is an helical domain found at the C-terminal of fungal sequences, whose function is unknown.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It is predicted to fold into an alpha-helical structure composed of three helices.
This domain is found in uncharacterised fungal proteins. It is predicted to adopt an alpha-helical structure consisting of four helices.
This entry represents a domain found in a family of uncharacterised phage proteins. Structure prediction suggests that this protein may homodimerise (A0A377YTN9 ipTM=0.68).

This family consists of several plant proteins of unknown function. Three of the sequences (from Gossypium hirsutum) in this family are described as cotton fibre expressed proteins [[cite:PUB00011314]]. The remaining sequences, found in Arabidopsis thaliana, are uncharacterised.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. It is predicted to adopt three-helical bundle.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It is predicted to fold into a beta-barrel with a PH-like topology.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It is predicted to fold into a beta-barrel with a PH-like topology.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It is predicted to fold into a beta-barrel with a PH-like topology.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It is predicted to fold into a beta-barrel with a PH-like topology.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. This domain is predicted to fold into an alpha-helical hairpin.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins from enterobacterial phage. The proteins are around 56 residues in length.

This domain is found in multiple copies in a number of bacterial proteins mainly from Actinomycetales. It is closely related to domains represented by [pfam:PF01345] and [pfam:PF24346]. Similarly to them, this domain contains a conserved N-terminal lysine and a C-terminal asparagine with central aspartate/glutamate residues suggesting that some members may contain an isopeptide bond. This domain is sometimes found in combination with [pfam:PF01345] or [pfam:PF24346].
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins frequently in multiple copies. Some proteins containing this domain contain LPXTG cell wall anchor motif [pfam:PF00746] at the C-terminus. It is likely that some members of this entry contain an intramolecular isopeptide bond.

Pfam_Description: Coxiella burnetii protein of unknown function (DUF762)
Pfam_name: Coxiella burnetii protein of unknown function (DUF762)
Pfam_description: This family consists several of several uncharacterised proteins from the bacterium Coxiella burnetii. Coxiella burnetii is the causative agent of the Q fever disease.
This entry represents a family of small uncharacterised phage proteins that are predicted to form a coiled-coil. However, structure predictions do not predict homodimeric or homotrimeric complexes.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised phage proteins.
This domain is found several times in a group of uncharacterised proteins from nematodes. It is predicted to adopt a mainly beta configuration.
Several copies of this domain of unknown function are found in a group of uncharacterised proteins from lower eukaryotes. It is often found associated to [pfam:PF00648] and [pfam:PF01067].

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure composed of alpha-helices. This domain has a number of conserved positively changed residues that in the predicted structure define a large positively charged patch on the surface.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. This domain is predicted to fold into a globular structure with a winged helix HTH topology.
This is a HTH-like domain found in uncharacterised sequences from fungi.
This entry represents a domain found in the uncharacterised protein B0303.14 from C.elegans and related sequences from nematodes.
This is a domain of unknown function found in uncharacterised sequences from Plasmodium and related sequences from Plasmodiidae.
This is an Ig-like domain found at the N-terminal of proteins from Plasmodium falciparum and related sequences from Plasmodiidae. The function of these protein is unknown.
This family consists of several uncharacterised bacterial and archaeal proteins of unknown function.
This presumed domain is found in uncharacterised sequences from Plasmodium falciparum and similar sequences from Apicomplexa. This domain may adopt a TNF receptor-like fold.
This presumed domain is found in uncharacterised sequences from Plasmodium falciparum and similar sequences from Apicomplexa. This domain may adopt a TNF receptor-like fold.
This is a presumed helical domain found at the C-terminal of a group of uncharacterised sequences from Plasmodium falciparum and related sequences from Apicomplexa.

This presumed domain is found at the C-terminal of uncharacterised sequences from diatoms, which is usually associated with a beta-solenoid at the N-terminal. This domain may adopt a beta-sandwich fold.
This is a presumed beta-sandwich domain found near the central region of uncharacterised sequences from Plasmodium falciparum (SwissProt:Q8IBR8) and similar sequences from Apicomplexa.

This is a presumed domain found in uncharacterised sequences from plasmodium falciparum (SwissProt:Q8IBR8) and similar sequences from Apicomplexa. It may adopt a beta-propeller-like fold, which, from structure predictions, it seems incomplete.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from nematodes. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of a three-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet and three alpha-helices packed on one side of it.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from nematodes. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of a four-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet and two alpha-helices packed on one side of it.
This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to adopt an alpha/beta structure consisting of curved beta-sheet and alpha-helices packed on the concave side of it.
This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure composed of a three helical bundle.

Pfam_Description: Borrelia burgdorferi protein of unknown function (DUF764)
Pfam_name: Borrelia burgdorferi protein of unknown function (DUF764)
Pfam_description: This family consists of proteins of unknown function from Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease spirochete).
This is a presumed domain found in a group of uncharacterised sequences from diatoms. This domain may adopt a beta-solenoid fold and in some members is repeated twice or three times.
This entry includes uncharacterised sequences from Plasmodium sp. and similar sequences from Apicomplexa. This entry may represent transmembrane helices.
This domain is found in uncharacterised sequences from plants.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised staphylococcal phage proteins. Structure prediction suggests they form a compact domain composed of a three stranded beta sheet packed against an alpha helix.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. It is predicted to fold into a three helical bundle.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. It has detectable similarity to winged helix HTH domains and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of array of helices.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of array of helices.
This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to adopt a non-compact structure consisting of four highly hydrophobic alpha-helices that could potentially dimerise.
This family consists of several short (27-30aa) porcine and bovine circovirus ORF6 proteins of unknown function.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants. It is predicted to adopt mainly helical structure.

This domain is found in the Polycomb group protein EMBRYONIC FLOWER 2 (EMF2) from Arabidopsis thaliana and related proteins. EMF2 is involved in flowering processes by repressing unknown target genes and preventing reproductive development. This domain is predicted to adopt a globular structure that resembles barrel-sandwich hybrid. The beta-sandwich has a topology most similar to C2 domains found in diverse proteins such as CEP120, Dysferlin and Myoferlin.
This is an Ig-like domain found towards the C-terminal of a group of uncharacterised sequences from Strongyloides spp. and similar sequences from nematodes.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from plants.
This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular alpha/beta structure.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised eukaryotic proteins. It shares detectable similarity to the Thioredoxin-like SNTX domain ([pfam:PF18078]) and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.
This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It contains a semi-conserved sequence motif TxYPGxR. It is likely that this domain is a transmembrane domain composed of alpha-helices.
This is a presumed domain found towards the C-terminal of a group of uncharacterised sequences from C. elegans and similar proteins from nematodes.

This family of uncharacterised proteins is found in bacteria and phage. Proteins in this family are typically between 128 and 147 amino acids in length. The proteins contain two subdomains separated by an alpha-helical linker.
This family represents a set of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. Structure prediction shows them to be composed of three alpha helices.
This entry represents a family of small uncharacterised bacterial proteins that adopts a compact domain composed of 5 beta strands and a single alpha helix.

This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is frequently found in combination with [pfam:PF21818] and [pfam:PF20815] which suggests that it may be involved in DNA binding and recognition. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of a three-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet and alpha-helices packed on one side of it.

This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is frequently found in combination with [pfam:PF21818]. It is predicted to adopt a complex alpha/beta structure composed of a curved beta-sheet that encloses an alpha-helix and a number of helices packed on its exterior.
This entry represents a small accessory domain found at the N-terminus of a small family of archaeal AGOG proteins. These proteins have 8-oxoguanine DNA glycosylase activity.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised bacterial protein. Proteins in this family are about 150 residues in length.

This entry represents an uncharacterised protein domain that is sometimes found associated with [pfam:PF01469]. The family also includes an N-terminal domain found in the Pseudomonas syringae InaZ ice nucleation protein.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. Structure prediction shows these proteins are alpha helical with a long central alpha helix packed against two shorter N and C-terminal helices. Structure prediction suggests these proteins may form homodimers.
This entry represents a bacterial protein domain of unknown function.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins primarily found in Bacteria. It has a detectable similarity to winged helix HTH domain and it is predicted to adopt similar structure. This domain is frequently found in combination with [pfam:PF21818] and [pfam:PF20815].
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised bacterial membrane proteins that contain four transmembrane alpha helices.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. The protein forms a single beta barrel domain which shows some structural similarity to the N-terminal domain of the PriA protein. However, structure prediction does not support this protein having a DNA-binding function like PriA.

This family of uncharacterised proteins is found in bacteria (Bacteroidota and Chloroflexi). Proteins in this family are approximately 80 amino acids in length. The proteins are likely to be integral membrane proteins with two transmembrane alpha helices. Structural modelling suggests that these proteins form a dimeric arrangement with the pairs of alpha helices tilted at close to 45 degrees angle compared to the lipid membrane. Based on the positive inside rule it is likely that the N and C-terminii of the proteins have a cytoplasmic location. Given the geometry of the protein complex it may not span the entire membrane.

This entry represents an uncharacterised family of proteins, which are typically between 100 and 122 amino acids in length. This protein is often found to be plasmid borne and in a few cases is associated with ParBc domains that are critical for plasmid segregation. This suggests that this domain may play a role in chromosome segregation or plasmid partitioning. Structural modelling suggests this domain will form a homodimeric complex.
This family of proteins is found in bacteria. Proteins in this family are typically between 113 and 127 amino acids in length.
This entry represents an uncharacterised family of proteins is found in bacteria and viruses. Proteins in this family are typically between 69 and 93 amino acids in length.

This entry represents a family of bacterial proteins that based on structural similarities are likely to bind to heme or a related derivative molecule. Structural modelling suggests these proteins are likely to form homodimers and that this complex can bind to two heme-like molecules. Each heme binding site is composed of parts of both subunits.
This entry represents a group of uncharacterised proteins found in bacteria. These proteins are predicted to adopt globular structure that folds into a three helical bundle.

This entry represents a conserved domain of unknown function (DUF7678) found in various bacterial species. The domain is approximately 75-100 amino acids in length and contains several highly conserved residues. The function of this domain remains to be determined. Structure prediction suggests this domain is composed of a 6 stranded beta sheet with an Alpha helix packed on one side.

This entry represents a small family of Lactobacillus proteins of unknown function. The predicted structure suggests these proteins contain two subdomains, with an N-terminal partly open beta barrel and C-terminal alpha/beta subdomain.
This family consists of several uncharacterised hypothetical proteins from Rhizobium loti.

This entry represents a group of uncharacterised prokaryotic proteins. These proteins share a common semi-conserved EExxWY sequence motif which is predicted as a solvent-exposed in a alpha/beta structure consisting of a four-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet and alpha-helices packed on one side of it.

This entry represents a small zinc-binding domain found to the N-terminus of proteins that belong to the ParE toxin superfamily. The exact function of this domain is unknown. The zinc ligands are composed of the cys and his in the N-terminal CGH motif and the cys residues in the C-terminal CHXC motif.

This family represents uncharacterised proteins found in bacteria. These proteins are related to members of [pfam:PF03513] which are described as immunity proteins. They are predicted to adopt similar structure composed of a four-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet with alpha-helices packed on one side of it.
This entry represents a group of uncharacterised bacterial proteins found in bacteria. They are predicted to adopt a globular alpha/beta structure that has some similarity to MurD C-terminal domain.

This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It contains two pairs of conserved cysteine residues and it is predicted to adopt a fold typical for treble clef zinc fingers. It has a detectable similarity to the N-terminal zinc finger domain of the bacterial AAA+ disaggregase ClpG, which confers extreme heat resistance to bacteria. The latter is is crucial for structural integrity and disaggregase functionality of ClpG.

This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is usually found next to [pfam:PF24734]. It is predicted to adopt alpha/beta structure consisting of a four-stranded beta-sheet curved around an alpha-helix.

This entry represents a domain found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It shares detectable similarity to a number of type II restriction endonucleases such as DpnII and Ecl18kI and it is predicted to adopt similar structure. It is likely to possess endonuclease activity given the conservation of putative functional site residues.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised protein found in bacteria. They are predicted to adopt alpha+beta structure defined as beta(2)alpha(2)beta(2) structural elements in which the beta-strands form an antiparallel beta-sheet.The function of these proteins is unknown.

This entry represents a group of uncharacterised proteins. They are predicted to adopt a fold typical for cysteine proteinases and topology similar to that of NlpC/P60 family proteins. These proteins are likely enzymes as they have similar active site architecture.

Pfam_Description: Xylella fastidiosa protein of unknown function (DUF769)
Pfam_name: Xylella fastidiosa protein of unknown function (DUF769)
Pfam_description: This family consists of several uncharacterised hypothetical proteins of unknown function from Xylella fastidiosa, the organism that causes Pierce's disease in plants.

This entry represents a domain found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is found N-terminal to [pfam:PF24736]. This domain is predicted to adopt a globular structure composed of four alpha- helices.

This entry represents a group of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They share detectable similarity to proteins members of [pfam:PF08974] whose function is unknown. Their predicted structures resemble the structure of DNA mimic protein DMP12 but elaborated with additional alpha helices.

This domain is found in a group of proteins from Halobacteria. It is predicted to adopt a structure that is reminiscent of ribbon-helix-helix fold. Members of this entry are likely to form dimers. They have a stretch of positively charged residues at the N terminus.

This entry represents a group of uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of a five-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet and helices packed on one side of it.

This entry represents a domain found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. They are predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of an antiparallel beta-sheet and alpha helix packed on it. Most members contain a highly conserved HhW sequence motif where h is hydrophobic residue.
This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It contains a pair of conserved cysteines and it is predicted to adopt a fold which is typical for zinc-ribbon domains.
This entry represents a small uncharacterised protein family. Members are composed of an N-terminal beta hairpin followed by three alpha helices.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised proteins. Although apparently having a bacterial origin these proteins appear in genomic contexts suggesting they are part of an integrated phage genome. Structurally these proteins are composed of a beta hairpin followed by a pair of alpha helices.

This entry represents a domain from uncharacterised proteins found mainly in Firmicutes. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of a curved beta-sheet and alpha-helices packed on one side of it. It contains a number of conserved aromatic hydrophobic residues, some of which are predicted to be solvent-exposed.

This domain of unknown function is found in Zinc finger CCCH domain-containing protein 62 from Oryza sativa (C3H62) and similar proteins from plants. Members of this family also show a SAP domain ([pfam:PF02037]). This domain is predicted to adopt a mainly beta configuration.

This domain is usually found in tandem in uncharacterised bacterial proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of a curved anti-parallel beta-sheet and alpha helices packed on one side of it. It contains highly conserved aspartate and histidine residues that may constitute a metal binding site.

This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from bacteria. It is predicted to adopt an alpha-helical structure with a highly conserved DVHDxWxxW sequence motif which may constitute a ligand binding site. This domain is likely to form a homodimer. Investigation of STRING networks suggests this protein may functionally interact with [pfam:PF24838] a likely octameric membrane complex.

This entry represents a domain found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It has a detectable similarity to domains members of Lipid-translocating exporter superfamily and are predicted to adopt similar structure.
This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It is predicted to contain seven transmembrane helices.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised eukaryotic proteins. It has a detectable similarity to Tumor protein p53-inducible protein 11 (TP53I11) and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.

This domain is found in a group of uncharacterised plant proteins. It has remote similarity to some glucanases and it is predicted to adopt similar beta-sandwich structure but elaborated with additional strands.

This entry represents an uncharacterised family of bacterial proteins. Structure prediction ([swissprot:B2VAQ8] AF3 iPTM=0.93) suggests that these proteins form dimers. The monomer is composed of three alpha helices. STRING provides some weak evidence that these proteins may be immunity proteins or perhaps part of a plasmid addiction system.

This domain is found in uncharacterised fungal proteins. It contains a set of highly conserved cysteine residues that are predicted to form disulfide bonds. It is likely that proteins containing this domain are secreted.
This domain is found N-terminal in uncharacterised fungal proteins. It shares detectable similarity to the N-terminal domain of NACHT proteins and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of array of helices followed by a beta-hairpin.
Family of uncharacterised ORFs found in Bacteriophage and Lactococcus lactis.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins.

This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised Actinomycete proteins. These proteins may form homodimers (AlphaFold3 A6WE73 ipTM = 0.79). The dimerisation is mediated by a C-terminal alpha helical subdomain.
This entry represents a small family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins.
This entry represents a protein domain that forms an intimate self-self dimer. The domain is found at the C-terminus of proteins that often have a [pfam:PF24735] domain.

This entry represents a group of uncharacterised prokaryotic proteins. They are likely to contain two domains that create a compact elongated structure. Toward the C terminus, these proteins have two highly conserved pairs of cysteines which are likely to be involved in metal coordination.
This entry represents a family of uncharacterised actinobacterial proteins that are related to [pfam:PF20115].

This domain is found in uncharacterised bacterial proteins either standalone or in combination with other domains. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of an antiparallel three-stranded beta-sheet and alpha-helices packed on one side of it.
This entry represents a group of uncharacterised proteins mainly from tailed bacteriophages.

This domain is found in uncharacterised prokaryotic proteins. It is predicted to adopt alpha/beta structure consisting of a meander beta-sheet and a kinked alpha-helix. It contains several conserved aspartate and histidine residues that are predicted to come close in space and may constitute a metal binding site.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins mainly from fungi. It is predicted to fold into three transmembrane helices.
This presumed domain is found at the N-terminus of many proteins found in transposons.
This entry represents a small domain found in streptococcal phage proteins. Structurally the domain is composed of a three stranded beta sheet followed by an alpha helix.
This domain is found in uncharacterised proteins from fungi. It is predicted to adopt globular structure consisting of array of helices.
This domain is found in uncharacterised plant proteins. It is predicted to contain helix-extended loop-helix (HeH) structure and has similarity to domains containing this motif.
This small family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins are often found adjacent to proteins from [pfam:PF13711]. Structure prediction shows that these proteins are very likely to form a complex.

This entry represents a family of bacterial proteins composed of an all beta strand domain composed of 7 beta strands. Structure prediction suggests that these proteins will form a complex with proteins from [pfam:PF24848].
This domain is found in uncharacterised plan proteins. It has detectable similarity to winged helix HTH domains and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.
This domain is found in uncharacterised fungal proteins. It has detectable similarity to HTH domains and it is predicted to adopt similar structure.

This domain is found in uncharacterised fungal proteins. It has detectable similarity to proteins members of the Cytochrome b558 subunit alpha family and it is predicted to adopt similar structure composed of four helices.
This domain is found in uncharacterised fungal proteins. It is predicted to fold into a beta-sandwich. It contains highly conserved cysteine residues that are predicted to form a disulfide bond.

This domain is found in uncharacterised fungal proteins. It is predicted to adopt a globular structure consisting of array of alpha helices. It contains several conserved cysteine residues that are predicted to form disulfide bonds. It is likely that the proteins containing this domain are secreted.
This family consists of several highly related mouse and human proteins of unknown function.

Pfam_Description: Borrelia burgdorferi protein of unknown function (DUF777)
Pfam_name: Borrelia burgdorferi protein of unknown function (DUF777)
Pfam_description: This family consists of several hypothetical proteins of unknown function from Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease spirochete).
This family consists of several bacterial proteins of unknown function.

Pfam_Description: Caenorhabditis elegans protein of unknown function (DUF780)
Pfam_name: Caenorhabditis elegans protein of unknown function (DUF780)
Pfam_description: This family consists of several short C. elegans proteins of unknown function.

Pfam_Description: Borrelia burgdorferi protein of unknown function (DUF787)
Pfam_name: Borrelia burgdorferi protein of unknown function (DUF787)
Pfam_description: This family consists of several hypothetical proteins of unknown function from Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease spirochete).
This family consists of several plant proteins of unknown function.
This family consists of several hypothetical archaeal proteins of unknown function.

Pfam_Description: Borrelia burgdorferi protein of unknown function (DUF792)
Pfam_name: Borrelia burgdorferi protein of unknown function (DUF792)
Pfam_description: This family consists of several hypothetical proteins from the Lyme disease spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi.
This region is found as two or more repeats in a small number of hypothetical proteins.
This family consists of several bacterial proteins of unknown function.
This family consists of several Siphovirus and Lactococcus proteins of unknown function. The viral sequences are thought to be tail component proteins.

Pfam_Description: Coxiella burnetii protein of unknown function (DUF807)
Pfam_name: Coxiella burnetii protein of unknown function (DUF807)
Pfam_description: This family consists of several proteins of unknown function from Coxiella burnetii (the causative agent of a zoonotic disease called Q fever).
This family consists of several bacterial proteins of unknown function.
This family consists of several proteins of unknown function Raphanus sativus (Radish) and Brassica napus (Rape).
This family consists of several bacterial proteins of unknown function.

This family includes proteins that are about 200 amino acids in length. The proteins are all from baculoviruses. This family includes ORF107 from Orgyia pseudotsugata multicapsid polyhedrosis virus (OpMNPV) and a variety of other numbered ORF proteins, such as ORF52 [swissprot:Q91F03], ORF140 [swissprot:Q9YMI8]. The function of these proteins is unknown.
This family consists of several bacterial proteins of unknown function.
This family consists of several Chlamydia CHLPS proteins, the function of which are unknown.
This family contains proteins of unknown function from archaeal, bacterial and plant species.
This family consists of several enterobacterial and siphoviral sequences of unknown function.
This family consists of several uncharacterised eukaryotic proteins.
This family consists of several herpesvirus proteins of unknown function.

This short presumed domain is found in a large number of hypothetical plant proteins. The domain is quite rich in conserved glycine residues. It occurs in some putative transposons but currently has no known function.
The members of this archaebacterial protein family are around 250-300 amino acid residues in length. The function of these proteins is not known.
This family consists of a number of conserved eukaryotic proteins of unknown function. The sequences carry three sets of CxxxC motifs, which might suggest a type of zinc-finger formation.
This family consists of several of unknown function from a variety of eukaryotic organisms.
This family consists of several uncharacterised proteins from the Gammaherpesvirinae.
This family consists of several uncharacterised proteins from the Siphoviruses and other bacterial viruses. Some members of this family are described as putative minor structural proteins.
This family consists of a number of hypothetical proteins from Arabidopsis thaliana and Oryza sativa. The function of this family is unknown.
This family consists of several hypothetical proteins from Arabidopsis thaliana and Oryza sativa. The function of this family is unknown.

This entry represents the central domain found in archaeal proteins such as DNA double-strand break repair helicase HerA ([ec:3.6.4.12]). HerA is a helicase which is able to utilise either 3' or 5' single-stranded DNA extensions for loading and subsequent DNA duplex unwinding [[cite:PUB00076694]]. It forms a complex with NurA nuclease, this complex has the 5'-3' DNA end resection activity and is essential for cell viability in the crenarchaeon Sulfolobus islandicus [[cite:PUB00076695]]. This domain includes the the central RecA-like catalytic core and a flanking four-helix bundle [[cite:PUB00078094]]. The function of this prokaryotic domain is unknown. It contains several conserved aspartates and histidines that could be metal ligands.

Pfam_Description: Caenorhabditis elegans protein of unknown function (DUF870)
Pfam_name: Caenorhabditis elegans protein of unknown function (DUF870)
Pfam_description: This family consists of a number of hypothetical proteins which seem to be specific to Caenorhabditis elegans. The function of this family is unknown.

Pfam_Description: Helicobacter pylori protein of unknown function (DUF874)
Pfam_name: Helicobacter pylori protein of unknown function (DUF874)
Pfam_description: This family consists of several hypothetical proteins specific to Helicobacter pylori. The function of this family is unknown.

This family consists of a series of hypothetical bacterial proteins. One of the family members [swissprot:Q45543] from Bacillus subtilis is thought to be involved in cell division and sporulation [[cite:PUB00011928]].
This family consists of several hypothetical bacterial proteins of unknown function. The N-terminal domain found in this entry is related to [pfam:PF05532].
This family corresponds to the C-terminal presumed transmembrane helix found in DUF883 proteins. The helix contains a glycine zipper motif suggestive of dimerisation.
This family consists of several hypothetical Nucleopolyhedrovirus proteins of unknown function.
This family consists of several hypothetical bacterial proteins several of which are putative membrane proteins.

This protein family is found in bacteria, including Protein YciF from Escherichia coli. This protein is produced by bacteria in response to stress conditions. It adopts a dimeric configuration in which each monomer shows five alpha-helices. Its function is still unknown [[cite:PUB00041161]].

In B. subtilis, one small SOS response operon under the control of LexA, the yneA operon, is comprised of three genes: yneA, yneB, and ynzC [[cite:PUB00053936]]. This family consists of several short, hypothetical bacterial proteins of unknown function. These proteins are mainly found in gram-positive firmicutes. Structures show that the N-terminus is composed of two alpha helices forming a helix-loop-helix motif. The structure of ynzC from B. subtilis forms a trimeric complex [[cite:PUB00047592]]. Structural modelling suggests this domain may bind nucleic acids [[cite:PUB00070793]]. This family is also known as UPF0291.

This entry consists of several bacterial proteins of unknown function. Some of the family members are described as inner membrane proteins. These proteins have a beta/alpha/alpha/beta/alpha hairpin structure that is repeated.
This family consists of several uncharacterised bacterial proteins of unknown function.
This family consists of several hypothetical proteins of unknown function mostly found in Rhizobium species. Members of this family have an alpha/beta hydrolase fold.
This family consists of several small bacterial proteins several of which are classified as putative lipoproteins. The function of this family is unknown.

This family consists of several short hypothetical Enterobacteria proteins of unknown function. Structural analysis of the surface features of the protein YvyC has revealed a single cluster of highly conserved residues on the surface. Additionally, these residues fall into two groups which lie within the two largest of the three cavities identified over the surface. The conclusion from this is that these two cavities with, Leu 58, Glu 75, Ile 82, and Glu 83 and Pro 86, conserved, are likely to be important for the molecular function and reflect the cavities found on the surface of the FlaG proteins in [pfam:PF03646].
Members of this family are found in various ubiquitin protein ligases.
This family consists of several bacterial proteins of unknown function. Members of this family have an alpha/beta hydrolase fold.

Pfam_Description: Protein of unknown function DUF917, C-terminal

Pfam_description: This family consists of several Nucleopolyhedrovirus proteins with no known function.
This family consists of several short Nucleopolyhedrovirus proteins of unknown function.

Members of this family have several predicted transmembrane helices. One member of the family has been characterised as protein PGR (AtPGR). PGR is suggested to be a potential glucose-responsive regulator in carbohydrate metabolism in plants. This entry also includes protein VTE6, which is a Pphytyl-phosphate kinase catalysing the conversion of phytyl-monophosphate to phytyl-diphosphate [[cite:PUB00092523]].
This family of proteins has a conserved HEXXH motif, suggesting they are putative peptidases of zincin fold [[cite:PUB00075429]].
This family consists of several hypothetical bacterial proteins of unknown function. Structurally, this family resembles TPR-like repeats.
This entry represents a domain found in bacterial proteins of unknown function. The crystal structure has been solved for a protein containing this domain SWISS:Q0WXP6 [[cite:PUB00085154]].
Family of uncharacterised bacterial protein.
Family of proteins from the archaeon Sulfolobus, with undetermined function. According to structure prediction this protein has a thioredoxin fold.
Family of bacterial proteins with undetermined function. All bacteria in this family are from the Rhizobiales order.
Family of prokaryotic proteins with unknown function. Contains a number of highly conserved polar residues that could suggest an enzymatic activity.

This family consists of several bacterial proteins of unknown function, however members have been suggested to be an accessory protein for sulfite reduction. This is based on the observation that they strongly cofit with various genes in the sulfate assimilation pathway in various Pseudomonas as well as in Marinobacter adhaerens HP15 and C. basilensis 4G11 (see Supplementary note 5 in [[cite:PUB00093610]].)
This entry consists of several hypothetical proteins from plants, whose function is unknown. According to structure predictions, this domain may adopt and OB-fold.
This family consists of several hypothetical bacterial proteins of unknown function.
This family consists of several hypothetical proteins from both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. The function of this family is unknown.

This family consists of several hypothetical putative membrane proteins from Escherichia coli, Yersinia pestis and Salmonella typhi. Recently, it was proposed that members of this family along with members of DUF3289 ([pfam:PF11692]) should be recognised as a putative toxin-antitoxin pair in which DUF3289 ([pfam:PF11692]) is a homolog of Colicin M and DUF943 acts as its cognate immunity protein [[cite:PUB00154362]].
This family consists of several hypothetical bacterial proteins of unknown function.
This family consists of bacterial sequences several of which are thought to be general stress proteins.
This family consists of several short hypothetical bacterial proteins of unknown function. Structural modelling suggests this domain may bind nucleic acids [[cite:PUB00070793]].
This family consists of several hypothetical bacterial and plant proteins of unknown function.
Family of bacterial sequences with undetermined function.
This N-terminal domain is not expressed in the 'Short' isoform of Collagen A [[cite:PUB00012268]].
This family consists of several hypothetical proteins from several species of Staphylococcus. The function of this family is unknown.
This family consists of several hypothetical bacterial proteins of unknown function.

Pfam_Description: Schizosaccharomyces pombe repeat of unknown function (DUF963)
Pfam_name: Schizosaccharomyces pombe repeat of unknown function (DUF963)
Pfam_description: This family consists of a series of repeated sequences from one hypothetical protein ([swissprot:Q96WV6]) found in Schizosaccharomyces pombe. The function of this family is unknown.
Family of uncharacterised prophage proteins found in Gammaproteobacteria. These may be HNH-nucleases, as there are several conserved cysteines and histidines.
Family of uncharacterised bacterial membrane proteins.
This family consists of several hypothetical archaeal proteins of unknown function.
Family of uncharacterised bacterial proteins.
This family consists of several hypothetical bacterial proteins from Escherichia coli and Salmonella typhi. The function of this family is unknown.
This family consists of several putative bacterial membrane proteins. The function of this family is unclear.
Family of uncharacterised proteins found in bacteria and archaea.

This family consists of several hypothetical proteins from Rhizobium meliloti, Rhizobium loti and Agrobacterium tumefaciens. The function of this family is unknown. Structural modelling suggests this domain may bind nucleic acids [[cite:PUB00070793]].
This family consists of several bacterial proteins of unknown function.
This family consists of several bacterial putative membrane proteins of unknown function.
Family of bacterial proteins that are related to the hypothetical protein yeeT.

This family includes uncharacterised archaebacterial proteins. Sequence and structure analysis to identify RNase H-like superfamily members, has clustered this family in endonuclease Clade V, thus suggesting endonuclease activity of these proteins [[cite:PUB00098031]].
This family consists of several hypothetical bacterial proteins of unknown function.
This family consists of several hypothetical bacterial proteins of unknown function.
Family of uncharacterised Proteobacteria proteins.
Family of uncharacterised bacterial and archaeal proteins.
Family of predicted bacterial membrane protein with unknown function.
Family of conserved bacterial and archaeal proteins.
Family of conserved Schizosaccharomyces pombe proteins with unknown function.

This domain family is found in eukaryotes, and is approximately 70 amino acids in length. The family is found in association with [pfam:PF05424]. This family contains the N terminus of the Duffy receptor binding domain.

This domain is found in Plasmodium Duffy binding proteins. Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium knowlesi merozoites invade human erythrocytes that express Duffy blood group surface determinants. The Duffy receptor family is localised in micronemes, an organelle found in all organisms of the phylum Apicomplexa [[cite:PUB00011323]]. This family is closely associated on PfEMP1 proteins with PFEMP, [pfam:PF03011].

This entry represents the DPY repeat module described in dumpy from Drosophila melanogaster, a gigantic extracellular matrix protein that contains epidermal growth factor (EGF) modules interspersed with DPY modules. The DPY module forms a compact fold consisting of a small N-terminal 3-10 helix packed against a double-stranded anti-parallel disulphide-stabilised beta-sheet motif capable of linking end-to-end with EGF modules to form a fibre [[cite:PUB00029455]].

This entry contains two domain copies of the OB fold. There is nearly absolutely conserved cysteine, serine/threonine, arginine, and aspartate residues which are predicted to line a deep cleft formed at the interface of the two OB domains. The predicted spatial arrangement of the tandem OB domains closely parallels OB-dyads from single-stranded nucleic acid-end binding proteins, such as the telomere-binding domain alpha-subunit, with the nucleic acid being lodged in a cleft formed by the two OB domains. Drawing an analogy to the SRAP domain, it has been suggested that the DuOB domain could potentially form crosslinks to DNA at the abasic sites via its conserved cysteine. It is found on the genome adjacent to DUF488 and DUF4326 proteins, which could potentially also catalyse thiotransfer reactions required for forming or resolving the cysteine-DNA crosslinks, paralleling recent findings where HD phosphatases mediate the transfer of a phosphorylated substrate to a hydroxyl-group-containing residue [[cite:PUB00153826]].

DuoxA (Dual oxidase maturation factor) is the essential protein necessary for the final release of DUOX2 (an NADPH:O2 oxidoreductase flavoprotein) from the endoplasmic reticulum. Dual oxidases (DUOX1 and DUOX2) constitute the catalytic core of the hydrogen peroxide generator, which generates H2O2 at the apical membrane of thyroid follicular cells, essential for iodination of thyroglobulin by thyroid peroxidases. DuoxA carries five membrane-integral regions including a reverse signal-anchor with external N-terminus (type III) and two N-glycosylation sites [[cite:PUB00044237]]. It is conserved from nematodes to humans.

This family consists of several yeast proteins of unknown functions. Swiss-prot annotates these as belonging to the DUP family. Several members of this family contain an internal duplication of this region.

This entry represents a member of a biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC). This BGC (BGC0001577) is described by MIBiG as an example of the following biosynthetic class, RiPP (ribosomally synthesised and post-translationally modified peptide). It includes lantibiotic duramycin, duramycin B and cinnamycin. Duramycin B is a potent inhibitor of human phospholipase A2 [[cite:PUB00151902]].

This entry represents a member of a biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) involved in duramycin biosynthesis, a ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptide (RiPP) produced by various actinomycetes and marine symbionts. Duramycin binds phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), a major structural phospholipid in mammalian and microbial cell membranes which contains 19 amino acids and 5 post-translational modifications (PTMs). This entry represents DurN, an enzyme that forms (2S,9S)-Lal one of the two last PTMs. DurN catalyses stereospecific and diastereoselective Lal formation in an unusual substrate-assisted mechanism in which the active site residues that make the reaction proceed come from the substrate itself, manoeuvred into position by DurN [[cite:PUB00152101]].

Members of this family catalyse the reduction of the 5,6-double bond of a uridine residue on tRNA. Dihydrouridine modification of tRNA is widely observed in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and also in some archae. Most dihydrouridines are found in the D loop of t-RNAs. The role of dihydrouridine in tRNA is currently unknown, but may increase conformational flexibility of the tRNA. It is likely that different family members have different substrate specificities, which may overlap. Dus 1 ([swissprot:Q9HGN6]) from Saccharomyces cerevisiae acts on pre-tRNA-Phe, while Dus 2 ([swissprot:P53720]) acts on pre-tRNA-Tyr and pre-tRNA-Leu. Dus 1 is active as a single subunit, requiring NADPH or NADH, and is stimulated by the presence of FAD [[cite:PUB00014304]]. Some family members may be targeted to the mitochondria and even have a role in mitochondria [[cite:PUB00014304]].

The DUSP (domain present in ubiquitin-specific protease) domain is found at the N-terminus of Ubiquitin-specific proteases. The structure of this domain has been solved [[cite:PUB00038034]]. Its tripod-like structure consists of a 3-fold alpha-helical bundle supporting a triple-stranded anti-parallel beta-sheet [[cite:PUB00038034]].
dUTPase hydrolyses dUTP to dUMP and pyrophosphate.

2-Deoxyuridine 5-triphosphate nucleotidohydrolase (dUTPase) catalyses the hydrolysis of dUTP to dUMP and pyrophosphate ([ec:3.6.1.23]). Members of this family have a novel all-alpha fold and are unrelated to the all-beta fold found in dUTPases of the majority of organisms [[cite:PUB00032166]]. This family contains both dUTPase homologues of dUTPase including dCTPase of phage T4.
dUTPase hydrolyses dUTP to dUMP and pyrophosphate.

2-Deoxyuridine 5-triphosphate nucleotidohydrolase (dUTPase) catalyses the hydrolysis of dUTP to dUMP and pyrophosphate ([ec:3.6.1.23]). Members of this family have a novel all-alpha fold and are unrelated to the all-beta fold found in dUTPases of the majority of organisms [[cite:PUB00032166]]. This family contains both dUTPase homologues of dUTPase including dCTPase of phage T4.

This family consists of the DVL family of proteins. In a gain-of-function genetic screen for genes that influence fruit development in Arabidopsis, DEVIL (DVL) gene was identified. DVL is a small protein and overexpression of the protein results in pleiotropic phenotypes featured by shortened stature, rounder rosette leaves, clustered inflorescences, shortened pedicles, and siliques with pronged tips. DVL family is a novel class of small polypeptides and the overexpression phenotypes suggest that these polypeptides may have a role in plant development [[cite:PUB00016535]].

Dinoflagellate viral nucleoprotein (DVNPs) are known to function in DNA packaging in Dinoflagellate as a histone replacement. It displaces nucleosomes when expressed in yeast [[cite:PUB00095059]]. This family is predominantly found in Phycodnaviridae.

DWNN is a ubiquitin like domain found at the N terminus of the RBBP6 family of splicing-associated proteins [[cite:PUB00035393]]. The DWNN domain is independently expressed in higher vertebrates so it may function as a novel ubiquitin-like modifier of other proteins [[cite:PUB00035393]].

Pfam_Description: Sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase regulator DWORF
Pfam_name: Sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase regulator DWORF
Pfam_description: This family includes human Sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase regulator DWORF and similar sequences from vertebrates. DWORF is a micropeptide that enhances the activity of the SERCA1 ATPase in the sarcoplasmic reticulum by displacing its inhibitors, thereby acting as a key regulator of skeletal muscle activity. It also enhances sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ uptake and myocyte contractility [[cite:PUB00096362],[cite:PUB00096365]]. DWORF shows an alpha-helical topology with a kink that separates two helical domains. This adaptive configuration seems to be directly linked to its activating effect on SERCA [[cite:PUB00153917]].
This domain has no known function. It is found in several C. elegans proteins. The domain contains 6 conserved cysteines that probably form three disulphide bridges.
This is the C-terminal domain of the 1-deoxy-D-xylulose-5-phosphate reductoisomerase enzyme. This domain forms a left handed super-helix.

This domain is found to the C-terminus of [pfam:PF02670] domains in bacterial and plant 1-deoxy-D-xylulose 5-phosphate reductoisomerases which catalyse the formation of 2-C-methyl-D-erythritol 4-phosphate from 1-deoxy-D-xylulose-5-phosphate in the presence of NADPH [[cite:PUB00020977]].

This is a family of 1-deoxy-D-xylulose 5-phosphate reductoisomerases. This enzyme catalyses the formation of 2-C-methyl-D-erythritol 4-phosphate from 1-deoxy-D-xylulose-5-phosphate in the presence of NADPH [[cite:PUB00020977]]. This reaction is part of the terpenoid biosynthesis pathway.

This family contains 1-deoxyxylulose-5-phosphate synthase (DXP synthase), an enzyme which catalyses the thiamine pyrophosphoate-dependent acyloin condensation reaction between carbon atoms 2 and 3 of pyruvate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, to yield 1-deoxy-D- xylulose-5-phosphate, a precursor in the biosynthetic pathway to isoprenoids, thiamine (vitamin B1), and pyridoxol (vitamin B6).

This entry includes dynein heavy chain (DYN1) from yeast, which is a cytoplasmic dynein that acts as a motor for intracellular retrograde motility of vesicles and organelles along microtubules. This entry represents the AAA+ ATPase lid domain [[cite:PUB00152713],[cite:PUB00055821],[cite:PUB00059369],[cite:PUB00151944],[cite:PUB00151945]].

This domain family is found in eukaryotes, and is approximately 280 amino acids in length. The family is found in association with [pfam:PF01302]. There is a single completely conserved residue E that may be functionally important. Dynactin has been associated with Dynein, a kinesin protein which is involved in organelle transport, mitotic spindle assembly and chromosome segregation. Dynactin anchors Dynein to specific subcellular structures.

This family contains p22, the smallest subunit of dynactin, a complex that binds to cytoplasmic dynein and is a required activator for cytoplasmic dynein-mediated vesicular transport. Dynactin localises to the cleavage furrow and to the midbodies of dividing cells, suggesting that it may function in cytokinesis [[cite:PUB00013145]]. Family members are approximately 170 residues long.

Dynactin is a multi-subunit complex and a required cofactor for most, or all, of the cellular processes powered by the microtubule-based motor cytoplasmic dynein. p62 binds directly to the Arp1 subunit of dynactin [[cite:PUB00011592],[cite:PUB00011591]].

This is the helical region from bacterial dynamin-like proteins which covers the middle and GED domains which mediate extensive protein-protein contacts [[cite:PUB00041888],[cite:PUB00072536]]. These proteins are large GTPases with the same multidomain architecture that is found in dynamin-like proteins.

This is the stalk region which lies between the GTPase domain, see [pfam:PF00350], and the pleckstrin homology (PH) domain, see [pfam:PF00169]. This region dimerises in a cross-like fashion forming a dynamin dimer in which the two G-domains are oriented in opposite directions [[cite:PUB00072539]].

Dynamitin is a subunit of the microtubule-dependent motor complex and in implicated in cell adhesion by binding to macrophage-enriched myristoylated alanine-rice C kinase substrate (MacMARCKS) [[cite:PUB00008705]].

Pfam_Description: Cytoplasmic dynein 2 heavy chain 1, AAA+ ATPase domain
Pfam_name: Cytoplasmic dynein 2 heavy chain 1, AAA+ ATPase domain
Pfam_description: This domain is found in Cytoplasmic dynein 2 heavy chain 1 from humans (DYNC2H1) and similar sequences from eukaryotes. Dynein-2 is essential for the dynamic remodelling of the ciliary proteome and is associated with human skeletal ciliopathies. DYNC2H1, one of its specific components, is the motor-domain- containing heavy chain. This protein consists of a compact N-terminal region, an elongated tail and a C-terminal AAA+ motor domain. There are two copies of this protein in the complex, each adopting a different configuration, which contributes to the asymmetry of Dynein-2. This entry covers one of the six motor's ring AAA+ domains (ATPases associated with various cellular activities) [[cite:PUB00085943],[cite:PUB00151745]].

Pfam_Description: Dynein heavy chain AAA lid domain
Pfam_name: Dynein heavy chain AAA lid domain
Pfam_description: This entry corresponds to the extension domain of AAA domain 5 in the dynein heavy chain [[cite:PUB00062447]]. This domain is composed of 8 alpha helices [[cite:PUB00062447]].

Pfam_Description: Dynein heavy chain AAA lid domain
Pfam_name: Dynein heavy chain AAA lid domain
