This family also the sequence-related yellow protein of drosophila which controls pigmentation of the adult cuticle and larval mouth parts.

This entry represents the receptor binding domain of MrkD from Klebsiella pneumoniae and similar sequences [[cite:PUB00154079]]. MkrD is an adhesin protein that specifically interacts with type IV and/or V collagen [[cite:PUB00154079]].

This entry represents the YcgR-like domain found at the N-terminal of MrkH ([swissprot:G3FT00]) from Klebsiella pneumoniae and similar sequences [[cite:PUB00154080]] which contain a PilZ domain at the C-terminal. MrkH is a c-di-GMP-related transcriptional regulator that affects type 3 fimbrial expression in response to cellular c-di-GMP level, playing and important role in biofilm formation. This protein binds to the promoter regulation fragments of mrkHI and mrkA mainly through its PilZ domain and this YcgR-like domain also participates in DNA-binding [[cite:PUB00154080]].

MRM3 catalyses the formation of 2'-O-methylguanosine at position 1370 Gm1370) in the 16S mitochondrial large subunit ribosomal RNA (mtLSU rRNA), a conserved modification in the peptidyl transferase domain of the mtLSU rRNA [[cite:PUB00016836],[cite:PUB00032343],[cite:PUB00154081]]. This entry represents the substrate binding domain of MRM3 from animals and related sequences from bacteria.
This family represents the ATP binding catalytic domain of the mRNA capping enzyme.
The C-terminal domain of mRNA-decapping enzyme in Metazoa is responsible for trimerisation [[cite:PUB00066161]].

This entry represents mRNA (guanine-N(7))-methyltransferase, which can either be found as a single domain protein, or as a domain within the mRNA-capping enzyme catalytic subunit. mRNA (guanine-N(7))-methyltransferase methylates the N7 position of the added guanosine to the 5'-cap structure of mRNAs. It binds RNA containing 5'-terminal GpppC [[cite:PUB00020157],[cite:PUB00058114],[cite:PUB00058116],[cite:PUB00090973],[cite:PUB00100699]]. Viral mRNA capping enzymes, meanwhile, are multidomain proteins that catalyse the first two reactions in the mRNA cap formation pathway [[cite:PUB00100699]]. They are heterodimers consisting of a large (catalytic) and small subunit.
This domain is an mRNA stabilisation factor [[cite:PUB00057313]].

The beta chain of mRNA capping enzyme has triphosphatase activity. The function of the capping enzyme also depends on the guanylyltransferase activity conferred by the alpha chain (see [pfam:PF01331])

This family is found in eukaryotes. Family members include MRN complex-interacting protein (MRNIP), which plays a role in preventing the accumulation of damaged DNA in cells. It associates with the MRE11-RAD50-NBS1 (MRN) damage-sensing complex and is rapidly recruited to sites of DNA damage. Phosphorylation of a serine promotes nuclear localization of MRNIP [[cite:PUB00083234]].

MRP1 and MRP2 are mitochondrial RNA binding proteins that form a heteromeric complex. The MRP1/MRP2 heterotetrameric complex binds to guide RNAs and stabilises them in an unfolded conformation suitable for RNA-RNA hybridisation. Each MRP subunit adopts a 'whirly' transcription factor fold [[cite:PUB00041062]].
This family of proteins is present in the intact 55S subunit of the mitochondrial ribosome. It is not known if it belongs to the 28S or to the 39S subunit [[cite:PUB00044378]].
Members of this family of proteins are components of the mitochondrial ribosome large subunit. They are also involved in apoptosis and cell cycle regulation.

Members of this family are components of the mitochondrial large ribosomal subunit. Mature mitochondrial ribosomes consist of a small (37S) and a large (54S) subunit. The 37S subunit contains at least 33 different proteins and 1 molecule of RNA (15S). The 54S subunit contains at least 45 different proteins and 1 molecule of RNA (21S) [[cite:PUB00044374]][[cite:PUB00044375]].
This is the L46 subunit of the mammalian mitochondrial ribosome, conserved from plants and fungi.

This family represents the N-terminal region (approximately 8 residues) of the eukaryotic mitochondrial 39-S ribosomal protein L47 (MRP-L47). Mitochondrial ribosomal proteins (MRPs) are the counterparts of the cytoplasmic ribosomal proteins, in that they fulfil similar functions in protein biosynthesis. However, they are distinct in number, features and primary structure [[cite:PUB00012961]].

MRP-L51 is a family of small proteins from the intact 55 S mitochondrial ribosome [[cite:PUB00044377]]. It has otherwise been referred to as bMRP-64 [[cite:PUB00044378]]. The exact function of this family is not known.

This is the conserved N-terminus and central portion of the mitochondrial small subunit 28S ribosomal protein S22. Mammalian mitochondria carry out the synthesis of 13 polypeptides that are essential for oxidative phosphorylation and, hence, for the synthesis of the majority of the ATP used by eukaryotic organisms. The number of proteins produced by prokaryotes is smaller, reflected in the lower number of ribosomal proteins present in them [[cite:PUB00019768]].

MRP-S23 is one of the proteins that makes up the 55S ribosome in eukaryotes from nematodes to humans. It does not appear to carry any common motifs, either RNA binding or ribosomal protein motifs [[cite:PUB00019768]]. All of the mammalian MRPs are encoded in nuclear genes that are evolving more rapidly than those encoding cytoplasmic ribosomal proteins. The MRPs are imported into mitochondria where they assemble coordinately with mitochondrially transcribed rRNAs into ribosomes that are responsible for translating the 13 mRNAs for essential proteins of the oxidative phosphorylation system [[cite:PUB00044379]]. MRP-S23 is significantly up-regulated in uterine cancer cells [[cite:PUB00044380]].
This family of proteins corresponds to mitochondrial ribosomal subunit S24 in eukaryotes [[cite:PUB00019768],[cite:PUB00044378]].
This is the family of fungal 37S mitochondrial ribosomal S25 proteins.
This family of proteins corresponds to mitochondrial ribosomal subunit S26 in eukaryotes [[cite:PUB00014866]]

Members of this family of small ribosomal proteins possess one of three conserved blocks of sequence found in proteins that stimulate the dissociation of guanine nucleotides from G-proteins, leaving open the possibility that MRP-S27 might be a functional partner of GTP-binding ribosomal proteins [[cite:PUB00044381]].

This is a conserved region of approx. 125 residues of one of the proteins that makes up the small subunit of the mitochondrial ribosome. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae the protein is MRP-S24 whereas in humans it is MRP-S28. The human mitochondrial ribosome has 29 distinct proteins in the small subunit and these have homologues in, for example, Drosophila melanogaster, Caenorhabditis elegans, and in the genomes of several fungi [[cite:PUB00044381]].

MRP-S31 is the mitochondrial 28S ribosomal subunit S31. This family of proteins is found in eukaryotes. Proteins in this family are typically between 246 and 395 amino acids in length. There are two conserved sequence motifs: RHFMELV and GLSKN.
This entry is of a family of short, approximately 100 amino acid residues, proteins which are mitochondrial 28S ribosomal proteins named as MRP-S32. Their exact function could not be confirmed.

This family of proteins corresponds to mitochondrial ribosomal subunit S27 in prokaryotes [[cite:PUB00019866]] and to subunit S33 in humans [[cite:PUB00044381]]. It is a small 106 residue protein.The evolutionary history of the mitoribosomal proteome that is encoded by a diverse subset of eukaryotic genomes, reveals an ancestral ribosome of alpha-proteobacterial descent that more than doubled its protein content in most eukaryotic lineages. Several new MRPs have originated via duplication of existing MRPs as well as by recruitment from outside of the mitoribosomal proteome [[cite:PUB00044382]].

This is a family of short mitochondrial ribosomal proteins, less than 200 amino acids long. that are highly conserved from worms to humans. The structure has previously been referred to as MRP-S18 but the current numbering fits the preferred nomenclature from these authors.

Pfam_Description: Multiple resistance and pH regulation protein F (MrpF / PhaF)
Pfam_name: Multiple resistance and pH regulation protein F (MrpF / PhaF)
Pfam_description: Members of the PhaF / MrpF family are predicted to be an integral membrane proteins with three transmembrane regions, involved in regulation of pH. PhaF is part of a potassium efflux system involved in pH regulation. It is also involved in symbiosis in Rhizobium meliloti [[cite:PUB00010603]]. MrpF is part of a Na+/H+ antiporter complex, also involved in pH homeostasis. MrpF is thought to be an efflux system for Na+ and cholate [[cite:PUB00009818]]. The Mrp system in Bacilli may also have primary energisation capacities [[cite:PUB00009819]].

This entry represents the C-terminal domain of fimbrial adhesin MrpH from bacteria. This protein is associated to strain virulence and is involved in surface adherence, biofilm formation and autoaggregation, essential for bladder and kidney colonization [[cite:PUB00155749]]. This domain attaches to bacterial fimbrial tip [[cite:PUB00155750]].

This entry represents the N-terminal domain of fimbrial adhesin MrpH protein from bacteria. This protein is associated to strain virulence and is involved in surface adherence, biofilm formation and autoaggregation, essential for bladder and kidney colonization [[cite:PUB00155749]]. This domain binds to surface receptor and coordinates one Zn cation necessary for attachment and biofilm formation [[cite:PUB00150666]].
Members of this family include the mamalian mitoribosomal proteins mL52 which is found in the 39S subunit. The mL52 has no homologues in yeast [[cite:PUB00089007],[cite:PUB00108680]].
This is the C-terminal domain of mitochondrial 54S ribosomal protein L8.

This family includes the MrpR protein from Bacillus subtilis (also known as YopR), the master repressor of the lytic cycle of the temperate phage SPbeta. MrpR, a DNA-binding protein that has lost its recombinase function, shows a tyrosine recombinase fold with an N-terminal all-alpha domain ([pfam:PF22822]) and a C-terminal catalytic domain (this entry) [[cite:PUB00154082]].

This family includes the MrpR protein from Bacillus subtilis (also known as YopR), the master repressor of the lytic cycle of the temperate phage SPbeta. MrpR, a DNA-binding protein that has lost its recombinase function, shows a tyrosine recombinase fold with an N-terminal core-binding (CB) domain with four alpha -helices (this entry) and a C-terminal catalytic domain [[cite:PUB00154082]].
MRP-L53 is also known as Mrp144. It is part of the 39S ribosome [[cite:PUB00044382]].

Prokaryotic family found in type II restriction enzymes containing the hallmark (D/E)-(D/E)XK active site. Presence of catalytic residues implicates this region in the enzymatic cleavage of DNA [[cite:PUB00010098],[cite:PUB00010100]].

Prokaryotic family found in type II restriction enzymes containing the hallmark (D/E)-(D/E)XK active site. Presence of catalytic residues implicates this region in the enzymatic cleavage of DNA [[cite:PUB00010098],[cite:PUB00010100]]

Prokaryotic family found in type II restriction enzymes containing the hallmark (D/E)-(D/E)XK active site. Presence of catalytic residues implicates this region in the enzymatic cleavage of DNA [[cite:PUB00010098],[cite:PUB00010100]].

Prokaryotic family found in type II restriction enzymes containing the hallmark (D/E)-(D/E)XK active site. Presence of catalytic residues implicates this region in the enzymatic cleavage of DNA [[cite:PUB00010098],[cite:PUB00010100]]

This domain is found at the N-terminus of the Mrr restriction endonuclease catalytic domain, [pfam:PF04471] [[cite:PUB00010100],[cite:PUB00057935]]. Fold recognition analysis predicts that it is a diverged member of the winged helix variant of helix turn helix proteins. It may play a role in DNA sequence recognition [[cite:PUB00057935]].

This entry represents eukaryotic membrane transporters distantly related to prokaryotic CorA transporters, including the inner mitochondrial membrane Mg2+ transporters Mfm1p/Lpe10p and Mrs2p from yeast, MRS2/MRSL from human and the homologues from plants [[cite:PUB00154083]].

This family consists of mammalian MRVI1 proteins which are related to the lymphoid-restricted membrane protein (JAW1) and the IP3 receptor associated cGMP kinase substrates A and B (IRAGA and IRAGB). The function of MRVI1 is unknown although mutations in the Mrvi1 gene induces myeloid leukaemia by altering the expression of a gene important for myeloid cell growth and/or differentiation so it has been speculated that Mrvi1 is a tumour suppressor gene [[cite:PUB00011374]]. IRAG is very similar in sequence to MRVI1 and is an essential NO/cGKI-dependent regulator of IP3-induced calcium release. Activation of cGKI decreases IP3-stimulated elevations in intracellular calcium, induces smooth muscle relaxation and contributes to the antiproliferative and pro-apoptotic effects of NO/cGMP [[cite:PUB00011375]]. Jaw1 is a member of a class of proteins with COOH-terminal hydrophobic membrane anchors and is structurally similar to proteins involved in vesicle targeting and fusion. This suggests that the function and/or the structure of the ER in lymphocytes may be modified by lymphoid-restricted resident ER proteins [[cite:PUB00011376]].
This entry includes budding yeast MIOREX complex component 7 (Mrx7), which associates with mitochondrial ribosome [[cite:PUB00076405]]. Its function is not clear.
This domain appears at the C-terminus of many of the proteins that carry the MR_MLE_N [pfam:PF02746] domain. [ec:4.2.1.40].

Pfam_Description: Mandelate racemase / muconate lactonizing enzyme, N-terminal domain
Pfam_name: Mandelate racemase / muconate lactonizing enzyme, N-terminal domain
Pfam_description: SCOP reports fold similarity with enolase N-terminal domain.

She1 seems to be related to the spindle integrity function of the Dam1 complex. She1 is a dynein regulator and limits dynein offloading by gating the recruitment of dynactin to the astral microtubule plus end. Aurora B phosphorylates She1, modulating its potency against dynein [[cite:PUB00110797]].

This domain of unknown function is found in fungal proteins including Mug8 from Schizosaccharomyces pombe which may have a role in meiosis and septation [[cite:PUB00044889]]. Saccharomyces cerevisiae homologue MSB1 (swiss:P21339) may be involved in positive regulation of 1,3-beta-glucan synthesis and the Pkc1p-MAPK pathway [[cite:PUB00087082]].

MAN1 is an integral protein of the inner nuclear membrane which binds to chromatin associated proteins and plays a role in nuclear organisation. The C terminal nucleoplasmic region forms a DNA binding winged helix and binds to Smad [[cite:PUB00040011]]. This C-terminal tail is also found in S. cerevisiae and is thought to consist of three conserved helices followed by two downstream strands [[cite:PUB00057231]].

The small mechanosensitive channel, MscS, is a part of the turgor-driven solute efflux system that protects bacteria from lysis in the event of osmotic shock. The MscS protein alone is sufficient to form a functional mechanosensitive channel gated directly by tension in the lipid bilayer. The MscS proteins are heptamers of three transmembrane subunits with seven converging M3 domains, and this MscS_porin is towards the N-terminal of the molecules. The high concentration of negative charges at the extracellular entrance of the pore helps select the cations for efflux.

Pfam_Description: Mechanosensitive ion channel inner membrane domain 1
Pfam_name: Mechanosensitive ion channel inner membrane domain 1
Pfam_description: The small mechanosensitive channel, MscS, is a part of the turgor-driven solute efflux system that protects bacteria from lysis in the event of osmotic shock. The MscS protein alone is sufficient to form a functional mechanosensitive channel gated directly by tension in the lipid bilayer. The MscS proteins are heptamers of three transmembrane subunits with seven converging M3 domains, and this domain is one of the inner membrane domains.
This domain is found in bacterial deaminases. Some members of this family also contain RHS repeats.

This is a novel repeat in Pneumocystis carinii Major surface glycoprotein (MSG) some members of the alignment have up to nine repeats of this family, the repeats containing several conserved cysteines. The MSG of P. carinii is an important protein in host-pathogen interactions [[cite:PUB00008113]]. Surface glycoprotein A [swissprot:O59920] from Pneumocystis carinii is a main target for the host immune system, this protein is implicated in the attachment of Pneumocystis carinii to the host alveolar epithelial cells, alveolar macrophages, host surfactant and possibly accounts in part for the hypoxia seen in Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (PCP) [[cite:PUB00008112]].

This domain family is found in eukaryotes, and is approximately 30 amino acids in length. The family is found in association with [pfam:PF02349]. This family is the C terminal of major surface glycoprotein 2 of virulent bacteria. It is a virulence factor antigen.

Pfam_Description: Malate synthase G, alpha-beta insertion domain
Pfam_name: Malate synthase G, alpha-beta insertion domain
Pfam_description: Malate synthase (MS) catalyses the aldol condensation of glyoxylate with acetyl-CoA to form malate as part of the second step of the glyoxylate bypass and an alternative to the tricarboxylic acid cycle in bacteria, fungi and plants. There have been identified two isoforms, A and G (MSA and MSG, respectively) that differ in size and is attributed to an inserted alpha/beta domain in MSG that may have regulatory function [[cite:PUB00051135],[cite:PUB00029759],[cite:PUB00014321],[cite:PUB00032598]]. Members of the isoform G family are only found in bacteria. This entry represents the alpha/beta insertion domain from MSG, which buttressed one side of the TIM-barrel domain [[cite:PUB00051135]].

This domain is found at the N-terminus of the Type II secretion secretion system protein E (GspE) and type IV pilus extensin ATPase PilB and near the C-terminus of the glycosyltransferase NfrB. A variant of this domain, called MshEN, binds cyclic di-GMP [[cite:PUB00151574],[cite:PUB00106044],[cite:PUB00104722]], which modulates the activity of the respective protein. The structure of this domain is now known [[cite:PUB00033663],[cite:PUB00033664],[cite:PUB00151574]].

MSL1_dimer is the short coiled dimerisation domain of higher eukaryotic MSL1, part of the MSL or Male-Specific Lethal complex. This complex regulates the dosage compensation of the male X chromosome in Drosophila and other eukaryotes. The structure of the MSL1/MSL2 core shows that two MSL2 subunits bind to a dimer formed by two molecules of MSL1. MSL11 is a substrate for MSL2 E3 ubiquitin ligase activity [[cite:PUB00065184]].

Pfam_Description: CXC domain of E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase MSL2
Pfam_name: CXC domain of E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase MSL2
Pfam_description: MSL2-CXC is an autonomously folded domain containing that binds three zinc ions. It lies on the E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase MSL2 in eukaryotes. The CXC domain critically contributes to the DNA-binding activity of MSL2 [[cite:PUB00062525]]. It carries 9 invariant cysteines within about a 50 residue region.

This domain is found in Male-specific lethal-3 (MSL3) and other related proteins such as MRG15 transcription factor. MSL3 resides in the MSL (male-specific lethal) complex, which upregulates transcription by spreading the histone H4 Lys16 acetyl mark. The MSL3 chromo domain implicated in chromatin targeting and its deletion leads to the disruption of MSL targeting. The MRG15 chromo domain is involved in chromatin remodelling and transcription regulation. This domain consists of a SH3-like beta-barrel and a long alpha-helix.

This entry represents a domain predicted to be an active, minimal version of the SLOG domain. It is found N-terminally fused to the DUF4326 domain ([pfam:PF14216]). It may play a role in base cleavage, potentially forming abasic sites acted on by DuOB domain ([pfam:PF22557]) [[cite:PUB00153826]].

Members of this entry are restricted to members of the Actinobacteria that synthesise PQQ. These are small proteins 155 amino acids long on average, found regularly next to a much larger protein, a PQQ-dependent oxidoreductase, and might be a companion subunit or an accessory protein such as chaperone involved in cofactor insertion.

Mso1p is a component of the secretory vesicle docking complex whose function is closely associated with that of Sec1p. It is a small hydrophilic protein that is enriched in the microsomal membrane fraction [[cite:PUB00067508]], and this binding domain is towards the N-terminus of Mso1. The yeast Sec1p protein functions in the docking of secretory transport vesicles to the plasma membrane [[cite:PUB00067509]]. Mso1p and Sec1p interact at sites of exocytosis and the Mso1p-Sec1p interaction site depends on a functional Rab GTPase Sec4p and its GEF Sec2p [[cite:PUB00067510]]. The C-terminal region of Mso1 (not built) assists in targetting Sec1 to the sites of polarised membrane transport [[cite:PUB00067511]].

This family consists of the 33 KDa photosystem II polypeptide from the oxygen evolving complex (OEC) of plants and cyanobacteria. The protein is also known as the manganese-stabilising protein as it is associated with the manganese complex of the OEC and may provide the ligands for the complex [[cite:PUB00003726]].

MSP1a is part of the A.marginale major surface protein 1 (MSP1) complex and exists as a heterodimer with MSP1b. The complex has adhesive functions in bovine erythrocytes invasion [[cite:PUB00053534]].

The major surface protein (MSP1) of the cattle pathogen Anaplasma is a heterodimer comprised of MSP1a and MSP1b. This family is the MSP1b chain. There MSP1 proteins are putative adhesins for bovine erythrocytes.

This entry represents a beta barrel domain found towards the N-terminal of phage Tuc2009 receptor binding protein (RBP) which forms the head domain, involved in carbohydrate recognition [[cite:PUB00151805]].

This family represents the C-terminal region of merozoite surface protein 1 (MSP1) which are found in a number of Plasmodium species. MSP-1 is a 200-kDa protein expressed on the surface of the P. vivax merozoite. MSP-1 of Plasmodium species is synthesised as a high-molecular-weight precursor and then processed into several fragments. At the time of red cell invasion by the merozoite, only the 19-kDa C-terminal fragment (MSP-119), which contains two epidermal growth factor-like domains, remains on the surface. Antibodies against MSP-119 inhibit merozoite entry into red cells, and immunisation with MSP-119 protects monkeys from challenging infections. Hence, MSP-119 is considered a promising vaccine candidate [[cite:PUB00013167]].
MSP7 is a protein family the malaria parasite that has been found to be associated with processed fragments from the MSP1 protein in a complex involved in red blood cell invasion.

MspA is a membrane porin produced by Mycobacteria, allowing hydrophilic nutrients to enter the bacterium. The protein forms a tightly interconnected octamer with eightfold rotation symmetry that resembles a goblet and contains a central channel. Each subunit fold contains a beta-sandwich of Ig-like topology and a beta-ribbon arm that forms an oligomeric transmembrane barrel [[cite:PUB00031908]].

Pfam_Description: Selenoprotein methionine sulfoxide reductase A, helical domain
Pfam_name: Selenoprotein methionine sulfoxide reductase A, helical domain
Pfam_description: This domain is found in 1-Cys type selenoprotein methionine sulfoxide reductase A (MsrA) from the bacteria Clostridium oremlandii, a repair enzyme for proteins that have been inactivated by oxidation that is found both in prokaryotes and eukaryotes. MsrA catalyses the reduction of methionine sulfoxide in proteins to methionine. This enzyme is organised into a catalytic domain ([pfam:PF01625]) and a helical domain (this entry) absent in most of the known MsrA structures. It consists of five helices, interacts with the catalytic domain and is essential for the active site formation [[cite:PUB00151656],[cite:PUB00151657]].
This presumed domain is found at the C-terminus of the MSS51 protein.
This family of drosophila proteins are typified by the repetitive motif C-G-P.

This is a SH3-like domain associated with the MutS-like ABC ATPase and Smr domains. It has been predicted to play a role in lesion recognition or alternatively in mediating contacts with RNA primers or misincorporated ribonucleotides during DNA repair or interacting with the ribosome at the intersection between DNA repair and ribosome rescue [[cite:PUB00101219]].

Pfam_Description: C terminal SARAH domain of Mst1
Pfam_name: C terminal SARAH domain of Mst1
Pfam_description: This family of proteins represents the C terminal SARAH domain of Mst1. SARAH controls apoptosis and cell cycle arrest via the Ras, RASSF, MST pathway. The Mst1 SARAH domain interacts with Rassf1 and Rassf5 by forming a heterodimer which mediates the apoptosis process [[cite:PUB00041953]].

This family includes Male-specific sperm protein Mst87F from Drosophila melanogaster, the product of a transcript expressed in the germline from late pupal stages onward that overlaps with one of the enhancers of the pri transcriptional unit, which encodes the smORF peptides represented in [pfam:PF22856] [[cite:PUB00154084]].
This domain was identified by Iyer and colleagues [[cite:PUB00010111]].

The MsyB protein has been found to be able to restore protein export defects caused by a temperature-sensitive secY or secA mutation [[cite:PUB00057923]]. However, its exact molecular function is still unknown, but it may play a role in protein export. Proteins in this family are approximately 120 amino acids in length. This family of proteins is found in bacteria.

Malate synthase (MS) catalyses the aldol condensation of glyoxylate with acetyl-CoA to form malate as part of the second step of the glyoxylate bypass and an alternative to the tricarboxylic acid cycle in bacteria, fungi and plants. There have been identified two isoforms, A and G (MSA and MSG, respectively) that differ in size and is attributed to an inserted alpha/beta domain in MSG that may have regulatory function [[cite:PUB00051135],[cite:PUB00029759]]. In malate synthases, the TIM beta/alpha-barrel fold and the C-terminal helical domain are well conserved and the cleft between them forms the active site [[cite:PUB00051135],[cite:PUB00029759],[cite:PUB00014321],[cite:PUB00032598]]. This entry represents the C-terminal domain which consists of a five-helix 'plug' connected to the barrel by an extended loop and caps the active site.

This entry includes small conductance mechanosensitive channels (MscS), which assembles to a homoheptameric complex [[cite:PUB00019883],[cite:PUB00019884],[cite:PUB00019885],[cite:PUB00101037],[cite:PUB00064132],[cite:PUB00062568]]. Each monomer consists of a N-terminal transmembrane region and a large cytoplasmic segment composed of a five-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet (middle/second) domain and a C-terminal alpha/beta-domain [[cite:PUB00101037],[cite:PUB00064132],[cite:PUB00062568]]. The N-terminal region consists of three membrane spanning helices (TM1, TM2 and TM3), TM2 and TM3 are represented in this entry. In the heptamer, the permeation pathway is formed by the packing of TM3s, flanked by TM1-TM2 helical hairpins [[cite:PUB00101037]].

Pfam_Description: Mechanosensitive ion channel, conserved TM helix
Pfam_name: Mechanosensitive ion channel, conserved TM helix
Pfam_description: This alignment represents a conserved transmembrane helix, often found in small conductance mechanosensitive channels (MscS) in association with [pfam:PF00924] [[cite:PUB00101037],[cite:PUB00062568],[cite:PUB00064132]], such as [swissprot:Q57634] and [swissprot:Q58543] MscS assembles to a homoheptameric complex; each monomer consists of a N-terminal transmembrane region and a large cytoplasmic segment composed of a five-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet (middle/second) domain ([pfam:PF00924]) and a C-terminal alpha/beta-domain ([pfam:PF21082]) [[cite:PUB00101037],[cite:PUB00062568],[cite:PUB00064132]]. The N-terminal region consists of three membrane spanning helices (TM1, TM2 and TM3), TM1 is represented in this entry. In the heptamer, the permeation pathway is formed by the packing of TM3s, flanked by TM1-TM2 helical hairpins [[cite:PUB00101037],[cite:PUB00062568],[cite:PUB00064132]].

This entry includes small conductance mechanosensitive channels (MscS), which assembles to a homoheptameric complex [[cite:PUB00019883],[cite:PUB00019884],[cite:PUB00019885],[cite:PUB00101036],[cite:PUB00062568],[cite:PUB00101037]]. Each monomer consists of a N-terminal transmembrane region and a large cytoplasmic segment composed of a five-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet (middle/second) domain and a C-terminal alpha/beta-domain [[cite:PUB00101036],[cite:PUB00062568],[cite:PUB00101037],[cite:PUB00064132]]. This is the beta domain which adopts a SH3-like barrel structure.

This entry includes small conductance mechanosensitive channels (MscS), which assembles to a homoheptameric complex [[cite:PUB00019883],[cite:PUB00019884],[cite:PUB00019885],[cite:PUB00101036],[cite:PUB00101037],[cite:PUB00064132]]. Each monomer consists of a N-terminal transmembrane region and a large cytoplasmic segment composed of a five-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet domain (beta-domain, [pfam:PF00924]) and a C-terminal alpha/beta-domain [[cite:PUB00019883],[cite:PUB00019884],[cite:PUB00019885]]. This is the C-terminal domain of McsS which, together with the middle beta-domain, creates a framework that connects to the cytoplasm through distinct openings [[cite:PUB00101036],[cite:PUB00101037],[cite:PUB00064132]].

Malate synthase (MS) catalyses the aldol condensation of glyoxylate with acetyl-CoA to form malate as part of the second step of the glyoxylate bypass and an alternative to the tricarboxylic acid cycle in bacteria, fungi and plants. There have been identified two isoforms, A and G (MSA and MSG, respectively) that differ in size and is attributed to an inserted alpha/beta domain in MSG that may have regulatory function [[cite:PUB00051135],[cite:PUB00029759]]. They consist of an N-terminal alpha-helical claps, a central TIM barrel and a C-terminal alpha-helical plug. This entry represents the N-terminal clasp that wraps around one side of the TIM barrel and buttressed it [[cite:PUB00051135],[cite:PUB00029759],[cite:PUB00014321],[cite:PUB00032598]].

Malate synthase (MS) catalyses the aldol condensation of glyoxylate with acetyl-CoA to form malate as part of the second step of the glyoxylate bypass and an alternative to the tricarboxylic acid cycle in bacteria, fungi and plants. There have been identified two isoforms, A and G (MSA and MSG, respectively) that differ in size and is attributed to an inserted alpha/beta domain in MSG that may have regulatory function [[cite:PUB00014321],[cite:PUB00051135]]. In malate synthases, the TIM beta/alpha-barrel fold and the C-terminal domain are well conserved and the cleft between them forms the active site [[cite:PUB00014321],[cite:PUB00051135],[cite:PUB00029759],[cite:PUB00032598]]. MSA and MSG consist of an N-terminal alpha-helical clasp domain, a central TIM barrel domain and a C-terminal helical plug domain. This is the TIM barrel domain of malate synthases.

the 380 kDa motor unit of dynein belongs to the AAA class of chaperone-like ATPases. The core of the 380 kDa motor unit contains a concatenated chain of six AAA modules, of which four correspond to the ATP binding sites with P-loop signatures described previously, and two are modules in which the P loop has been lost in evolution. This family is the region between D4 and D5 and is the two predicted alpha-helical coiled coil segments that form the stalk supporting the ATP-sensitive microtubule binding component [[cite:PUB00028625]].
MT-A70 is the S-adenosylmethionine-binding subunit of human mRNA:m6A methyl-transferase (MTase), an enzyme that sequence-specifically methylates adenines in pre-mRNAs.
This protein family represents human Mitochondrial-derived peptide MOTS-c (MT-RNR1), a 16-residue peptide that regulates insulin sensitivity and metabolic homeostasis [[cite:PUB00154085]].

This family of proteins contains the MT0933 protein [swissprot:O05901] which has been identified as an antitoxin to /protein MT0934 [[cite:PUB00067485]]. This family of proteins is found in bacteria. Proteins in this family are typically between 61 and 90 amino acids in length.

This family of proteins is found in bacteria and archaea. Proteins in this family are approximately 460 amino acids in length. MtaB folds as a TIM barrel and contains a novel zinc-binding motif. Zinc(II) lies at the bottom of a funnel formed at the C-terminal beta-barrel end and ligates to two cysteinyl sulfurs (Cys-220 and Cys-269) and one carboxylate oxygen (Glu-164). The function of this protein is to catalyse the cleavage of the C O bond in methanol by an SN2 mechanism. It complexes with MtaA and MtaC to perform this function.

Pfam_Description: Mitochondrial ABC-transporter N-terminal five TM region
Pfam_name: Mitochondrial ABC-transporter N-terminal five TM region
Pfam_description: MTABC_N is the N-terminal five transmembrane helices of eukaryotic mitochondrial ABC-transporters.
This is a globular domain found across several restriction- modification systems [[cite:PUB00101219]].

The R1 domain is found in the MTA1 protein and its homologues. The domain is composed of 4 alpha helices [[cite:PUB00085227]]. It has been shown to bind to the RBBP4 protein [[cite:PUB00085227]]. The MTA proteins contain a second partial copy of this domain called R2. The R2 domain is matched by this model for some proteins.

MTBP, or MDM2-binding protein, binds to MDM2. The MDM2 protein, through its interaction with p53, plays an important role in the regulation of the G1 checkpoint of the cell cycle [[cite:PUB00070069]]. MTBP promotes MDM2-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of p53 and also MDM2 stabilisation in an MDM2 RING finger-dependent manner [[cite:PUB00068081]]. MTBP differentially regulates the E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of MDM2 towards two of its most critical targets (itself and p53) and in doing so significantly contributes to MDM2-dependent p53 homeostasis in unstressed cells [[cite:PUB00068081]]. MTBP inhibits cancer cell migration by interacting with a protein involved in cell motility. This motility protein is alpha-actinin-4 (ACTN4) [[cite:PUB00070070]]. It is unclear which regions of MTBP interact with which binding-partner. See PF14919, PF14920.
