Nrap appears to be associated with ribosome biogenesis by interacting with pre-rRNA primary transcript [[cite:PUB00008443]].

NRBF2 plays an essential role in autophagy, the cellular pathway that degrades long-lived proteins and other cytoplasmic contents through lysosomes. NRBF2 binds Atg14L - a Beclin-binding protein - directly via the MIT domain and enhances Atg14L-linked Vps34 kinase (a class III phosphatidylinositol-3 kinase) activity and autophagy induction [[cite:PUB00078728]].

Pfam_Description: MIT domain of nuclear receptor-binding factor 2
Pfam_name: MIT domain of nuclear receptor-binding factor 2
Pfam_description: This MIT domain is the microtubule interaction and trafficking of nuclear receptor-binding factor 2 - NRBF2 - in higher eukaryotes. It is a coiled-coil region at the N-terminus of [pfam:PF08961] [[cite:PUB00078727]]. NRBF2 plays an essential role in autophagy, the cellular pathway that degrades long-lived proteins and other cytoplasmic contents through lysosomes. NRBF2 binds Atg14L - a Beclin-binding protein - directly via the MIT domain and enhances Atg14L-linked Vps34 kinase (a class III phosphatidylinositol-3 kinase) activity and autophagy induction [[cite:PUB00078728]].

Nrd1 is a heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein (hnRNP)-like RNA-binding protein, part of the Nrd1-Nab3-Sen1 (NNS) complex which is involved in the termination and processing of short RNA polymerase II transcripts [[cite:PUB00140673]]. Seb1 is the Nrd1 homologue from S. pombe that is essential for cell viability and binds directly to Rpb7 subunit of RNA polymerase II. It functions in terminating all classes of Pol II-transcribed genes genome-wide. These proteins have a RNA-recognition motif (RRM, [pfam:PF00076]) fused to a second alpha/beta domain described as domain 2 (also referred to as the split domain, SD, in [[cite:PUB00151774]]) from Nrd1 and Seb1. This domain is essential and forms a rigid body with the canonical RRM that interacts with RNA [[cite:PUB00140673],[cite:PUB00152056],[cite:PUB00151774]].

This entry comprises two domains found in the nitrogen regulatory protein NrpR that bind DNA and repress transcription of nitrogen assimilation genes. The two NrpR regulatory domains (NRD1 and NRD2) that sense and bind 2-oxoglutarate (2OG) are both structurally and functionally homologous and share a high degree of sequence conservation. Mutational analysis of NrpR from Methanococcus maripaludis (MmNrpR) indicated that the two most critical residues for 2OG binding are Cys389 and His435 (Cys395 and His441, respectively in thermophilic archaeon Methanocaldococcus jannaschii (MjNrpR)). Both the Cys395 and His441 are conserved among NrpR proteins from diverse species [[cite:PUB00086621]].

This is a family of eukaryotic proteins. Eukaryotic cells express a wide variety of endogenous small regulatory RNAs that regulate heterochromatin formation, developmental timing, defence against parasitic nucleic acids, and genome rearrangement. Many small regulatory RNAs are thought to function in nuclei, and in plants and fungi small interfering (si)RNAs associate with nascent transcripts and direct chromatin and/or DNA modifications. This family protein, NRDE-2, is required for small interfering (si)RNA-mediated silencing in nuclei. NRDE-2 associates with the Argonaute protein NRDE-3 within nuclei and is recruited by NRDE-3/siRNA complexes to nascent transcripts that have been targeted by RNA interference, RNAi, the process whereby double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) directs the sequence-specific degradation of mRNA [[cite:PUB00057435]].
This conserved region is found in the C-terminal region of archaeal Nre proteins. While most archaeal organisms encode only a single Nre protein, some encode two, NreA and NreB.
This conserved region is found in the N-terminal region of archaeal Nre proteins. While most archaeal organisms encode only a single Nre protein, some encode two, NreA and NreB.

Pfam_Description: Nrf1 activator activation site binding domain
NLS-binding and DNA-binding and dimerisation domains of Nrf1
Pfam_name: NLS-binding and DNA-binding and dimerisation domains of Nrf1
Pfam_description: In Drosophila, the erect wing (ewg) protein is required for proper development of the central nervous system and the indirect flight muscles. The fly ewg gene encodes a novel DNA-binding domain that is also found in four genes previously identified in sea urchin, chicken, zebrafish, and human [[cite:PUB00044398]]. Nuclear respiratory factor-1 is a transcriptional activator that has been implicated in the nuclear control of respiratory chain expression in vertebrates. The first 26 amino acids of nuclear respiratory factor-1 are required for the binding of dynein light chain. The interaction with dynein light chain is observed for both ewg and Nrf-1, transcription factors that are structurally and functionally similar between humans and Drosophila [[cite:PUB00044399]]. The highest level of expression of both ewg and Nrf-1 was found in the central nervous system, somites, first branchial arch, optic vesicle, and otic vesicle. In the mouse Nrf-1 protein, Swiss-Prot:Q8C4C0, there is also an NLS domain at 88-116, and a DNA binding and dimerisation domain at 127-282. Ewg is a site-specific transcriptional activator, and evolutionarily conserved regions of ewg contribute both positively and negatively to transcriptional activity [[cite:PUB00044400]].

NrfD is an integral transmembrane protein with loops in both the periplasm and the cytoplasm. NrfD is thought to participate in the transfer of electrons, from the quinone pool into the terminal components of the Nrf pathway [[cite:PUB00006649]].

Bacterial polysulfide reductase is an integral membrane protein complex responsible for quinone-coupled reduction of polysulfide, a process important in extreme environments such as deep-sea vents and hot springs. Polysulfides are a class of compounds composed of chains of sulfur atoms, which in their simplest form are present as an anion with general formula Sn(2-). In nature, polysulfides are found in particularly high concentrations in extreme volcanic or geothermically active environments. Here, the reduction and oxidation of polysulfides are vital processes for many bacteria and are essential steps in the global sulfur cycle. In particular, the reduction of polysulfide to hydrogen sulfide in these environments is usually linked to energy-generating respiratory processes, supporting growth of many microorganisms, particularly hyperthermophiles.
This is the N-terminal domain of rhomboid protease [[cite:PUB00041146]].
This domain is the first (N-terminal) repression domain of nuclear receptor-interacting protein 1 [[cite:PUB00075793],[cite:PUB00060898]].
This domain is the second repression domain of nuclear receptor-interacting protein 1 [[cite:PUB00075793],[cite:PUB00060898]].
This domain is the third repression domain of nuclear receptor-interacting protein 1 [[cite:PUB00075793],[cite:PUB00060898]].
This domain is the fourth (C-terminal) repression domain of nuclear receptor-interacting protein 1 [[cite:PUB00075793],[cite:PUB00060898]].

The domain family Neuritin1 (NRN1) is a GPI-anchored protein expressed in post-mitotic-differentiating neurons in the developing nervous system [[cite:PUB00060119]]. NRN1 is a glutamate and neurotrophin receptor target encoding a neuronal protein that functions extracellularly to modulate neurite outgrowth (OMIM:607409). This family of proteins is found in eukaryotes. Proteins in this family are typically between and 158 amino acids in length.

In fission yeast, this protein is a positive regulator of the stability of Sre1N, the sterol regulatory element-binding protein which is an ER membrane-bound transcription factor that controls adaptation to low oxygen-growth [[cite:PUB00055996]]. In addition, the fission yeast Nro1 is a direct inhibitor of a protein that inhibits SreN1 degradation, Ofd1 (an oxoglutamate deoxygenase). The outcome of this reactivity is that Ofd1 acts as an oxygen sensor that regulates the binding of Nro1 to Ofd1 to control the stability of Sre1N [[cite:PUB00045331]]. Solution of the structure of Nro1 reveals it to be made up of a number of TPR coils [[cite:PUB00056187]]. TPR proteins are composed of three to 16 tandem peptide repeat motifs of 34 amino acids with degenerate sequence. The helical pairs adopt a helix-turn-helix anti-parallel arrangement with interacting helices. In general, TPR motifs are stacked together so that helix A from TPRn is packed between helix B from TPRn and helix A from TPRn+1. In Nro1, the 12 alpha helices forming the six TPR motifs are organised as follows from N terminus to C terminus - TPR1A, TPR1B, TPR2A, TPR2B, TPR3A, TPR3B, TPR4A, TPR4B, TPR5A, TPR5B, TPR6A, and TPR6B with the C-terminal helix (hC) running above the sixth TPR motif with an angle of approx 45 degrees with TPR6A and TPR6B. The corresponding TPRs structural motifs are longer (50 residues) than are canonical ones (34 amino acids) and are organised into two subdomains - Nro1-N (residues 55-225) and Nro1-C (residues 226-393). The Nro1/Etti protein plays a role in nuclear import suggesting that it is residues 4-19 that are interacting with Ofd1 [[cite:PUB00056187]].
This entry represents the C-terminal region of fission yeast Negative regulator of ofd1 (Nro1) whose alpha-helices are grouped in six helical hairpins [[cite:PUB00154119],[cite:PUB00056187]].

Pfam_Description: Nuclear speckle splicing regulatory protein 1, RS-like domain
Pfam_name: Nuclear speckle splicing regulatory protein 1, RS-like domain
Pfam_description: This domain found at the C-terminal of Nuclear speckle splicing regulatory protein 1 (NRP1, also known as Nuclear speckle-related protein 70 and Coiled-coil domain-containing protein 55). This is the RS-like domain, that resembles the arginine/serine-rich (RS) domain in other SR proteins, interacts with two SR proteins and with target mRNA, being essential for NRP1 activity. NRP1 is a RNA-binding protein that mediates pre-mRNA alternative splicing regulation [[cite:PUB00093375],[cite:PUB00093376]].

This entry represents the head domain found in NrS-1 polymerase from Nitratiruptor phage NrS-1, the first known phage that can infect Epsilonproteobacteria, one of the predominant primary producers in the deep-sea hydrothermal vent ecosystems. NrS-1 polymerase is a multidomain enzyme and is a key component of the phage replisome [[cite:PUB00151922]]. This domain, together with the helicase and tail domains, is responsible for the DNA activity in this protein. It has a novel alpha/beta fold [[cite:PUB00151922]].

This entry represents the tail domain found in NrS-1 polymerase from Nitratiruptor phage NrS-1, the first known phage that can infect Epsilonproteobacteria, one of the predominant primary producers in the deep-sea hydrothermal vent ecosystems. NrS-1 polymerase is a multidomain enzyme and is a key component of the phage replisome [[cite:PUB00151922]]. This domain, together with the head ([pfam:PF22761]) and helicase ([pfam:PF19263]) domains, is responsible for the DNA activity in this protein. It has a novel alpha/beta fold [[cite:PUB00151922]].The tail domain is important for the hexamer assembly and polymerization activity of NrS-1 polymerase [[cite:PUB00151922]].

This family includes CC3252 (NrsF- Negative regulator of sigma F) from Caulobacter crescentus, which is proposed to be an anti-sigma factor. In particular, overexpression of NrsF prevents the induction of the sigF regulon after dichromate stress [[cite:PUB00086036]]. Family members also include the anti-sigma factor OsrA (blr3039) from Bradyrhizobium japonicum, which is involved in sensing reactive oxygen species. There is evidence that OsrA binds an ECF-type sigma factor (EcfF) in vivo. Furthermore, the conserved cysteine residues 129 and 179 of OsrA are shown to be required for normal function [[cite:PUB00109140]]. Family members have 6 predicted transmembrane regions.

This entry represents the C-terminal DNA-binding domain of bacterial transcriptional regulator NrtR which is involved in regulating the transcription of NAD biosynthetic genes. This domain has a winged helix-turn-helix structure [[cite:PUB00052992]].

This is a repeat domain involved in dimerisation of nuclear receptors proteins and in transcriptional regulation in general. It contains a Leu-Xaa-Xaa-Leu-Leu motif which has been characterized for the orphan nuclear receptor Dax-1, which represses the constitutively expressed protein Ad4BP/SF-1. The LXXLL motif plays in important role in binding of Dax-1 to Ad4BP/SF-1 [[cite:PUB00058216]]. The domain is subject to structure determination by the Joint Center of Structural Genomics.

This domain is the transactivation domain of the Parvovirus NS1 protein, located immediately C-terminal to the helicase [[cite:PUB00096849],[cite:PUB00083690]]. Parvovirus are some of the smallest viruses containing linear, non-segmented single-stranded DNA genomes, with an average genome size of 5000 nucleotides. They infect a wide range of invertebrates and vertebrates and are well known for causing enteric disease in mammals. Genomes contain two large ORFs: NS1 and VP1; other ORFs are found in some sub-types and different gene products can arise from splice variants and the use of different start codons [[cite:PUB00054921]]. NS1 protein is essential for viral life cycle stages, including DNA replication, trans-regulation of the two viral promoters and modulation of heterologous promoters. It exhibits DNA binding, endonuclease and helicase activities and is the major contributor to the toxic effect on host cells [[cite:PUB00096898]].

This is a family of proteins found in Densoviruses. Members of this family such as NS3 found in Junonia coenia have been shown to be involved in viral DNA replication. Generation of deletion mutants and replicative cycle analysis show that NS3 is required for viral DNA replication [[cite:PUB00085259]]. Bioinformatics analysis of Bombyx mori densovirus protein NS3, show that it has two putative zinc-finger motifs, 6 putative N glycosylation sites, and 4 putative phosphorylation sites [[cite:PUB00085260]].

Pfam_Description: NS3 RNA helicase, C-terminal helical domain
Pfam_name: NS3 RNA helicase, C-terminal helical domain
Pfam_description: This entry represents the C-terminal all-alpha helical domain (referred to as domain 3) of hepatitis C virus RNA helicase (NS3) [[cite:PUB00023240],[cite:PUB00028307],[cite:PUB00025639],[cite:PUB00040542],[cite:PUB00058566]]. NS3 helicase consists of three domains, separated by a series of clefts. Bound ssDNA lies in a channel that separates domain 3 from domains 1 and 2. The 5' end of the oligonucleotide resides at the interface of domains 2 and 3 and its 3' end is positioned at the interface of domains 1. This domain is associated with domain 2 by a pair of antiparallel beta-strands [[cite:PUB00023240],[cite:PUB00028307],[cite:PUB00025639],[cite:PUB00040542],[cite:PUB00058566]].

Pfam_Description: Binding domain of Nse4/EID3 to Nse3-MAGE
Pfam_name: Binding domain of Nse4/EID3 to Nse3-MAGE
Pfam_description: This family includes Nse4 and EID3 members [[cite:PUB00069904]], that bind over this region to the Nse3 pocket, in MAGE family [pfam:PF01454] [[cite:PUB00069905]].

Nse4 is the kleisin component of the Smc5/6 DNA repair complex. It bridges the heads of Smc5 and Smc6 [[cite:PUB00045053],[cite:PUB00035433],[cite:PUB00069904],[cite:PUB00095747]]. This is the C-terminal domain of Nse4 that interacts with the head domain of Smc5 [[cite:PUB00095747]].

Pfam_Description: DNA repair proteins Nse5 and Nse6
Pfam_name: DNA repair proteins Nse5 and Nse6
Pfam_description: Nse5 and Nse6 are non essential nuclear proteins that are critical for chromosome segregation in fission yeast [[cite:PUB00035434]]. Nse5 forms a dimer with Nse6 and facilitates DNA repair as part of the Smc5-Smc6 holocomplex.

This entry represents the ATPase lid domain of the second AAA+ ATP-binding domain (also known as D2) of NSF proteins [[cite:PUB00028321]], found at the C-terminal. NFS proteins are essential membrane fusion events. They play the role of a chaperone by activating SNAP receptor proteins (SNAREs) so that they can participate in membrane fusion [[cite:PUB00028321],[cite:PUB00022273],[cite:PUB00154121],[cite:PUB00154122],[cite:PUB00154123]].
This family probably forms a coiled-coil [[cite:PUB00010195]]. This important region of Nsp1 is involved in binding Nup82 [[cite:PUB00010195]].

Pfam_Description: Immunogenic region of nsp2 protein of arterivirus polyprotein
Pfam_name: Immunogenic region of nsp2 protein of arterivirus polyprotein
Pfam_description: This domain is in a non-essential part of the nsp2 (non-structural protein) subunit section of the arterivirus polyprotein. This domain carries seven small sequence-regions that are predicted to be potential B-cell epitopes.

Pfam_Description: Non-essential region of nsp2 of arterivirus polyprotein
Pfam_name: Non-essential region of nsp2 of arterivirus polyprotein
Pfam_description: This non-essential region of the nsp2 subunit of the arterivirus polyprotein of such as porcine arterivirus PRRSV and equine arterivirus EAV may offer immunogenic surfaces to B-cells. It is associated with Peptidase_C33, [pfam:PF05412].

This domain is found in Nsp2 protein of the RNA-arteriviruses, such as porcine arterivirus PRRSV and equine arterivirus EAV, which is a tetraspanning transmembrane protein. This domain resides adjacent to the peptidase C33 catalytic domain of Nsp2 [[cite:PUB00076813],[cite:PUB00052898]].

Avian infectious bronchitis virus (IBV) is a gammacoronavirus that belongs to Group III of coronaviruses. They have a large genome containing the replicase gene consisting of two large ORFs, ORF1a and 1b that encode two replicase polyproteins ppa1a/1ab, which are then auto-proteolytically processed into 15 or 16 matured nonstructural proteins to achieve viral genomic replication, assembly and maturation. This group contains avian viruses and differs from the other groups in that they do not encode the essential pathogenic factor non-structural protein 1 (NSP1) and instead start with NSP2. IBV NSP2 is one of the first replicase proteins to be translated and processed in the viral life cycle [[cite:PUB00095940]]. NSP2 is a weak protein kinase R (PKR) antagonist, which may suggest that it plays a role in interfering with intracellular immunity [[cite:PUB00095939]].

This domain is found in Non-structural protein 3 (nsP3) from Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) and similar proteins from Alphavirus. The function of nsP3, one of the four products of the polyprotein P1234, is still unknown. This protein consists of three domains: an amino-terminal Macro domain ([pfam:PF01661]), a central zinc- binding domain (ZBD, this entry), and a hypervariable-sequence carboxyl terminus. ZBD is essential for viral replication. It has two cysteines in a loop between alpha-helices and the other two cysteines at the end of two parallel beta-strands, which represent a structural scaffold for zinc-ion coordination [[cite:PUB00062497],[cite:PUB00151633]].

Pfam_Description: Nuclear speckle splicing regulatory protein 1, N-terminal
Pfam_name: Nuclear speckle splicing regulatory protein 1, N-terminal
Pfam_description: This domain is found at the N-terminal of Nuclear speckle splicing regulatory protein 1 (NRP1, also known as Nuclear speckle-related protein 70 and Coiled-coil domain-containing protein 55) and contains a coiled-coil domain that plays a critical role in NRP1 alternative splicing activity and self-oligomerization. NRP1 is a RNA-binding protein that mediates pre-mRNA alternative splicing regulation [[cite:PUB00093376],[cite:PUB00093375]].

Pfam_Description: Rift valley fever virus non structural protein (NSs) like
Pfam_name: Rift valley fever virus non structural protein (NSs) like
Pfam_description: This family contains several Phlebovirus non structural proteins which act as a major determinant of virulence by antagonising interferon beta gene expression [[cite:PUB00056025]].

NST1 is a family of proteins that seem to be involved, directly or indirectly, in the salt sensitivity of some cellular functions in yeast. It does this without affecting sodium accumulation. It negatively affects salt-tolerance through an interaction with the splicing factor Msl1p. This interaction stresses the importance of efficient RNA processing under salt stress conditions [[cite:PUB00057327]].
This is a novel domain of the STAND-superfamily of AAA+ ATPases found in bacterial conflict systems [[cite:PUB00100103]].

This is an inactive STAND-NTPase superfamily domain found in a mobile two-gene bacterial conflict systems. nSTAND2 is fused to various effector molecules. The neighbouring gene is an active STAND domain. These STAND NTPases define a novel family close to CR-ATPases, the mitochondrial apoptotic ribosomal protein S29/Dap3 and the mitochondria-associated STAND NTPase RNA12 [[cite:PUB00100103]].
This entry represents a novel domain of the STAND-superfamily of AAA+ ATPases found in bacterial conflict systems and in metazoan TRADD-N associated counter-invader proteins [[cite:PUB00100103]].

Pfam_Description: NOL1/NOP2/Sun domain family member 5, ferredoxin-like domain
Pfam_name: NOL1/NOP2/Sun domain family member 5, ferredoxin-like domain
Pfam_description: This is a ferredoxin-like domain of NOL1/NOP2/Sun domain family member 5, found at the N-terminal of the methyltransferase domain [[cite:PUB00026173]]. NSUN5 is a SAM-dependent methyltransferase that specifically methylates the C(5) position of cytosine 3782 in 28S rRNA [[cite:PUB00072550],[cite:PUB00151712]].

Pfam_Description: NOL1/NOP2/Sun domain family member 5, N-terminal domain
Pfam_name: NOL1/NOP2/Sun domain family member 5, N-terminal domain
Pfam_description: NSUN5 (and the homologue from yeast RCM1) is a SAM-dependent methyltransferase that specifically methylates the C(5) position of cytosine 3782 in 28S rRNA [[cite:PUB00151712]]. This is the N-terminal globular domain of NSUN5 which is required for targeting to nucleoli [[cite:PUB00151712]].

Pfam_Description: N-terminal C2 in EEIG1 and EHBP1 proteins
Pfam_name: N-terminal C2 in EEIG1 and EHBP1 proteins
Pfam_description: This version of the C2 domain was initally identified in the vertebrate estrogen early-induced gene 1 (EEIG1) [[cite:PUB00044243]], and its Drosophila ortholog required for uptake of dsRNA via the endocytotic machinery to induce RNAi silencing [[cite:PUB00057260]]. It is also in C.elegans ortholog Sym-3 (SYnthetic lethal with Mec-3) and the mammalian protein EHBP1 (EH domain Binding Protein-1) that regulates endocytotic recycling and two plant proteins, RPG that regulates Rhizobium-directed polar growth and PMI1 (Plastid Movement Impaired 1) that is essential for intracellular movement of chloroplasts in response to blue light [[cite:PUB00057260]].

Pfam_Description: 5' nucleotidase, deoxy (Pyrimidine), cytosolic type C protein (NT5C)
Pfam_name: 5' nucleotidase, deoxy (Pyrimidine), cytosolic type C protein (NT5C)
Pfam_description: This family consists of several 5' nucleotidase, deoxy (Pyrimidine), cytosolic type C (NT5C) proteins. 5'(3')-Deoxyribonucleotidase is a ubiquitous enzyme in mammalian cells whose physiological function is not known [[cite:PUB00012938]].

Agrin is a multidomain heparan sulphate proteoglycan, that is a key organiser for the induction of postsynaptic specialisations at the neuromuscular junction. Binding of agrin to basement membranes requires the amino terminal (NtA) domain [[cite:PUB00007702]]. This region mediates high affinity interaction with the coiled-coil domain of laminins. The binding of agrin to laminins via the NtA domain is subject to tissue-specific regulation. The NtA domain-containing form of agrin is expressed in non-neuronal cells or in neurons that project to non-neuronal cell such as motor neurons. The structure of this domain is an OB-fold [[cite:PUB00007703]].

Pfam_Description: Pol beta superfamily nucleotidyltransferase in conflict systems
Pfam_name: Pol beta superfamily nucleotidyltransferase in conflict systems
Pfam_description: This is a Pol beta superfamily nucleotidyltransferase domain found in bacterial conflict systems and predicted to function as an effector [[cite:PUB00100103]].

Nucleotidyltransferases (EC 2.7.7) comprise a large enzyme family with diverse roles in polynucleotide synthesis and modification. This domain is structurally related to kanamycin nucleotidyltransferase (KNTase) and forms a complex with HI0073, a sequence homolog of the nucleotide-binding domain of this nucleotidyltransferase superfamily [[cite:PUB00014788]].

Pfam_Description: NTD biosynthesis operon protein NtdA, N-terminal domain
Pfam_name: NTD biosynthesis operon protein NtdA, N-terminal domain
Pfam_description: This entry represents the N-terminal domain of NtdA, which is not found in other aminotransferases and consists of two-stranded parallel beta-sheet flanked by two alpha-helices [[cite:PUB00154124]]. This domain may be involved in protein-protein interactions. NtdA is a sugar aminotransferase involved in the biosynthesis of kanosamine.

This family represents the N-terminal region of proteins carrying the transposase enzyme, DDE_Tnp_1 (that was Transposase_11), [pfam:PF01609], at the C-terminus. The full-length members are Insertion Element 4, IS4. Within the collection of E.coli strains, ECOR, the number of IS4 elements varies from zero to 14, with an average of 5 copies/strain [[cite:PUB00056053]].

Pfam_Description: Neuropathy Target Esterase family P-loop like domain
Pfam_name: Neuropathy Target Esterase family P-loop like domain
Pfam_description: This domain is fond in a variety of Neuropathy Target Esterase family proteins. This domain appears to be structurally realted to P-loop ATPases, but it appears to not contain the typical APT-binding motifs. The NTE family comprises intracellular phospholipases B that catalyze the double deacylation of phosphatidylcholine (PC) to glycerophosphocholine (GroPCho). These enzymes play a crucial role in membrane lipid homeostasis and are responsible for the rapid turnover of PC in response to various stimuli such as inositol, elevated temperatures, or choline presence. Additionally, some members of the family, like the neuropathy target esterase (NTE), are involved in the signaling mechanisms between neurons and glia, regulating glia wrapping during brain development and ensuring cell survival. The family also includes lysophospholipases that preferentially deacylate unsaturated lysophosphatidylcholine, generating glycerophosphocholine and other lysophospholipids.
Structural comparisons with PDB:1kny indicate that this N-terminal domain resembles a nucleotidyltransferase fold.
This family includes the NTF2-like Delta-5-3-ketosteroid isomerase proteins.

This family represents the N-terminal region of neutrophin-3 (NTF3) which contains two precursor homology regions located upstream of the mature NTF3 sequence. These regions play important and specific roles in the folding, processing and transport of neurotrophic factors [[cite:PUB00034812]].

Bacteria of the Clostridium genus produce protein neurotoxins, which are complexes consisting of neurotoxin (NT), haemagglutinin (HA), nontoxic nonhaemagglutinin (NTNH), and RNA [[cite:PUB00020996],[cite:PUB00020995]]. The domain described here is found at the C-terminus of the NTNH component.

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an alpha+beta fold and conserved cysteine, histidine and glutamate residues that is usually exported by the Photorhabdus virulence cassette (PVC)-type export system [[cite:PUB00066726]].
A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an alpha+beta fold that is usually exported by the type 2 secretion system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin contains two structural domains, an N-terminal alpha/beta domain and a C-terminal all-beta domain. The domain contains conserved GxR, RxxxoH GxE and GxxH motifs and a conserved histidine residue. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is usually exported by the Photorhabdus virulence cassette (PVC)-type export system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an alpha+beta fold that is usually exported by the Photorhabdus virulence cassette (PVC)-type export system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses a most all-alpha helical fold and a conserved HxxD motif. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is usually exported by the type 2, type 6, type 7 or Photorhabdus virulence cassette (PVC)-type secretion systems [[cite:PUB00066726]]. This is shown to be a type IV secretion system protein that behaves as DNase [[cite:PUB00075355]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an all-alpha helical fold and conserved (DNE)xxH motif and arginine residue. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is exported by the type 2, type 6, or Photorhabdus virulence cassette (PVC)-type secretion system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses a mostly all-beta fold and a conserved ExD motif and a histidine residue. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is exported by the type 2, type 7 or TcdB/TcaC-type secretion system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

Bacterial genomes and plasmids encode a variety of peptide and protein toxins that mediate inter-bacterial competition. Bacteriocins are diffusible proteins that parasitize cell-envelope proteins to enter and kill bacteria. Contact-dependent growth inhibition (CDI) is one mechanism of inter-bacterial competition. Novel Toxin 21 (alternatively 16S rRNA endonuclease CdiA) belongs to a family of prokaryotic polymorphic toxin systems implicated in intra-specific conflicts [[cite:PUB00088209]]. This RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, is proposed to adopt the BECR (Barnase-EndoU-ColicinE5/D-RelE) fold, with two conserved lysine residues and [DS]xDxxxH, RxG[ST] and RxxD motifs. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is usually exported by the type 2, type 4, type 5 or type 7 secretion systems. This is also referred to as the E. cloacae CdiAC. The CdiAC proteins carry a variety of sequence-diverse C-terminal domains, which represent a collection of distinct toxins [[cite:PUB00066726]]. Many CdiA-CT toxins have nuclease activities. In accord with the structural homology, CdiA-CT cleaves 16S rRNA at the same site as colicin E3 and this nuclease activity is responsible for growth inhibition [[cite:PUB00088209]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses a mostly beta fold and two conserved histidines, two aspartates and a glutamate residue. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is usually exported by the type 5 secretion system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an all-beta fold and conserved ND and DxxR motifs and a histidine residue. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is exported by the type 2 or TcdB/TcaC secretion system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an all-beta fold and conserved ND and DxxR motifs and a histidine residue. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is exported by the type 2 or TcdB/TcaC secretion system. Interestingly, the toxin is also found in type-II toxin-antitoxin systems [[cite:PUB00066726]].

This domain family, predicted to have RNase activity, is found in a group of toxins mainly found in Enterobacterales. It shows a conserved FGPY motif and a histidine residue and is predicted to have a mostly all-beta fold. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is exported by the type 2 or type 5 secretion system [[cite:PUB00066726]]. Some members of this family are annotated as CdiA, a member of a contact-dependent growth inhibition system (CDI) that show diverse functions implicated in bacterial competition, including the dissipation of the proton motive force (PMF) and the degradation of DNA or RNA [[cite:PUB00152489],[cite:PUB00152488],[cite:PUB00057480]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an alpha+beta fold and conserved aspartate and glutamate residues, and an RxW motif. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is exported by the type 2 or type 7 secretion systems [[cite:PUB00066726]].

This entry represents the C-terminal RNase toxin domain found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an all alpha-helical fold and conserved aspartate and glutamate residues, and K[DE] and [DN]HxxE motifs. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is exported by the type 2, type 5 or type 7 secretion system [[cite:PUB00066726]]. This C-terminal domain cleaves within tRNA anticodon loops, tRNase activity that is stimulated by CysK which stabilises this domain and allows its binding to the tRNA substrate [[cite:PUB00111161],[cite:PUB00094027]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an all-beta fold and conserved aspartate, arginine, histidine and cysteine residues that is usually exported by the Photorhabdus virulence cassette (PVC)-type export system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an all-beta fold and two conserved histidines present in an RxH and THIP motif. The domain additionally has a highly conserved arginine residue. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is usually exported by the type 2, type 6 or type 7 secretion systems [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an alpha+beta fold and [DN]xHxxK and DxxxD motifs. It is usually exported by the Type 2 secretory system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an all-alpha helical fold and conserved lysine and cysteine residues, and GNxxD and WxCxH motifs. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is exported by the type 2 or type 6 secretion system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems that is proposed to adopt the BECR (Barnase-EndoU-ColicinE5/D-RelE) fold, and contains a conserved histidine residue and a KH motif. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is usually exported by the type 2 secretion system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an alpha+beta fold that is usually exported by the Photorhabdus virulence cassette (PVC)-type export system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an alpha+beta fold with two conserved histidine residues. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is usually exported by the type 2 or TcdB/TcaC-type secretion system [[cite:PUB00066726]]. An example of this, the Pseudomonas RhsT-C, has been experimentally characterised.

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an all-alpha-helical fold with conserved DxK, GNxxxG, and DxxxD motifs. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is exported by the type 2, type 6 or type 7 secretion systems [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted toxin domain found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an alpha+beta fold with a conserved glutamine residue and a [KR]STxxPxxDxx[ST] motif. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is exported by the type 2 or type 6 secretion system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems that is proposed to adopt the BECR (Barnase-EndoU-ColicinE5/D-RelE) fold, and contains two conserved aspartates, a glutamate, a histidine and an arginine residue and an RT motif. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is usually exported by the type 2, type 6 or type 7 secretion system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an alpha+beta fold that is usually exported by the Photorhabdus virulence cassette (PVC)-type export system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems that is proposed to adopt the BECR (Barnase-EndoU-ColicinE5/D-RelE) fold, and contains two conserved histidine, a serine, two lysine, and a threonine residue and a HxVP motif. In bacterial polymorphic toxin systems, the toxin is usually exported by the type 2, type 6, type 7, and MuF-type secretion systems [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an alpha+beta fold that is usually exported by the Photorhabdus virulence cassette (PVC)-type export system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

A predicted RNase toxin found in bacterial polymorphic toxin systems. The toxin possesses an alpha+beta fold and HxR and HxxxH motifs and is usually exported by the type 2 and type 6 secretion system [[cite:PUB00066726]].

This domain is found across all species from bacteria to human, and the function was determined first in a hyperthermophilic bacterium to be an NTPase [[cite:PUB00055956]]. The structure of one member-sequence represents a variation of the RecA fold, and implies that the function might be that of a DNA/RNA modifying enzyme [[cite:PUB00032635]]. The sequence carries both a Walker A and Walker B motif which together are characteristic of ATPases or GTPases. The protein exhibits an increased expression profile in human liver cholangiocarcinoma when compared to normal tissue [[cite:PUB00041591]].

NTPase_I-T is a family of NTPases with supreme activity against ITP and XTP. Active site analysis and structure comparison of YjjX strongly suggested that it is an NTP binding protein with nucleoside triphosphatase activity. YjjX exhibits a mixed alpha-beta fold [[cite:PUB00038960],[cite:PUB00037841]].

Pfam_Description: ATPase P4 of dsRNA bacteriophage phi-12
Pfam_name: ATPase P4 of dsRNA bacteriophage phi-12
Pfam_description: P4 is a packaging motor which is involved in the packaging of phi-12 genome into preformed capsids using ATP. P4 is located at the vertices of the icosahedral capsid. ATP drives RNA translocation through cooperative conformational changes [[cite:PUB00032176]].
This family includes a wide range of enzymes which transfer nucleotides onto phosphosugars.

Members of this family belong to a large family of nucleotidyltransferases [[cite:PUB00005745]]. This family includes kanamycin nucleotidyltransferase (KNTase) which is a plasmid-coded enzyme responsible for some types of bacterial resistance to aminoglycosides. KNTase in-activates antibiotics by catalysing the addition of a nucleotidyl group onto the drug.
This family includes the MobA protein (Molybdopterin-guanine dinucleotide biosynthesis protein A). The family also includes a wide range of other NTP transferase domain.
This is a probable sugar nucleotidyl transferase family.
This family is likely to be an uncharacterised group of nucleotidyltransferases.
This family consists of several hypothetical bacterial proteins of unknown function. This family was recently identified as belonging to the nucleotidyltransferase superfamily [[cite:PUB00066751]].

This family contains many hypothetical proteins. It also includes four nematode prion-like proteins. This domain has been identified as part of the nucleotidyltransferase superfamily [[cite:PUB00066751]].

This is a family of bacterial proteins that have a nucleotidyltransferase fold. The fold-prediction is backed up by conservation of three highly characteristic sequence motifs found in all other nucleotidyl transferases: i) pDhDhhh(h/p), where p is a polar residue and h is a hydrophobic residue; ii) upstream of the first, a GG/S; iii) a conserved D/E in a hydrophobic surround. In the classification of nucleotidyltransferases proposed in [[cite:PUB00066751]] this is a group XVIII NTP-transferase. Many of these sequences were classified in the COG database as COG5397. The exact function is not known.
This family consists of several hypothetical bacterial proteins of unknown function. This family was recently identified as belonging to the nucleotidyltransferase superfamily [[cite:PUB00066751]].

This family contains many hypothetical proteins. It also includes four nematode prion-like proteins. This domain has been identified as part of the nucleotidyltransferase superfamily [[cite:PUB00066751]].

This is a family of bacterial proteins that have a nucleotidyltransferase fold. The fold-prediction is backed up by conservation of three highly characteristic sequence motifs found in all other nucleotidyl transferases: i) pDhDhhh(h/p), where p is a polar residue and h is a hydrophobic residue; ii) upstream of the first, a GG/S; iii) a conserved D/E in a hydrophobic surround. In the classification of nucleotidyltransferases proposed in [[cite:PUB00066751]] this is a group XVIII NTP-transferase. Many of these sequences were classified in the COG database as COG5397. The exact function is not known.
This family consists of several hypothetical bacterial proteins of unknown function. This family was recently identified as belonging to the nucleotidyltransferase superfamily [[cite:PUB00066751]].

This family contains many hypothetical proteins. It also includes four nematode prion-like proteins. This domain has been identified as part of the nucleotidyltransferase superfamily [[cite:PUB00066751]].

This is a family of bacterial proteins that have a nucleotidyltransferase fold. The fold-prediction is backed up by conservation of three highly characteristic sequence motifs found in all other nucleotidyl transferases: i) pDhDhhh(h/p), where p is a polar residue and h is a hydrophobic residue; ii) upstream of the first, a GG/S; iii) a conserved D/E in a hydrophobic surround. In the classification of nucleotidyltransferases proposed in [[cite:PUB00066751]] this is a group XVIII NTP-transferase. Many of these sequences were classified in the COG database as COG5397. The exact function is not known.
This domain contains a beta-tent fold [[cite:PUB00078711]].

Sequence similarity between netrin UNC-6 and C345C complement protein family members, and hence the existence of the UNC-6 module, was first reported in [[cite:PUB00019944]]. Subsequently, many additional members of the family were identified on the basis of sequence similarity between the C-terminal domains of netrins, complement proteins C3, C4, C5, secreted frizzled-related proteins, and type I pro-collagen C-proteinase enhancer proteins (PCOLCEs), which are homologous with the N-terminal domains of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs). The TIMPs are classified as a separate family in Pfam ([pfam:PF00965]) [[cite:PUB00005058]]. This expanded domain family has been named as the NTR module [[cite:PUB00005058]].

Family members include the NTR2 or Nineteen complex-related protein 2 found in fungus and plants. NTR2 proteins form a complex with the DExD/H-box RNA helicase Prp43. Along with NTR1 it is an accessory factor of Prp43 in catalysing spliceosome disassembly. Disassembly of the spliceosome after completion of the splicing reaction is necessary for recycling of splicing factors to promote efficient splicing [[cite:PUB00054039]]. NTR2 and NTR1 associate with a post-splicing complex containing the excised intron and the spliceosomal U2, U5, and U6 snRNAs, that supports a link with a late stage in the pre-mRNA splicing process [[cite:PUB00067694]].
This entry represents the probable sensor region of the two component regulator protein NtrY [[cite:PUB00098912]]. This region includes four probable transmembrane helices.
This family represents the periplasmic protein NtrZ which functions to regulate the activity of the NtrY-NtrX two-component system [[cite:PUB00151631]]. NtrZ inhibits NtrY phosphatase activity.

This family, the N-terminal segment, is the most variable part of the variant surface antigen family of Plasmodium falciparum, the erythrocyte membrane protein-1 (PfEMP1) proteins. PfEMP1 is an important target for protective immunity and is implicated in the pathology of malaria through its ability to adhere to host endothelial receptors [[cite:PUB00066773]]. A structural and functional study of the N-terminal domain of PfEMP1 from the VarO variant comprising the N-terminal segment (NTS) and the first DBL domain (DBL1alpha1), shows this region is directly implicated in rosetting. NTS, previously thought to be a structurally independent component of PfEMP1, forms an integral part of the DBL1alpha domain that is found to be the important heparin-binding site [[cite:PUB00066775]]. This family is closely associated with PFEMP, [pfam:PF03011], and Duffy_binding, [pfam:PF05424].

Pfam_Description: N-terminal segments of P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein
Pfam_name: N-terminal segments of P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein
Pfam_description: NTS_2 is a family of the most variable part of the variant surface antigen family of Plasmodium falciparum, the erythrocyte membrane protein-1 (PfEMP1) [[cite:PUB00066773]]. However, in this group of proteins conservation is high. PfEMP1 is an important target for protective immunity and is implicated in the pathology of malaria through its ability to adhere to host endothelial receptors.

This entry represents the type II secretion system substrate NttA from Legionella pneumophila and related proteins found mainly in Legionellales species. Homologues of NttA are also found outside Legionella genus. NttA contains and N-terminal disordered region followed by a globular all-alpha helical domain consisting of four alpha-helices [[cite:PUB00155764]]. NttA was shown to interact with phosphoinositides with a clear preference for phosphatidylinositol -3,5-biphosphate [PtdIns(3,5)P2] [[cite:PUB00155764]]. NttA is likely targeted to host organelles, such as the Legionella containing vacuole, during intracellular infection.

This entry represents the T2SS protein NttC from Legionella pneumophila and related proteins found mainly in other Legionella species. NttC has a key role during L. pneumophila infection of V. vermiformis and W. magna amoeba. It folds into an Ig-like beta-sandwich containing ten beta-strands and an alpha-helix which provides one of the pair cysteines involved in the disulfide bond formation. NttC is unusual in that it lacks a compact core and instead contains a buried internal cavity [[cite:PUB00155764]]. This cavity was proposed to bind a variety of organic molecules [[cite:PUB00155764]].

This entry represents the type II secretion system substrate NttE from Legionella pneumophila and relate proteins found mainly in Legionellales species. NttE structure is composed of two intertwined alpha/beta domains, each of which is consisting of an antiparallel beta-sheet and alpha-helices packed on it [[cite:PUB00155764],[cite:PUB00105497]]. This protein forms stable dimers and the dimer interface is contributed by the C-terminal domain. The N-terminal domain of NttE is mobile which is likely essential for its function in modifying the bacterial cell surface and/or during intracellular infection [[cite:PUB00155764]].
This protein is conserved from plants to humans. It represents a family of N terminal glutamine amidases. The enzyme removes the NH2 group from a Gln, at the N-terminal, rendering it a Glu.

This domain is found N-terminal in fruit fly Neurotrophin 1 (NT) and related proteins from arthropods. NT binds to Toll-7 and probably acts as its ligand in promoting motor axon targeting and neuronal survival in the central nervous system (CNS) [[cite:PUB00155765]]. In larvae, NT is involved in the negative regulation of the tracheal immune response to bacterial infection by acting as a ligand for the Toll-related receptor Tollo [[cite:PUB00155766]]. This domain is predicted to fold into a globular structure consisting of alpha helices. It is frequently found N-terminal to [pfam:PF16077].

The NuA4 histone acetyltransferase (HAT) multisubunit complex is responsible for acetylation of histone H4 and H2A N-terminal tails in yeast [[cite:PUB00035438]]. NuA4 complexes are highly conserved in eukaryotes and play primary roles in transcription, cellular response to DNA damage, and cell cycle control [[cite:PUB00035439]].

This entry represents the C-terminal zinc finger domain of Zinc finger C3HC-type protein 1 (ZC3HC1, also known as Nuclear- interacting partner of ALK (NIPA)) and mRNA export factor Rsm1 which is a homologue from S. pombe [[cite:PUB00016374]]. These proteins contain a C3HC-type zinc finger at the N terminus followed by the domain represented in this entry. These N- and C-terminal zinc finger domains are homologous and both are related to BIR domains. The zinc ion coordination occurs exclusively via four invariant amino acids (C2HC), in a mode similar to the BIR domains [[cite:PUB00154435]]. This domain can harbour a large insert after the first two conserved cysteine residues, which is probably intrinsically disordered [[cite:PUB00154437]]. Both N- and C-terminal (this entry) zinc finger domains were found to be essential for binding TPR/Mlp1 and therefore denoted as the nuclear basket-interaction domain (NuBaID), representing an evolutionary conserved integral functional unit [[cite:PUB00154437]].

This is a nuclease (NUC) domain found in Cpf1, an RNA-guided endonuclease of a type V CRISPR-Cas system. Structural and functional analysis indicate that this domain is involved in DNA cleavage [[cite:PUB00091266]].
This C terminal domain is found in a novel family of hypothetical nucleolar proteins [[cite:PUB00016366]].
This small domain is found in a a novel nucleolar family [[cite:PUB00016366]].

This family consists of the anticodon nuclease activator proteins. Pre-existing host tRNAs are reprocessed during bacteriophage T4 infection of certain Escherichia coli strains. In this pathway, tRNA(Lys) is cleaved 5' by the anticodon nuclease to the wobble base and is later restored in polynucleotide kinase and RNA ligase reactions [[cite:PUB00016404]].

This is the N protein of the nucleocapsid. The nucleocapsid functions to protect the RNA against nuclease degradation and to promote it's reverse transcription [[cite:PUB00109581]]. The NC protein promotes viral RNA dimerisation and encapsidation and initiates reverse transcription by activating the annealing of the primer tRNA to the initiation site [[cite:PUB00109582]].
This family of nucleocapsid proteins is from ssRNA negative-strand viruses of plant origin.
This domain adopts a three helix fold resembling part of a winged helix motif. It binds nucleolin [[cite:PUB00057086]].

Nucleoplasmins are also known as chromatin decondensation proteins. They bind to core histones and transfer DNA to them in a reaction that requires ATP. This is thought to play a role in the assembly of regular nucleosomal arrays.

This is the C-terminal half of a family of nucleoporin proteins. Nucleoporins are the main components of the nuclear pore complex in eukaryotic cells, and mediate bidirectional nucleocytoplasmic transport, especially of mRNA and proteins. Two nucleoporin classes are known: one is characterised by the FG repeat [pfam:PF03093]; the other is represented by this family, and lacks any repeats. RNA undergoing nuclear export first encounters the basket of the nuclear pore and many nucleoporins are accessible on the basket side of the pore [[cite:PUB00019951]]. This region is composed of a long alpha solenoid repeat structure.
This family includes a number of FG repeats that are found in nucleoporin proteins. This family includes the yeast nucleoporins Nup116, Nup100, Nup49, Nup57 and Nup 145.

Nup133 is a nucleoporin that is crucial for nuclear pore complex (NPC) biogenesis. The N terminal forms a seven-bladed beta propeller structure [[cite:PUB00032448]]. This family now contains other sized nucleoporins, including Nup155, Nup8, Nuo132, Nup15 and Nup170.

A family of nucleoporins conserved from yeast to human. THe nuclear pore complex is a large assembly composed of two essential complexes: the heptameric Nup84 complex and the heteromeric Nic96-containing complex. The Nup84 complex is composed of one copy each of Nup84, Nup85, Nup120, Nup133, Nup145C, Sec13, and Seh1. The structure of a complex of Nup85 and Seh1 was solved [[cite:PUB00051815]]. The N-terminus of Nup85 is inserted and forms a three-stranded blade that completes the Seh1 6-bladed beta-propeller in trans. Following its N-terminal insertion blade, Nup85 forms a compact cuboid structure composed of 20 helices, with two distinct modules, referred to as crown and trunk [[cite:PUB00051815]].

This is a family of nucleoside transporters. In mammalian cells nucleoside transporters transport nucleoside across the plasma membrane and are essential for nucleotide synthesis via the salvage pathways for cells that lack their own de novo synthesis pathways [[cite:PUB00003000]]. Also in this family is mouse and human nucleolar protein HNP36 [swissprot:Q14542] a protein of unknown function; although it has been hypothesised to be a plasma membrane nucleoside transporter [[cite:PUB00003000]].

This family consists of nucleoside transport proteins. [swissprot:Q62773] is a purine-specific Na+-nucleoside cotransporter localised to the bile canalicular membrane [[cite:PUB00002907]]. [swissprot:Q62674] is a a Na+-dependent nucleoside transporter selective for pyrimidine nucleosides and adenosine it also transports the anti-viral nucleoside analogues AZT and ddC [[cite:PUB00002855]]. This alignment covers the C-terminus of this family of transporters.

This family consists of nucleoside transport proteins. [swissprot:Q62773] is a purine-specific Na+-nucleoside cotransporter localised to the bile canalicular membrane [[cite:PUB00002907]]. [swissprot:Q62674] is a a Na+-dependent nucleoside transporter selective for pyrimidine nucleosides and adenosine it also transports the anti-viral nucleoside analogues AZT and ddC [[cite:PUB00002855]]. This alignment covers the N terminus of this family
Proteins in this family have been been predicted to be nucleotide-diphospho-sugar transferases.
This family consists of several Nucleopolyhedrovirus late expression factor-12 (LEF-12) proteins. The function of this family is unknown [[cite:PUB00013412],[cite:PUB00013413]].
This family consists of several Nucleopolyhedrovirus capsid protein P87 sequences. P87 is expressed late in infection and concentrated in infected cell nuclei [[cite:PUB00013078]].

Endonuclease NucS cleaves both 3' and 5' ssDNA extremities of branched DNA structures and it binds to ssDNA [[cite:PUB00060574],[cite:PUB00052724]]. This entry represents the C-terminal domain of NucS.

Endonuclease NucS cleaves both 3' and 5' ssDNA extremities of branched DNA structures and it binds to ssDNA [[cite:PUB00060574],[cite:PUB00052724]]. This entry represents the N-terminal PH-like domain of NucS.
Nucleoside 2-deoxyribosyltransferase [ec:2.4.2.6] catalyses the cleavage of the glycosidic bonds of 2`-deoxyribonucleosides [[cite:PUB00010196]].
This is a conserved short region that is found in many bacterial polymorphic toxin proteins [[cite:PUB00057479]]. It is often located before C-terminal nuclease domains [[cite:PUB00057479]].

Nuclear receptors (NRs) are a family of ligand-inducible transcription factors, and, like other transcription factors, they contain a distinct DNA binding domain that allows for target gene recognition and several activation domains that possess the ability to activate transcription [[cite:PUB00063250]]. One of these activation domains is at the N-terminal, although there are two distinct motifs within this domain, between residues 20-36 and between 74 and the end of this domain, which are the binding regions. One of the co-activators is TIF1beta, which appears to bind at the first motif [[cite:PUB00063251]].
This region is found on eukaryotic nuclear receptor coactivators and forms an alpha helical structure.

This family of membrane proteins transport nucleotide sugars from the cytoplasm into Golgi vesicles. [swissprot:P78382] transports CMP-sialic acid, [swissprot:P78381] transports UDP-galactose and [swissprot:Q9Y2D2] transports UDP-GlcNAc.

This domain, approximately 40-50 residues in length, is mainly found in nuclear migration proteins in various Mammalia species [[cite:PUB00076533]]. It may play a role not only in mitosis and cytokinesis [[cite:PUB00076533]], but also in interkinetic nuclear migration and neuronal migration during neocortical development [[cite:PUB00076534]].

The N-terminus of nuclear distribution gene C homolog (NUDC) proteins contains a highly conserved region consisting of a predicted three helix bundle. In the human homolog this segment has been targeted for structure determination by the Joint Center for Structural Genomics. NUDC forms a complex with other NUD proteins and is involved in several cellular division activities. Recently it was shown that NUDC regulates platelet-activating factor (PAF) acetylhydrolase with PAF being a pro-inflammatory secondary lipidic messenger [[cite:PUB00058240]].
This family represents the C-terminal conserved region of the NUDE proteins. NUDE proteins are involved in nuclear migration [[cite:PUB00008687]].
The N-terminal domain in NADH pyrophosphatase, which has a rudiment Nudix fold according to SCOP.

Nudix hydrolases are found in all classes of organism and hydrolyse a wide range of organic pyrophosphates, including nucleoside di- and triphosphates, di-nucleoside and diphospho-inositol polyphosphates, nucleotide sugars and RNA caps, with varying degrees of substrate specificity.

Pfam_Description: NUDIX, or N-terminal NPxY motif-rich,  region of KRIT

Pfam_description: This domain is found just before the N-terminal region of nucleoside diphosphate-linked moiety (Nudix) hydrolases ([pfam:PF00293]). Nudix hydrolases catalyze the hydrolysis of nucleoside diphosphates which are often toxic metabolic intermediates and signalling molecules [[cite:PUB00091184]].

Pfam_Description: Hydrolase of X-linked nucleoside diphosphate N terminal

Pfam_description: This entry represents the NUDIX hydrolase domain of U8 snoRNA -decapping enzyme from Xenopus laevis (Nudt16) and similar proteins from animals and bacteria. Nudt16 was initially described as an RNA-binding and decapping enzyme but it was later reported to be specialised in the removal of hazardous (deoxy)inosine diphosphate from the nucleotide pool. It adopts a canonical NUDIX fold, an alpha-beta-alpha sandwich constituted by two beta-sheets whose strands interact in a way that could also be described as a single extended beta-sheet [[cite:PUB00154125]].

Members of this family are components of the mitotic spindle. It has been shown that Nuf2 from yeast is part of a complex called the Ndc80p complex [[cite:PUB00008439]]. This complex is thought to bind to the microtubules of the spindle. An arabidopsis protein has been included in this family that has previously not been identified as a member of this family, [swissprot:Q9C953]. The match is not strong, but in common with other members of this family contains coiled-coil to the C terminus of this region.

This domain is found at the C-terminal region of Nuf2 proteins. This domain was identified as MazG related domain also designated as Designed helical repeat protein 10 (DHR10) [[cite:PUB00091445]] that actually adopts a coiled-coil structure [[cite:PUB00049694]]. Nuf2 is part of the Ndc80 complex, which binds to the spindle and is required for chromosome segregation and spindle checkpoint activity [[cite:PUB00088250],[cite:PUB00068219]].

Proteins in this family have been implicated in the assembly of the large subunit of the ribosome [[cite:PUB00044401]] and in telomere maintenance [[cite:PUB00044402]]. Some proteins in this family contain a CCCH zinc finger. This family contains a protein called human FMR1-interacting protein NUFIP1 which is known to bind RNA [[cite:PUB00044403]] and is phosphorylated upon DNA damage [[cite:PUB00044404]].

This family represents the nuclease A inhibitor NuiA expressed by Anabaena sp ([swissprot:Q44296]) and similar bacterial proteins. This protein adopts an alpha+beta fold described as an 'open jaw', which shares some similarity to the PR-1-like fold [[cite:PUB00016584]]. NuiA regulates the activity of Nuclease A (NucA). The NucA inhibition by NuiA involves an unusual divalent metal ion bridge that connects the nuclease with its inhibitor. A highly conserved glutamate extends into the active site, mimicking the charge of a phosphate. In addition, a second interaction site located on one of the two 'jaws' of the NuiA structure, contribute to the specificity and strength of the NuiA-NucA interaction [[cite:PUB00042100]].

This entry represents a group of fungal proteins that are related to the nuclease A inhibitor NuiA ([pfam:PF07924]). NuiA is known to regulate the activity of NucA, one of the most potent nucleases involved in degradation of both single- and double-stranded DNA and RNA. The NucA inhibition by NuiA involves an unusual divalent metal ion bridge that connects the nuclease with its inhibitor. A highly conserved glutamate extends into the active site, mimicking the charge of a phosphate. The functionally essential glutamate is conserved within this family. In some members, it is replaced with aspartate. Most members of this family bear a deletion affecting the second interaction site located on one of the two 'jaws' of the NuiA structure and known to contribute to the specificity and strength of the NuiA-NucA interaction. The lack of this region indicates some functional differences of this group of potential inhibitors.
This presumed domain is found in the Numb family of proteins adjacent to the PTB domain..
This domain probably represents a DNA-binding helix-turn-helix based on its similarity to other families (Bateman A pers obs).

NUMOD3 is a DNA-binding motif found in homing endonucleases and related proteins. It occurs on its own or in tandem repeats in GIY-YIG ([pfam:PF01541]) and HTH proteins. It constitutes a beta-turn-loop-helix subregion of the the DNA-binding domain of I-TevI homing endonuclease ([swissprot:P13299]) [[cite:PUB00013165]].
NUMOD4 is a putative DNA-binding motif found in homing endonucleases and related proteins [[cite:PUB00013165]].
This family consists of several purine nucleoside permease from both bacteria and fungi [[cite:PUB00012638]].

This entry represents the helical domain of Nup120 from S. pombe referred to as the irregular helical bundle (IHB) [[cite:PUB00062495],[cite:PUB00151813]], which makes extensive contacts with the propeller and helical bundle at the N-terminal. Nup120 functions as a component of the nuclear pore complex (NPC). Deletion of this gene causes clustering of NPCs at one side of the nuclear envelope, moderate nucleolar fragmentation and slower cell growth.

This domain is found in Nucleoporin NUP120 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae and similar fungal sequences. NUP120 is a a component of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) involved in nuclear poly(A)+ RNA and pre-ribosome export, in GSP1 nuclear import, in NPC assembly and distribution, as well as in nuclear envelope organisation. This entry represents the alpha-helical domain of NUP120, which packs against the side of the beta-propeller [pfam:PF11715], located N-terminal of the protein [[cite:PUB00052893],[cite:PUB00053083],[cite:PUB00154129],[cite:PUB00154130]].

This entry represents the helical domain of Nup120 from S. pombe referred to as the irregular helical bundle (IHB) [[cite:PUB00062495],[cite:PUB00151813]], which makes extensive contacts with the propeller and helical bundle at the N-terminal. Nup120 functions as a component of the nuclear pore complex (NPC). Deletion of this gene causes clustering of NPCs at one side of the nuclear envelope, moderate nucleolar fragmentation and slower cell growth.

This domain is found in Nucleoporin NUP120 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae and similar fungal sequences. NUP120 is a a component of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) involved in nuclear poly(A)+ RNA and pre-ribosome export, in GSP1 nuclear import, in NPC assembly and distribution, as well as in nuclear envelope organisation. This entry represents the alpha-helical domain of NUP120, which packs against the side of the beta-propeller [pfam:PF11715], located N-terminal of the protein [[cite:PUB00052893],[cite:PUB00053083],[cite:PUB00154129],[cite:PUB00154130]].
This family contains both the nucleoporin Nup153 from human and Nup154 from fission yeast. These have been demonstrated to be functionally equivalent [[cite:PUB00033302]].

This entry represents the central helical domain of NUP160, which is found in animals, including humans, mice, and Drosophila melanogaster. NUP160 is one of up to 60 proteins that constitute the Nuclear Pore Complex (NPC) as a component of the NUP107-160 subcomplex [[cite:PUB00019951]]. NUP160, in conjunction with NUP133, interacts with NUP98 and NUP153, mediating mRNA export [[cite:PUB00019951]]. NUP160 mutations have been associated with Steroid-Resistant Nephrotic Syndrome (SRNS). Silencing Drosophila NUP160 specifically in nephrocytes results in functional abnormalities, reduced cell size and nuclear volume, as well as a disorganised nuclear membrane structure [[cite:PUB00155767]].

This entry represents a helical domain that can be found in NUP160, also known as SAR1, a nucleoporin protein in Arabidopsis thaliana. It is a member of the NUP107-160 nuclear pore sub-complex [[cite:PUB00085245]]. NUP160 plays a role in normal auxin signalling, which works in synergy with ethylene to control various ethylene-dependent phenomena [[cite:PUB00155768]]. Also, it contributes to pathogen defense [[cite:PUB00085247]], nucleocytoplasmic mRNA export [[cite:PUB00155768]], and is required for disease resistance [[cite:PUB00085246]].

Pfam_Description: Nuclear pore protein NUP188 C-terminal domain
Pfam_name: Nuclear pore protein NUP188 C-terminal domain
Pfam_description: This is C-terminal domain of Nup188. It is a right-handed arc-shaped superhelical structure built from 19 helices that form 6 helical repeats, which are stacked in regular order. The first helical pair (alpha1 and alpha2) forms a HEAT repeat followed by 5 ARM repeats [[cite:PUB00091656]].

Nup188 is one of the many peptides that make up the nucleoporin complex (NPC), and is found across eukaryotes [[cite:PUB00044405]]. The Nup188 subcomplex (Nic96p-Nup188p-Nup192p-Pom152p) is one of at least six that make up the NPC, and as such is symmetrically localised on both faces of the NPC at the nuclear end, being integrally bound to the C-terminal of Pom34p [[cite:PUB00044406]]. This protein folds into an extended stack of helices where the N-terminal forms a closed ring (subdivided into subdomains I-III in [[cite:PUB00091656]]) and the C-terminal forms a more regular, superhelical structure [[cite:PUB00091656]]. This entry represents the N-terminal helical repeats from Nup188.

Nup188 one of the many peptides that make up the nucleoporin complex (NPC), and is found across eukaryotes [[cite:PUB00044405],[cite:PUB00044406],[cite:PUB00091656]]. The Nup188 subcomplex (Nic96p-Nup188p-Nup192p-Pom152p) is one of the at least six that make up the NPC, and as such is symmetrically localised on both faces of the NPC at the nuclear end, being integrally bound to the C-terminus of Pom34p [[cite:PUB00044406]]. This protein folds into an extended stack of helices where the N-terminal forms a closed ring (subdivided into subdomains I-III in [[cite:PUB00091656]]) and the C-terminal forms a more regular, superhelical structure [[cite:PUB00091656]]. This entry represents the helical segment of subdomain III described in [[cite:PUB00091656]], which consists of an array of HEAT and ARM repeats with an inserted SH3-like domain [[cite:PUB00091656]].

This is a family of eukaryotic nucleoporins of several different sizes. All of them are long and form the scaffold of the nuclear pore complex. Nup192 in particular modulates the permeability of the central channel of the NPC central or nuclear pore complex [[cite:PUB00109663]].

This domain is found in the homologues of Nuclear pore membrane glycoprotein 210 (NUP210). NUP210 is essential for nuclear pore assembly and fusion, nuclear pore spacing, as well as for its structural integrity. NUP210 is composed of multiple immunoglobin-like (Ig-like) domains and forms a ring around the NPC within the NE lumen [[cite:PUB00154131]]. The domain represented by this entry is one of these constituent Ig-like domain and has a significant structural similarity to cadherin domains.

CRM1 is the major nuclear export receptor. During translocation through the nuclear pore, transport complexes transiently interact with phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeats of multiple nucleoporins. On the cytoplasmic side of the nuclear pore, CRM1 tightly interacts with the nucleoporin Nup214. Nup214 binds to N- and C-terminal regions of CRM1, thereby clamping CRM1 in a closed conformation and stabilizing the export complex. This entry represents an FG repeat region within the C terminus of Nup214 which is required for its interaction with CRM1 [[cite:PUB00091621]].

Members of this family belong to the nucleor pore complex, NPC, the only gateway between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. The NPC consists of several subcomplexes each one of which is made up of multiple copies of several individual Nup, Nic or Sec protein subunits. In yeast, this Nup or nucleoporin subunit is numbered Nup53, Nup40 in Schizo. pombe and in vertebrates as Nup35. This subunit forms part of the inner ring within the membrane and interacts directly with Nup-Ndc1, considered to be an anchor for the NPC in the pore membrane [[cite:PUB00109194]]. This region of the Nup is the RNA-recognition region [[cite:PUB00038167]].

Nucleoporin 50 kDa (NUP50) acts as a cofactor for the importin-alpha:importin-beta heterodimer, which in turn allows for transportation of many nuclear-targeted proteins through nuclear pore complexes. The C terminus of NUP50 binds importin-beta through RAN-GTP, the N terminus binds the C terminus of importin-alpha, while a central domain binds importin-beta. NUP50:importin-alpha:importin-beta then binds cargo and can stimulate nuclear import. The N-terminal domain of NUP50 is also able to actively displace nuclear localisation signals from importin-alpha [[cite:PUB00035440]].

This is the human Nup54 subunit of the nucleoporin complex, equivalent to Nup57 of yeast. Nup54, Nup58 and Nup62 all have similar affinities for importin-beta. It seems likely that they are the only FG-repeat nucleoporins of the central channel, and as such they would form a zone of equal affinity spanning the central channel. The diffusion of importin-beta import complexes through the central channel may be a stochastic process as the affinities are similar, whereas movement from cytoplasmic fibrils to the central channel and from the central channel to the nuclear basket would be facilitated by the subtle differences in affinity between them [[cite:PUB00016425],[cite:PUB00057912]].

The mammalian nuclear pore complex (NPC) conducts nucleocytoplasmic transport and contains multiple copies of nucleoporins (nups). This is the C-terminal interacting domain found on Nup54. Nup45 is a splice variant of Nup58 with an identical alpha-helical region. Nup54 along with Nup62 and Nup58 are essential for nuclear transport. The C-terminal part of the alpha-helical region of Nup54 interacts with a C-terminal part of the alpha-helical region of Nup58. Interestingly, this region appears in two distinct conformations: a single helix and a helix-loop-helix, termed 'straight' and 'bent'. Whereas the straight conformer consists of a 34 residues long alpha helix (residues 460-493), the bent conformer is composed of two alpha helices, each 13 residues long, connected by a central loop (N helix, residues 460-472; C helix, residues 477-489) [[cite:PUB00057913]].

Nup84p forms a complex with five proteins, of which Nup120p, Nup85p, Sec13p, and a Sec13p homologues. This Nup84p complex in conjunction with Sec13-type proteins is required for correct nuclear pore biogenesis [[cite:PUB00009851]].

Nup88 can be divided into two structural domains; the N-terminal two-thirds of the protein has no obvious structural motifs but is the region for binding to Nup98, one of the components of the nuclear pore. the C-terminal end is a predicted coiled-coil domain [[cite:PUB00044407]]. Nup88 is overexpressed in tumour cells [[cite:PUB00044408]].

Nup96 (often known by the name of its yeast homolog Nup145C) is part of the Nup84 heptameric complex in the nuclear pore complex. Nup96 complexes with Sec13 in the middle of the heptamer. The function of the heptamer is to coat the curvature of the nuclear pore complex between the inner and outer nuclear membranes. Nup96 is predicted to be an alpha helical solenoid. The interaction between Nup96 and Sec13 is the point of curvature in the heptameric complex. [[cite:PUB00050622]] [[cite:PUB00019948]]

Pfam_Description: Nucleoporin homology of Germinal-centre associated nuclear protein
Pfam_name: Nucleoporin homology of Germinal-centre associated nuclear protein
Pfam_description: NupH_GANP is the nucleoporin-homology domain at the N-terminus of human GANP or germinal-centre associated nuclear proteins. GANP is part of the TREX-2 complex that links transcription with nuclear messenger RNA export, and it associates with the mRNP particle through the interaction of the NupH_GANP with NXF1, the export factor. This attachment mediates efficient delivery of mRNPs to nuclear pore complexes [[cite:PUB00069584]].

This is the highly conserved C-terminal motif GRKIxxxxxRRKx of nucleoporins that plays a critical and unique role in the nuclear import of retro-transposons in both yeasts and higher organisms. It would appear that the arginine residues at positions 2 and 9-10 constitute a bipartite nuclear localisation signal, with two basic peptide motifs separated by an interchangeable spacer sequence, that is crucial for the retro-transposon activity [[cite:PUB00044409]].

This family includes NurA a nuclease exhibiting both single-stranded endonuclease activity and 5'-3' exonuclease activity on single-stranded and double-stranded DNA from the hyperthermophilic archaeon Sulfolobus acidocaldarius [[cite:PUB00044410]].
This family of microtubule-associated proteins has a role in spindle microtubule organisation [[cite:PUB00061766],[cite:PUB00061767]]
This domain represents the RNA polymerase binding domain of NusA.
The NusB protein is involved in the regulation of rRNA biosynthesis by transcriptional antitermination.

This domain is found in Thermotoga maritima NusG, which interacts with RNA polymerase and other proteins to form multi-component complexes that modulate transcription. This domain is referred to as Domain II and is an additional domain inserted into the N-terminal domain [[cite:PUB00065139]].

This domain is found in some NusG proteins where it forms domain II [[cite:PUB00017610]]. However most NusG proteins are missing this domain. In other cases this domain is found in isolation [[cite:PUB00075435]]. The function of this domain is unknown.

This family includes the NUT protein. The gene encoding for NUT protein (Nuclear Testis protein) is found fused to BRD3 or BRD4 genes, in some aggressive types of carcinoma, due to chromosomal translocations [[cite:PUB00055988],[cite:PUB00055989]]. Proteins of the BRD family contain two bromodomains that bind transcriptionally active chromatin through associations with acetylated histones H3 and H4 [[cite:PUB00055988],[cite:PUB00055989]]. Such proteins are crucial for the regulation of cell cycle progression. On the other hand, little is known about NUT protein. NUT is known to have a Nuclear Export Sequence (NES) as well as a Nuclear Localisation Signal (NLS), both located towards the C-terminal end of the protein [[cite:PUB00055988],[cite:PUB00055989]]. A fused NUT-GFP protein showed either cytoplasmic or nuclear localisation, suggesting that it is subject to nuclear/cytoplasmic shuttling. Consistent with this possibility, treatment with leptomycin B an inhibitor of CRM1-dependent nuclear export resulted in re-distribution of NUT-GFP to the nucleus [[cite:PUB00021074],[cite:PUB00055990]]. Inspection of NUT revealed a C-terminal sequence similar to known nuclear export sequences (NES) which are often regulated by phosphorylation [[cite:PUB00021074],[cite:PUB00055990]]. This family carries some natively unstructured sequence.

This family of proteins is functionally uncharacterised. This family of proteins is found in bacteria. Proteins in this family are typically between 75 and 92 amino acids in length. There is a conserved NVEALA sequence motif.

Pfam_Description: Nuclear RNA export factor, NTF2 domain
Pfam_name: Nuclear RNA export factor, NTF2 domain
Pfam_description: This entry represents the NTF2 domain of nuclear RNA export factors (NFX), proteins that are involved in the nuclear export of mRNAs [[cite:PUB00018169],[cite:PUB00021156],[cite:PUB00025422],[cite:PUB00026326],[cite:PUB00026433]].

NYAP_N is an N-terminal family of eukaryotic proteins that are substrates of tyrosine kinase in the brain. When first identified, the family members were referred to as unconventional myosin XVI, or Myr 8 [[cite:PUB00070020]]. However, proteins have now been identified as being integrally involved in neuronal function and morphogenesis. The family is involved in both the activation of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) and the recruitment of the downstream effector WAVE complex to the close vicinity of PI3K; it also appears to regulate the brain size and neurite outgrowth in mice [[cite:PUB00061705]].

NYAP_C is a C-terminal family of eukaryotic proteins that are substrates of tyrosine kinase in the brain. When first identified, the family members were referred to as unconventional myosin XVI, or Myr 8 [[cite:PUB00070020]]. However, proteins have now been identified as being integrally involved in neuronal function and morphogenesis. The family is involved in both the activation of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) and the recruitment of the downstream effector WAVE complex to the close vicinity of PI3K; it also appears to regulate the brain size and neurite outgrowth in mice [[cite:PUB00061705]].

NYD-SP12, also known as SPATA16, is a germ-cell specific participant in the Golgi apparatus, and its expression is confined to spermatogenic epithelium, not being found in interstitial cells [[cite:PUB00069831]]. Computer analysis of the protein-sequence showed that NYD-SP12 contains a cluster of phosphorylation sites for protein kinase C as well as for cyclic nucleotide-dependent protein kinases [[cite:PUB00069832],[cite:PUB00069833]]. It is postulated that since the mutation of some Golgi apparatus' proteins are responsible for male infertility that NYD-SP12 might play a role in modification and sorting of acrosomal enzymes [[cite:PUB00069833]]. OMIM:102530.
