It has been suggested that this domain may be involved in interactions with ubiquitin, ubiquitin-like protein modifiers, or ubiquitin-like domains, such as Ubx. Furthermore, the domain may possess a putative adaptor or substrate binding site, allowing for peroxisomal biogenesis, membrane fusion and protein translocation [[cite:PUB00035447]].

Members of this family adopt a Cdc48 domain 2-like fold, with a beta-alpha-beta(3) arrangement. It has been suggested that this domain may be involved in interactions with ubiquitin, ubiquitin-like protein modifiers, or ubiquitin-like domains, such as Ubx. Furthermore, the domain may possess a putative adaptor or substrate binding site, allowing for peroxisomal biogenesis, membrane fusion and protein translocation [[cite:PUB00035447]].

This family consists of several peroxisomal biogenesis factor 11 (PEX11) proteins from several eukaryotic species. The PEX11 peroxisomal membrane proteins promote peroxisome division in multiple eukaryotes.

This domain is centrally located in Peroxisomal membrane protein PEX14 from Arabidopsis thaliana and similar plant sequences. PEX14 is a component of the PEX13-PEX14 docking complex, a translocon channel that specifically mediates the import of peroxisomal cargo proteins bound to PEX5 receptor. It is often found between [pfam:PF04695] and [pfam:PF17733] and is predicted to adopt an all-alpha helical configuration.

Family of peroxisomal membrane anchor proteins which bind the PTS1 (peroxisomal targeting signal) receptor and are required for the import of PTS1-containing proteins into peroxisomes. Loss of functional Pex14p results in defects in both the PTS1 and PTS2-dependent import pathways. Deletion analysis of this conserved region implicates it in selective peroxisome degradation. In the majority of members this region is situated at the N-terminus of the protein [[cite:PUB00008550],[cite:PUB00008551]].
Pex16 is a peripheral protein located at the matrix face of the peroxisomal membrane [[cite:PUB00033311]].

Peroxisomes play diverse roles in the cell, compartmentalising many activities related to lipid metabolism and functioning in the decomposition of toxic hydrogen peroxide. Sequence similarity was identified between two hypothetical proteins and the peroxin integral membrane protein Pex24p [[cite:PUB00012364]].

This family consists of Pex26 and related mammalian proteins. Pex26 is a type II peroxisomal membrane protein which recruits Pex6-Pex1 complexes to peroxisomes [[cite:PUB00013022]]. Mutations in Pex26 can lead to human disorders [[cite:PUB00013023]].

This region is found at the N terminal of a number of known and predicted peroxins including Pex2, Pex10 and Pex12. This conserved region is usually associated with a C terminal ring finger ([pfam:PF00097]) domain.

This domain is found in the yeast Peroxisomal ATPase PEX6 and related proteins. PEX6 is a component of the PEX1-PEX6 AAA ATPase complex, a protein dislocase complex that mediates the ATP-dependent extraction of the PEX5 receptor from peroxisomal membranes, an essential step for PEX5 recycling [[cite:PUB00057423],[cite:PUB00057424]]. The domain represented in this entry is predicted to adopt a globular structure with some topological similarity to AAA ATPase p97.

This entry represents homologous WY domains of the RxLR effector PexRD54 and other related proteins. The WY domain is a conserved structural unit consisting of three alpha-helices and two characteristic hydrophobic amino acids, frequently W (Trp) and Y (Tyr), which contribute to a stable hydrophobic core.
This domain is found at the C-terminal end of the transcription factor PF0095 from Pyrococcus furiosus and similar archaeal sequences.

This domain is found in PF0610 from Pyrococcus furiosus. This protein has a Zn ribbon-embedded wHTH fold. This entry represents the N-terminal domain, which is composed of three helices [[cite:PUB00041110]].

This domain is found at the C-terminal end of NAD(P)H:rubredoxin oxidoreductase from Pyrococcus furiosus (PF1197) and similar sequences mainly found in archaea. PF1197 catalyses the NADH -dependent reduction of rubredoxin (Rd), a small iron -containing redox protein. This domain, likely to be involved in dimerisation, is often found associated with [pfam:PF07992].

Pfam_Description: Fatty acid synthase subunit PfaD N-terminal domain
Pfam_name: Fatty acid synthase subunit PfaD N-terminal domain
Pfam_description: This domain is found in N-terminal region of PfaD, an enoyl reductase enzyme present in Bacillus subtilis. PfaD plays a role in the biosynthesis of polyunsaturated fatty acids. The domain is typically found just before the N-terminal region of a nitronate monooxygenase domain ([pfam:PF03060]) [[cite:PUB00091383]].

This family contains lipoproteins from the Lyme disease spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi and related bacteria. This entry contains proteins from Paralogous family 54 (PFam54) and 60 and (PFam60). The first crystal structure of B. burgdorferi PFam54 member BBA68 revealed a previously unseen novel fold, which, according to the CATH protein domain classification, was named the Bbcrasp-1 fold because of the common name used for the protein BBA68 [[cite:PUB00038017]].

Pcf11 is a subunit and an essential component of the cleavage and polyadenylation factor CFIA from yeast and the orthologue from human CFII which is involved in pre-mRNA 3' end processing and in transcription termination [[cite:PUB00042008],[cite:PUB00100171]]. Pcf11-mediated termination is essential for vertebrate development [[cite:PUB00100182]]. Pcf11 binds to Clp1, another subunit of CFIA/CFII, whose interaction is responsible for maintaining a tight coupling between the Clp1 nucleotide binding subunit and the other components of the polyadenylation machinery [[cite:PUB00042008],[cite:PUB00100182],[cite:PUB00100171]]. This entry represents the Clp1-interaction region (Clp1 ID) of Pcf11 from yeast and vertebrates.

This entry represents the RNA14/15 interacting domain (Rna14/15-ID) of Pfc11 from yeast [[cite:PUB00154152]]. Pfc11 is a multidomain protein that links transcriptional elongation, 3'-end processing, and transcription termination.

PfEMP1 (Plasmodium falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein) has been identified as the rosetting ligand of the malaria parasite P. falciparum [[cite:PUB00007454],[cite:PUB00020082]]. Rosetting is the adhesion of infected erythrocytes with uninfected erythrocytes in the vasculature of the infected organ, and is associated with severe malaria. PfEMP1 interacts with Complement Receptor One on uninfected erythrocytes to form rosettes [[cite:PUB00020082]]. The extreme variation within these proteins and the grouping of var genes implies that var gene recombination preferentially occurs within var gene groups. These groups reflect a functional diversification that has evolved to cope with the varying conditions of transmission and host immune response met by the parasite [[cite:PUB00066773]]. A recombination hotspot was uncovered between Duffy-binding-like (DBL) subdomains [[cite:PUB00066774]]. Solution of the crystal structure of the N-terminal and first DBL region of PfEMP1 from the VarO variant of the PfEMP1 protein is found to be directly implicated in rosetting as the heparin-binding site [[cite:PUB00066775]].

This domain is found in the surface protein PfEMP1 from Plasmodium falciparum. PfEMP1 is essential for the virulence of this organism. This protein interacts with the endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) through its cysteine-rich interdomain region (CIDRalpha1, this entry). This domain show binding surfaces that are conserved in shape and bonding potential, despite dramatic sequence diversity. The domain is built around a long three-helical core bundle, with a four-stranded beta-sheet on one side and two alpha-helices on the opposite side [[cite:PUB00091594],[cite:PUB00151884]].

This entry includes fungal vacuolar membrane proteases, such as PFF1 from yeast, which may be involved in vacuolar sorting and osmoregulation [[cite:PUB00151250]]. It is an homologue of human ERMP1 [[cite:PUB00101324]]. According to AlphaFold structure prediction, these proteins consist of a M28 peptidase domain ([pfam:PF04389]) at the N-terminal, a central transmembrane domain and a C-terminal domain with an elongated beta-sandwich-like fold, similar to the Mu homology domain (MHD) ([pfam:PF00928]). This entry represents the C-terminal MHD-like domain of PFF1 and its fungal homologues.

This entry includes fungal vacuolar membrane proteases, such as PFF1 from yeast, which may be involved in vacuolar sorting and osmoregulation [[cite:PUB00151250]]. It is the homologue of human ERMP1 [[cite:PUB00101324]]. According to AlphaFold structure prediction, these proteins consist of a M28 peptidase domain ([pfam:PF04389]) at the N-terminal, a central transmembrane domain (TM) and a C-terminal domain with an elongated beta-sandwich-like fold ([pfam:PF22250]), similar to the Mu homology domain (MHD) ([pfam:PF00928]). This entry represents the TM domain of PFF1 and fungal its homologues.

Members of this family are essential for gametocytogenesis in Plasmodium falciparum. They contain a fold composed of two pseudo dyad-related repeats of the helix-turn-helix motif, serving as a platform for RNA and Src homology-3 (SH3) binding [[cite:PUB00029012]].

FiwA-like proteins are fertility inhibition factors (FIN), which are employed by plasmids to block import of rival plasmids [[cite:PUB00085711],[cite:PUB00085716]]. FiwA is encoded by plasmid RP1 and blocks the transfer of plasmid R388 [[cite:PUB00085714]]. A FiwA-like protein called Osa (oncogenic suppressive activity) inhibits the oncogenic properties of Agrobacterium tumefaciens [[cite:PUB00154164]]. Osa is structurally similar to the ParB/Sulfiredoxin fold [[cite:PUB00085711]]. Osa has been shown to have ATPase and DNAse activities, and can block T-DNA transfer into plants [[cite:PUB00085712],[cite:PUB00085713]].
This family includes a variety of carbohydrate and pyrimidine kinases.

This is a phosphofructokinase (Pfk) N-terminal domain found in yeast ATP-dependent 6-phosphofructokinase subunit alpha. ATP-dependent 6-phosphofructokinases (Pfks, EC 2.7.1.11) catalyze the phosphorylation of fructose 6-phosphate (F-6-P) to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, a key control step of glycolysis in most organisms. The N-terminal domain contains the active site and is related to glyoxalase I (E.C. 4.4.1.5) [[cite:PUB00081275]].

This family of enzymes includes pyruvate formate lyase [[cite:PUB00007412]], choline trimethylamine lyase [[cite:PUB00074193]], glycerol dehydratase [[cite:PUB00030576]], 4-hydroxyphenylacetate decarboxylase [[cite:PUB00105268]], and benzylsuccinate synthase [[cite:PUB00017117]].

This entry represent the helical insertion domain of NDH2, a NADH-ubiquinone oxidoreductase from Plasmodium falciparum [[cite:PUB00154098]], an interesting target for antimalarial drug development. This domain seems to be present exclusively in Plasmodium sequences.

PFOR_II is a core domain of the anaerobic enzyme pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase and is necessary for inter subunit contacts in conjunction with domains I and IV [[cite:PUB00005843],[cite:PUB00078738]].

Pfam_Description: Pyruvate ferredoxin oxidoreductase beta subunit C terminal
Pfam_name: Pyruvate ferredoxin oxidoreductase beta subunit C terminal
Pfam_description: This domain family is found in bacteria and archaea, and is approximately 70 amino acids in length. The family is found in association with [pfam:PF02775]. There are two completely conserved residues (A and G) that may be functionally important. PFO is involved in carbon dioxide fixation via a reductive TCA cycle. It forms a heterodimer (alpha/beta). The beta subunit has binding motifs for Fe-S clusters and thiamine pyrophosphate.
This domain is found N terminal to [pfam:PF08324] and binds to ubiquitin [[cite:PUB00035448]].

UIS3 is a membrane protein essential for sporozoite development in infected hepatocytes. This family is 130-229 of the Plasmodium falciparum UIS3 protein which is compact and has an all alpha-helical structure.PfUIS3(130-229) interacts with lipids, phospholipid lysosomes, the human liver fatty acid-binding protein and with the lipid phosphatidylethanolamine. The interaction with liver fatty acid-binding protein provides the parasite with a method to import essential fatty acids/lipids during rapid growth phases of sporozoites [[cite:PUB00049933]].

Pga1 is found only in yeasts and not in mammals. It localises in the ER as a glycosylated integral membrane protein. It binds to the GPI-mannosyltransferase II subunit of the GPI and it is responsible for the second mannose addition to GPI precursors. The GPI-anchoring complex is a glycolipid that functions as a membrane anchor for many cell-surface proteins [[cite:PUB00044430]].
A Saccharomyces cerevisiae member of this family (PGA2) is an ER protein which has been implicated in protein trafficking [[cite:PUB00044766]].

The partially de-N-acetylated poly-beta-1,6-N-acetyl-d-glucosamine (dPNAG) polymer serves as an intercellular biofilm adhesin that plays an essential role for the development and maintenance of integrity of biofilms of diverse bacterial species. Translocation of dPNAG across the bacterial outer membrane is mediated by a tetratricopeptide repeat-containing outer membrane protein, PgaA [[cite:PUB00151721]]. This entry represents the PgaA membrane beta barrel domain [[cite:PUB00151721]].

This family includes the PgaD protein from E. coli [swissprot:P69432]. The homopolymer poly-beta-1,6-N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (beta-1,6-GlcNAc; PGA) serves as an adhesin for the maintenance of biofilm structural stability in eubacteria. The pgaABCD operon is required for its synthesis and export. It has been shown that PgaD is essential for this process [[cite:PUB00055022]].

This domain is found in the human PGAP2-interacting protein (PGAP2IP) and its homologues in yeast CWH43. PGAP2IP is composed of three domains. Two of these domains are predicted to adopt very similar structure consisting of six transmembrane helices, which suggests a possible duplication event in these proteins. These two domains have significant similarity to domains belonging to major facilitator superfamily (MFS). The PGAP2IP yeast homologue, CWH43, is involved in the remodeling of the lipid moiety of GPI anchors to ceramides [[cite:PUB00063839]].

This domain is found in the human PGAP2-interacting protein (PGAP2IP) and its homologues in yeast CWH43. PGAP2IP is composed of three domains. Two of these domains are predicted to adopt very similar structure consisting of six transmembrane helices, which suggests a possible duplication event in these proteins. Its yeast homologue CWH43 is involved in the remodeling of the lipid moiety of GPI anchors to ceramides [[cite:PUB00063839]].

PgaPase_1 is a family of functionally diverse Caenorhabditis proteins. The family is homologous to the cysteine-peptidases, but lack of a strictly conserved Glu-Cys-His catalytic triad or pGlu binding site implies that it has other functions that could have resulted in a change in reaction-specificity or even of catalytic activity [[cite:PUB00075353]].

This protein is a putative poly-gamma-glutamate capsule biosynthesis protein found in bacteria. Poly-gamma-glutamate is a natural polymer that may be involved in virulence and may help bacteria survive in high salt concentrations. It is a surface-associated protein [[cite:PUB00044431]].

PGBA_C is an C-terminal family of bacterial proteins that bind plasminogen. This activity was identified in Helicobacter pylori where it is thought to contribute to the virulence of this bacterium. Both PgbA and PgbB are surface-exposed proteins that mediate binding to plasminogen such that it can be converted into plasmin in the presence of a plasminogen activator.

PGBA_N is an N-terminal family of bacterial proteins that bind plasminogen. This activity was identified in In Helicobacter pylori where it is thought to contribute to the virulence of this bacterium. Both PgbA and PgbB are surface-exposed proteins that mediate binding to plasminogen such that it can be converted into plasmin in the presence of a Pg activator.

The domain belongs to a fast evolving family known only from the placental mammals [[cite:PUB00069812],[cite:PUB00069813],[cite:PUB00069811]]. The PGC7/Stella/Dppa3 protein protects imprinted regions from demethylation post-fertilization [[cite:PUB00069811]]. This suggests that it might bind methylated DNA sequences directly [[cite:PUB00069716]]. The conserved core includes a postively charged helical segment and a C-terminal CXCXXC motif that is predicted to chelate a metal ion [[cite:PUB00069716]]. Most placental mammals contain 3-6 paralogs of this domain family. The CXCXXC motif is also conserved in a subset of fungal MBD4-like proteins [[cite:PUB00069716]].

This is the N-terminal and middle domain found in Streptococcus pneumoniae peptidoglycan GlcNAc deacetylase (SpPgdA). PgdA protects the Gram-positive bacterial cell wall from host lysozymes by deacetylating peptidoglycan GlcNAc residues. It is a member of the family 4 carbohydrate esterases (CE-4) [[cite:PUB00039846]].
PGDH_C is the C-terminal domain of putative bacterial phosphogluconate dehydrogenase proteins.

This domain is found in the D-3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase enzyme. In the structure of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis enzyme this domain was described as the intervening domain, also known as the allosteric substrate binding domain (ASB) [[cite:PUB00032650],[cite:PUB00051336],[cite:PUB00069764]]. The intervening domain between the substrate-binding and regulatory domains is not present in E. coli PGDH. This domain is closely related to [pfam:PF03315]. It serves as an anion-binding site and may function as an allosteric site for the control of enzyme activity [[cite:PUB00069764]].

This family of proteins is functionally uncharacterised. This family of proteins is found in bacteria. Proteins in this family are approximately 150 amino acids in length. There is a conserved PGDYG motif.

This family catalyses the synthesis of thymidine monophosphate (dTMP) from deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP). The physiological co-substrate has not yet been identified. Previous designation of this famliy as being thymidylate synthase from one paper, [cite:PUB00075419], has been shown to be erroneous [[cite:PUB00057368]]. The proteins are uncharacterised.

EKR is a short, 33 residue, domain found in bacterial and some lower eukaryotic species which lies between a POR (pyruvate ferredoxin/flavodoxin oxidoreductase) [pfam:PF01558] and the 4Fe-4S binding domain Fer4 [pfam:PF00037]. It contains a characteristic EKR sequence motif. The exact function of this domain is not known.

This domain of about 280 residues is found in eukaryotes. There are two conserved sequence motifs: GFC and GLL. This family is also known as UPF0704. This domain is found FAP206 [swissprot:Q23H79], a protein associated with cilia and flagella. In the ciliate Tetrahymena, the cilium has radial spokes, each of which is a macromolecular complex essential for motility. A triplet of three radial spokes, RS1, RS2, and RS3, is repeated every 96 nm along the doublet microtubule. Each spoke has a distinct base that docks to the doublet and is linked to different inner dynein arms. Knockout of the FAP206 gene results in slow cell motility and the 96-nm repeats lack RS2 and dynein c. FAP206 is probably part of the front prong and docks RS2 and dynein c to the microtubule [[cite:PUB00082324]].
This is a family of uncharacterised Clostridiales proteins.
The PGG domain is named for the highly conserved sequence motif found at the startt of the domain. The function is not known.

Members of this family carry two distinct, highly conserved sequence motifs, CPPPLYYTHL and HPHLAWLY. The family is found in eukaryotes, and the function is not known. This family lies at the C-terminus of members.
YdiH is a family of proteins found in bacteria. Proteins in this family are typically between 62 and 80 amino acids in length. The function is not known.
This family around 100 residues locates in the C-terminal of some uncharacterized proteins in various Bacteroides, Prevotella and Prevotella species. The function of this family remains unknown.

This domain is found in Rhamnogalacturonan lyase from Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron ([swissprot:Q8AAW3]) and other bacterial proteins. It shows an alpha/beta structure [[cite:PUB00100662]] and locates C-terminal to [pfam:PF07944]. The specific function of this domain is still unknown.
This family around 150 residues locates in the C-terminal of some uncharacterized proteins in various Bacteroides and Prevotella species. The function of this family remains unknown.

This family around 200 residues locates in the N-terminal of some uncharacterised proteins in various Bacteroides and Alistipes species. The function of this family remains unknown. The N-terminus of this model has been clipped by ~30 residues as it was capturing parts of collagen sequences, [pfam:PF01391].
This family around 150 residues locates in the N-terminal of some uncharacterized proteins in various Bacteroides and Prevotella species. The function of this family remains unknown.
This family around 100 residues locates in the N-terminal of some uncharacterized proteins and glucuronyl hydrolases in various Bacteroides species. The function of this family remains unknown.

This domain of around 100 residues locates at the C-terminal of some glycerophosphoryl diester phosphodiesterases and uncharacterized proteins in various Bacteroides and Prevotella species. The function of this domain is not yet clear, however, it is described as a putative glycerophosphoryl diester phosphodiesterase (PDBe:3i10).
This family around 75 residues locates in the N-terminal of F5/8 type C domain proteins and some uncharacterized proteins in various Bacteroides species. The function of this family remains unknown.
This family around 200 residues locates in the C-terminal of some uncharacterized proteins in various Bacteroides and Parabacteroides species. The function of this family remains unknown.
This is a family of unknown function, however family members such as B277 have been suggested to play a role in viral function [[cite:PUB00046115]].
Phosphoglucose isomerase catalyses the interconversion of glucose-6-phosphate and fructose-6-phosphate.
This alpha/beta domain is found at the N-terminus of proteins such as PglD [[cite:PUB00049741]]. This domain binds a UDP-sugar substrate [[cite:PUB00061322]].

PglL_A is a pilin glycosylation ligase domain found in Gram negative bacteria [[cite:PUB00076005]]. PglL protein O-oligosaccharyltransferases differ from the wider Wzy_C family, [pfam:PF04932], which contains both WaaL O-antigen ligases, in its substrate-specificity. PglL O-oligosaccharyltransferases (O-OTase) transfer oligosaccharide to serine or threonine in a protein. A further indication that the genes identified are PglL rather than WaaL homologues is that they are not located within lipopolysaccharide biosynthetic loci [[cite:PUB00076006]]. The specific pilin glycosylation ligases are a subset of the more general bacterial protein o-oligosaccharyltransferases [[cite:PUB00076006]].
This family is a member of the Alkaline phosphatase clan.
This is the C-terminal domain found in PGM1 present in Streptomyces cirratus. PGM1 is a gene product that links precursor peptides together to form the antibiotic Pheganomycin [[cite:PUB00091247]].

This domain is found in Immunodominant antigen Pgp3, a virulence protein from Chlamydia trachomatis involved in stimulating host immune responses and thought to be required for growth within mammalian cells. Pgp3 consists of globular N- and C-terminal domains ([pfam:PF05475] is the latter) connected by a triple-helical coiled coil (THCC). The N-terminal domain (this entry), which includes several structural motifs typically found in trimeric viral proteins, folds into a fairly flat surface [[cite:PUB00081208],[cite:PUB00152088],[cite:PUB00011294]].

This family represents a family of bacterial phosphatidylglycerophosphatases ([ec:3.1.3.27]), known as PgpA. It appears that bacteria possess several phosphatidylglycerophosphatases, and thus, PgpA is not essential in Escherichia coli [[cite:PUB00010084]].
Proteins in this entry are putative Actinobacterial proteins of about 150 amino acids in length, with three predicted transmembrane helices and an unusual motif with consensus sequence PGPGW.

This is a family of proteins that acts as a mitochondrial phosphatase in cardiolipin biosynthesis. Cardiolipin is a unique dimeric phosphoglycerolipid predominantly present in mitochondrial membranes. The inverted phosphatase motif includes the highly conserved DKD triad [[cite:PUB00066452]].

PE_PGRSs are a large family of Mtb proteins implicated in tuberculosis (TB) pathogenesis that show a modular structure: the N-terminal PE domain, highly homologous to the domain found in tens of others PE proteins and whose structure has been already solved by crystallography; a C-terminal domain that is unique for each protein; the polymorphic glycine-rich domain (PGRS) that varies in length from few tens to more than 1,000 amino acids [[cite:PUB00151826]].

This domain is found at the C-terminal end of [swissprot:Q7MX90] from Porphyromonas gingivalis (PG_0320) and similar bacterial sequences. This domain is usually found associated with [pfam:PF07610]. It is functionally uncharacterised.

This entry represents a ferredoxin-like domain found in a group of poorly characterised sequences, including the putative methyltransferase PG_1098 from Porphyromonas gingivalis ([swissprot:Q7MVG6], PDB:3ll7). Members of this entry contain a THUMP-like domain at the C-terminal ([pfam:PF18096]), following this domain.

Pfam_Description: N-terminal domain in putative methyltransferase PG_1098
Pfam_name: N-terminal domain in putative methyltransferase PG_1098
Pfam_description: This small alpha-helical domain is found at the N-terminus of putative methyltransferase proteins.

This domain is composed of three alpha helices [[cite:PUB00003979]]. This domain is found at the N or C terminus of a variety of enzymes involved in bacterial cell wall degradation [[cite:PUB00003115]]. This domain may have a general peptidoglycan binding function. This family is found N-terminal to the catalytic domain of matrixins [[cite:PUB00003911]]. The domain is found to bind peptidoglycan experimentally [[cite:PUB00109212]].
This family may be a peptidoglycan binding domain.

This domain is found associated with the L,D-transpeptidase domain [pfam:PF03734]. The structure of this domain has been solved and shows a mixed alpha-beta fold composed of nine beta strands and four alpha helices. This domain is usually found to be duplicated. Therefore, it seems likely that this domain acts to bind the two unlinked peptidoglycan chains and bring them into close association so they can be cross linked by the transpeptidase domain (Bateman A pers. observation).

This domain is composed of three alpha helices [[cite:PUB00003979]]. This domain is found at the N or C terminus of a variety of enzymes involved in bacterial cell wall degradation [[cite:PUB00003115]]. This domain may have a general peptidoglycan binding function. This family is found N-terminal to the catalytic domain of matrixins [[cite:PUB00003911]]. The domain is found to bind peptidoglycan experimentally [[cite:PUB00109212]].
This family may be a peptidoglycan binding domain.

This domain is found associated with the L,D-transpeptidase domain [pfam:PF03734]. The structure of this domain has been solved and shows a mixed alpha-beta fold composed of nine beta strands and four alpha helices. This domain is usually found to be duplicated. Therefore, it seems likely that this domain acts to bind the two unlinked peptidoglycan chains and bring them into close association so they can be cross linked by the transpeptidase domain (Bateman A pers. observation).
This family contains a potential peptidoglycan binding domain.

This domain is composed of three alpha helices [[cite:PUB00003979]]. This domain is found at the N or C terminus of a variety of enzymes involved in bacterial cell wall degradation [[cite:PUB00003115]]. This domain may have a general peptidoglycan binding function. This family is found N-terminal to the catalytic domain of matrixins [[cite:PUB00003911]]. The domain is found to bind peptidoglycan experimentally [[cite:PUB00109212]].
This family may be a peptidoglycan binding domain.

This domain is found associated with the L,D-transpeptidase domain [pfam:PF03734]. The structure of this domain has been solved and shows a mixed alpha-beta fold composed of nine beta strands and four alpha helices. This domain is usually found to be duplicated. Therefore, it seems likely that this domain acts to bind the two unlinked peptidoglycan chains and bring them into close association so they can be cross linked by the transpeptidase domain (Bateman A pers. observation).
This entry represents a putative peptidoglycan binding domain.
This domain is found in the N-terminal region of glucose-6-phosphate isomerase-like protein, just before the phospho-glucose isomerase C-terminal SIS domain ([pfam:PF10432]).
PH stands for pleckstrin homology.
This PH domain is found in IQ motif and SEC7 domain-containing proteins.
This entry contains a PH domain.
This entry corresponds to the PH domain found at the N-terminus of phospholipase C enzymes [[cite:PUB00043827]].
This entry represents the C-terminal part of the split PH domain from syntrophin proteins [[cite:PUB00038781]].
This entry represents a PH domain found in a variety of fungal proteins [[cite:PUB00057291],[cite:PUB00059482]].

This domain is found in uncharacterised fungal proteins. It shares significant sequence similarity to known Pleckstrin homology domains (PH-domains) and it is predicted to adopt similar structure. Proteins containing this domain also contain a DH-domain located downstream the PH-domain and are likely members of the Dbl family of guanine nucleotide exchange factors.

This domain is found at the N-terminal end of PH0730 from Pyrococcus horikoshii and similar archaeal proteins that contain the domain [pfam:PF14544] at the C-terminal. This domain adopts a winged helix fold.
This is a hypothetical protein from Pyroccous horikoshii of unknown function. It contains six alpha helices and eight beta strands and is thought to be monomeric.

SSRP1 is a component of FACT (facilitator of chromatin transcription), an essential chromatin reorganizing factor. This entry represents the first of two PH-like domains in these proteins [[cite:PUB00041003],[cite:PUB00101032],[cite:PUB00101034]].

This family represents the protein product of the gene pha-1 which coordinates with lin-35 Rb during animal development. The protein is expressed during embryonic development and functions in the cytoplasm. PHA-1 acts in a parallel pathway with UBC-18 to regulate the activity of a common cellular target [[cite:PUB00053702]].

This entry represents a domain found in an uncharacterised protein from a sulfolobus phage. ECOD notes structural similarity to [pfam:PF08796] that includes the YkuJ protein from Bacilli [[cite:PUB00054436]].

This family represents the N-terminal region of the bacterial poly-beta-hydroxybutyrate polymerase (PhaC). Polyhydroxyalkanoic acids (PHAs) are carbon and energy reserve polymers produced in some bacteria when carbon sources are plentiful and another nutrient, such as nitrogen, phosphate, oxygen, or sulfur, becomes limiting. PHAs composed of monomeric units ranging from 3 to 14 carbons exist in nature. When the carbon source is exhausted, PHA is utilised by the bacterium. PhaC links D-(-)-3-hydroxybutyrl-CoA to an existing PHA molecule by the formation of an ester bond [[cite:PUB00013025]]. This family appears to be a partial segment of an alpha/beta hydrolase domain.
PHAF1 and BCAS3 form a complex that affects the recruitment of several core autophagy proteins to the phagophore assembly site [[cite:PUB00097858]].
This domain is found in bacteriophage and is thought to have a gp45 function within the phage tail-fibre system.

Members of this family of viral baseplate structural proteins adopt a structure consisting of a three-layer beta-sandwich with two finger-like loops containing an alpha-helix at the opposite sides of the sandwich. The two peripheral, five-stranded, antiparallel beta-sheets are stacked against the middle, four-stranded, antiparallel beta-sheet. Attachment of this family of proteins to the baseplate during assembly creates a binding site for subsequent attachment of Gp6 [[cite:PUB00029011]].

Pfam_Description: Mu B transposition protein, C terminal
Pfam_name: Mu B transposition protein, C terminal
Pfam_description: The C terminal domain of the B transposition protein from Bacteriophage Mu comprises four alpha-helices arranged in a loosely packed bundle, where helix alpha1 runs parallel to alpha3, and anti-parallel to helices alpha2 and alpha4. The domain allows for non-specific binding of Mu to double-stranded DNA, allowing for integration into the bacterial genome, and mediates dimerisation of the protein [[cite:PUB00013250]].
Members of this family of scaffolding proteins are produced by various bacteriophages [[cite:PUB00028571]].

Members of this family adopt a beta barrel structure with a Greek key topology, which is topologically similar to the FMN-binding split barrel. They are structural component of the viral baseplate, predominantly found in the structural protein gp27 [[cite:PUB00012803]].

Members of this family adopt a beta barrel structure with a Greek key topology, which is topologically similar to the FMN-binding split barrel. They are structural component of the viral baseplate, predominantly found in the structural protein gp27 [[cite:PUB00012803]].
This putative domain is found in the large gene transfer agent protein. These produce defective phage like particles. This domain is similar to other phage-tail protein families.
This entry represents a probable metallopeptidase found in a variety of phage and bacterial proteomes.
Members of this family are found in putative phage tail tape measure proteins.

Members of this family of viral domains adopt a structure consisting of a single-stranded right-handed beta-helix, which in turn is made of parallel beta-strands and short turns. They are required for recognition of the 0-antigenic repeating units of the cell surface, and for subsequent infection of the bacterial cell [[cite:PUB00031615]].

Members of this family are phage shock protein PspD, found in a minority of bacteria that carry the defining genes of the phage shock regulon (pspA, pspB, pspC, and pspF). It is found in Escherichia coli, Yersinia pestis, and closely related species, where it is part of the phage shock operon. It is known to be expressed but its function is unknown.

This protein was previously designated as YjbO in Escherichia coli. It is found only in genomes that have the phage shock operon (psp), but it is only rarely encoded near other psp genes. The psp regulon is upregulated in response to a number of stress conditions, including ethanol, expression of the filamentous phage secretin protein IV and other secretins and heat shock.
This family is represented by Bacteriophage 186, Fil, a protein that causes filamentation. The characteristics of the protein distribution suggest prophage matches in addition to the phage matches.

Gene 1.1 in Bacteriophage T7 encodes a 42 amino acid protein, rich in basic amino acids suggesting its interaction with nucleic acids [[cite:PUB00017170]]. Many homologs are present in different T7 and T3-like bacteriophage.
Proteins in this family are bacteriophage GP30.3 proteins. Their function is poorly characterised [[cite:PUB00016570]][[cite:PUB00017073]].
This family consists of several GP30.8 proteins from the T4-like phages. The function of this family is unknown.

This domain is found in a prophage protein BC1872 found in B. cereus. The domain forms a three-layer beta/alpha/beta sandwich. Three alpha-helices, alpha1, alpha2, and alpha3, are sandwiched on one side by three-stranded antiparallel beta-sheet (beta3, beta4, and beta5) and on the other by a beta-hairpin (beta1 and beta2) [[cite:PUB00037487]].

This family consists of several short bacterial and phage proteins which are related to the E. coli protein AlpA. AlpA suppress two phenotypes of a delta lon protease mutant, overproduction of capsular polysaccharide and sensitivity to UV light [[cite:PUB00011917]]. Several of the sequences in this family are thought to be DNA-binding proteins.

This family consists of several phage antitermination protein Q and related bacterial sequences. Phage 82 gene Q encodes a phage-specific positive regulator of late gene expression, thought, by analogy to the corresponding gene of phage lambda, to be a transcription antiterminator [[cite:PUB00012323]].

This family consists of several phage antitermination protein Q and related bacterial sequences. Antiterminator proteins control gene expression by recognising control signals near the promoter and preventing transcriptional termination which would otherwise occur at sites that may be a long way downstream [[cite:PUB00012642]].

This family consists of several phage antitermination protein Q and related bacterial sequences. Phage 82 gene Q encodes a phage-specific positive regulator of late gene expression, thought, by analogy to the corresponding gene of phage lambda, to be a transcription antiterminator [[cite:PUB00012323]].

This family consists of several phage antitermination protein Q and related bacterial sequences. Antiterminator proteins control gene expression by recognising control signals near the promoter and preventing transcriptional termination which would otherwise occur at sites that may be a long way downstream [[cite:PUB00012642]].
Family members are found in Caudovirales such as Salmonella virus P22. Family members have a recombination accessory function [[cite:PUB00085216]].
This family was identified by Iyer and colleagues [[cite:PUB00010111]]. It includes the Ash protein from bacteriophage P4.

This entry includes the phage lambda head-tail attachment protein FII that is required for the joining of phage heads and tails at the last step of morphogenesis [[cite:PUB00010497]]. Plays a role in virion assembly by joining the head and the tail at the last step of morphogenesis. Six FII proteins probably bind protein W that closes the DNA-filled capsid, as well as the U tail terminator protein of the pre-assembled tail.

This is a family of proteins from single-stranded DNA bacteriophages. Scaffold proteins B and D are required for procapsid formation. Sixty copies of the internal scaffold protein B are found in the procapsid.

Pfam_Description: Type VI secretion system/phage-baseplate injector OB domain
Pfam_name: Type VI secretion system/phage-baseplate injector OB domain
Pfam_description: Family of bacterial and phage baseplate assembly proteins responsible for forming the small spike at the end of the tail or bacterial pathogenic needle-shaft [[cite:PUB00008577]]. This entry represents the OB fold part of the structure. This structure contains an unusual extra beta hairpin that forms the foundation of the spike protein's beta helix [[cite:PUB00091638]].

This entry represents a small family of short uncharacterised phage proteins. Structure prediction of A0A1J0MI44 suggests the protein adopts a four stranded sheet that can form homo-oligomers, with a homohexamer forming a beta propeller structure (iPTM=0.93). The function of these protein is unknown.

This entry describes a family of proteins found almost exclusively in phage or in prophage regions of bacterial genomes, including the phage-like Rhodobacter capsulatus gene transfer agent, which packages DNA. An apparent exception is Wolbachia pipientis wMel, a bacterial endosymbiont of the fruit fly, which has several candidate phage-related genes physically separate from obvious prophage regions.
This family of phage proteins is functionally uncharacterised. Proteins in this family are typically between 68 to 86 amino acids in length.
Family of bacteriophage hypothetical proteins and capsid proteins.
This entry represents a family of phage capsid protein. This family of proteins is found in bacteria and phage. Proteins in this family are approximately 280 amino acids in length.

The P3 major capsid protein adopts a 'double-barrel' structure comprising two eight-stranded viral beta-barrels or jelly rolls, each of which contains a 12-residue alpha-helix. This protein then trimerises through a 'trimerisation loop' sequence, and is incorporated within the viral capsid [[cite:PUB00028629]].
Major capsid protein E is involved with the stabilisation of the condensed form of the DNA molecule in phage heads [[cite:PUB00008451]].

Pfam_Description: Phage major capsid protein, P2 family
Pfam_name: Phage major capsid protein, P2 family

Pfam_description: E217 is a Pseudomonas phage used in an experimental cocktail to eradicate cystic fibrosis-associated Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Gp24 is a trimeric structural protein and component of the E217 icosahedral head.Gp24 adopts a beta-tulip fold similar to the gp87 protein found in the thermophilic phage P74-26. Each gp24 subunit consists of two anti-parallel beta-sheets, that form a tulip-like structure. Gp24 structural protein probably stabilises the E217 capsid. This entry includes the cement protein gp6 of cyanophage Pam3. It consists of an N-terminal beta-tulip domain followed by a C-terminal domain of seven antiparallel beta-strands. Gp6 trimers sit at the icosahedral threefold and quasi-threefold axes, stabilizing the capsid shell.
This entry represents a large family of phage proteins. These proteins form a trimeric arrangement which stabilises the phage capsid. The proteins have what is known as a beta-tulip fold.
This entry represents a large family of phage proteins. These proteins form a trimeric arrangement which stabilises the phage capsid. The proteins have what is known as a beta-tulip fold.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage proteins. Based on structural similarity These proteins form a trimeric arrangement which stabilises the phage capsid. The proteins have what is known as a beta-tulip fold.
This family consists of several phage CII regulatory proteins. CII plays a key role in the lysis-lysogeny decision in bacteriophage lambda and related phages [[cite:PUB00010448]].
The C-terminal domain of the CI repressor functions in oligomer formation [[cite:PUB00040693]].

This family consists of several phage CI repressor proteins and related bacterial sequences. The CI repressor is known to function as a transcriptional switch, determining whether transcription is lytic or lysogenic [[cite:PUB00012984]].
This is the A subunit of bacteriophage DNA clamp loader required for loading of sliding clamps onto chromosomal DNA. These clamps are involved in processivity of DNA replication [[cite:PUB00065743]].
Members of this family form the capsid of P. aeruginosa phage PP7. They adopt a secondary structure consisting of a six stranded beta sheet and an alpha helix [[cite:PUB00028377]].
Class I phage major coat protein Gp8 or B. The coat protein is largely alpha-helix with a slight curve [[cite:PUB00010511]].

Infection of Escherichia coli by filamentous bacteriophages is mediated by the minor phage coat protein A and involves two distinct cellular receptors, the F' pilus and the periplasmic protein TolA. These two receptors are contacted in a sequential manner, such that binding of TolA by the extreme N-terminal domain is conditional on a primary interaction of the second coat protein A domain with the F' pilus [[cite:PUB00010500]].

The major coat protein in the capsid of filamentous bacteriophage forms a helical assembly of about 7000 identical protomers, with each protomer comprised of 46 amino acid, after the cleavage of the signal peptide. Each protomer forms a slightly curved helix that combine to form a tubular structure that encapsulates the viral DNA [[cite:PUB00010499]].

The head-tail connector of bacteriophage 29 is composed of 12 36 kDa subunits with 12 fold symmetry. It is the central component of a rotary motor that packages the genomic dsDNA into pre-formed proheads. This motor consists of the head-tail connector, surrounded by a 29-encoded, 174-base, RNA and a viral ATPase protein [[cite:PUB00020085],[cite:PUB00020086]].

This family of proteins contain head-tail connector proteins related to gp6 from bacteriophage HK97 [[cite:PUB00067867]]. A structure of this protein shows similarity to gp15 a well characterised connector component of bacteriophage SPP1 [[cite:PUB00067867]].

This entry represents a family of phage proteins that are structurally related to the HK97 gp6 protein that forms a head to tail connection. It is likely that these proteins form large homo-oligomeric rings.

This family of phage Cox proteins is expressed by Enterobacteria phages. The Cox protein is a 79-residue basic protein with a predicted strong helix-turn-helix DNA-binding motif. It inhibits integrative recombination and it activates site-specific excision of the HP1 genome from the Haemophilus influenzae chromosome, Hp1. Cox appears to function as a tetramer. Cox binding sites consist of two direct repeats of the consensus motif 5'-GGTMAWWWWA, one Cox tetramer binding to each motif. Cox binding interferes with the interaction of HP1 integrase with one of its binding sites, IBS5. This competition is central to directional control. Both Cox binding sites are needed for full inhibition of integration and for activating excision, because it plays a positive role in assembling the nucleoprotein complexes that produce excisive recombination, by inducing the formation of a critical conformation in those complexes [[cite:PUB00044432]].
This family consists of several phage regulatory protein CII (CP76) sequences which are thought to be DNA binding proteins which are involved in the establishment of lysogeny [[cite:PUB00012905]].

The phage replication protein CRI, also known as Replication-associated protein G2P or Gene II, is essential for DNA replication. This entry represents the N-terminal TBP-like domain, a DNA binding fold composed of a curved antiparallel beta-sheet.
This family contains the bacteriophage helix-destabilising protein, or single-stranded DNA binding protein, required for DNA synthesis.

DsbA is a double stranded binding protein found in bacteriophage T4 which is involved in transcriptional regulation. DsbA, along with other viral proteins, interacts with the host RNA polymerase core enzyme enabling initiation of transcription. DsbA acts as an enhancer protein of late genes in vitro. The protein consists of mainly alpha helices [[cite:PUB00053255]].
The bacteriophage endonuclease I is a nuclease that is selective for the structure of the four-way Holliday DNA junction [[cite:PUB00010506]].
This is a family of proteins from single-stranded DNA bacteriophages. Protein F is the major capsid component, sixty copies of which are found in the virion.
This repeat is found in the tail fibres of phage. For example protein K [swissprot:Q37842] [[cite:PUB00007726]]. The repeats are about 40 residues long.
This repeat is found in the tail fibres of phage. For example protein K [swissprot:Q37842] [[cite:PUB00007726]]. The repeats are about 40 residues long.
This family represents the C-terminus of a prophage tail fibre protein found mostly in E. coli. All family members contain a conserved RLGP motif.
This entry represents a small repeat found in phage tail proteins from tailed bacteriophages and prophages mainly from flavobacteria.
This family consists of bacteriophage FRD3 proteins.
This is a family of proteins from single-stranded DNA bacteriophages. Five G proteins, each a tight beta barrel, from twelve surface spikes.

This entry represents a family of phage proteins related to gene 29 protein from Mycobacterium phage D29 and L5. The function of the proteins in this family is unknown. AlphaFold multimer shows that the proteins in the family adopt a confident dimeric structure. The individual proteins are not compact in isolated structure predictions.

This entry represents the gene 47 protein found in Mycobacterium phage L5. This protein forms a small globular beta domain that is related to LSM superfamily proteins such as Hfq. AlphaFold modelling suggests this protein forms an unusual octameric arrangement. Based on similarity to LSM proteins these proteins may bind to RNA.

GL forms a complex with gH, a glycoprotein known to be essential for entry of HSV-1 into cells and virus-induced cell fusion [[cite:PUB00109835]]. It is a hetero-oligomer of gH and gL which is incorporated into virions and transported to the cell surface which acts during entry of virus into cells [[cite:PUB00109835]]
This family consists of several Streptococcus thermophilus bacteriophage Gp111 proteins of around 110 residues in length. The function of this family is unknown.
This family consists of bacteriophage Gp15 proteins and related bacterial sequences. The function of this family is unknown

Family members such as protein 17 (gene product 17/gp17) found in Bacillus phage phi29, is involved in DNA replication and in pulling the phage DNA into the cell during the injection process [[cite:PUB00085236]].
This family of proteins are functionally uncharacterised. They are found in a variety of bacteriophage.
This family consists of several phage minor structural protein GP20 sequences of around 180 residues in length. The function of this family is unknown.
This is the highly conserved family of the major tail subunit protein.

The gene product 38 (gp38) from Lactococcus phage P008 is a short protein consisting of 71 amino acids. It is also known as the AbiQ resistance protein due to its involvement in escaping bacterial killing mediated by the AbiQ protein. Gp38 is expressed early in the viral replication cycle and is essential for virus function.

Pfam_Description: Phage protein (N4 Gp49/phage Sf6 gene 66) family
Pfam_name: Phage protein (N4 Gp49/phage Sf6 gene 66) family
Pfam_description: This family of phage proteins is functionally uncharacterised. The family includes bacteriophage Sf6 gene 66 [swissprot:Q716B1] as well as phage N4 GP49 protein [swissprot:A0MZD7]. Proteins in this family are typically between 87 and 154 amino acids in length. There is a conserved NGF sequence motif.

The baseplate of bacteriophage T4 controls host cell recognition, attachment, tail sheath contraction and viral DNA ejection. The structure of the baseplate suggests a mechanism of baseplate structural transition during the initial stages of T4 infection. The baseplate is assembled from six identical wedges that surround the central hub. Gp53, along with other T4 gene products, combine sequentially to assemble a wedge [[cite:PUB00029807]].

This entry represents a family of phage proteins. One example is the Gp84 protein from Mycobacteriophage L5 [swissprot:Q05301]. An AlphaFold model of a family member:K5BEF7 has a compact fold of one alpha helix followed by a three stranded beta sheet. The function of these proteins is unknown.

This family consists of a group of bacteriophage replication gene A protein (GPA) like sequences from both viruses and bacteria. The members of this family are likely to be endonucleases [[cite:PUB00011666],[cite:PUB00011665],[cite:PUB00011664]].

This family consists of several phage head completion protein (GPL) as well as related bacterial sequences. Members of this family allow the completion of filled heads by rendering newly packaged DNA in the heads resistant to DNase. The protein is thought to bind to DNA filled capsids [[cite:PUB00011914]].

Pfam_Description: Phage capsid scaffolding protein (GPO) serine peptidase
Pfam_name: Phage capsid scaffolding protein (GPO) serine peptidase
Pfam_description: This family consists of several bacteriophage capsid scaffolding proteins (GPO) and some related bacterial sequences. GPO is thought to function in both the assembly of proheads and the cleavage of GPN [[cite:PUB00011914]]. The family is found to function as a serine peptidase, with a conserved Asp, His and Ser catalytic triad, as in subtilisin, and as represented in MEROPS:S73. The family includes SwissProt:P25478 from Enterobacteria phage P2 which cleaves itself and then becomes the scaffold protein upon which the bacteriophage prohead is built - a mechanism quite common amongst phages [[cite:PUB00056601]].

This head assembly protein is also refereed to as gene product 40 (Gp40). A specific gp20-gp40 membrane insertion structure constitutes the T4 prohead assembly initiation complex [[cite:PUB00053307]]. This protein in T4 stimulates head formation [[cite:PUB00109680]].
This head fiber protein is also refereed to as Gp8.5. Gp8.5 is a structural protein in phage. It is a dispensable head protein.

This entry represents a phage protein that contains a central Hfq-like domain. This suggests that this protein may have an RNA binding function. AlphaFold prediction suggests a confident homohexameric structure. This entry represents a hypothetical protein found in several mycobacteriophages, including Bxz1, Mangeria, Derek, DrPhinkDaddy, Phusco and Jedediah. The proteins are typically around 155 amino acids in length.
This family consists of the tail length tape measure protein from bacteriophage HK97 and related sequences from Escherichia coli O157:H7.

This family of holins is found in several staphylococcal and streptococcal bacteriophages. Holins are a diverse family of proteins that cause bacterial membrane lysis during late-protein synthesis. It is thought that the temporal precision of holin-mediated lysis may occur through the buildup of a holin oligomer which causes the lysis [[cite:PUB00010120]].

This entry represents a family of bacteriophage holin proteins. Holins are small membrane proteins that control the timing of host cell lysis during the phage lytic cycle. Holins typically have 2-4 transmembrane helices. The exact mechanism of how holins trigger cell lysis is not fully understood. The holin family is found in phages that infect Actinobacteria, primarily Mycobacteria and Gordonia species.

This entry represents a family of putative holin proteins found in various phages infecting actinobacterial hosts, particularly Gordonia, Mycobacterium, Arthrobacter, and Microbacterium. Holins are small membrane proteins involved in the timing of host cell lysis during bacteriophage infection. Members of this family typically range from 94 to 151 amino acids in length and contain 3 to 4 predicted transmembrane helices. While some members have an N-terminal signal peptide or lipoprotein signal, most do not. It is unclear where the annotation for these proteins as holins arose. However it appears plausible based on their sequence features. This entry shows similarity to [pfam:PF19447] a bacterial family of unknown function.

Phage_holin_2_1 is a family of small hydrophobic holin proteins with one or more transmembrane domains. Members of this family fall into the holin superfamily II, and Phage 21 S holin is the prototype for this superfamily. It has two transmembrane segments with both the N- and C-termini on the cytoplasmic side of the inner membrane in E. coli. Holins are a diverse family of proteins that cause bacterial membrane lysis during late-protein synthesis. It is thought that the temporal precision of holin-mediated lysis may occur through the build up of a holin oligomer which causes the lysis [[cite:PUB00008724],[cite:PUB00084995]].

Pfam_Description: Phage holin T7 family, holin superfamily II
Pfam_name: Phage holin T7 family, holin superfamily II
Pfam_description: Holins are a diverse family of proteins that cause bacterial membrane lysis during late-protein synthesis.

Phage_holin_2_3 is a family of small hydrophobic phage proteins called holins with one transmembrane domain. Holins are produced by double-stranded DNA bacteriophages that use an endolysin-holin strategy to achieve lysis of their hosts. The endolysins are peptidoglycan-degrading enzymes that are usually accumulated in the cytosol until access to the cell wall substrate is provided by the holin membrane lesion 1,2].

Phage_holin_2_4 is a family of small hydrophobic phage proteins called holins with one transmembrane domain. Holins are produced by double-stranded DNA bacteriophages that use an endolysin-holin strategy to achieve lysis of their hosts. The endolysins are peptidoglycan-degrading enzymes that are usually accumulated in the cytosol until access to the cell wall substrate is provided by the holin membrane lesion.

This family represents one of a large number of mutually dissimilar families of phage holins. Holins act against the host cell membrane to allow lytic enzymes of the phage to reach the bacterial cell wall. This family includes the product of the S gene of phage lambda.

Holins are a diverse family of proteins that cause bacterial membrane lysis during late-protein synthesis. It is thought that the temporal precision of holin-mediated lysis may occur through the buildup of a holin oligomer which causes the lysis [[cite:PUB00010120]].

Pfam_Description: LydA holin phage, holin superfamily III
Pfam_name: LydA holin phage, holin superfamily III
Pfam_description: Phage_holin_3_3 is a family of small hydrophobic holin proteins with one or more transmembrane domains. Holins are encoded within the genomes of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria as well as those of the bacteriophages of these organisms. Their primary function appears to be transport of murein hydrolases across the cytoplasmic membrane to the cell wall where these enzymes hydrolyse the cell wall polymer as a prelude to cell lysis. When chromosomally encoded, these enzymes are therefore autolysins. Holins may also facilitate leakage of electrolytes and nutrients from the cell cytoplasm, thereby promoting cell death. Some may catalyse export of nucleases. LydA and lydB are encoded on the dar operon. The phenotype of a rapid lysis in the absence of active LydB suggests that this protein might be an antagonist of the holin LydA [[cite:PUB00076211]].

Phage_holin_6_2 is a family of holins classified as 1.E.20 in the TC database. The hol gene (PRF9) product (117 aas) of Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1 exhibits a hydrophobicity profile similar to holins of P2 and phiCTX phages with two peaks of hydrophobicity that might correspond to either one or two TMSs. Hol functions in conjunction with the lytic enzyme, Lys, a glycosyl hydrolase that breaks-up the murein in the bacterial cell-wall, causing lysis of the cell and hence entry of phage particles [[cite:PUB00076212]]. Several members are annotated as pyocin R2_PP when encoded on the chromosome.

Pfam_Description: Putative Actinobacterial Holin-X, holin superfamily III
Pfam_name: Putative Actinobacterial Holin-X, holin superfamily III
Pfam_description: Phage_holin_3_6 is a family of small hydrophobic proteins with two or three transmembrane domains of the Hol-X family. Holin proteins are produced by double-stranded DNA bacteriophages that use an endolysin-holin strategy to achieve lysis of their hosts. The endolysins are peptidoglycan-degrading enzymes that are usually accumulated in the cytosol until access to the cell wall substrate is provided by the holin membrane lesion.
This is a family of putative proteobacterial phage three-transmembrane-domain holins.

Phage holins and lytic enzymes are both necessary for bacterial lysis and virus dissemination. This family also includes TcdE/UtxA involved in toxin secretion in Clostridium difficile [[cite:PUB00009740]]. The 1.E.10 family is represented by Bacillus subtilis phi29 holin [[cite:PUB00075698],[cite:PUB00075699]]; 1.E.16 represents the Cph1 holin[[cite:PUB00075700]]; and the 1.E.19 family is represented by the Clostridium difficile TcdE holin. Toxigenic strains of C. difficile produce two large toxins (TcdA and TcdB) encoded within a pathogenicity locus. tcdE, encoded between tcdA and tcdB, encodes a 166 aa protein which causes death to E. coli when expressed, and the structure of TcdE resembles holins. TcdE acts on the bacterial membrane. Since TcdA and TcdB lack signal peptides, they may be released via TcdE either prior to or subsequent to cell lysis [[cite:PUB00009740]].

Pfam_Description: Mycobacterial 4 TMS phage holin, superfamily IV
Pfam_name: Mycobacterial 4 TMS phage holin, superfamily IV
Pfam_description: These proteins are predicted transmembrane proteins with probably four transmembrane spans. The 1.E.40 is represented by the mycobacterial 4 phage holin, but it also contains many cyanobacterial. proteobacterial and firmicute proteins. Holins are encoded within the genomes of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria as well as in those of the bacteriophage of these organisms. The primary function of holins appears to be transport of murein hydrolases across the cytoplasmic membrane to the cell wall where these enzymes hydrolyse the cell wall polymer as a prelude to cell lysis. When chromosomally encoded the enzymes are therefore autolysins. Holins may also facilitate leakage of electrolytes and nutrients from the cell cytoplasm, thereby promoting cell death. Some may catalyse export of nucleases.

This family consists of several Listeria bacteriophage holin proteins and related bacterial sequences. Holins are a diverse family of proteins that cause bacterial membrane lysis during late-protein synthesis. It is thought that the temporal precision of holin-mediated lysis may occur through the build up of a holin oligomer which causes the lysis [[cite:PUB00010120]].

Pfam_Description: Phage holin family Hol44, in holin superfamily V
Pfam_name: Phage holin family Hol44, in holin superfamily V
Pfam_description: Phage_holin_V_2 is a family of small hydrophobic proteins with three transmembrane domains of the Hol44 family. These proteins are produced by double-stranded DNA bacteriophages that use an endolysin-holin strategy to achieve lysis of their hosts. The endolysins are peptidoglycan-degrading enzymes that are usually accumulated in the cytosol until access to the cell wall substrate is provided by the holin membrane lesion. Full activity of the endolysin Lys44 from oenophage fOg44 requires sudden ion-nonspecific dissipation of the proton motive force, undertaken by the fOg44 holin during phage-infection [[cite:PUB00110742],[cite:PUB00076205],[cite:PUB00110743]].

Phage_holin_6_1 or Holin_LLH identifies a family of phage holins from a number of phage and prophage regions of Gram-positive bacteria. Like other holins, it is large for holins (about 100-160 amino acids) with stretches of hydrophobic sequence and is encoded adjacent to lytic enzymes. Holin LLH family is found in phage of Firmicutes and have an N-terminal transmembrane segment.

Pfam_Description: Mycobacterial 2 TMS Phage Holin (M2 Hol) Family
Pfam_name: Mycobacterial 2 TMS Phage Holin (M2 Hol) Family
Pfam_description: Phage_holin_8_1 is a family of two transmembrane mycobacteriophage holins, small hydrophobic proteins that effect lysis of host mycobacterial cells in conjunction with a mycobacteria-specific lysin, lysB. The product of lysB gene targets the mycobacteria outer membrane, the last barrier to bacteriophage release [[cite:PUB00076209],[cite:PUB00075704]].

This family of holins is found in several staphylococcal and streptococcal bacteriophages. Holins are a diverse family of proteins that cause bacterial membrane lysis during late-protein synthesis. It is thought that the temporal precision of holin-mediated lysis may occur through the buildup of a holin oligomer which causes the lysis [[cite:PUB00010120]].

This entry represents a family of bacteriophage holin proteins. Holins are small membrane proteins that control the timing of host cell lysis during the phage lytic cycle. Holins typically have 2-4 transmembrane helices. The exact mechanism of how holins trigger cell lysis is not fully understood. The holin family is found in phages that infect Actinobacteria, primarily Mycobacteria and Gordonia species.
Phage_holin_Dp1 is a family of putative phage-holins from Gram-positive bacteria, largely Firmicutes, with two probable TMSs. The family shows lytic activity.

Bacteriophage effects host lysis with T holin along with an endolysin. T disrupts the membrane allowing sequential events which lead to the attack of the peptidoglycan. T has an usual periplasmic domain which transduces environmental information for the real-time control of lysis timing [[cite:PUB00053276]].
This family is represented by Bacteriophage HP1, Orf24, whose function is unknown. The characteristics of the protein distribution suggest prophage matches in addition to the phage matches.

These baseplate proteins are also referred to as Gp28. Gp28 is the structural component of the central part of the bacteriophage T4 baseplate, which possesses a hydrophobic region and is membrane bound [[cite:PUB00056064]]. Gp28 forms a complex with gp27 which is another structural component of the baseplate [[cite:PUB00056064]].

Members of this family cleave DNA substrates by a series of staggered cuts, during which the protein becomes covalently linked to the DNA through a catalytic tyrosine residue at the carboxy end of the alignment. The catalytic site residues in CRE recombinase ([swissprot:P06956]) are Arg-173, His-289, Arg-292 and Tyr-324.
Catalyses cleavage and ligation of DNA [[cite:PUB00061161],[cite:PUB00076085]].

This is the central domain of phage integrases. This domain is known to mediate DNA binding and binds to the major groove adjacent to the site of DNA cleavage [[cite:PUB00029750]]. It consists of two pairs of antiparallel helices that pack together at nearly a right angle and form a four-helix bundle.
This domain is found in a variety of phage integrase proteins.
This is a family of DNA-binding prophage integrases. It is found largely in Proteobacteria.
This domain is found in a variety of phage integrase proteins.
This domain is found in a variety of phage integrase proteins.
A family of uncharacterised proteins found by clustering human gut metagenomic sequences [[cite:PUB00055601]]. This family appears related to the N-terminal domain of phage integrases.

Xer recombinases are members of the tyrosine site-specific recombinase superfamily, a large group of enzymes that catalyze DNA breakage and rejoining using a conserved tyrosine nucleophile. Tyrosine recombinases promote various programmed DNA rearrangements including the monomerization of phage, plasmid and chromosome multimers, resolution of hairpin telomeres, and the movement of virulence and antibiotic resistance carrying integrative mobile genetic elements. Structural analysis of Helicobacter pylori XerH indicates that this N-terminal domain consisting of six alpha-helices contacts the DNA using a four-helix bundle [[cite:PUB00091525]].
A family of uncharacterised proteins found by clustering human gut metagenomic sequences [[cite:PUB00055601]]. This family appears related to the N-terminal domain of phage integrases.

Xer recombinases are members of the tyrosine site-specific recombinase superfamily, a large group of enzymes that catalyze DNA breakage and rejoining using a conserved tyrosine nucleophile. Tyrosine recombinases promote various programmed DNA rearrangements including the monomerization of phage, plasmid and chromosome multimers, resolution of hairpin telomeres, and the movement of virulence and antibiotic resistance carrying integrative mobile genetic elements. Structural analysis of Helicobacter pylori XerH indicates that this N-terminal domain consisting of six alpha-helices contacts the DNA using a four-helix bundle [[cite:PUB00091525]].

This family consists of several Bacteriophage lambda replication protein P like proteins. The bacteriophage lambda P protein promoters replication of the phage chromosome by recruiting a key component of the cellular replication machinery to the viral origin. Specifically, P protein delivers one or more molecules of Escherichia coli DnaB helicase to a nucleoprotein structure formed by the lambda O initiator at the lambda replication origin [[cite:PUB00012966]].

This protein is involved in host lysis. This family is not considered to be a peptidase according to the MEROPs database. This family Rz and the Rz1 protein ([pfam:PF06085]) represent a unique example of two genes located in different reading frames in the same nucleotide sequence, which encode different proteins that are both required in the same physiological pathway [[cite:PUB00034469]].
This family includes lambda phage lysozyme and E. coli endolysin.
This domain has a lysozyme like fold. It is found in the tail protein of various phages probably giving them the ability to degrade the host cell wall peptidoglycan layer [[cite:PUB00051120]].
Family of related phage minor capsid proteins.
This family consists of a series of phage minor tail proteins and related sequences from several bacterial species.

This entry represents putative lysis proteins from Bacteriophage MS2 and Bacteriophage BZ13. The bacteriophage MS2 lysin protein swiss:C0M1L5 was identified as an overlapping cistron in the bacteriophage MS2 RNA [[cite:PUB00053761]]. This proteins induces the formation of specific membrane adhesion sites between the inner and outer membranes, apparently leading to host cell lysis. Lysis may be performed via activation of host murein hydrolases [[cite:PUB00097482],[cite:PUB00097483]].

Pfam_Description: Phage Mu protein F like protein
Pfam_name: Phage Mu protein F like protein
Pfam_description: Members of this family are found in double-stranded DNA bacteriophages, and in some bacteria. A member of this family is required for viral head morphogenesis in bacteriophage SPP1 ([swissprot:Q38577]). This family is possibly a minor head protein. This family may be related to the family TT_ORF1 ([pfam:PF02956]).

This family consists of bacterial and phage Gam proteins. The gam gene of bacteriophage Mu encodes a protein which protects linear double stranded DNA from exonuclease degradation in vitro and in vivo [[cite:PUB00013109]].

This family is represented by Bacteriophage Mu, Gp27. It is probably the small subunit of terminase, which recognises viral DNA, binding to the packaging initiation site (pac) and regulates the ATPase activity of the terminase large subunit [[cite:PUB00097490]]. The characteristics of the protein distribution suggest prophage matches in addition to the phage matches.
This family is represented by the Bacteriophage Mu, Gp36. The characteristics of the protein distribution suggest prophage matches in addition to the phage matches.

This family is represented by Bacteriophage Mu, Gp37 (also known as Probable tail terminator protein) which may stop tail tube polymerization by capping the rapidly polymerising tail tube once it has reached its requisite length and prevent its depolymerization [[cite:PUB00052083]]. This family also has prophages matches, such as the Gp37 protein from the FluMu prophage.

This entry represents the N-terminal domain of Bacteriophage Mu Gp45 and related proteins from both phages and bacteria. Gp45 is a component of the baseplate that forms a central needle-like spike used to puncture the host cell membrane for tube insertion during virus entry. It serves as the distal plug of tail tube channel and might regulate the process of the phage DNA and protein ejection into the host cell [[cite:PUB00077063],[cite:PUB00065189]]. According to structure predictions and comparison, this domain may adopt and OB-fold.

Members of this family of proteins comprise various hypothetical and putative bacteriophage tail proteins, including Gp48 from Bacteriophage Mu and other Mu-like prophages such as FluMu [[cite:PUB00015900]].
This family consists of several phage NinH proteins. The function of this family is unknown.

Terminase, the DNA packaging enzyme of bacteriophage lambda, is a heteromultimer composed of subunits Nu1 and A. The smaller Nu1 terminase subunit has a low-affinity ATPase stimulated by non-specific DNA [[cite:PUB00013172]].

Pfam_Description: Cyanophage outer membrane protein like beta barrel domain
Pfam_name: Cyanophage outer membrane protein like beta barrel domain
Pfam_description: This entry represents a family of small uncharacterised membrane bound beta barrel-like proteins found in cyanophage. The putative membrane beta barrel is incomplete composed of only 6 beta strands. However, the proteins form a confident homodimer (ipTM=0.78) composed of a flattened 12 stranded beta barrel. The proteins likely contain an N-terminal signal peptide that is cleaved during membrane insertion.

This family of proteins is found in bacteriophage such as Bacteriophage phiMH2K and Bacteriophage Chp1. Proteins in this family are typically between 81 and 96 amino acids in length. These proteins appear to have a role in phage packaging.
Family of conserved bacteriophage open reading frames.
This family is represented by Bacteriophage P22, NinX. The characteristics of the protein distribution suggest prophage matches in addition to the phage matches.
This family consists of several phage and bacterial proteins which are closely related to the GpE tail protein from Phage P2.

This family consists of several bacterial and phage proteins of around 130 residues in length which seem to be related to the bacteriophage P2 GpU protein ([swissprot:O64315]) which is thought to be involved in tail assembly [[cite:PUB00012968]].

ORF12 from Lactococcus lactis phage p2 is thought to be a chaperone for the tape measure protein that might help to maintain the tape measure protein in solution during tail assembly. This late- expressed protein shows an all-alpha structure with five alpha- helices oriented to form a hydrophobic cleft on the inner surface of the protein. It adopts a trimeric assembly, forming long spirals [[cite:PUB00051292]].

Bacteriophage capsids constitute icosahedral shells of exceptional stability that protect the viral genome. Many capsids display on their surface decoration proteins whose structure and function remain largely unknown. The decoration protein pb10 of phage T5 binds at the centre of the 120 hexamers formed by the major capsid protein [[cite:PUB00151784]]. Pb10 consists of an N-terminal alpha-helical capsid-binding domain (this entry) and an Ig-like domain [[cite:PUB00151784]].

This domain is found in a family of proteins found almost exclusively in phage or in prophage regions of bacterial genomes, including the phage-like Rhodobacter capsulatus (Rhodopseudomonas capsulata) gene transfer agent, which packages DNA.

Bacteriophage portal proteins form a dodecamer and is located at a five-fold vertex of the viral capsid. The portal complex forms a channel through which the viral DNA is packaged into the capsid, and exits during infection. The portal protein is though to rotate during DNA packaging [[cite:PUB00008675]]. Portal proteins from different phage show little sequence homology, so this family does not represent all portal proteins.

This family represents phage and prophage portal proteins that form the portal of the phage particle [[cite:PUB00155786],[cite:PUB00153918],[cite:PUB00154413]]. These proteins form a dodecamer assembly that defines a channel for DNA entry and exit. The dodecamer structure resembles a flying saucer with a central channel, which is filled with a rope-like DNA chain [[cite:PUB00154413]]. Each subunit of the dodecamer is involved in interaction with capsomers. The dodecameric portal is connected with the neck, which comprises a dodecameric adaptor, a hexameric connector, and a hexameric terminator gp12, forming a continuous DNA injection channel at the center [[cite:PUB00154413]].
This protein forms a hole, or portal, that enables DNA passage during packaging and ejection. It also forms the junction between the phage capsid and the tail proteins.

Members of this protein family are found in temperate phage and bacterial prophage regions. Members include the product of the rha gene of the lambdoid phage phi-80, a late operon gene. The presence of this gene interferes with infection of bacterial strains that lack integration host factor (IHF), which regulates the rha gene. It is suggested that Rha is a phage regulatory protein.

This entry represents a family of uncharacterised phage and bacterial proteins. Structurally the proteins include an N-terminal beta barrel domain that shows some structural similarity to the C-terminal domain of the ProQ RNA-binding domain. That domain has been described as being similar to the Tudor domains.

Pfam_Description: Putative lactococcus lactis phage r1t holin
Pfam_name: Putative lactococcus lactis phage r1t holin
Pfam_description: Phage_r1t_holin is a family of putative phage r1t holins from lactococcus. these holins carry two hydrophobic putative TMs separated by a short beta-turn region [[cite:PUB00110820]].

Pfam_Description: Phage 5-bladed beta propeller receptor binding platform domain
Pfam_name: Phage 5-bladed beta propeller receptor binding platform domain
Pfam_description: This entry represents the receptor binding domain of a variety of bacteriophage. The cell wall of S. aureus typically contains poly-ribitol phosphate type wall teichoic acid (WTA), which is modified with D-alanine and N-acetyl-glucosamine (GlcNAc). It has been shown that phage psi11 requires GlcNAc residues on WTA for adsorption8. Gp45 of phage psi11 was identified and characterized as the receptor-binding protein (RBP) [[cite:PUB00151757]]. This entry represents the 5 bladed beta propeller platform domain that has been suggested to bind to the GlcNac substrate [[cite:PUB00151758]].

Replication protein O is necessary for the initiation of bacteriophage DNA replication. Protein O interacts with the lambda replication origin, and also with replication protein P to form an oligomer [[cite:PUB00010025]]. It is speculated that the N-terminal half interacts with the replication origin while the C terminal half mediates protein-protein interaction (annotation of Swiss: P14815).

This entry represents the N-terminal domain of a small family of phage proteins. The protein contains a region of low-complexity sequence that reflects DNA direct repeats able to function as an origin of phage replication. The region is N-terminal to the low-complexity region.

Upon infection the RpbA encode phage protein binds to the ADP-ribosylated core RNA polymerase and modulates function to preferentially bind T4 promoters. This is a non-essential protein to the phage life cycle.

Pfam_description: This entry represents the second domain in a variety of phage tail sheath proteins. According to ECOD this domain has a subtilisin-like structure.

Bacteriophages penetrate the host cell membrane using their tail to inject genetic material into the host [[cite:PUB00061271]]. In this penetration process, they use central spike domain located beneath their baseplate [[cite:PUB00065189]]. The spike domain folds as a trimeric iron-binding structure [[cite:PUB00061271]]. This entry contains three copies of the repeat unit.
