This is the C-terminal domain of 54S ribosomal protein L2 (also known as Mitochondrial large ribosomal subunit protein bL27m). bL27 C-terminal region interacts with an expansion segment of 21S rRNA to form part of the central protuberance [[cite:PUB00087081]].

The ribosomal 28 family includes L28 proteins from bacteria and chloroplasts. The L24 protein from yeast [swissprot:P36525] also contains a region of similarity to prokaryotic L28 proteins. L24 from yeast is also found in the large ribosomal subunit

Ribosomal protein L3 (also known as uL3) is one of the proteins from the large ribosomal subunit. In Escherichia coli, L3 is known to bind to the 23S rRNA and may participate in the formation of the peptidyltransferase centre of the ribosome.
This family includes prokaryotic L30 and eukaryotic L7.
This presumed domain is found at the N-terminus of Ribosomal L30 proteins and has been termed RL30NT or NUC018 [[cite:PUB00016366]].
This family includes ribosomal protein L32 from eukaryotes and archaebacteria.
This family includes yeast MRPL37 a mitochondrial ribosomal protein [[cite:PUB00033319]].
This ribosomal protein is found in archaebacteria and eukaryotes. It contains four conserved cysteine residues that may bind to zinc.
This family includes ribosomal protein L37 from eukaryotes and archaebacteria. The family contains many conserved cysteines and histidines suggesting that this protein may bind to zinc.
This family includes Ribosomal L4/L1 from eukaryotes and archaebacteria and L4 from eubacteria. L4 from yeast has been shown to bind rRNA [[cite:PUB00000678]].
Bovine L40 has been identified as a secondary RNA binding protein [[cite:PUB00004350]]. L40 is fused to a ubiquitin protein [[cite:PUB00000250]].

The 39S ribosomal protein appears to be a subunit of one of the larger mitochondrial 66S or 70S units [[cite:PUB00044461]]. Under conditions of ethanol-stress in rats the larger subunit is largely dissociated into its smaller components [[cite:PUB00044462]]. In E. coli, in the absence of the enzyme pseudouridine synthase (RluD) synthase, there is an accumulation of 50S and 30S subunits and the appearance of abnormal particles (62S and 39S), with concomitant loss of 70S ribosomes [[cite:PUB00044462]].

Pfam_Description: Ribosomal large subunit proteins 60S L5, and 50S L18
Pfam_name: Ribosomal large subunit proteins 60S L5, and 50S L18
Pfam_description: This family contains the large 60S ribosomal L5 proteins from Eukaryota and the 50S L18 proteins from Archaea. It has been shown that the amino terminal 93 amino acids of [swissprot:P09895] are necessary and sufficient to bind 5S rRNA in vitro [[cite:PUB00002952]], suggesting that the entire family has a function in rRNA binding [[cite:PUB00123343],[cite:PUB00079817],[cite:PUB00123344],[cite:PUB00110894]].
This region is found associated with [pfam:PF00281].

This family includes: Ribosomal L7A from metazoa, Ribosomal L8-A and L8-B from fungi, 30S ribosomal protein HS6 from archaebacteria, 40S ribosomal protein S12 from eukaryotes, Ribosomal protein L30 from eukaryotes and archaebacteria. Gadd45 and MyD118 [[cite:PUB00007297]].
This family includes small ribosomal subunit S10 from prokaryotes and S20 from eukaryotes.

This is a family of unknown function. Family members are ribosomal proteins found in the mitochondria (RPS12). Homologus RPS12 proteins in bacterial ribosoms participate in stabilizing the second base pair of the codon-anticodon duplex in the A site and is likely to be critical for the fidelity of decoding process. A similar role can be anticipated for this protein in mitochondrial ribosomes. This has been shown where the product of edited RPS12 mRNA translation represented a component of the mitoribosome's small subunit [[cite:PUB00085312]].
This family includes ribosomal protein S13 from prokaryotes and S18 from eukaryotes.
This domain is found at the N-terminus of ribosomal S13 and S15 proteins. This domain is also identified as NUC021 [[cite:PUB00016366]].
This family includes both ribosomal S14 from prokaryotes and S29 from eukaryotes.
This short N-terminal region is found in a number of higher eukaryotic ribosomal subunit 17 proteins.
Bacterial ribosomal protein S20 interacts with 16S rRNA [[cite:PUB00003228]].

This family of ribosomal proteins consists mainly of the 40S ribosomal protein S27a which is synthesised as a C-terminal extension of ubiquitin (CEP). The S27a domain compromises the C-terminal half of the protein. The synthesis of ribosomal proteins as extensions of ubiquitin promotes their incorporation into nascent ribosomes by a transient metabolic stabilisation and is required for efficient ribosome biogenesis [[cite:PUB00004044]]. The ribosomal extension protein S27a contains a basic region that is proposed to form a zinc finger; its fusion gene is proposed as a mechanism to maintain a fixed ratio between ubiquitin necessary for degrading proteins and ribosomes a source of proteins [[cite:PUB00004045]].

Pfam_Description: Sigma 54 modulation protein / S30EA ribosomal protein
Pfam_name: Sigma 54 modulation protein / S30EA ribosomal protein
Pfam_description: This Pfam family contains the sigma-54 modulation protein family and the S30AE family of ribosomal proteins which includes the light- repressed protein (lrtA) ([swissprot:P47908]) [[cite:PUB00009462]].
This family contains a central domain [pfam:PF00013], hence the amino and carboxyl terminal domains are stored separately. This is a minimal carboxyl-terminal domain. Some are much longer.

This family includes small ribosomal subunit S9 from prokaryotes and S16 from metazoans. This domain is predicted to bind to ribosomal RNA [[cite:PUB00001317]]. This domain is composed of four helices in the known structure. However the domain is discontinuous in sequence and the alignment for this family contains only the first three helices.
This family contains ribosomal protein S7 from prokaryotes and S5 from eukaryotes.
This family includes small ribosomal subunit S9 from prokaryotes and S16 from eukaryotes.

This family contains the C-terminal domain of ribosomal protein TL5. The N-terminal domain, which binds to 5S rRNA, is contained in family Ribosomal_L25p, [pfam:PF01386]. Full length (N- and C-terminal domain) homologues of TL5 are also known as CTC proteins. TL5 or CTC are not found in Eukarya or Archaea. In some Bacteria, including E. coli, this ribosomal subunit occurs as a single domain protein (named Ribosomal subunit L25), where the only domain is homologous to TL5 N-terminal domain (hence included in family [pfam:PF01386]). The function of the C-terminal domain of TLC is at present unknown.

Pfam_Description: Small ribosomal subunit protein uS5m, N-terminal
Pfam_name: Small ribosomal subunit protein uS5m, N-terminal
Pfam_description: This entry represents an extension found at the N-terminal of the mitochondrial 28S Small ribosomal subunit protein uS5m [[cite:PUB00151742],[cite:PUB00151743]]. This region lines a part of the mRNA entry path and connects the 28S subunit body to the head forming a latch across the mRNA channel entrance [[cite:PUB00151743]].
This protein is known as S12 in bacteria and archaea and S23 in eukaryotes.

Pfam_Description: Sigma 54 modulation/S30EA ribosomal protein C terminus
Pfam_name: Sigma 54 modulation/S30EA ribosomal protein C terminus
Pfam_description: This domain often occurs at the C-terminus of proteins containing [pfam:PF02482].
This family is found at the very C-terminal of 60 ribosomal L4 proteins.

This family represents the C-terminal domain of some putative ribosome biogenesis proteins in archaea. It has also been identified in the eukaryotic protein Tsr3, which is involved in ribosomal RNA biogenesis [[cite:PUB00076727]].
This enzyme catalyses the conversion of D-ribulose 5-phosphate into D-xylulose 5-phosphate.
This family consists of several ribose 5-phosphate isomerase A or phosphoriboisomerase A ([ec:5.3.1.6]) from bacteria, eukaryotes and archaea.
ADP-ribosyl cyclase [ec:3.2.2.5] (also know as cyclic ADP-ribose hydrolase or CD38) synthesises cyclic-ADP ribose, a second messenger for glucose-induced insulin secretion.

Pfam_Description: Small ribosomal subunit protein mS39, PPR
Pfam_name: Small ribosomal subunit protein mS39, PPR
Pfam_description: This entry represents the a PPR section found at the N-terminal of Small ribosomal subunit protein mS39 (also known as PPR domain protein 3 (PTCD3)), a mitochondrial RNA-binding protein that has a role in mitochondrial translation [[cite:PUB00151742],[cite:PUB00090551],[cite:PUB00154208],[cite:PUB00152699],[cite:PUB00154029]].
This highly conserved region is found towards the C-terminus of the transmembrane domain [[cite:PUB00010217]]. The function is unclear.

RIC1 has been identified in yeast as a Golgi protein involved in retrograde transport to the cis-Golgi network. It forms a heterodimer with Rgp1 and functions as a guanyl-nucleotide exchange factor [[cite:PUB00035455]].

Pfam_Description: Resistance to inhibitors of cholinesterase homologue 3
Pfam_name: Resistance to inhibitors of cholinesterase homologue 3
Pfam_description: RIC3 is a protein associated with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), neurotransmitter-gated ion channels expressed at the neuromuscular junction and within the central and peripheral nervous systems. It can enhance functional expression of multiple nAChR subtypes. RIC3 promotes functional expression of homomeric alpha-7 and alpha-8 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the cell surface.
Ric8 is involved in the EGL-30 neurotransmitter signalling pathway [[cite:PUB00011692]]. It is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor [[cite:PUB00044463]] that regulates neurotransmitter secretion.

This presumed domain is about 85 residues in length and very rich in charged residues, hence the name RICH (Rich In CHarged residues). It is found in secreted proteins such as PspC [swissprot:Q9KK19], SpsA [swissprot:O33742] and IgA FC receptor [swissprot:P27951] from Streptococcus agalactiae. This domain could be involved in bacterial adherence or cell wall binding.
This entry represents the catalytic domain of a subset of ubiquitin-like proteases from the CE clan, including RickCE from Rickettsia [[cite:PUB00117515],[cite:PUB00154209]].

This is a presumed domain found at the N-terminal of rickCE ubiquitin-like proteases, such as [swissprot:Q1RK35], which may have a Rossmann-like fold similar to that in glycosyltransferases (Foldseek structural comparison).

This family includes a putative two transmembrane alpha-helical region that contains glycine zipper motifs [[cite:PUB00055608]]. This family includes several Rickettsia genus specific 17 kDa surface antigen proteins [[cite:PUB00020255]].

Pfam_Description: Rapamycin-insensitive companion of mTOR, middle domain
Pfam_name: Rapamycin-insensitive companion of mTOR, middle domain
Pfam_description: Rictor appears to serve as a scaffolding protein that is important for maintaining mTORC2 integrity. The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a conserved Ser/Thr kinase that forms two functionally distinct complexes, mTROC1 and mTORC2, important for nutrient and growth-factor signalling. This region is the more conserved central section that may include several individual domains. Rictor can be inhibited in the short-term by rapamycin.

Rictor appears to serve as a scaffolding protein that is important for maintaining mTORC2 integrity. The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a conserved Ser/Thr kinase that forms two functionally distinct complexes, mTROC1 and mTORC2, important for nutrient and growth-factor signalling. This region is the N-terminal conserved section that may include several individual domains. Rictor can be inhibited in the short-term by rapamycin.

Rictor appears to serve as a scaffolding protein that is important for maintaining mTORC2 integrity. The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a conserved Ser/Thr kinase that forms two functionally distinct complexes, mTROC1 and mTORC2, important for nutrient- and growth-factor signalling. This short region is the phoshorylation site. Rictor does interact with 14-3-3 in a Thr1135-dependent manner. Rictor can be inhibited by short-term rapamycin treatment showing that Thr1135 is an mTORC1-regulated site.

Rictor appears to serve as a scaffolding protein that is important for maintaining mTORC2 integrity. The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a conserved Ser/Thr kinase that forms two functionally distinct complexes, mTROC1 and mTORC2, important for nutrient and growth-factor signalling. These long eukaryotic proteins carry several well-conserved domains, and this is No.5.

The rieske domain has a [2Fe-2S] centre. Two conserved cysteines coordinate one Fe ion, while the other Fe ion is coordinated by two conserved histidines. In hyperthermophilic archaea there is a SKTPCX(2-3)C motif at the C-terminus. The cysteines in this motif form a disulphide bridge, which stabilises the protein [[cite:PUB00109198]].

This domain is comprised of the iron-sulphur cluster and Rieske subunit found in the large subunit of arsenite oxidase. Arsenite oxidase is a 100 kDa molybdenum- and iron-sulfur-containing protein located on the outer surface of the inner membrane of Gram-negative organisms. The large subunit of arsenite oxidase is similar to other members of the dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO) reductase family of molybdenum enzymes. The large subunit of arsenite oxidase is divided into four domains, with domain I binding the [3Fe-4S] cluster . Domain I, consists of three antiparallel beta sheets and six helices. The [3Fe-4S] cluster is coordinated by the motif Cys21-X2-Cys24-X3-Cys28 near the interface with domains III and IV. A large, flattened funnel-like cavity bounded by domains I, II, and III leads to the molybdenum center [pfam:PF00384] located near the center of the molecule [[cite:PUB00025173]].
This entry represents soluble Rieske-type ferredoxins from animals , referred to as MRF and HRF for the mouse and human proteins, respectively, whose function is not yet known [[cite:PUB00051288]].

This domain family is found in eukaryotes, and is typically between 135 and 146 amino acids in length. Rif1 is a protein which interacts with Rap1 to regulate telomere length. Interaction with telomeres limits their length. The N terminal region contains many HEAT- and ARMADILLO- type repeats. These are helical folds which form extended curved proteins or RNA interface surfaces.

RIF2 is involved in transcriptional silencing and telomere length regulation [[cite:PUB00141895]]. It belongs to the ATPase family associated with diverse cellular activities. This domain represents the ASCE (NTPase) domain described in [[cite:PUB00141895]].

RIF2 is involved in transcriptional silencing and telomere length regulation [[cite:PUB00141895]]. It belongs to the ATPase family associated with diverse cellular activities. This domain represents the alpha-helical AAA+ lid domain described in [[cite:PUB00141895]].
Staphylococcus nuclease (SNase) domain family found in the Trypanosoma brucei TbRIF5 protein, which could contribute to the processing of dsRNA targets [[cite:PUB00091015]].
Staphylococcus nuclease (SNase) domain family found in the Trypanosoma brucei TbRIF5 protein, which could contribute to the processing of dsRNA targets [[cite:PUB00091015]].

Plasmodium falciparum is the causative agent of deadly malaria disease. It encodes repetitive interspersed families of polypeptides (RIFINs), which are expressed on the surface of infected erythrocytes [[cite:PUB00085063]]. All RIFIN sequences contain the PEXEL motif (a pentameric sequence RxLxE/Q/D, known as the Plasmodium export element) required for correct export and surface expression or host-targeting (HT) signal which plays a central role in the export of proteins into the host cell [[cite:PUB00085061]]. It has been reported that PEXEL is preferably located 15-20 amino acids downstream of an N-terminal hydrophobic signal sequence [[cite:PUB00085062]]. The RIFIN protein family can be divided into A and B types based on the presence or absence of a 25 amino acid motif located approximately 66 amino acids downstream of the PEXEL motif [[cite:PUB00085062]], with A- and B-types serving different roles in distinct parasite stages [[cite:PUB00085061]]. The specific type B RIFIN variant (PF13_0006) is expressed on the surface of free merozoites, internally in developing gametocytes and on the surface of gametes at the point of emerging from activated, mature stage V gametocytes. While type A RIFIN are expressed on the infected erythrocyte surface, potentially contributing to the antigenic variation capacity of the parasite [[cite:PUB00085061]].

This is the C-terminal domain of Innate Immune Pattern-Recognition Receptor RIG-I present in homo sapiens. RIG-I is a key cytosolic pattern-recognition receptors of the vertebrate innate immune system that form the first line of defense against RNA viral infection. RNA binding to RIG-I is mediated both by the C-terminal domain and by the helicase domain. The C-terminal domain specifically binds the 5'triphosphate end with a 10-fold higher affinity compared to 5'OH-dsRNA [[cite:PUB00057056]].

This family of proteins represents the regulatory domain RD of RIG-I, a protein which initiates a signalling cascade that provides essential antiviral protection for the host. The RD domain binds viral RNA, activating the RIG-I ATPase by RNA-dependant dimerisation. The structure of RD contains a zinc-binding domain and is thought to confer ligand specificity [[cite:PUB00048985]].

This eukaryotic domain is found in ryanodine receptors (RyR) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptors (IP3R) which together form a superfamily of homotetrameric ligand-gated intracellular Ca2+ channels [[cite:PUB00020904]]. There seems to be no known function for this domain [[cite:PUB00006473]]. Also see the IP3-binding domain [pfam:PF01365] and [pfam:PF02815].

Pfam_Description: Regulatory subunit of type II PKA R-subunit
Pfam_name: Regulatory subunit of type II PKA R-subunit

Pfam_description: This domain is found is a wide variety of AKAPs (A kinase anchoring proteins) [[cite:PUB00011239]]. The domain is also found on micro-tubule-associated proteins.

RILP contains a domain which contains two coiled-coil regions and is found mainly in the cytosol. RILP is recruited onto late endosomal and lysosomal membranes by Rab7 and acts as a downstream effector of Rab7. This recruitment process is important for phagosome maturation and fusion with late endosomes and lysosomes [[cite:PUB00037685]].

This entry represents the zinc finger domain of Regulating synaptic membrane exocytosis protein 2 (RIM2a) and related proteins. This domain alone is responsible for the interaction with Munc13-1 by engaging with the Munc13-1 C2A domain [[cite:PUB00039109]]. Structurally, this domain is similar to FIVE zinc fingers.

RAB7A-interacting MON1-CCZ1 complex subunit 1 (RIMC1, previously known as UPF0600 protein C5orf51) plays an important role in the removal of damaged mitochondria via mitophagy by controlling the stability and localization of RAB7A. It is required for the recruitment of RAB7A and ATG9A vesicles to damaged mitochondria and promotes the stability of RAB7A by inhibiting its proteasomal degradation during mitophagy [[cite:PUB00100228]].
This ATP-grasp domain is found in the ribosomal S6 modification enzyme RimK [[cite:PUB00020972]].
This is the N-terminal domain found in Escherichia coli RimK proteins (Ribosomal protein S6-L-glutamate ligase). This domain precedes the ATP-grasp domain [pfam:PF08443] [[cite:PUB00091443]].

The RimM protein is essential for efficient processing of 16S rRNA [[cite:PUB00002319]]. The RimM protein was shown to have affinity for free ribosomal 30S subunits but not for 30S subunits in the 70S ribosomes [[cite:PUB00002319]]. This N-terminal domain is found associated with a PRC-barrel domain [[cite:PUB00010437]].

This entry represents the N-terminal domain of the ribosome maturation factor RimP (also known as yhbC). RimP facilitates the maturation of the 30S ribosomal subunit [[cite:PUB00053910]]. The N-terminal domain contains two alpha-helices and a three-stranded beta-sheet. It is suggested that the N-terminal domain of SP14.3 (RimP orthologue) could function as a protein module that binds to other proteins, especially those that contain highly positively charged surfaces. [[cite:PUB00021814]].

This family consists of several Staphylococcus aureus bacteriophage RinB proteins and related sequences from their host. The int gene of staphylococcal bacteriophage phi 11 is the only viral gene responsible for the integrative recombination of phi 11. rinA and rinB, are both required to activate expression of the int gene [[cite:PUB00009648]].

CBP (CREB-binding protein) and p300 (also known as CREBBP or KAT3A and EP300 or KAT3B, respectively) are two histone acetyltransferases (HATs) that associate with and acetylate transcriptional regulators and chromatin. The catalytic core of animal CBP-p300 contains a bromodomain, a CH2 region containing a discontinuous PHD domain interrupted by this RING domain, and a HAT domain. Bromodomain-RING-PHD forms a compact module in which the RING domain is juxtaposed with the HAT substrate-binding site. This RING domain contains only a single zinc ion-binding cluster instead of two; instead of a second zinc atom, a network of hydrophobic interactions stabilizes the domain. The RING domain has an inhibitory role. Disease mutations that disrupt RING attachment lead to upregulation of HAT activity. HAT regulation may require repositioning of the RING domain to facilitate access to an otherwise partially occluded HAT active site. Plant CBP-p300 type HATs lack a bromodomain whose role in the animal animal CBP-p300's is to bind acetylated histones; it has been suggested that these plant proteins may utilise a different domain or another bromodomain protein to perform this function [[cite:PUB00074827]]. This RING domain has also been referred to as DUF902.
This family is the catalytic domain of aromatic-ring- hydroxylating dioxygenase systems. The active site contains a non-heme ferrous ion coordinated by three ligands.
This subunit has a similar structure to NTF-2 and scytalone dehydratase.

This family includes TIP-1 (also known as Tip20) protein from yeast which is part of the Dsl1 complex, a multisubunit tethering complex involved in retrograde trafficking of vesicles from Golgi to ER [[cite:PUB00010001],[cite:PUB00051798],[cite:PUB00053456],[cite:PUB00100039]], its homologue from animals RINT-1, a Rad50 interacting protein which participates in radiation induced checkpoint control [[cite:PUB00010117],[cite:PUB00100047]] and in membrane trafficking from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the Golgi complex; and MAIGO2 (Mag2) from plants which functions in the transport of storage protein precursors between the ER and Golgi complex [[cite:PUB00072936]]. They are part of the CATCHR (complexes associated with tethering containing helical rods) family which includes proteins from the GARP/EARP, exocyst, conserved oligomeric Golgi (COG), and Dsl1 complexes and share a structural fold consisting of helical bundles [[cite:PUB00100039],[cite:PUB00100047]].

Members of this family are found in Rio2, and are structurally homologous to the winged helix (wHTH) domain. They adopt a structure consisting of four alpha helices followed by two beta strands and a fifth alpha helix. The domain confers DNA binding properties to the protein, as per other winged helix domains [[cite:PUB00031542]].

Pfam_Description: Ribosomal oxygenase 1, C-terminal winged helix domain
Pfam_name: Ribosomal oxygenase 1, C-terminal winged helix domain
Pfam_description: This domain is found in Ribosomal oxygenase 1 from humans (RIOX1) and similar proteins from animals. RIOX1 catalyse histidine- hydroxylation in ribosomal protein rpL28. The protein shows a JmjC domain followed by an helical dimerization domain and a C-terminal winged-helix (WH)-domain (this entry) [[cite:PUB00099121],[cite:PUB00151734]].

The precise function of this family is not clear, but it is thought to play a role in somitogenesis, development and transcriptional repression. Ripply is also known by an alternative name, Bowline. Bowline, is an associate protein of the transcriptional co-repressor XGrg-4 [[cite:PUB00067537]]. This family contains two conserved sequence motifs: WRPW and FPVQATI. The WRPW motif is thought to be required for binding to tle/groucho proteins [[cite:PUB00067538]]. Ripply3 is also known as Down Syndrome Critical Region Protein 6 homolog [[cite:PUB00067539]]. This family of proteins is found in eukaryotes. Proteins in this family are typically between 109 and 154 amino acids in length.

This family represents the RNAP Inhibitory Protein (RIP) and its paralog, the major capsid protein (MCP) P131. These proteins adopt very similar bundle structures consisting of six alpha-helices [[cite:PUB00154210],[cite:PUB00154211]]. RIP factor binds inside the DNA-binding channel of RNAP, inhibiting transcription by occlusion of binding sites for nucleic acid and the transcription initiation factor TFB. MCP P131 is a building block of the viral capsid.

Pfam_Description: Periplasmic domain of Sensor histidine kinase RisS
Pfam_name: Periplasmic domain of Sensor histidine kinase RisS
Pfam_description: RisS_PPD is the periplasmic domain of the sensor histidine kinase RisS. It is purported to be the region of the kinase that senses the pH of the environs.

This domain is the N-terminal domain from the enzyme ([ec:2.4.2.-]) which modifies exclusively the initiator tRNA in position 64 using 5'-phosphoribosyl-1'-pyrophosphate as the modification donor. As the initiator tRNA participates both in the initiation and elongation of translation, the 2'-O-ribosyl phosphate modification discriminates the initiator tRNAs from the elongator tRNAs [[cite:PUB00009892]]. The N-terminal domain is the most conserved region of the protein [[cite:PUB00078750]].

RITA is a highly conserved protein that binds to tubulin and shuttles between the cytoplasm and nucleus. It is responsible for export of RBP-J/CBF-1 from the nucleus, which modulates Notch-mediated transcription [[cite:PUB00075806]].

Rix1 is a nucleoplasmic particle involved in rRNA processing/ribosome assembly [[cite:PUB00016366],[cite:PUB00073776]]. It associates with two other proteins, Ipi1 and Ipi3, to form the RIX1 complex that allows Rea1 - the AAA ATPase - to associate with the 60S ribosomal subunit. More than 170 assembly factors are involved in the construction and maturation of yeast ribosomes, and after these factors have completed their function they need to be released from the pre-ribosomes. Rea1 induces the release of the assembly protein complex in a mechanical fashion [[cite:PUB00073777]]. This family is usually associated with NUC202, [pfam:PF08166].

This domain represents the N-terminal region of the E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase RKP from plants. It was demonstrated that RKP is a functional ubiquitin E3 ligase and is able to interact with cell-cycle inhibitor ICK/KRP proteins.
The RRM-like (RL) domain is found in the N-terminal region of the polyA polymerase PAPD1. It contributes to PAPD1 dimerization and has a fold similar to RNP-type RBDs [[cite:PUB00058875]].

Pfam_Description: Insertion domain in 60S ribosomal protein L10P
Pfam_name: Insertion domain in 60S ribosomal protein L10P
Pfam_description: This domain is found in prokaryotic and archaeal ribosomal L10 protein [[cite:PUB00057768]].

Pfam_Description: Glycoprotein encoding membrane proteins RL5A and RL6
Pfam_name: Glycoprotein encoding membrane proteins RL5A and RL6
Pfam_description: RL5A and RL6 are part of the RL11 family which are predicted to encode membrane glycoproteins. Two adjacent open reading frames potentially encode a domain that is the hallmark of proteins encoded by the RL11 family.

An uncharacterized alpha+beta fold domain that is mostly fused to a RimK-like ATP-grasp and is found in bacteria and euryarchaea. Members of this family are almost always associated in gene neighborhoods with a GNAT-like acetyltransferase fused to a papain-like petidase. Additionally M20-like peptidases, GCS2, 4Fe-4S Ferredoxins, a distinct metal-sulfur cluster protein and ribosomal proteins are found in the gene neighborhoods. Contextual analysis suggests a role for these in peptide biosynthesis [[cite:PUB00057486]].

Pfam_Description: RNA repair pathway DNA polymerase beta family
Pfam_name: RNA repair pathway DNA polymerase beta family
Pfam_description: Family of the DNA polymerase beta superfamily, with closest affinities to the Minimal Nucleotide Transferase clade (MNT). Observed in diverse RNA repair genome contexts centered on both RtcB and Rnl-type (ATP-grasp fold) repair ligases [[cite:PUB00091037]]. Members of this family of bacterial proteins catalyze the transfer of nucleotide residues from nucleoside diphosphates or triphosphates into dimer or polymer forms.

Pfam_Description: Possible Fer4-like domain in RNase L inhibitor, RLI
Pfam_name: Possible Fer4-like domain in RNase L inhibitor, RLI
Pfam_description: Possible metal-binding domain in endoribonuclease RNase L inhibitor. Found at the N-terminal end of RNase L inhibitor proteins, adjacent to the 4Fe-4S binding domain, fer4, [pfam:PF00037]. Also often found adjacent to the DUF367 domain [pfam:PF04034] in uncharacterised proteins. The RNase L system plays a major role in the anti-viral and anti-proliferative activities of interferons [[cite:PUB00009821]], and could possibly play a more general role in the regulation of RNA stability in mammalian cells. Inhibitory activity requires concentration-dependent association of RLI with RNase L [[cite:PUB00009822]].

This domain is found in RLIP76 (also known as RalA-binding protein 1, RalBP1), a multifunctional protein that interacts with multiple small G protein families and endocytosis proteins. The Ral binding domain is a coiled-coil. The orientation of its alpha-helices and the loop between them slightly changes upon binding to RalB. This interaction appears to be related to the cellular localization of the complex [[cite:PUB00059679],[cite:PUB00152115],[cite:PUB00152116]].

Pfam_Description: RNA transcription, translation and transport factor protein
Pfam_name: RNA transcription, translation and transport factor protein
Pfam_description: This entry represents RNA transcription, translation and transport factor protein (RTRAF, also known as hCLE/C14orf166) from eukaryotes. It is part of the DDX1-HSPC117-FAM98B complex that shuttles between the nucleus and the cytoplasm transporting RNAs [[cite:PUB00088063]]. It is also a component of the tRNA-splicing ligase complex and is required for tRNA ligation [[cite:PUB00088064]]. Human RTRAF works as a positive modulator of the RNA polymerase II activity [[cite:PUB00088061]]. It also interacts with influenza virus polymerase subunit PA and plays an important role in influenza virus replication [[cite:PUB00088066]]. Family members carry a characteristic RLL sequence-motif.

This entry represents the ferredoxin-like domain found at the N-terminal of RmlL, referred to as NFLD domain usually fused to the THUMP domain [[cite:PUB00100798]]. Ribosomal RNA large subunit methyltransferase K/L from E.coli (also known as YcbY) specifically methylates the guanine in positions 2445 and 2069 of 23S rRNA before its assembly into 50S subunits [[cite:PUB00100798]].

This domain is found in Ribosomal methyltransferase RlmM (YdgE) present in E. coli. RlmM catalyzes the S-adenosyl methionine (AdoMet)-dependent 2'O methylation of C2498 in 23S ribosomal RNA. The domain is ferredoxin-like and forms part of the THUMP domain which binds RNA. THUMP domains typically have low sequence similarity [[cite:PUB00062661]].

Pfam_Description: Ribosomal RNA large subunit methyltransferase M, N-terminal
Pfam_name: Ribosomal RNA large subunit methyltransferase M, N-terminal
Pfam_description: This is the THUMP-like domain of Ribosomal RNA large subunit methyltransferase M (RLMM), adjacent the ferredoxin-like domain ([pfam:PF18125]), which together constitutes the N-terminal domain [[cite:PUB00062661]]. RlmM specifically catalyses the 2'-O-methylation of nucleotide C2498 in the peptidyl transferase loop of 23S rRNA [[cite:PUB00062661]].

Pfam_Description: Ribosomal RNA large subunit methyltransferase N-terminal domain
Pfam_name: Ribosomal RNA large subunit methyltransferase N-terminal domain
Pfam_description: This entry represents the N-terminal domain from the dual-specificity RNA methyltransferase RlmN.

This family includes the RloB protein that is found within a bacterial restriction modification operon. This family includes the AbiLii protein that is found as part of a plasmid encoded phage abortive infection mechanism [[cite:PUB00057366]]. Deletion within abiLii abolished the phage resistance. The family includes some proteins annotated as CRISPR Csm2 proteins.

Pfam_Description: Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 14, RM2
Pfam_name: Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 14, RM2
Pfam_description: This entry represents an alpha/beta motif that is found tandemly repeated in the homologues of human Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 14 (Med14). Med14 is a component of the Mediator complex, a coactivator involved in the regulated transcription of nearly all RNA polymerase II-dependent genes. Med14 along with Med17 are scaffold subunits in nucleating Mediator [[cite:PUB00154060],[cite:PUB00151584]]. The major portion of Med14 exists in the Head-Shoulder module of the Mediator and consists of nine tandem repeats (RM1 to RM9), which are arranged in an atypical right-handed helix [[cite:PUB00151584]]. This entry represents repeat RM2.

Pfam_Description: Large ribosomal subunit protein mL44, endonuclease domain
Pfam_name: Large ribosomal subunit protein mL44, endonuclease domain
Pfam_description: Large ribosomal subunit protein mL44 (RM44) is a component of the 39S subunit of mitochondrial ribosome. It may play a role in the assembly/stability of nascent mitochondrial polypeptides exiting the ribosome. This entry represents the endonuclease (RNase III-like) domain [[cite:PUB00089007],[cite:PUB00108679],[cite:PUB00108680]].

Pfam_Description: Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 14, RM6
Pfam_name: Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 14, RM6
Pfam_description: This entry represents an alpha/beta motif that is found tandemly repeated in the homologues of human Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 14 (Med14). Med14 is a component of the Mediator complex, a coactivator involved in the regulated transcription of nearly all RNA polymerase II-dependent genes. Med14 along with Med17 are scaffold subunits in nucleating Mediator [[cite:PUB00154060],[cite:PUB00151584]]. The major portion of Med14 exists in the Head-Shoulder module of the Mediator and consists of nine tandem repeats (RM1 to RM9), which are arranged in an atypical right-handed helix [[cite:PUB00151584]]. This entry represents repeat RM6.

Pfam_Description: Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 14, RM8
Pfam_name: Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 14, RM8
Pfam_description: This entry represents an alpha/beta motif that is found tandemly repeated in the homologues of human Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 14 (Med14). Med14 is a component of the Mediator complex, a coactivator involved in the regulated transcription of nearly all RNA polymerase II-dependent genes. Med14 along with Med17 are scaffold subunits in nucleating Mediator [[cite:PUB00154060],[cite:PUB00151584]]. The major portion of Med14 exists in the Head-Shoulder module of the Mediator and consists of nine tandem repeats (RM1 to RM9), which are arranged in an atypical right-handed helix [[cite:PUB00151584]]. This entry represents repeat RM8.

This family represents the C-terminus (approximately 160 residues) of a number of Regulator of MON1-CCZ1 complex (RMC1, also known as colon cancer-associated protein Mic1). This is an alpha-helical region that serves as a scaffold for CCZ1-MON1 recruitment and bridges the membrane and GEF complex [[cite:PUB00090867]].

This is the N-terminal beta-propeller of Regulator of MON1-CCZ1 complex (RMC1). RMC1 is a component of the the CCZ1-MON1 complex, which functions as a guanine exchange factor (GEF) for RAB7 during endocytic and autophagic flux to the lysosome [[cite:PUB00090867]]. This region may function analogously to the WIPI proteins to bind phosphoinositides at the membrane [[cite:PUB00090867]].

This is the C-terminal domain of Regulator of microtubule dynamics proteins 1-3 (RMD1-3) which consists of alpha-helical repeats. These are microtubule-binding proteins. RMD3 is involved in cellular calcium homeostasis regulation, and it may participate in differentiation and apoptosis of keratinocytes [[cite:PUB00071995]]. RMD1 from C. elegans functions in chromosome segregation [[cite:PUB00151668]].

DNAJ protein RME-8 (receptor-mediated endocytosis-8; Gvr2 in Arabidopsis) is involved in membrane trafficking through early endosomes and in the regulation of endosomal membrane tubulation. It regulates the dynamics of SNX1 (sorting nexin 1) on the endosomal membrane. It coordinates the function of the WASH complex and the retromer SNX dimer through its interaction with FAM21 subunit in WASH complex. This is the N-terminal domain of RME-8, which is required for membrane association and interaction with FAM21 tail domain [[cite:PUB00091010]]. It contains critical residues mediating phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI(3)P) binding, required for its association with endosomes [[cite:PUB00099024]].

This protein associates with 70s ribosomes and converts them to a dimeric form (100S ribosomes) which appear during the transition from the exponential growth phase to the stationary phase of Escherichia coli cells.

Pfam_Description: Recq-mediated genome instability protein 1, C-terminal OB-fold
Pfam_name: Recq-mediated genome instability protein 1, C-terminal OB-fold
Pfam_description: RMI1_C is a C-terminal oligo-nucleotide binding domain of Recq-mediated genome instability proteins. This domain interacts with RMI2-OB folds to make up the RMI core complex. The RMI core interface is crucial for BLM, Bloom syndrome, dissolvasome assembly and may have additional cellular roles as a docking hub for other proteins [[cite:PUB00075424],[cite:PUB00076224]].

This is the OB-fold domain found at the N-terminal of RecQ-mediated genome instability protein 1 (RMI1), which forms a stable complex with Bloom syndrome protein BLM and DNA topoisomerase 3-alpha [[cite:PUB00075424],[cite:PUB00075425],[cite:PUB00058799]].

The N-terminal domain of RecQ-mediated genome instability protein 1 carries an oligo-nucleotide-binding domain or OB-fold, and forms a stable complex with Bloom syndrome protein BLM and DNA topoisomerase 3-alpha [[cite:PUB00075424],[cite:PUB00075425],[cite:PUB00058799]]. At the very N-terminal, it has a 3-helix bundle, represented in this entry, which protrudes to one side of the structure and makes extensive hydrophobic contacts with the convex side of the beta-barrel [[cite:PUB00058799]].

RMI2 is a eukaryotic family of an OB3, oligo-nucleotide-binding proteins. It is an essential component of the RMI complex that plays a vital role in the processing of homologous recombination intermediates in order to limit DNA-crossover-formation in cells [[cite:PUB00076224]].

L-rhamnose is a saccharide required for the virulence of some bacteria. Its precursor, dTDP-L-rhamnose, is synthesised by four different enzymes the final one of which is RmlD. The RmlD substrate binding domain is responsible for binding a sugar nucleotide [[cite:PUB00009948],[cite:PUB00009949]].

The metallo-beta-lactamase fold contains five sequence motifs. The first four motifs are found in [pfam:PF00753] and are common to all metallo-beta-lactamases. This, the fifth motif [[cite:PUB00014290]], appears to be specific to Zn-dependent metallohydrolases such as ribonuclease J 2 [[cite:PUB00078730]] which are involved in the processing of mRNA [[cite:PUB00041631],[cite:PUB00054497]]. This domain adds essential structural elements to the CASP-domain and is unique to RNA/DNA-processing nucleases, showing that they are pre-mRNA 3'-end-processing endonucleases [[cite:PUB00041631],[cite:PUB00054497],[cite:PUB00078730]].

Members of this family are about 220 amino acids long. It includes Rhamnosyl O-methyltransferase which catalyses the O-methylation of the hydroxyl group located on C-2 of the first rhamnosyl residue linked to the phenolic group of glycosylated phenolphthiocerol dimycocerosates (PGL) and p-hydroxybenzoic acid derivatives (p-HBAD) [[cite:PUB00053670]]. This entry also includes CmcI protein [swissprot:O85726] which was previously presumed to represent the cephalosporin-7--hydroxylase [[cite:PUB00008735]]. However, it is apparently a methyltransferase that works with hydroxylase CmcJ, and its most likely function is to catalyse the transfer of a methyl group from SAM to the 7alpha-hydroxy cephalosporin in the second catalytic reaction of cephamycin formation. Studies using recombinant proteins purified from E. coli suggest that the complex, but not the separate proteins, exhibits a strong interaction with SAM and cephalosporin C [[cite:PUB00039678]].

RMP is encoded for by a gene, C8orf37. Mutations in the gene cause two types of retinal dystrophies: cone-rod dystrophy type 16 (CORD16) and retinitis pigmentosa type 64 (RP64). CORD16 affects the cone receptors which detect red, green or blue wavelengths of light and RP64 affects the cone receptors first and then the rod receptors. Both of these affect the photo-receptors in the eye leading to colour blindness or blindness respectively [[cite:PUB00069920]].

This family represents Ribonuclease MRP protein subunit RMP1 from yeast, a component of ribonuclease MRP (RNase MRP), which is involved in rRNA processing in mitochondria [[cite:PUB00102196]]. This protein is found only in RNase MRP and is involved in extensive interactions with RNA, contributing to the formation of the substrate binding pocket of MRP [[cite:PUB00102197]]. It is, likely, orthologue to human NEPRO.

This family contains several bacterial RmuC DNA recombination proteins. The function of the RMUC protein is unknown but it is suspected that it is either a structural protein that protects DNA against nuclease action, or is itself involved in DNA cleavage at the regions of DNA secondary structures [[cite:PUB00020261]]

This family includes RNA12 from S. cerevisiae. That protein contains an RRM domain. This region is C-terminal to that and includes a P-loop motif suggesting this region binds to NTP. The RNA12 proteins is involved in pre-rRNA maturation [[cite:PUB00044464]].
Ribonucleases. Members include pancreatic RNAase A and angiogenins. Structure is an alpha+beta fold -- long curved beta sheet and three helices.

Ribonuclease D is a bacterial 3'-5' exonuclease that acts on tRNA. It contributes to the 3' maturation of several stable RNAs [[cite:PUB00038621]]. It consists of a catalytic domain ([pfam:PF01612]) and two alpha- helical domains at the C-terminal that closely resemble the HRDC domain seen in RecQ-family helicases. This is the second HRDC domain from RNAse D. The first one is included in [pfam:PF00570].

Members of this family are found in T4 RNaseH ribonuclease, and adopt a SAM domain-like fold, consisting of a bundle of four/five helices. These residues may have a role in providing a docking site for other proteins or enzymes in the replication fork [[cite:PUB00011713]].

RNaseH_like is a family of uncharacterised eubacterial proteins that are distant homologues of Ribonuclease H-like. The family maintains all the core secondary structure elements of the RNase H-like fold and shares several conserved, presumably active site residues with RNase HI. This finding suggests that it functions as a nuclease [[cite:PUB00020735]].

RNaseH domain of the pPIWI_RE PIWI/Argonaute module. pPIWI_RE is found in a conserved three-gene island that also contains a DinG-type helicase and an REase nuclease. This three gene island is predicted to form a conflict system which targets R-loop formation of invasive plasmids during plasmid replication [[cite:PUB00091016]].

This is the N-terminal domain of eukaryotic ribonuclease 3 (RNase III, [ec:3.1.26.3]). Structure analysis of Saccharomyces cerevisiaeRNase III (Rnt1p) :RNA revealed specific contacts between the N-terminal domain (NTD) dimer and the 5' end region of the tetraloop. Deletion of the NTD led to cleavage at alternative site(s), suggesting that this region increases the precision of the cleavage site selectivity [[cite:PUB00091154]].

Contact-dependent growth inhibition (CDI) is an important mechanism of inter-bacterial competition found in many Gram-negative pathogens. CDI+ cells express cell-surface CdiA proteins that bind neighboring bacteria and deliver C-terminal toxin domains (CdiA-CT) to inhibit target-cell growth. Structure analysis of CdiA-CT shows that it adopts the same fold (with two beta-sheets forming an overall kidney shape) as angiogenin and other RNase A paralogs, but the toxin does not share sequence similarity with these nucleases and lacks the characteristic disulfide bonds of the superfamily. Furthermore, structural comparison analysis identified human angiogenin, Rana pipiens protein P-30 (onconase) and mouse pancreatic ribonuclease (RNase 1) as the closest structural homologs of CdiA-CT [[cite:PUB00091451]].
Ribonuclease E and Ribonuclease G are related enzymes that cleave a wide variety of RNAs [[cite:PUB00033641]].

Both RNase E and its homologue RNase G are endoribonucleases that play central roles in RNA processing. RNase E shows two globular domains. This entry represents the smaller domain, which shows a thioredoxin-like fold [[cite:PUB00033641],[cite:PUB00049806],[cite:PUB00151990]].

RNase H digests the RNA strand of an RNA/DNA hybrid. Important enzyme in retroviral replication cycle, and often found as a domain associated with reverse transcriptases. Structure is a mixed alpha+beta fold with three a/b/a layers.

Pfam_Description: Ydr279p protein family (RNase H2 complex component) wHTH domain
Pfam_name: Ydr279p protein family (RNase H2 complex component) wHTH domain
Pfam_description: RNases H are enzymes that specifically hydrolyse RNA when annealed to a complementary DNA and are present in all living organisms. In yeast RNase H2 is composed of a complex of three proteins (Rnh2Ap, Ydr279p and Ylr154p), this family represents the homologues of Ydr279p [[cite:PUB00044465]]. It is not known whether non yeast proteins in this family fulfil the same function.

This entry represents the non-catalytic subunit of RNase H2, which in S. cerevisiae is Ylr154p/Rnh203p [swissprot:Q12338] (. Whereas bacterial and archaeal RNases H2 are active as single polypeptides, the Saccharomyces cerevisiae homologue, Rnh2Ap, when expressed in Escherichia coli, fails to produce an active RNase H2. For RNase H2 activity three proteins are required [Rnh2Ap (Rnh201p), Ydr279p (Rnh202p) and Ylr154p (Rnh203p)]. Deletion of any one of the proteins or mutations in the catalytic site in Rnh2A leads to loss of RNase H2 activity [[cite:PUB00044465]]. RNase H2 ia an endonuclease that specifically degrades the RNA of RNA:DNA hybrids. It participates in DNA replication, possibly by mediating the removal of lagging-strand Okazaki fragment RNA primers during DNA replication.

Pfam_Description: RNase II-type exonuclease C-terminal S1 domain
Pfam_name: RNase II-type exonuclease C-terminal S1 domain
Pfam_description: This entry describes the C-terminal S1 domain found in type 2 RNase exonucleases. DrR63 proteins from Deinococcus radiodurans are an RNase II-type enzymes (DrII). Structure analysis of DrII indicates that it has an N-terminal HTH domain which interacts with a flexible loop that connects two beta-strands from the conserved C-terminal S1 domain, forming a beta-wing fold common in wHTH domains [[cite:PUB00057529]].

This domain is found in Ribonuclease J from Thermus thermophilus (RNaseJ) and similar bacterial proteins. RNaseJ is an RNase that has endonuclease and possibly 5'-3' exonuclease activity. It is probably involved in maturation of rRNA and in some organisms also mRNA maturation and/or decay. This protein shows three globular domains: the beta lactamase core (formed by two separate regions, [pfam:PF12706] and [pfam:PF07521]), the beta-CASP (this entry) and the C-terminal domain (Pfam: PF17770). This domain consists of a central five-stranded parallel beta-sheet that is surrounded by five alpha-helices [[cite:PUB00050660],[cite:PUB00138074]].
This domain is found at the C-terminus of Ribonuclease J proteins. Its function is unknown, but deletion of this domain causes dissociation to monomers [[cite:PUB00050660]].

This family consists of several archaeal and eukaryotic proteins. The archaeal proteins are found to be expressed within ribosomal operons and several of the sequences are described as ribonuclease P protein subunit p29 proteins [[cite:PUB00042726],[cite:PUB00028005]]. The structure of the RNase P subunit, Rpp29, from Methanobacterium thermoautotrophicum has been determined. Mth Rpp29 is a member of the oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide binding fold family. It contains a structured beta-barrel core and unstructured N- and C-terminal extensions bearing several highly conserved amino acid residues that could be involved in RNA contacts in the protein-RNA complex [[cite:PUB00028005]]. Rpp29 catalyses the endonucleolytic cleavage of RNA, removing 5'-extranucleotides from tRNA precursor. It interacts with the Rpp25 and Pop5 subunits.

This family includes 3'-5' exoribonucleases. Ribonuclease PH contains a single copy of this domain, and removes nucleotide residues following the -CCA terminus of tRNA. Polyribonucleotide nucleotidyltransferase (PNPase) contains two tandem copies of the domain. PNPase is involved in mRNA degradation in a 3'-5' direction. The exosome is a 3'-5' exoribonuclease complex that is required for 3' processing of the 5.8S rRNA. Three of its five protein components, [swissprot:P46948] [swissprot:Q12277] and [swissprot:P25359] contain a copy of this domain [[cite:PUB00000954]]. [swissprot:Q10205], a hypothetical protein from S. pombe appears to belong to an uncharacterised subfamily. This subfamily is found in both eukaryotes and archaebacteria.

This family includes 3'-5' exoribonucleases. Ribonuclease PH contains a single copy of this domain, and removes nucleotide residues following the -CCA terminus of tRNA. Polyribonucleotide nucleotidyltransferase (PNPase) contains two tandem copies of the domain. PNPase is involved in mRNA degradation in a 3'-5' direction. The exosome is a 3'-5' exoribonuclease complex that is required for 3' processing of the 5.8S rRNA. Three of its five protein components, [swissprot:P46948] [swissprot:Q12277] and [swissprot:P25359] contain a copy of this domain [[cite:PUB00000954]]. [swissprot:Q10205], a hypothetical protein from S. pombe appears to belong to an uncharacterised subfamily. This subfamily is found in both eukaryotes and archaebacteria.
This protein is part of the RNase P complex that is involved in tRNA maturation [[cite:PUB00020266]].

This family of fungal proteins form a subunit of RNase P, the ribonucleoprotein enzyme that cleaves the leader sequence of precursor tRNAs to generate mature tRNAs. The structure of Pop3 has been assigned the L7Ae/L30e fold [[cite:PUB00017150]]. This RNA-binding fold is also present in human RNase P subunit Rpp38, raising the possibility that Pop3p and Rpp38 are functional homologs.

tRNA processing enzyme ribonuclease P (RNase P) is a ubiquitous ribozyme that catalyzes a Mg2-dependent hydrolysis to remove the 5'-leader sequence of precursor tRNA (pre-tRNA). Archaeal and eukaryotic RNase P consist of a single RNA and archaeal RNase P has four or five proteins, while eukaryotic RNase P consists of 9 or 10 proteins [[cite:PUB00007201]]. Human RNase P is composed of a singular protein Pop1 and three subcomplexes, the Rpp20-Rpp25 heterodimer, Pop5-Rpp14- (Rpp30)2-Rpp40 heteropentamer, and Rpp21-Rpp29-Rpp38 heterotrimer. This family includes Rnp2 (also known as Pop5) from archaea [[cite:PUB00097410]] and Pop5/Rpp14 from eukaryotes [[cite:PUB00100655],[cite:PUB00097413]].
This family includes a variety of exonuclease proteins, such as ribonuclease T and the epsilon subunit of DNA polymerase III.;

This domain is found in the Zc3h12a protein which has shown to be a ribonuclease that controls the stability of a set of inflammatory genes [[cite:PUB00053552]]. It has been suggested that this domain belongs to the PIN domain superfamily [[cite:PUB00053552]]. This domain has also been identified as part of the NYN domain family [[cite:PUB00056584]].
This family is found to be a divergent form of the NYN-domain- containing RNAse family.

This domain is found in the Zc3h12a protein which has shown to be a ribonuclease that controls the stability of a set of inflammatory genes [[cite:PUB00053552]]. It has been suggested that this domain belongs to the PIN domain superfamily [[cite:PUB00053552]]. This domain has also been identified as part of the NYN domain family [[cite:PUB00056584]].
This family is found to be a divergent form of the NYN-domain- containing RNAse family.
This domain corresponds to the RNA binding domain of Poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN).

PH1010 [swissprot:O58738] is composed of five alpha-helices (1-5) and eight beta-strands (1-8) with the following topology: beta-1, alpha-1, beta-2, beta-3, alpha-2, alpha-3, beta-4, beta-5, alpha-4, beta-6, alpha-5, beta-7, beta-8. The first six beta-strands (1-6) form a slightly twisted antiparallel beta-sheet and face five alpha-helices on one side. The last two beta-strands form an antiparallel beta-sheet in the C-terminus. PH1010 forms a characteristic homodimer structure in the crystal. Dimerisation of the molecule is crucial for function. The structure resembles that of some ribosomal proteins such as the 50S ribosomal protein L5 [[cite:PUB00051274]]. Although the structure resembles that of the RRM-type RNA-binding domain of the ribosomal L5 protein, the residues involved in RNA-binding in the L5 protein are not conserved in this family [[cite:PUB00048377]]. Despite this, these proteins bind to double-stranded RNA in a non-sequence specific manner [[cite:PUB00066786]].
This family includes RNA helicases thought to be involved in duplex unwinding during viral RNA replication. Members of this family are found in a variety of single stranded RNA viruses.

Pfam_Description: Putative ATP-dependent RNA helicase, helical bundle
Pfam_name: Putative ATP-dependent RNA helicase, helical bundle
Pfam_description: This domain is found in the putative ATP-dependent RNA helicase from Pyrococcus furiosus (PF2015) and similar archaeal proteins. PF2015 is a Hef helicase that processes flap- or fork-DNA structures. This protein shows an SF2 helicase domain in the N-terminal two-thirds and an XPF/Mus81-type nuclease domain in the C-terminal one-third. The SF2 helicase domain is organised into three structural subdomains. This entry represents the second of them, which is composed of six alpha-helices that are tightly assembled into a hydrophobic core. Its surface is positively charged, suggesting that it is a potential DNA binding region [[cite:PUB00032295]].
This is a family of RNA ligases. The enzyme repairs RNA strand breaks in nicked DNA:RNA and RNA:RNA but not in DNA:DNA duplexes.

Members of this family include T4 phage proteins with ATP-dependent RNA ligase activity. Host defence to phage may include cleavage and inactivation of specific tRNA molecules; members of this family act to reverse this RNA damage. The enzyme is adenylated, transiently, on a Lys residue in a motif KXDGSL. This family also includes fungal tRNA ligases that have adenylyltransferase activity [[cite:PUB00017112]]. tRNA ligases are enzymes required for the splicing of precursor tRNA molecules containing introns.i
This is a family of RNA ligases. The enzyme repairs RNA strand breaks in nicked DNA:RNA and RNA:RNA but not in DNA:DNA duplexes.

Members of this family include T4 phage proteins with ATP-dependent RNA ligase activity. Host defence to phage may include cleavage and inactivation of specific tRNA molecules; members of this family act to reverse this RNA damage. The enzyme is adenylated, transiently, on a Lys residue in a motif KXDGSL. This family also includes fungal tRNA ligases that have adenylyltransferase activity [[cite:PUB00017112]]. tRNA ligases are enzymes required for the splicing of precursor tRNA molecules containing introns.i
This is a family of single chain RNA polymerases.

Pfam_Description: Yeast RNA polymerase I subunit RPA14
Pfam_name: Yeast RNA polymerase I subunit RPA14
Pfam_description: This is a family of yeast proteins. A14 is one of the final two subunits of Saccharomyces cerevisiae RNA polymerase I and is proposed to play a role in the recruitment of pol I to the promoter [[cite:PUB00017151]]. Members of this entry has a HRDC domain, which is equivalent to that in subunit F from archaeal RNA polymerase II and RPB4 from the eukaryotic RNA polymerase II [[cite:PUB00092063]].

Pfam_Description: DNA-directed RNA polymerase I subunit RPA34.5
Pfam_name: DNA-directed RNA polymerase I subunit RPA34.5
Pfam_description: This is a family of proteins conserved from yeasts to human. Subunit A34.5 of RNA polymerase I is a non-essential subunit which is thought to help Pol I overcome topological constraints imposed on ribosomal DNA during the process of transcription [[cite:PUB00017113]].

Pfam_Description: DNA-directed RNA polymerase III subunit Rpc31
Pfam_name: DNA-directed RNA polymerase III subunit Rpc31
Pfam_description: RNA polymerase III contains seventeen subunits in yeasts and in human cells. Twelve of these are akin to RNA polymerase I or II and the other five are RNA pol III-specific, and form the functionally distinct groups (i) Rpc31-Rpc34-Rpc82, and (ii) Rpc37-Rpc53. Rpc31, Rpc34 and Rpc82 form a cluster of enzyme-specific subunits that contribute to transcription initiation in S.cerevisiae and H.sapiens. There is evidence that these subunits are anchored at or near the N-terminal Zn-fold of Rpc1, itself prolonged by a highly conserved but RNA polymerase III-specific domain [[cite:PUB00056102]].
Members of this family include: alpha subunit from eubacteria alpha subunits from chloroplasts Rpb3 subunits from eukaryotes RpoD subunits from archaeal

Pfam_Description: Bacterial RNA polymerase, alpha chain C terminal domain
Pfam_name: Bacterial RNA polymerase, alpha chain C terminal domain
Pfam_description: The alpha subunit of RNA polymerase consists of two independently folded domains, referred to as amino-terminal and carboxyl terminal domains. The amino terminal domain is involved in the interaction with the other subunits of the RNA polymerase. The carboxyl-terminal domain interacts with the DNA and activators. The amino acid sequence of the alpha subunit is conserved in prokaryotic and chloroplast RNA polymerases. There are three regions of particularly strong conservation, two in the amino-terminal and one in the carboxyl- terminal [[cite:PUB00001064]].

This bacteriophage protein inhibits the bacterial host RNA polymerase by interacting with the RpoC subunit and inhibiting the formation of a promoter complex [[cite:PUB00076018],[cite:PUB00097435],[cite:PUB00076019]].

Pfam_Description: A49-like RNA polymerase I associated factor
Pfam_name: A49-like RNA polymerase I associated factor
Pfam_description: Saccharomyces cerevisiae A49 is a specific subunit associated with RNA polymerase I (Pol I) in eukaryotes. Pol I maintains transcription activities in A49 deletion mutants. However, such mutants are deficient in transcription activity at low temperatures. Deletion analysis of the fusion yeast homolog indicate that only the C-terminal two thirds are required for function. Transcript analysis has demonstrated that A49 is maximising transcription of ribosomal DNA [[cite:PUB00012886]].

The two eukaryotic subunits Rpb3 and Rpb11 dimerise to from a platform onto which the other subunits of the RNA polymerase assemble (D/L in archaea). The prokaryotic equivalent of the Rpb3/Rpb11 platform is the alpha-alpha dimer. The dimerisation domain of the alpha subunit/Rpb3 is interrupted by an insert domain ([pfam:PF01000]). Some of the alpha subunits also contain iron-sulphur binding domains ([pfam:PF00037]). Rpb11 is found as a continuous domain. Members of this family include: alpha subunit from eubacteria, alpha subunits from chloroplasts, Rpb3 subunits from eukaryotes, Rpb11 subunits from eukaryotes, RpoD subunits from archaeal spp, and RpoL subunits from archaeal spp.

The two eukaryotic subunits Rpb3 and Rpb11 dimerise to from a platform onto which the other subunits of the RNA polymerase assemble (D/L in archaea). The prokaryotic equivalent of the Rpb3/Rpb11 platform is the alpha-alpha dimer. The dimerisation domain of the alpha subunit/Rpb3 is interrupted by an insert domain ([pfam:PF01000]). Some of the alpha subunits also contain iron-sulphur binding domains ([pfam:PF00037]). Rpb11 is found as a continuous domain. Members of this family include: alpha subunit from eubacteria, alpha subunits from chloroplasts, Rpb3 subunits from eukaryotes, Rpb11 subunits from eukaryotes, RpoD subunits from archaeal spp, and RpoL subunits from archaeal spp. Many of the members of this family carry only the N-terminal region of Rpb11.

The two eukaryotic subunits Rpb3 and Rpb11 dimerise to from a platform onto which the other subunits of the RNA polymerase assemble (D/L in archaea). The prokaryotic equivalent of the Rpb3/Rpb11 platform is the alpha-alpha dimer. The dimerisation domain of the alpha subunit/Rpb3 is interrupted by an insert domain ([pfam:PF01000]). Some of the alpha subunits also contain iron-sulphur binding domains ([pfam:PF00037]). Rpb11 is found as a continuous domain. Members of this family include: alpha subunit from eubacteria, alpha subunits from chloroplasts, Rpb3 subunits from eukaryotes, Rpb11 subunits from eukaryotes, RpoD subunits from archaeal spp, and RpoL subunits from archaeal spp.

The two eukaryotic subunits Rpb3 and Rpb11 dimerise to from a platform onto which the other subunits of the RNA polymerase assemble (D/L in archaea). The prokaryotic equivalent of the Rpb3/Rpb11 platform is the alpha-alpha dimer. The dimerisation domain of the alpha subunit/Rpb3 is interrupted by an insert domain ([pfam:PF01000]). Some of the alpha subunits also contain iron-sulphur binding domains ([pfam:PF00037]). Rpb11 is found as a continuous domain. Members of this family include: alpha subunit from eubacteria, alpha subunits from chloroplasts, Rpb3 subunits from eukaryotes, Rpb11 subunits from eukaryotes, RpoD subunits from archaeal spp, and RpoL subunits from archaeal spp. Many of the members of this family carry only the N-terminal region of Rpb11.

Rpc25 is a strongly conserved subunit of RNA polymerase III and has homology to Rpa43 in RNA polymerase I, Rpb7 in RNA polymerase II and the archaeal RpoE subunit. Rpc25 is required for transcription initiation and is not essential for the elongating properties of RNA polymerase III [[cite:PUB00017156]].

Pfam_Description: RNA polymerase I, Rpa2 specific domain
Pfam_name: RNA polymerase I, Rpa2 specific domain
Pfam_description: This domain is found between domain 3 ([pfam:PF04565]) and domain 5 ([pfam:PF04565]), but shows no homology to domain 4 of Rpb2. The external domains in multisubunit RNA polymerase (those most distant from the active site) are known to demonstrate more sequence variability [[cite:PUB00008731]].

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). This domain, domain 1, represents the clamp domain, which a mobile domain involved in positioning the DNA, maintenance of the transcription bubble and positioning of the nascent RNA strand [[cite:PUB00002975],[cite:PUB00008731]].

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). This domain, domain 2, contains the active site. The invariant motif -NADFDGD- binds the active site magnesium ion [[cite:PUB00002975],[cite:PUB00008731]].

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). This domain, domain 3, represents the pore domain. The 3' end of RNA is positioned close to this domain. The pore delimited by this domain is thought to act as a channel through which nucleotides enter the active site and/or where the 3' end of the RNA may be extruded during back-tracking [[cite:PUB00002975],[cite:PUB00008731]].

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). This domain, domain 4, represents the funnel domain. The funnel contain the binding site for some elongation factors [[cite:PUB00002975],[cite:PUB00008731]].

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). This domain, domain 5, represents the discontinuous cleft domain that is required to from the central cleft or channel where the DNA is bound [[cite:PUB00002975],[cite:PUB00008731]].

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). This domain, domain 6, represents a mobile module of the RNA polymerase. Domain 6 forms part of the shelf module [[cite:PUB00002975],[cite:PUB00008731]]. This family appears to be specific to the largest subunit of RNA polymerase II.

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). This domain, domain 7, represents a mobile module of the RNA polymerase. Domain 7 forms a substantial interaction with the lobe domain of Rpb2 ([pfam:PF04561]) [[cite:PUB00002975],[cite:PUB00008731]].

The repetitive C-terminal domain (CTD) of Rpb1 (RNA polymerase Pol II) plays a critical role in the regulation of gene expression. The activity of the CTD is dependent on its state of phosphorylation [[cite:PUB00010210]].

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). This domain forms one of the two distinctive lobes of the Rpb2 structure. This domain is also known as the protrusion domain [[cite:PUB00003220]]. The other lobe ([pfam:PF04561]) is nested within this domain.

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). Rpb2 is the second largest subunit of the RNA polymerase. This domain forms one of the two distinctive lobes of the Rpb2 structure. This domain is also known as the lobe domain [[cite:PUB00008731]]. DNA has been demonstrated to bind to the concave surface of the lobe domain, and plays a role in maintaining the transcription bubble [[cite:PUB00008731]]. Many of the bacterial members contain large insertions within this domain, as region known as dispensable region 1 (DRI).

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). Domain 3, s also known as the fork domain and is proximal to catalytic site [[cite:PUB00008731]].

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). Domain 4, is also known as the external 2 domain [[cite:PUB00008731]].

Pfam_Description: RNA polymerase beta subunit external 1 domain
Pfam_name: RNA polymerase beta subunit external 1 domain
Pfam_description: RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA-dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared with three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial or chloroplast polymerases). This domain in prokaryotes spans the gap between domains 4 and 5 of the yeast protein. It is also known as the external 1 region of the polymerase and is bound in association with the external 2 region [[cite:PUB00008731]].

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). Domain 5, is also known as the external 2 domain [[cite:PUB00008731]].

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). This domain represents the hybrid binding domain and the wall domain [[cite:PUB00008731]]. The hybrid binding domain binds the nascent RNA strand / template DNA strand in the Pol II transcription elongation complex. This domain contains the important structural motifs, switch 3 and the flap loop and binds an active site metal ion[[cite:PUB00008731]]. This domain is also involved in binding to Rpb1 and Rpb3 [[cite:PUB00008731]]. Many of the bacterial members contain large insertions within this domain, as region known as dispensable region 2 (DRII).

RNA polymerases catalyse the DNA dependent polymerisation of RNA. Prokaryotes contain a single RNA polymerase compared to three in eukaryotes (not including mitochondrial. and chloroplast polymerases). Rpb2 is the second largest subunit of the RNA polymerase. This domain comprised of the structural domains anchor and clamp [[cite:PUB00008731]]. The clamp region (C-terminal) contains a zinc-binding motif [[cite:PUB00008731]]. The clamp region is named due to its interaction with the clamp domain found in Rpb1. The domain also contains a region termed "switch 4". The switches within the polymerase are thought to signal different stages of transcription [[cite:PUB00008731]].

This family includes the Rpb4 protein. This family also includes C17 (aka CGRP-RCP) is an essential subunit of RNA polymerase III. C17 forms a subcomplex with C25 [[cite:PUB00040054]] which is likely to be the counterpart of subcomplex Rpb4/7 in Pol II [[cite:PUB00045118]].
The assembly domain of Rpb5 [[cite:PUB00008457]]. The archaeal equivalent to this domain is subunit H. Subunit H lacks the N-terminal domain.

Rpb5 has a bipartite structure which includes a eukaryote-specific N-terminal domain and a C-terminal domain resembling the archaeal RNAP subunit H [[cite:PUB00008455],[cite:PUB00008456]]. The N-terminal domain is involved in DNA binding and is part of the jaw module in the RNA pol II structure [[cite:PUB00008457]]. This module is important for positioning the downstream DNA.

Rpb6 is an essential subunit in the eukaryotic polymerases Pol I, II and III. This family also contains the bacterial equivalent to Rpb6, the omega subunit. Rpb6 and omega are structurally conserved and both function in polymerase assembly [[cite:PUB00007936]].
Rpb8 is a subunit common to the three yeast RNA polymerases, pol I, II and III. Rpb8 interacts with the largest subunit Rpb1, and with Rpb3 and Rpb11, two smaller subunits.
RNA_pol_RpbG is a family of archaeal and fungal subunit G of DNA-directed RNA polymerase.

Subunit specific to RNA Pol III, the tRNA specific polymerase. The C34 subunit of yeast RNA Pol III is part of a subcomplex of three subunits which have no counterpart in the other two nuclear RNA polymerases. This subunit interacts with TFIIIB70 and is therefore participates in Pol III recruitment [[cite:PUB00010211]].
Specific subunit for Pol III, the tRNA specific polymerase.

This family consists of several DNA-directed RNA polymerase III polypeptides which are related to the Saccharomyces cerevisiae RPC82 protein. RNA polymerase C (III) promotes the transcription of tRNA and 5S RNA genes. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the enzyme is composed of 15 subunits, ranging from 160 to about 10 kDa [[cite:PUB00011444]].

Pfam_Description: RNA polymerase Rpo13 subunit HTH domain
Pfam_name: RNA polymerase Rpo13 subunit HTH domain
Pfam_description: This domain is found in archaea, and is about 40 amino acids in length. It has a single completely conserved residue E that may be functionally important. It is found in the archaeal DNA dependent RNA polymerase. The domain is a 'helix-turn-helix' (HTH) domain in the Rpo13 subunit of the RNA polymerase. This domain is involved in downstream DNA binding, and the entire subunit has also been implicated in contacting transcription factor II B.
This family is of Leviviridae RNA replicases. The replicase is also known as RNA dependent RNA polymerase.
This domain is the catalytic domain of ribonuclease II [[cite:PUB00045119]].

This is a family of integral membrane proteins including Rhodobacter-specific nitrogen fixation (rnf) proteins RnfA and RnfE [[cite:PUB00008135]] and Na+-translocating NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (Na+-NQR) subunits NqrD and NqrE.
This domain is found at the N-terminus of E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase Arkadia [[cite:PUB00069988]].

This family represents the C-terminal region of the E3 ubiquitin ligase RNF152 containing the hydrophobic transmembrane domain, responsible for the lysosomal localisation of the protein as well as its ubiquitination activity. This protein polyubiquitinates several proteins and itself, which leads to proteasome degradation. It has been shown that RNF152 has also pro-apoptotic activity, dependent on its RING finger and transmembrane domains [[cite:PUB00079274]]. In addition, the transmembrane domain of RNF152 is necessary for negative regulation of the mTORC1 pathway in an amino-acid-sensitive manner, as it mediates RNF152-RagA interaction and RagA ubiquitination [[cite:PUB00079275]].

This family represents the C-terminal region of the E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase RNF180 (Also known as Rines: RING finger protein in neural stem cells) which comprises its transmembrane domain. This is an integral membrane protein located mainly on the cytoplasmic side of the endoplasmic reticulum and functions as an E3 ubiquitin ligase. It is thought that it is involved in modulation of neuronal function, such as regulation of synaptic structure and synaptic plasticity due to its high expression in mature brain [[cite:PUB00078285]].
This family represents the central region of the E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase RNF220 [[cite:PUB00053927]].

This entry represents a domain found in human E3 ubiquitin -protein ligase rififylin (RNF34L) and similar eukaryotic proteins. RNF34L regulates several biological processes through the ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation of various target proteins. This domain is predicted to adopt an helix-extended loop-helix (HeH) structure.

This domain is part of the barrel sandwich hybrid superfamily. It is found at the N-terminus of the RnfC Electron transport complex protein. It appears to be most related to the N-terminal NQRA domain ([pfam:PF05896]).
This family of proteins is found in bacteria. Proteins in this family are typically between 94 and 143 amino acids in length. There is a conserved RNHCP sequence motif.
This domain occurs at the N-terminus of Rnk, an RNA polymerase-interacting protein of the GreA/GreB family ([pfam:PF01272]). It has a coiled coil structure [[cite:PUB00050693]].

Pfam_Description: RNase LS, bacterial toxin DBD domain
Pfam_name: RNase LS, bacterial toxin DBD domain
Pfam_description: RnlA toxin is an RNase LS and a putative toxin of a bacterial toxin-antitoxin pair. Toxin-antitoxin systems consist of a stable toxin and an unstable antitoxin. In this case, a novel type II system, RnlA is the stable toxin that causes inhibition of cell growth and rapidly degrades T4 late mRNAs to prevent their expression, and this is neutralised by the activity of the unstable antitoxin RnlB [[cite:PUB00075651],[cite:PUB00076076]]. This entry represents the C-terminal DBD domain, responsible for the RNA cleavage activity and toxicity. Through interaction between DBDs, RnlA dimerises in solution. T4 Dmd binds to DBD for inhibition of RnlA toxicity and RnlB also inhibits the toxicity of DBD [[cite:PUB00094670]].

RnlA_toxin is an RNase LS and a putative toxin of a bacterial toxin-antitoxin pair. Toxin-antitoxin systems consist of a stable toxin and an unstable antitoxin. In this case, a novel type II system, RnlA is the stable toxin that causes inhibition of cell growth and rapidly degrades T4 late mRNAs to prevent their expression, and this is neutralised by the activity of the unstable antitoxin RnlB [[cite:PUB00075651],[cite:PUB00076076]].

RnlA_toxin is an RNase LS and a putative toxin of a bacterial toxin-antitoxin pair. Toxin-antitoxin systems consist of a stable toxin and an unstable antitoxin. In this case, a novel type II system, RnlA is the stable toxin that causes inhibition of cell growth and rapidly degrades T4 late mRNAs to prevent their expression, and this is neutralised by the activity of the unstable antitoxin RnlB [[cite:PUB00075651],[cite:PUB00076076]]. This entry represents the N-terminal domain composed of four-stranded twisted antiparallel beta-sheet and two alpha-helices [[cite:PUB00094670],[cite:PUB00094671]].

Pfam_Description: Antitoxin to bacterial toxin RNase LS or RnlA
Pfam_name: Antitoxin to bacterial toxin RNase LS or RnlA
Pfam_description: RnlB_antitoxin, formerly known as yfjO, has been found to be the antidote protein to RNase LS or RnlA in E. coli. Bacterial toxin-antitoxin systems consist of a stable toxin and an unstable antitoxin. In this case, a novel type II system, RnlA is the stable toxin that causes inhibition of cell growth and rapidly degrades T4 late mRNAs to prevent their expression, and this is neutralised by the activity of the unstable antitoxin RnlB [[cite:PUB00076076]].

The bacterial PIcR helix-turn-helix transcription factor includes five TPR units of different lengths [[cite:PUB00065033]]. This entry represents the TPR containing domain as a whole. This family is called RNPP after (Rapm NprR, PrgX, and PlcR).

This entry represents the insertion domain of adenosylcobalamin-dependent ribonucleoside-triphosphate reductases (class II RNRs) from Lactococcus leichmannii and related sequences. RNR's are responsible for the conversion of the ribose sugar of RNA into the deoxyribose sugar of DNA, a rate-limiting step of DNA biosynthesis. RNRs are classified in class I, II and III [[cite:PUB00007088]]. Class II RNRs are less complex and function as a monomer in contrast to class I and III RNRs, which controls substrate specificity as efficiently as a multimeric enzymes.
